items.title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
Enterprise Article Published
October 22, 2026 Upvote 21
+15
Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft
This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.
We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.
Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts.
We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.
Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.
Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+
So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.
Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.
We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.
What happened after training
We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds
ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.
In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.
And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.
If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.
The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.
Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.
The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.
Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.
Where the gains landed
Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.
Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).
What dependability costs

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.
The single-attempt view
Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.
Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.
The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.
The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.
These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.
The training loop
Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.
Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.
Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).
Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.
For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.
Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.
That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.
Offline policy-relative difficulty
Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:
No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.
ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.
Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++
A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.
The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?
We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.
So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.
Estimating difficulty from limited probes
Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:
success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)
Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.
We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:
Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop
Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep
Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep
Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT
Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop
Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.
One task, end to end
Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.
Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.
When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.
The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.
What earns a reward
Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.
When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.
In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.
Two reward paths, one binary verdict
Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed.
Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test.
Run the training stack
We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:
docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting;
docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration;
docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20.
Before you start
Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.
The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.
Install
Keep the three repositories side by side:
mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git
git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git
git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training
git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1
git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0
Create the validated environment
The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate
uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy
uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
-e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools
uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \
-e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606
python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install
python scripts/verify_verl_install.py
uv pip check
The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.
Prepare the training data
Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
python data/prepare_data.py --help
The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.
Configure and inspect the launch
Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history.
Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command:
DRY_RUN=true ./scripts/run_train.sh \
trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
trainer.save_freq=5
It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run.
Train
The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:
# head node
ROLE=head NODE_IP="$HEAD_IP" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
./scripts/start_ray.sh
# each worker node
ROLE=worker NODE_IP="$WORKER_IP" \
HEAD_ADDRESS="$HEAD_IP:6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \
./scripts/start_ray.sh
After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node:
export RAY_ADDRESS=auto
export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
./scripts/run_train.sh \
trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \
trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \
trainer.total_training_steps=50 \
trainer.save_freq=5
Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv
The first ThinkingBox
post
covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained
checkpoint following
docs/evaluation.md,
then serve it with vLLM.
From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model
directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The
historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration:
vllm serve "$MERGED_MODEL" \
--served-model-name q38-rlft \
--host 127.0.0.1 \
--port 8001 \
--tensor-parallel-size 8 \
--dtype bfloat16 \
--max-model-len 262144 \
--gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \
--max-num-seqs 16 \
--max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \
--language-model-only \
--enable-chunked-prefill \
--enable-prefix-caching \
--reasoning-parser qwen3 \
--enable-auto-tool-choice \
--tool-call-parser qwen3_xml
In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:
cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training
source .venv/bin/activate
bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh
Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:
curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz
Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration:
orchestrator:
agent_model:
type: aoai
endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions
deployment: q38-rlft
credential:
type: api-key
api_key: <your_api_key>
is_reasoning: true
temperature: 1.0
top_k: 20
top_p: 0.95
max_completion_tokens: 8192
timeout: 1800
Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this
thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once
/ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:
uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \
thinkingbox-eval \
--config "$PWD/thinkingbox.yaml" \
--base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \
--dataset "$THINKINGBOX_DATA" \
--output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \
--errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \
--repeat 20 \
--coverage-profile full \
--aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \
--message-timeout 1800
The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before
aggregation.
Where this goes next
The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.
If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records:
Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look at the band histogram. In our experience teams often have not inspected this distribution, and it is usually more lopsided than expected.
Check your parity. Replay the same recorded model output through the training and evaluation parsers, and verify that both extract identical tool names and arguments. Otherwise, training may reward behavior that evaluation interprets differently.
Report both coverage and repeatability. State how many tasks pass at least once in k attempts and how many pass all k. A model that occasionally finds a solution is not necessarily one that repeats it consistently.
Further details can be found in the following links:

Framework: microsoft/thinkingbox · tutorial
Benchmark: microsoft/thinkingbox-data
Dataset viewer: microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench

items.title: Uber brings ChatGPT Work to all employees with OpenAI
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 22, 2026
Company
Uber brings ChatGPT Work to all employees with OpenAI
Uber announced the company-wide rollout of ChatGPT Work, an agent that helps employees take on a wide range of tasks within ChatGPT Enterprise, starting today. The rollout will make ChatGPT Work available to more than 30,000 employees across Uber’s global workforce.
Expanding from an initial pilot of 1,000 employees, the rollout will give teams across Uber access to an agentic platform designed to take on complex, multi-step tasks and deliver finished work. The expansion makes ChatGPT Work Uber’s first company-wide deployment of an agentic platform tailored for knowledge work.
ChatGPT Work connects with tools companies like Uber use on a daily basis, including Google Drive, Gmail, Google Calendar, and Slack, enabling workers to research information, prepare meeting briefs, create presentations, analyze data and complete workflows across applications.
ChatGPT Work also gives Uber access to OpenAI’s portfolio of frontier models. Uber will benefit from models like GPT‑6.1 Sol⁠ which will be deployed as the default capability within ChatGPT Work, balancing frontier performance and cost efficiency. Uber teams will also be supported by OpenAI multimodal capabilities, including voice and image generation, giving them the flexibility to choose the right models and tools for different needs.
The rollout will be supported by Uber’s internal AI skills library, approved integrations and dedicated employee training, helping teams across functions including operations, finance, marketing and product put the technology to work. Uber’s developers and software engineering teams will also continue using Codex to accelerate software development and streamline coding workflows.
“Uber has always been a company of builders, and every day, millions of people around the world rely on what we create. As AI transforms how we work, we want to give everyone the tools to innovate, solve problems and help shape Uber’s future. Rolling out ChatGPT Work across the company is an exciting step toward that ambition, and I can’t wait to see what our teams build with it.”
—Praveen Neppalli Naga, CTO of Uber
“Uber is putting AI to work across its business, and bringing ChatGPT Work to tens of thousand employees is a big step toward expanding access to frontier AI capabilities and tools. Now teams across Uber can tap into our portfolio of frontier models and agents to take on more complex work, connect the tools they use every day, and get more done.”
—Greg Brockman, president and co-founder of OpenAI
The expansion marks another step in Uber’s broader AI strategy and its collaboration with OpenAI. The companies plan to share further insights into adoption, use cases and measurable outcomes as the rollout progresses.

items.title: What FDE means at OpenAI
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 22, 2026
AI AdoptionGuides
What FDE means at OpenAI
What we do, how we work, and how we solve enterprise’s toughest problems to deliver real impact.
By: Colin Jarvis, Head of Forward Deployed Engineering at OpenAI
Learn moreWatch the livestream(opens in a new window)Share
When Codex came out, someone on the team asked me, “What do we do when Codex can just one-shot the use cases we spent the last few months building?”
That question gets to the heart of what FDE means at OpenAI. We work alongside customers to understand their hardest problems and build solutions they can depend on. What we learn helps shape our products and gives Research concrete problems to solve.
That is progress. If we make ourselves obsolete every couple of months, our FDE team is doing its job.
I founded the team in early 2025 to close what we call “the deployment gap”: the distance between what models appear capable of and what people can reliably use to do their work.
Model capabilities have moved faster than the systems and processes needed to put them to use. Sometimes the missing piece is a product. Sometimes a model performs well on a benchmark but cannot do the job with real-life variables and constraints.
We focus on customers’ hardest problems. Where our models can do the job today, we work with Product and our customer to make the solution repeatable and, where they fall short, we work with customers and Research to define the gap and make improvements. Our goal is for each engagement to leave the next customer with a better starting point—if we raise the floor to the point our customers don’t need FDEs to solve this class of problem the next time, we have done our job well.
The challenge for John Deere, a 200 year-old agriculture business, was how to scale personalized advice for farmers.
One example is See & Spray, its precision weed-control technology, which uses cameras and machine learning to identify and spray weeds rather than treating entire fields to reduce chemical use by up to 70%.
But realizing those benefits depends on farmers knowing how to configure the technology, plan their season, and adjust their practices as conditions change.
John Deere deployed OpenAI’s APIs to help make that support personalized and scalable.
AI can answer farmers’ questions in natural language, provide tailored setup guidance and recommendations, identify when equipment may not be delivering its full potential, and help farmers understand the value they’re getting from the technology.
The opportunity extends beyond any single interaction: to deliver relevant guidance throughout the customer journey, helping farmers make better use of their equipment while improving efficiency and sustainability.
This is the kind of challenge OpenAI FDEs work to solve: helping organizations move from AI capabilities to systems that deliver practical value in complex, real-world environments.
But the problems are often wide open, there may be no established ground truth, and there is no playbook. Everyone wants to build something that has never existed. Fewer people want to do what it takes to get there.
Finding talented FDEs while raising the baseline for “good enough” has meant constant experimentation and application.
Start with the outcome
At the start of every FDE team session, I put up a slide with one core value: “Start with the outcome, do what it takes to succeed, then follow with scale”.
An impressive demo can go a long way before anyone asks whether it works in the real world.
Our job is to solve the customer’s problem to a standard we can stand behind in production.
In mid-2025, we had around 15 FDEs working with a large semiconductor customer on 10+ use cases. The ambition was to make their verification process AI-native, covering:
Directed test generation
Root cause analysis and debugging
An architecture assistant
Verification can account for ~70% of a project’s effort in this industry. The opportunity was enormous, and there were many possible places to start.
Some FDEs had joined OpenAI just days earlier and had never worked in semiconductors. They embedded with the customer’s verification team, studied chip design in their spare time, and built evals with the engineers to test whether the AI could generate useful tests and correctly diagnose chip failures.
Alongside that learning, we built custom harnesses for the individual use cases. Over the first 3-6 months, all of them reached production and early user adoption. The payoff was seeing the metrics:
~48% time saved through AI-based directed test generation.
22% median performance improvement through kernel optimisation.
Weeks of debugging compressed into hours
When we played this all back the Chief Hardware Officer asked, “Did you guys work as chip designers before coming here?”
Our FDEs don’t need to know the industry on day one but it is their responsibility to learn it.
As coding assistants make software faster to build, understanding the customer’s business becomes even more important. We build teams with a mix of generalists and domain experts.
You need enough knowledge to make sound judgments, and enough curiosity to question assumptions about the status quo.
In life sciences, for example, our FDEs’ scientific backgrounds help them earn trust with researchers working on pre-clinical drug discovery tasks such as target validation and prioritization, gene-expression analysis, and chemical synthesis-route reconstruction. That expertise lets them contribute informed judgment about how those workflows could improve.
Make success repeatable
We had shown that these workflows could deliver value, but each still required too much custom integration to extend to another team. The next challenge was to preserve those results while making the software easier to deploy and maintain.
By then, Codex had grown in capability. One FDE tested rebuilding their application around it, then worked with the team to move the use cases onto a common harness with Codex at its core.
Custom applications became plugins and skills built on common Codex primitives. Codex also became the interface, allowing us to retire the separate terminal UIs and CLIs we had written for individual use cases.
We were able to remove roughly 90% of the custom code from each project, and this changed how we built, maintained and scaled these workflows:
We could benefit from centralized improvements to Codex, reducing the amount of glue code required for each individual use case
Key functionalities were bundled as skills and plugins, making them easier to share with each other and to be centrally controlled by the AI CoE. This meant that extending from one team to the next could be as simple as swapping in new connectors/MCP servers, building fresh evals (which we also had a skill for) and getting up and running.
In one August 2026 example, the initial deployment took two months. Extending the solution to a second team took one day. The next teams onboarded faster as we scaled—this has continued, with a use case in August 2026 taking 1 day for the second team after the initial deployment took 2 months.
That is one version of making ourselves obsolete. The work we had done to reach production established what mattered. As the underlying product improved, we could replace much of our custom implementation and keep the value it delivered.
This is why the order matters. LLMs let us build fast. Use that speed to get something valuable into users’ hands, learn what holds up in practice, and then scale what works.
The same principle applies across all engagements.
OpenAI Presence, our product for enterprise voice and chat agents, grew out of real customer deployments. The work began with Swarm⁠(opens in a new window) and evolved through the Agents API, and today one customer now handles more than half of its calls with AI.
Getting those deployments into production taught us which problems needed a custom solution and which building blocks other teams could use. We brought those building blocks into Presence, making it easier for developers to automate regulated workflows without rebuilding the underlying infrastructure. Each deployment helped shape the product and gave the next customer a better starting point.
With Thrive Holdings, OpenAI FDEs and researchers worked alongside engineers and accountants to build Tax AI for Current’s accounting firms. During its pilot, Tax AI processed 7,000 tax returns and increased throughput by about 50%.
One of the hardest challenges was automating rental-property returns, which required six weeks of engineering and practitioner review to reach 90% precision and recall. The work created reusable patterns that made it easier to extend Tax AI to other complex tax schedules.
The teams are now applying the same approach to bookkeeping, audit, and IT support—building systems that improve through practitioner feedback and real-world use.
Close the intelligence gaps as they appear
Sometimes a better product lets us simplify what we built but sometimes the model itself cannot yet do the job.
If we only build what today’s models already make possible, we will not uncover the intelligence gaps Research needs to close next. Therefore a lot of our important engagements start at those limits with the customer, FDE and Research committed to working through them together.
We had already developed a customer-service platform with a large telecommunications customer, and they wanted to extend it to voice.
Voice accounted for around 90% of their customer-service volume. These cases were more expensive to contain than chat, and brought a range of new technical challenges in getting accents, tone and latency/accuracy up to production grade. Getting it right would make a substantial difference to their business.
During scoping, our model scored around 60% on the key evals we used to assess whether it could do the job in production. We had reached the limits of its capabilities. Function calling and instruction following in customer-service scenarios needed to improve.
We explained that to the customer and brought Research into the work. FDE worked with the customer to build the platform and define what the model needed to do. Research worked on closing the capability gaps, with successive model snapshots letting us test progress against the customer’s requirements.
Over six months, performance on the key evals rose from around 60% to 80% and then 90%+, reaching the levels needed for production.
The resulting voice model now supports that customer’s deployment, other custom customer-service deployments, and managed deployments through Presence. A problem encountered in one customer’s business helped identify improvements that could serve many others.
Each part mattered. The customer committed to working on a problem the model could not yet solve. FDE stayed close enough to frame that problem, build the platform and drive the engagement from start to finish. Research improved the underlying model capabilities.
This is the other version of making ourselves obsolete: helping turn a problem today’s models cannot solve into a capability future models can deliver. The return on our work extends beyond the hours we spend with any one customer.
Go find the harder problem
I joined OpenAI to help make AI useful in people’s everyday work. That still guides the team. I often say to the team that in most cases in LLM development, Occam’s Razor applies—the simplest solution is the best. In a company that is defined by its cutting edge research and in an industry that is tainted by hyperbole, we want to build stuff that works reliably which people in the field can depend on.
The goal is for each engagement to improve what comes next: a product that is easier to deploy, a model that can handle a harder task, or less custom work for the next customer.
If you have a hard problem you want to solve, we’d love to work with you. If you want to help solve those problems, we’d love you to join us.
So what do we do when Codex can handle the work we spent months building?
Go find the harder problem.

items.title: 从 LOOP 到图探索 —— 算法模型的 AutoResearch 自进化系统架构演进之路
items.summary: 算法工程师的一天是“改代码—提交训练—等待—看日志—决定下一步”，过程中还经常被打断。我们团队从 Karpathy 的 AutoResearch 出发，经过三次架构重构，搭建出一套可在企业云端训练平台使用的算法研究自进化系统：系统从单线程 LOOP 探索升级为 CyclicGraph Engine 图探索架构，用状态机保证长周期运行的稳定性，并通过“业务知识库 + 真实大闭环 + 经验自动沉淀”实现系统自进化、越用越好用。 在结构、目标与场景均不相同的两个业务建模项目中，单任务完成耗时较人工基线分别减少约 85% 与 83%，其中一个算法模型已将系统自主推导的方案推全上线，并取得线上收益；另一个多目标项目中，系统产出的方案在全部 12 个预估目标上同时超过人工基线。两个项目唯一的共同点是同一套系统架构，说明增益来自架构本身。本文分享这套系统的设计理念、架构演进与可信度设计，希望对大家有所帮助或启发。 1 背景：算法工程师的时间都去哪了？ 一个算法工程师的典型工作流是：修改代码、推送代码、提交训练、等待、查看日志提取指标、与上一轮对比、决定下一步。等待的间隙，工程师会切换到其他任务，但切换有成本，时间利用不充分；如果训练在凌晨完成，还要等到第二天继续。一天下来，大约完成 2~3 次实质性迭代。真正需要判断力的环节，反而被切换和等待挤压得所剩无几。 2025 年底，Andrej Karpathy 开源了 AutoResearch：一个在单张 H100 上训练 5000 万参数教学级 GPT 的实验原型。仓库只有三个文件：program.md 用自然语言描述研究规则，train.py 是 Agent 唯一可自主修改的训练代码，prepare.py 负责评估。正是这个极简组合，让 LLM 驱动的研究在夜间和周末自动运行。约两天内，系统运行约 700 次实验，产出约 20 个针对 val_bpb 的正向提交。这套循环背后有一个刻意的信任设计：负责评估的 prepare.py 被冻结为不可修改文件，Agent 只能改训练代码而不能改评估函数，从机制上杜绝了“篡改裁判”的可能；而 keep/reset 的 Git 棘轮机制让每一步改进都可审计、可回滚。 这让我们看到了“让 Agent 自主迭代”的可能性。但把它搬进企业场景后，三个问题很快暴露： 可信度问题：规则全部以自然语言 Prompt 声明，模型幻觉会导致执行不完全可信； 运行环境差异：本地单机与企业云端训练平台差异巨大，Agent 需要异步执行，评价指标要体现业务差异性； LOOP 架构的根本局限：keep/reset 本质是可回滚的单线程串行 LOOP，效果改善就 commit、退化就 reset，同一时刻只能维护一条时间线。多数 AutoResearch 实践者（包括最初的我们）都沿用了这套单线程思路。 Karpathy AutoResearch 的 LOOP 机制：keep/reset 单线程串行循环 本文要讲的，是我们如何在三个月内经历三次架构重构，最终跳出 LOOP 架构，从“跑起来”走到“能自动化、自进化”：V1 回答“能不能跑”，V2 回答“能不能稳定地跑”，V3 回答“能不能跑得又快又准”。 2 设计理念：我们想造一个什么样的系统？ 在展开架构细节之前，先说清楚我们的五条设计理念，后面所有取舍都由此推导： 高效、高性价比。Agent 的夜间与周末算力是“闲置产能”，系统要能把人的注意力从执行中解放出来，只保留在高价值判断上。 与底层 Agent 基座解耦。Agent 基座能力在快速进步，模型每几个月就有性价比更优的选择。系统不应该绑死在任何一家基座上，而是通过良好的 Harness 设计“搭便车”——基座升级，系统免费受益。 系统自进化，越用越好用。经验、工具、Skill 不应该每次从零开始，而应在使用中自动总结、经人工校验后沉淀回系统。 用真实的大闭环获取优质数据。离线指标提升只是中间站，方案上线后的真实反馈回流知识库，才是垂直场景里最稀缺的数据。系统在使用中不断积累业务知识，形成自进化的飞轮。 可信优先。无人值守的长周期循环里，一次错误会成为下一轮决策的输入，逐轮放大。凡是能用代码表达的约束，一律不放在 prompt 里。 3 三次架构演进：从 LOOP 到 CyclicGraph Engine 三个版本不是提前规划的路线图，而是被真实问题驱动的演进。 AutoResearch 架构演进：V1 LOOP → V2 状态机 → V3 图探索（Spawn-Converge） 3.1 V1 把 LOOP 搬上企业云端 定时任务 + Shell 脚本周期性触发，单个 Agent 串行完成检查、提取、分析、改代码的全链路，报告归档到云端协作文档。V1 实现了企业云端的 AutoResearch，但上下文爆炸、状态同步不及时等问题造成了低效。 3.2 V2 异步循环与显式状态机 每次触发创建全新会话，状态持久化在 JSON 状态文件中，解决了长会话带来的上下文爆炸问题。架构拆分为 Monitor 与 Iterator 两个角色，依靠状态文件的 phase 字段互斥路由，同一时刻只有一个角色工作。状态文件只保留决策所需的最小信息，目标是把探索结果压缩为可复用的决策依据；这是针对 ML 迭代场景的定制设计，与通用图编排框架的“全量状态”思路不同。另一个关键决策是“无状态触发 + 有状态文件”：Agent 不同步等待训练（训练动辄数小时，长会话等待既浪费上下文也不可靠），而是靠定时触发的新会话在下一次唤起时从状态文件恢复现场，这为 V3 的异步并行打下了地基。 3.3 V3 CyclicGraph Engine 图探索架构 V3 打破了 V1、V2 沿用的单线程 LOOP 限制，核心机制是 Spawn-Converge： Spawn：决策层的主 Agent 把一个大问题拆成 3~4 个互斥的差异化假设（例如“特征不足”与“结构不足”），派发给执行层； 执行：子 Agent 通过上下文隔离并行地各自修改代码、提交训练，互不知情，因而不会被彼此的中间结论带偏； Converge：训练完成后，主 Agent 汇总对比几份独立结果、提炼洞察，并决策下一轮方向组合。 AutoResearch V3 全景架构：论文雷达 + CyclicGraph Engine 图探索 需要强调的是，这与“多开几个实验同时跑”有本质区别。并行只是手段，配套的是三步闭环：主 Agent 先拆互斥假设，子 Agent 各自独立验证，主 Agent 最后收拢对比做决策。如果只并行、不收拢，就退化成了多开实验。 调度层面，系统自 V2 起逐步演进为状态机驱动：异步触发 + 状态恢复，Agent 不同步等待训练，而是依靠状态机在下次触发时查询结果。这是对“训练需要数小时”这一物理约束的合理架构回应，也显著提升了系统稳定性与流程灵活度。 3.4 图架构带来的探索效率跃升 图架构的效率收益可以直接量化。在同一个建模项目上：LOOP 架构下 10 次迭代耗时 3 天（0.14 次/小时）且未取得突破；切换为图架构后，12 次迭代仅耗时 4.7 小时（2.55 次/小时）并达成目标，迭代速度相差 18 倍（完整效果见第 8 节）。 差异并非来自单次训练变快，而是来自四点：正交并行把每轮的信息获取量提升约 3 倍；“汇总—分发”的组织形式提高了单位时间内的有效决策数；边界探针快速确定参数的上下界；单变量控制避免了因变量混淆产生的无效迭代。 4 垂直耦合：把 AutoResearch 长在业务场景里 通用 Agent 不懂你的业务。让系统真正可用的关键，是把它垂直耦合到具体业务场景，而这靠的是业务知识库 + 真实大闭环。 4.1 业务知识库 系统的“入职培训” 初始化一个新项目时，系统会要求提供基础业务知识库（建模目标、样本口径、历史结论、约束边界），并结合自动化的初始调研构建方向池，保证知识库的起点是干净的。 4.2 渐进式调研机制 系统的调研方式分三层： 初始化调研：项目启动时建立方向池，对调研来源做筛选； 渐进式调研：研究过程中按需补充，而不是一次性塞满上下文； 强制调研：当指标边际提升缓慢、连续多轮在同一方案内打转时，触发逃逸机制，强制切换维度并重新调研——避免系统在局部最优里空转烧资源。 4.3 真实大闭环 自进化飞轮的燃料 离线指标提升只是中间站。方案上线后的真实反馈（线上实验结论、业务口径的指标变化）会回流进知识库，成为系统在垂直场景内最稀缺的优质数据。离线指标升降是明确的、可机器判读的；线上闭环数据则校准“离线好”与“线上好”之间的偏差。在系统使用过程中，通过知识、经验与工具的持续积累与回流，实现系统在垂直场景的自进化。 5 可信度设计：无人值守时，凭什么相信系统？ 长周期自动循环中，Agent 的不可靠行为分为两类，成因和治理手段完全不同： 认知层幻觉：输出在语言上自洽、在事实上错误，例如把训练波动归因为某个并不存在的因素，或把参数填成不存在的取值。它不会报错，只会悄悄把后续决策引向错误方向。 执行层偏差：工具调用失败、返回结果与预期不符，例如平台接口超时、任务 ID 过期、日志字段缺失导致指标解析为空。 治理原则是一句话：凡是能用代码表达的约束，一律不放在 Prompt 里。Prompt 里写“不要重复已证伪方向”并不足够，Agent 仍可能认为“这次情况不同”；但已证伪方向一旦写入状态文件的硬约束列表，下一轮就会在代码逻辑层面被直接跳过。针对执行层偏差，系统在三个环节设防：关键状态以状态文件为唯一事实源，易过期字段（如任务 ID）每轮强制重新读取，禁止复用上下文旧值；所有平台调用封装为幂等化工具，返回值做结构化校验，字段缺失或格式异常即判定失败，而非带着空值继续执行；区分代码故障与基础设施故障，前者计入证伪记录并触发方案调整，后者自动重试且不占用轮次预算。 5.1 原始证据优先：指标与 diff 都要“原件” 系统保留每一轮探索的原始指标提升和原始代码 diff。Agent 的分析可能有幻觉，但指标数据和代码修改本身是确定真实的。任何一轮的结论都可以回溯到证据链，而不是回溯到某段叙述。这一点来自我们对幻觉复合效应的观察：循环里错误结论一旦被喂入下一轮上下文，就会在错误前提上叠加错误推理，步步错但步步“看起来合理”；唯一的反制，是让训练结果这样的物理事实成为不可绕过的校验锚点——模型可以幻觉“学习率太小”，但训练跑完后的指标曲线不会配合它幻觉。 5.2 上下文隔离与交叉验证 子 Agent 探索时上下文相互隔离，或改用不同模型，从两条路径验证同一个假设，检测分歧。汇总时主 Agent 对照几份独立结果再做决策，天然带一层交叉验证。交叉验证并非每轮都做（成本太高），而是在主 Agent 置信度偏低、连续多轮指标同向恶化、或归因涉及方向性决策时触发；分歧结论同时保留并转入人工审查，而非简单投票取多数。 5.3 二级人机校验 Skill 草稿机制 系统在执行过程中会自动总结工具使用经验与踩坑处理方法，沉淀出可复用的 Skill 草稿，经过“系统初筛 + 人工审核”的两级校验后，正式写入系统工具集。一个真实例子：早期批次中训练平台参数服务器连接异常的处理经验被系统自动整理为 Skill 草稿，人工审核后反哺至工具集，此后系统自主应对数百次同类基础设施故障，全程无需人工介入。已入库的 Skill 也会在后续使用中通过审核机制持续自完善。这背后是一条反幻觉的晋升链：经验先作为带证据的低层级记录存在，满足复用规则并通过人工审核后才晋升为正式 Skill，未经外部验证的结论永远不进入知识库，只暂存在临时区。 主 Agent 与系统记忆交互架构 5.4 归因：自进化系统的“慢变量” Agent 的归因（“为什么这个方向有效”）仍是开放难题。我们的答案不是某个单点技术，而是三方面积累：知识库的积累让归因有业务依据，调研的积累让归因有论文依据，真实实验数据的积累让归因有证据依据。归因能力是慢变量——Harness 建设得好，它会随使用时长持续变好；这本身就是自进化系统设计的一部分。 5.5 Harness 决定系统上限 我们把套在通用 Agent 外、让它在生产流程中稳定行动的一组运行规则（状态文件、工具返回校验、失败恢复、经验库、硬约束、提示词）称为 Harness。外部也有同方向的实证：LangChain 的编码 Agent 全程使用同一个模型，仅调整 System Prompt、Tools、Middleware 三个 Harness 维度，在 Terminal Bench 2.0 的 89 个跨领域任务上得分从 52.8% 提升至 66.5%。同一个模型，换一套工作机制，差异达到 14 个百分点。我们的三次重构，本质上就是在与底层通用 Agent 解耦的前提下，打磨这套领域特定的 Harness，它决定系统是加速发现真理，还是加速传播错误。基座模型的能力红利人人可得，而 Harness 是差异化竞争力的所在。 Agent Harness 与能力层级：L2 状态记忆 → L3 自主调度 → L4 自主研究 6 与 Agent 基座解耦，享受 Agent 红利 系统与底层 Agent 基座彻底解耦，核心设计是“无状态触发 + 有状态文件”：状态全部落在 JSON 文件里，每次触发都是全新会话。这个设计带来三重收益：随时可触发——不受会话生命周期限制，定时、手动、事件驱动任意唤起；零空转——Agent 不同步等待动辄数小时的训练，触发即工作、完成即退出，长周期任务中也能充分利用计算资源；基座自由——不依赖任何基座的会话记忆或专有能力，Agent 基座升级后，系统可无缝切换。 在前端交互层，我们尝试过 IM 机器人、内部 Agent 平台、自建沙箱等多种形态，框架设计与交互形态完全解耦——换个入口，系统照常运转。 7 真实使用体验：从一句需求到自主迭代 对使用者来说，开启一个新项目非常轻： 用户：我要开始一个新项目，需要给你提供什么？ 系统：需要提供基础业务知识库（若有缺失，会询问补充）、需要优化的业务指标、报告归档的云端文档目录、迭代上限和阈值指标（主要用来防止无限制消耗资源），并给出一份可直接填写的需求模板。 用户：填写模板文档，把链接发给系统。 系统：启动自动迭代。中途用户可随时询问进度、打断；如果不打断，系统会在达成目标或达到上限时自行停止。 项目启动后的典型体验是：周五启动，周一回来发现系统已自主完成十余轮迭代，核心指标显著改善，期间零人工介入。这直接修正了我们对人机分工的初始设定（“AI 执行、人监督每一轮方向”）；实践后收敛出的分工边界是：人的价值集中在少数几个高杠杆节点上，而非分散在每一轮的执行监督中。 8 效果、验证与边界 8.1 效果：效率增益来自架构本身 在两个模型结构、优化目标、场景均不相同的建模项目上，系统给出了高度一致的答案：单任务完成耗时较人工基线分别减少约 85% 与 83%。两个项目唯一的共同点是同一套系统架构，这说明增益来自架构，而不是某个项目的特殊性。其中一个项目中，系统自主推导出的优化方案（不在任何参考论文中）已通过全部验证并推全上线，取得线上收益；另一个多目标项目中，全部 12 个预估目标均超过人工基线。 8.2 与传统 AutoML 的差异 最关键的一点：工程界主流的 AutoML 默认“正确答案在预定义搜索空间内”。而在我们的实际案例中，正确答案恰恰不在初始空间内——系统需要先证伪并退出一个错误的问题框架，再从论文的数学结构中推导出新的候选方案。这是能力层级的差异（从“执行给定方向”到“自主生成假设”），而非搜索效率的差异。 8.3 三层验证：自主方案上线和反哺经验 验证覆盖三件事：离线指标、线上实验、可解释性检验。前两件决定上线和推全——离线指标达标后，用线上 A/B 实验结果的置信区间判断是否推全；第三件决定能不能进硬约束库——若 Agent 给不出合理的推导，即使指标好也不入库，避免错误经验污染知识库，无法判断是否可入库时转人工审核。 8.4 适用边界与诚实的局限 这套架构适用于同时满足三个条件的场景：有明确的可量化指标；单次实验成本可接受；实验结果可逆。它不适用于评价高度主观、搜索空间完全开放、或单次实验成本极高且不可逆的场景。 基础设施依赖：训练资源是最大的外部瓶颈，系统只能降低资源消耗，无法从根源消除资源紧张； 经验迁移的幻觉风险：涉及垂直业务领域的经验库跨项目复用，可能把局部经验错误泛化，当前靠人工审核卡点拦截； 归因可解释性有限：系统能推导出有效方案，但“为什么有效”的归因解释仍不够严谨，需人工交叉验证后才能进入硬约束库。 下一步的方向：一是提升自进化稳定性 —— 自进化技术架构方向已确定，后续持续打磨状态机与流程稳定性；二是知识迁移中的幻觉问题 —— 如何稳定复用跨业务的经验，保证经验库干净稳定；三是探索更友好的交互与使用体验。 9 结语：从 Karpathy 出发，走到更远的地方 Karpathy 的 AutoResearch 是一个在单张 H100 上跑教学级 GPT 的实验原型。我们所做的，是把这套理念搬进企业云端的真实业务场景：在工程化过程中发现单线程 LOOP 的根本局限，用 CyclicGraph Engine 的图探索架构打破它；用状态机保障长周期运行的稳定性；用业务知识库和真实大闭环，让系统在垂直场景里越用越好用。 我们相信，Agent 自主研究的真正价值不在于“比人更快地搜索已有空间”，而在于“能够证伪错误的前提，并主动扩展搜索空间”。当系统能够从论文的数学结构中推导出人类未给定的方案，并在真实业务中验证有效时，它已经从“执行工具”走向了“研究伙伴”。这条路才刚刚开始。 最后回到方法论本身。三个月三次重构给我们的最大启发是：自主研究系统的核心工程量不在模型侧，而在 Harness 侧——状态机、硬约束、证据链、晋升门槛这些“不性感”的基础设施，才是决定系统可信度的分水岭。评估这套系统的正确方式也不是看它跑得多快，而是看它犯错之后能否被证据纠正、被约束拦住、被经验库记住。可复现、可审计、可回滚，是自主研究系统比效率更重要的底座。 10 参考文献及补充说明 [1] Andrej Karpathy. AutoResearch. GitHub, 2025 [2] Ryan Lopopolo. Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world. OpenAI, 2026 [3] LangChain. The Anatomy of an Agent Harness. LangChain Blog [4] 统计口径说明：本文统一以“一个训练任务”作为一次迭代的计数单位（并行方向分别计入），含因指标崩溃被证伪的探索性失败；人工基线按实际投入迭代的工作日折算；系统侧仅统计正常执行批次，基础设施故障导致的批次不计入分母。18 倍为图架构相对本系统自身 LOOP 架构的提升；85% 与 83% 为相对人工基线的单任务耗时减少，两者分母不同。

items.title: Broad access through consistent standards
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 21, 2026
SafetyCompany
Broad access through consistent standards
Over the past few months, we’ve worked with customers and partners to align safety policies across services that provide our models. We’re also updating our Usage Policies to make those requirements clearer and easier for developers to follow.
Models such as GPT‑6 Astra expand what developers and businesses can build. As those capabilities grow, we’re working to keep safeguards effective and consistently applied across the services that offer our models.
Responsibility starts with us
Before deploying a model, we evaluate its capabilities and risks, train it to follow safety requirements, and test whether its safeguards hold up when people deliberately try to bypass them. As we describe in our approach to safety and alignment, we combine safeguards designed to reinforce one another.
After deployment, we monitor for potential abuse and investigate concerns. To mitigate cyber misuse, for example, we train models to refuse harmful requests and use systems that look for suspicious patterns across interactions to decide how to respond. Trusted access programs provide another layer of protection and set eligibility requirements and conditions for access to our most powerful capabilities.
Some safeguards are built into the model and others depend on the systems and people around it. Both need to be effective whether people access our models directly or through a partner.
Consistent standards across services
Developers and businesses should be able to choose where they access our models, with consistent safeguards across those services. We developed policies to align our safeguards across providers and are working with each of our partners to ensure their implementation meets or exceeds our safety standards. These policies apply whether people access our models directly through OpenAI, partners that host them, or through reseller partners.
These policies require partners that provide access to OpenAI models to maintain safeguards consistent with our own, investigate potential violations, and take appropriate action when concerns are identified. That includes coordinating on enforcement so that restrictions remain effective across services providing access to our models.
Putting this into practice means accounting for how different services work and how customers use them. Our work with customers and partners on Private Safety Processing is one example of how we can develop effective safeguards while giving customers greater choice and control over their sensitive data.
Clear policies and predictable enforcement
We’re also updating our Usage Policies, effective November 20, 2026, to clarify the rules for safe model development and sensitive uses of AI. The updated Usage Policies build on that work by requiring services that provide direct access to our models such as model routers or AI gateways to get our review and approval before offering that access.
We’ll keep explaining what’s allowed, what’s restricted, and how customers and partners can ask questions or resolve compliance concerns.
As our models become more capable, we’ll keep improving how we detect, investigate, and respond to misuse. Customers can face misuse through their end users, compromised accounts, or leaked API keys and we work with them to understand and address those problems.
We’re also working with customers to introduce SafetyIDs, which customers can provide to help us distinguish between individual end users in an investigation without OpenAI learning those users’ identities. With SafetyIDs, we can respond to potential misuse more precisely while reducing disruption to others.
We base enforcement decisions on documented conduct and risk, apply our rules consistently, and respond in proportion to the circumstances. When we restrict access, we revisit those restrictions if meaningful changes in conduct, commitments, or safeguards address the concerns behind our decision.
We want more people to benefit from AI. Clear rules and consistent safeguards should make it easier for developers and businesses to build, compete, and choose the services that work best for them.

items.title: ChatGPT Ads expands to 26 new countries as over 100,000 advertisers have used the platform
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 21, 2026
Product
ChatGPT Ads expands to 26 new countries as over 100,000 advertisers have used the platform
From local businesses to global brands, more advertisers can now reach people as they explore, compare and decide what to buy in ChatGPT.
Start advertising in ChatGPT(opens in a new window)Share
More than 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week to explore ideas, compare options and make decisions. Ads can help people discover products and services that fit their needs, including options they might not have found otherwise.
Since we launched ads just over eight months ago, over 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns on ChatGPT. Today, we’re expanding ChatGPT Ads to 26 additional countries, extending availability to 89 countries worldwide. This launch builds on our recent expansions across Europe and Southeast Asia and Taiwan.
Advertising helps support free and low-cost access to ChatGPT for people around the world. Our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. Ads will appear only on the Free and Go plans. Plus, Pro, and Enterprise subscriptions will remain ad-free.
Supporting more businesses around the world
Following our launches in Mexico and Brazil, we’re bringing ChatGPT Ads to 14 more Latin American countries, including Argentina, Chile, Colombia, and Peru. We’re also launching in more markets across Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, including Nigeria, South Africa, Serbia, Ukraine, Cambodia, Bangladesh, and Pakistan.
Advertisers can access ChatGPT Ads in these countries through technology partners or self-service access through Ads Manager⁠(opens in a new window).
Reach people as they explore their options
In ChatGPT, people can explain what they’re looking for, ask follow-up questions, and refine their options through conversation. Someone training for their first marathon might start by exploring meal ideas for race week, then narrow their options based on their dietary preferences and how much time they have to cook. An ad relevant to that conversation could introduce them to a grocery delivery service they hadn’t considered.
For local businesses, regional brands, and international companies, ChatGPT Ads gives businesses a way to introduce their products during these moments of consideration, when people are still evaluating their options and deciding what’s right for them.
“At L’Oreal our culture is to ‘seize what is starting.’ Today, as billions of consumers use AI models to discover and explore beauty, our mission remains centered on delivering meaningful value and building deeper connections. Testing early with OpenAI enables us to pioneer helpful experiences and journeys, from discovery, to evaluation, to agentic commerce, ensuring L’Oréal remains the most trusted, expert answer wherever beauty conversations take place.”
Asmita Dubey, L’Oréal Group CDMO
Guided by our ads principles
Protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT is foundational to our approach to advertising.
Guided by OpenAI’s ads principles, we keep conversations private from advertisers and do not sell customer data. Ads in ChatGPT are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT’s answers, and advertising does not influence the answers ChatGPT provides.
Our goal is to make ads useful to people as they pursue their goals and make decisions—and effective for the businesses that advertise with us.
What’s next
Our focus remains expanding access to AI while staying true to our principles.
With ChatGPT Ads now available in 89 countries, our next phase of growth will include the development of additional formats, objectives, buying options, and measurement capabilities. We are also continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.
As more people turn to ChatGPT to explore needs, evaluate options, and make decisions, we see an opportunity to help them discover products and services—and to help businesses of every size grow and thrive.
Businesses interested in advertising on ChatGPT can learn more at ads.openai.com⁠(opens in a new window).

items.title: Claude Security now scans continuously and tracks fixes
items.summary:
Claude Security now scans continuously and tracks fixes
Claude Security now keeps up with your repositories as code changes, tracks findings until they’re fixed, learns from the context your team adds, and connects to your tools through an API and MCP. Available in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers.
CategoryProduct updates
ProductClaude Security
DateOctober 21, 2026
Reading time5 min
ShareCopy link
Since Claude Security entered public beta in April, thousands of organizations have used it to find over a million vulnerabilities.
Instead of waiting for someone to start a scan, Claude Security now keeps up with your repositories as your code changes, keeps track of which findings get fixed, and uses what your team tells it about your environment to decide what matters. Claude Security is powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos, with no Cyber Verification Program access required.
The latest version of Claude Security is available today in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers. Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.
Continuous monitoring keeps up with your code
A scan captures one moment, and code changes every day. Teams told us they wanted coverage that stays current without anyone having to schedule it.
Create a project, connect your repositories through the Claude GitHub app (including GitHub Enterprise Server) or with an access token from GitLab and other Git providers, and choose the branch and scope for each. Claude runs a deep baseline scan, then scans changes regularly based upon their risk and complexity, so your list of findings stays close to the current state of your code.
A project can hold multiple repositories, so Claude can catch issues that live between services, like a backend that trusts input a client was supposed to validate.
Findings are marked fixed when the fix ships
Most fixes happen outside the tool that found the issue. Claude Security checks open findings against the code that changed and marks them fixed when the fix lands, whether your team fixed it in Claude Code or in a separate process. If Claude Security finds the issue again later, the finding reopens automatically.
Your team’s knowledge shapes the scan
Every environment has controls a scanner can’t see from the code alone. Teams wanted a way to tell Claude Security about those controls, and to look across services that depend on each other. Now, each project has a knowledge base where you can describe how your code is deployed, which security policies apply, and anything a new security engineer on your team would need to know.
Claude Security also generates a threat model from your code that your team can review and edit. Subsequent scans use those threat models to decide what’s worth flagging. Added context also helps Claude Security skip risks your environment already handles.
Severity and exploit paths for every finding
Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project’s threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what’s actually reachable first. Findings can include a diagram of the attack path.
Findings reach your tools, with controls for larger rollouts
The new API lets you integrate Claude Security into your existing workflows. You can list and read projects and findings, resolve or reopen findings, and create and manage projects and their repositories. Users can create a personal access token in Claude Security settings, and it can only see and change what the user can. Webhooks can also notify your systems when a new finding lands.
Claude Security is also available as an MCP connector in Claude.ai and Claude Code. An engineer can pull up a finding, ask Claude about it, start the fix, and mark it resolved in the same session.
New role-based access controls let admins decide who can view projects, triage findings, and create projects. Organizations can open Claude Security to more teams that own the code without giving everyone access to create projects.
Getting started
The latest version of Claude Security is available in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers starting today. Admins can enable it in the admin console and set who on their team can access it.
Use the Getting Started Guide to set up your first project, and visit the Help Center for more details.
Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

Cloudflare links vulnerability discovery to defense with OpenAI
Cloudflare uses OpenAI Daybreak with live traffic and security signals to investigate vulnerabilities and propose fixes for customer review.

Cloudflare operates one of the world’s largest networks and proxies roughly 20% of the web’s traffic. Organizations depend on that network to keep their applications and services secure, fast, and reliable.
Cloudflare combines OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak with its global network and threat context in Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation⁠(opens in a new window), an early-access service offered through Cloudflare Managed Defense. The models investigate code and assess potential vulnerabilities. Cloudflare adds live traffic data, security signals, and validation to prioritize findings and prepare proposed mitigations and patches for customers to review.
Codex extends OpenAI’s role across Cloudflare’s engineering organization, where developers use it to increase output and improve code quality.
“The beauty of the automation that Daybreak and Codex provide is that you can assign machines to do the grunt work so humans can exercise their judgment on the most important engineering and security decisions.”
—Mark Anderson, President of Revenue, Cloudflare
Scaling security analysis with Daybreak
Security teams face a constant stream of vulnerability information and alerts. Manually sifting through that data takes time and effort, leaving teams with less capacity to investigate and address critical issues. “Traditional security teams have a ton of useful data. They just don’t have the people and time to deal with it,” Anderson says.
Cloudflare’s approach is to connect a vulnerability in source code to what is happening in production. Is the affected route active? Is it receiving suspicious traffic? Are existing security controls already protecting it? Those signals give security teams more context for deciding what to investigate first.
Through Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation⁠(opens in a new window), Cloudflare uses OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code, identify potential vulnerabilities, and check the evidence supporting each finding. The service prepares proposed code patches and, where appropriate, custom web application firewall rules to reduce exposure while developers review a fix. Cloudflare runs automated checks on these proposals, and its team reviews them before sharing them with customers.
For Cloudflare customers, the benefit is a clear path from identifying a vulnerability to protecting the affected application. The service gives them evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities, proposed edge protections to reduce exposure, and code fixes to review, while they retain control over which changes to implement.
Rebuilding a product in 3 days with Codex
Protecting applications also depends on the code teams write and maintain. Anderson connects Cloudflare’s use of Codex to greater developer productivity, better code quality, and fewer bugs introduced during development.
“At Cloudflare, a third of our company are software developers building services and features for our platform, and 100% of them use Codex to boost their output and deliver better code.”
—Mark Anderson, President of Revenue, Cloudflare
Anderson describes a recent rebuild the team had postponed. “We were putting off building it because we didn’t have the manpower to do it,” he says. With Codex scaling developer productivity, the question shifts from “Can we take this on?” to “Why not?”
Anderson estimates that the work would have required months of sequencing and “maybe 10x more developers.” With Codex, a Cloudflare team of four developers took on the build. “We built it in three days, rolled it out and tested it, and spent $1,100 on tokens,” he says.
Shaping cyber defense around AI and human judgment
For Anderson, making AI part of everyday engineering means “rebuilding the internal process to build technology with machines in mind, not as a separate element, but as something that’s integrated into the build process.”
Cloudflare’s early-access security service puts that approach into practice by connecting code investigation with production evidence and proposed actions customers can review. The goal is to give security teams the information they need to decide which vulnerabilities to prioritize and how to protect and fix affected applications, while customers retain control over changes.

items.title: Democratic governance of frontier AI, part II: Empowering cyber defenders
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 21, 2026
Global AffairsSecurity
Democratic governance of frontier AI, part II: Empowering cyber defenders
Read the blueprint(opens in a new window)Share
AI is changing the speed, scale, and economics of cybersecurity. It can help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, detect intrusions, and respond to attacks—but those same capabilities can enable malicious actors and create new risks when AI systems act beyond their intended boundaries. We are in a defender’s window: a limited opportunity to put advanced AI into defenders’ hands and strengthen protections before advanced cyber offensive capabilities become widely available.
Today, we’re publishing a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders, building on our earlier cybersecurity action plan and frontier safety blueprint⁠(opens in a new window). Our experience with misalignment and security incidents involving our own models underscores the need for stronger safeguards and accountability across the industry. Drawing on those lessons, the blueprint puts forward concrete proposals for governments and industry in three areas:
Strengthening safety and security for advanced AI: Establish clearer responsibilities for securing frontier models and agents, detecting dangerous behavior, and maintaining reliable shutdown controls for operations under each organization’s control.
Modernizing cybersecurity for the intelligence age: Equip defenders with advanced tools, training, and technical support; address longstanding cybersecurity weaknesses; and invest in securing essential services and replacing outdated systems.
Building resilient and adaptive public institutions: Strengthen government evaluations and independent technical assessments, establish consistent incident reporting requirements, and improve coordinated response and recovery.
AI labs have a responsibility to address the risks their systems create and help strengthen society’s defenses. Governments must also have the expertise, resources, and authority to protect the public as capabilities advance. We encourage policymakers to act now—establishing safeguards, learning from experience, and strengthening requirements as the technology evolves.

Anthropic is partnering with HCLTech (opens in new tab), a global technology company with more than 230,000 people in 60 countries. HCLTech will build agentic solutions on Claude for its clients through a dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence, embed Claude in HCLSoftware products, and integrate Claude and Claude Code into AI Force, the platform it uses to run IT services for clients. HCLTech becomes a Global Premier Partner (opens in new tab) in the Claude Partner Network, the top tier, which requires 1,000 certified practitioners (opens in new tab).
HCLTech provides solutions for financial services, manufacturing, life sciences and healthcare, technology, semiconductor, telecom and media, retail and CPG, and mobility and public services. In these environments, a mistake is expensive and every change needs to be reviewed, logged, and approved. The partnership is built to put Claude into that work with the controls designed for those environments.
How HCLTech is putting Claude to work
HCLTech is bringing Claude into its business in three places and is designing each with guardrails and human review.
A dedicated Anthropic Business Unit and Center of Excellence. HCLTech’s forward-deployed engineers will set up secure sandbox environments where clients can test Claude against their own systems and data before deploying. The Center will train client workforces, help engineering teams adopt AI-native practices, and build the organizational controls for running agents safely at scale.
Claude inside HCLSoftware products. HCLSoftware becomes an Anthropic independent software vendor (ISV) partner and will embed Claude in select products across cybersecurity, automation, business process applications, and application development. The first are HCL BigFix for endpoint management, HCL AppScan for application security testing, and the Actian AI analyst for data and analytics.
Claude and Claude Code in AI Force. AI Force is how HCLTech delivers IT support, code remediation, and digital employee services for the enterprises it serves. Claude and Claude Code go into that platform with policy guardrails and exception handling. Agents handle the routine work, and HCLTech engineers oversee high-impact changes.
“Few technology companies combine the scale of a global systems integrator with the product depth of an ISV,” says C Vijayakumar, CEO and Managing Director at HCLTech. “That gives us a rare advantage to securely engineer and deploy Agentic AI at scale and deliver the business outcomes that matter most to our clients. Our partnership with Anthropic further strengthens our capabilities to achieve the same.”
"AI can only be as useful as it is trustworthy, and we build Claude to give companies the confidence to bring it into their most sensitive and valuable work,” says Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President at Anthropic. “HCLTech manages those kinds of systems for banks, hospitals, telecom companies and manufacturers, and we’re excited to partner with them as they integrate Claude and Claude Code. This partnership — and our broader commitment to advancing capability and safety together — is how AI will change the way entire industries run for the better.”

AT&T’s in-house legal department has hundreds of lawyers and legal professionals around the world. Before they can advise the business, they need to assemble facts, documents, and relevant past work, often drawing on expertise held across different teams. For David McAtee, AT&T’s Senior Executive Vice President and General Counsel, making that experience easier to access is central to how the department’s work can improve.
AT&T is working with OpenAI to build that next phase. “Our partnership with OpenAI is going to allow us to build that plumbing that powers the knowledge layer throughout the company and that all of us will draw into,” McAtee says.
The collaboration builds on LegalEdge, AT&T’s team of attorneys, legal professionals, technologists, and project managers focused on applying AI to major legal matters. The next step is to connect more of the company’s accumulated expertise to the work arriving on a lawyer’s desk.
Requests arrive from across the business, and legal teams need to respond quickly without overlooking risks. Before they can advise, they have to understand the issue, gather the relevant context and decide what needs attention first. That makes intake a critical part of protecting the business. Bill Ryan, AT&T’s Chief Compliance Officer, describes one planned initiative as an intake system with “a front door where we have natural language intake.” The system would classify and prioritize requests, connect them with relevant precedent, research, and past work, and give the responsible legal professional historical context and recommended first steps.
