items.title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
items.summary:
Back to Articles
How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
Team Article Published
October 21, 2026 Upvote 38
+32
Bernardo França de Aguiar bernardoaguiar Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI
Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.
The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.
One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.
The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.
We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.
A Vocabulary Built for Everyone
The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.
For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.
The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.
The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.
Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive
The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.
To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.
This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.
Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.
The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.
And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.
Why Existing Solutions Fell Short
Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.
They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.
They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.
How We Solved It
VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.
First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.
Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.
To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.
Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.
An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.
A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.
That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.
What Changed in the Grader
To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.
The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.
Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.
The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.
Beyond the Grader
To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.
VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.
Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter
VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.
Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.
The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

items.title: How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 21, 2026
Engineering
How we built ChatGPT’s novel ad stack for user trust and relevance
By Ritendra Datta and Karthik Gopalratnam, Members of Technical Staff
Traditional advertising systems are built to respond to discrete units of user intent. A user searches for or views something online, the ads system receives those queries and page views as events, and the system looks for matching ads based on those events. Building an ads stack for ChatGPT was different: user intent develops across conversations and shifts over multiple turns of a conversation, sometimes without a fitting advertising moment. To support this new paradigm, we built a bespoke ads delivery system. This new type of ad stack is based on a custom, post-trained frontier LLM that makes tool calls for retrieval (identifying the top options), ranking (predicting user engagement), relevance (evaluating the usefulness of the ad), and running auctions for final ad selection and pricing.
Our ads system supports the nuance of evolving user goals by making three key design decisions: 1) implementing stateful ads sessions, meaning information is remembered across turns of a conversation and across multiple conversations, 2) relying on a custom, post-trained LLM that uses a tool call architecture to interpret a conversation’s context and underlying intent, and then effectively select, rank, and deliver ads, and 3) running the ads selection process separately from ChatGPT’s answer generation, in its own service, to keep ads from influencing answers and maintain ChatGPT’s neutral voice. We use our post-trained LLM to orchestrate the entire ads flow, determining the right ad to surface at the right time based on both the user’s current turn and conversation history. While bootstrapping a self-improving ads system like this used to take years, ChatGPT Ads reached $1 billion in annualized revenue run rate less than 200 days after launch; now, more than 100,000 advertisers have run ads on ChatGPT since launch.
How should ads work in agentic chat?
A conventional advertising request usually starts with a well-defined event. A user submits a search query or opens a webpage and the ads system receives a request. This type of system is fairly simple: it retrieves potential ad candidates, ranks them, runs an auction to appropriately price the opportunity, and shows the resulting ad to the user. ChatGPT does not naturally produce such a concrete moment.
In a ChatGPT conversation, people arrive with goals rather than a one-answer search query. They might be planning a trip, choosing software for their business, furnishing a home, or learning a new hobby. This doesn’t all happen in one turn of a conversation. ChatGPT often helps the user clarify what matters along the way.
As an example, our engineering team asked ChatGPT how to train for a race: A conversation begins with a general question about running. Several turns later, they ask about shoes to help train. The commercial meaning of the conversation changes as each constraint arrives—and this personalized context evolves across multiple sessions. A system that acted on the first message could retrieve the wrong intent entirely, potentially degrading the user’s experience and getting in their way.
Building our ads system required us to move beyond the request-response advertising architecture and build an ads stack from scratch to find potential economic opportunities while prioritizing user trust and value.
Conversation memory, without influencing ChatGPT answers
Turning every message into a standalone request, like a traditional ads system, would have carried a few risks in our chat use case: 1) misreading the user goal by oversimplifying it, 2) beginning the advertising flow too soon, before the user’s real need has become clear, 3) showing ads that get in the way of the user journey instead of supporting it, and 4) inefficiently rerunning the ads flow every time the request changes, creating noise and wasting cost. Instead of building around individual events, the ads system (consisting of retrieval, ranking, and delivery) maintains a stateful session, meaning the ads session runs for the duration of an eligible turn, remembering and updating information as it evolves. ChatGPT sends the initial request context to the ads server. The ads system follows and adapts to the developing exchange rather than relying on a single flattened query.
The ads selection process runs alongside ChatGPT’s normal response generation to ensure the ads flow doesn’t influence ChatGPT’s responses. Ads are filtered and selected through a separate system consuming the conversation under its own eligibility, quality, and delivery constraints. This important architectural boundary—different services that use separate models and separate code—lets core ChatGPT servers handle generating the organic response; meanwhile, the ads system independently evaluates whether there’s an appropriate advertising opportunity and, if so, prepares a sponsored placement through a separate serving process.
Advertising runs alongside the ChatGPT answer path.
Beyond protecting the user experience, this separation has some practical consequences. ChatGPT has no dependency on the ads system—the services are in no way intertwined and don’t share a content generation model. So if the ads serving system is unavailable or slow, ChatGPT’s organic response continues unaffected. This means the ads system can’t take down or delay the ChatGPT product. The other benefit of this separation is that it keeps the bar very high for valuable ads. Returning no ad is an ordinary, successful outcome. The system only delivers an ad if it’s clearly beneficial to users and advertisers.
An LLM interprets conversations and calls tools
The other key architectural component in our ads stack is the post-trained LLM that interprets conversations and runs the entire ads flow in an agentic loop—making tool calls to the core functions of the ads system, from the retrieval stage to ranking to auction and, ultimately, delivery. We call this LLM the orchestrator.
The first part of an ads flow is understanding user intent to start the retrieval process, which is a fast and deliberately broad sourcing of potential ads to later filter through. Receiving the conversation incrementally creates a richer but more ambiguous retrieval problem because the ads system needs to distinguish current intent from stale context. The orchestrator must interpret references to earlier messages, recognize when a user is speaking hypothetically, and avoid treating every mention of a product or service as a request to buy something.
The ads orchestrator uses the available conversation and user context, iterating to find good ads and repeatedly choosing when to call which tool with the underlying goal of finding the most appropriate ad (the ad that balances high user value and high advertiser value) for that conversation and context. If the user chooses to personalize ads, the orchestrator also considers available nonsensitive information about the user’s past conversations to find the best ad matches.
The ads orchestrator iteratively calls ads delivery tools to find valuable ads.
As the conversation progresses and the ads orchestrator gets more updated information, the orchestrator can run a fresh set of tool calls with the updated context to find better ads and return them to the client, which can then use these new ads if they arrive in time.
User valueAdvertiser value
Printed Throw Pillow
Ineligible candidate
The orchestrator is designed to balance user value and advertiser value, always putting users first.
How the orchestrator calls ad tools in an agentic loop
The ads system consists of individual tools, and the orchestrator calls them iteratively to find the best ads for a conversation. At a high level, the orchestrator turns conversations into brief text summaries, which are then turned into semantic embeddings (stored meanings that are easier for an ads system to sift through), retrieves ad candidates using those semantic embeddings, filters those candidates for eligibility (based on budget, user settings, and other preliminary checks), assesses their quality and relevance, and does a final ranking to identify high value opportunities for placement at the end of a chat response. Each ad must therefore meet a high bar on eligibility and relevance in order to be eligible for placement.
Preparing retrieval queries that capture intent
The orchestrator LLM first prepares one or more queries representing the relevant commercial intent. This can include rewriting conversation context to broaden the commercial possibilities beyond 1:1 search queries and then creating semantic representations, where the orchestrator distills a multiturn conversation into a summarized version for the retrieval system—retrieving ads from our database in a focused way.
Ad placements will be better for both users and advertisers if they only appear when there’s deep understanding of the user’s intent. Multiple queries can preserve different aspects of intent. A conversation about planning a trip, for example, might contain distinct needs related to transportation, lodging, or activities. The retrieval system can preserve these distinctions rather than compressing the entire conversation into one literal string.
As an example, let’s look at a potential conversation sequence about hiking shoes:
What should I cover on a two-day trip to Yosemite?
Will it be cold next week?
New [insert brand] product lines?
Although the user hasn’t connected the shoe brand question to the Yosemite trip, this conversation might be represented in our ads system by two queries, such as [shoes appropriate for hiking trip] and [new [brand] product lines good for travel]. This might only be the first attempt; the orchestrator is designed to iterate on these representations until it finds ads in our inventory that are highly valuable to the user.
Retrieving possible ads
Retrieval is the process of creating a deliberately broad pool of ad options. Candidates may come from different retrieval strategies and can later compete under the same serving constraints. We build multiple indices that optimize for different system and product constraints (for example, the index for product feed ads is designed to be aware of positive or negative product reviews as it fetches the best possible ads. This is not relevant to other ads that may not have reviews associated with them). Each index is optimized for some version of approximate-nearest-neighbor (ANN) search, using embeddings representing the user’s intent. This ANN search is an approximation algorithm for retrieval over large semantic indices, meaning ads are fetched very quickly, getting close to a good solution rather than looking for “the right” solution, while retaining most of the relevant candidates.
The ads system uses rewritten queries to create semantic embeddings during the ad retrieval process and produce a broad pool of ad candidates.
Filtering ineligible candidates
The goal of filtering is to eliminate all ad candidates from consideration that don't meet the bar for placement when it comes to relevance, bids, and budget. Depending on the candidate and configuration, filtering checks can include creative and campaign availability (whether the campaign or ad-creatives are active), campaign targeting (e.g., which locales a campaign is allowed to operate in), policy restrictions (compliance requirements around what can be advertised), budget availability (whether or not a campaign still has budget available to spend), pacing (whether a campaign should be spending budget now versus another time in the day), placement compatibility (what kinds of conversations this advertisement is eligible for), and advertiser and campaign level deduplication (picking an appropriate number of ads per advertiser to ensure fair participation across businesses).
Evaluating relevance and quality
Candidates that survive eligibility checks move on to a scoring phase, where the orchestrator makes tool calls to various scoring systems—for serving considerations such as semantic relevance (is the ad relevant to the user’s goal?), predicted engagement (is the ad likely to get viewed, clicked, and converted into the advertiser’s desired outcome?), historical performance (has the ad performed well when shown to users so far?). The orchestrator also filters ads to ensure relevance and safety before the auction. These systems narrow the field into a smaller candidate pool ready for auction, but they still don’t determine the final delivered ad.
Running the ads auction
The orchestrator evaluates the prepared candidates in the context of the conversation and chooses which ad candidates are plausible enough to enter the final auction. The orchestrator doesn’t directly decide which ad will be served, nor does it set a price. It nominates contextually appropriate candidates for the auction tool to evaluate.
The auction applies the final serving mechanics, including auction admission (passing a minimum threshold of relevance and value), pacing (spending ad budget more evenly), bid and auction-feature computation, quality-adjusted ranking, pricing, and final selection.
Final eligibility checks
After the auction, there are two ways an ad might fail to deliver, both specific to the ChatGPT conversational medium.
The ad might not feel appropriate in the chat: Even though the conversation itself was deemed safe for ad placement by integrity models (the models that decide when it’s appropriate to serve an ad), and the ad itself was deemed policy-compliant, sometimes the ad might feel inappropriate in the context of certain conversations. The orchestrator blocks these ads from being shown.
The ad request might not arrive in time: If the ChatGPT model is ready to respond, but the ad is not yet ready to place, the ad request times out and the ad doesn’t get delivered. One goal of the ads system, therefore, is to run as fast as possible. The ChatGPT model response time is dynamic, and we don’t delay chat responses to wait for ads to load.
If all of the above checks are met, we send the ad to the frontend for rendering. We consider this a server-side ad delivery, but we still might not show the ad to the user—and this is by design.
The final step: showing the ads to the user
In a conversational product like ChatGPT, server-side delivery of an ad creative does not guarantee an ad will be displayed; the ad must also arrive in time to be included in the current turn. The ad creative includes the title, description, destination link, and any call to action. Additionally, a model-generated preamble, which is a short, neutral introduction explaining how the ad relates to the conversation, is also returned by the ads system. Keeping the preamble separate from the creative preserves the advertiser’s message while keeping ChatGPT’s voice neutral.
The ChatGPT frontend receives the preamble and ad creative as a bundle. If it arrives before ChatGPT's response is fully generated, the frontend displays the ad below ChatGPT’s response, clearly labeled as sponsored. If it arrives too late, the ad is not shown for that turn. This is the difference between server-side ad delivery and a user-facing ad impression.
Winner selection and delivery are separate events. A selected ad becomes a delivery only after ChatGPT approves and displays the placement and the delivery is acknowledged.
What happens after the ad is shown
Our advertising stack uses traditional logging and data pipelines, which have three main benefits: advertisers can more easily integrate their existing systems with our stack, advertisers can improve their strategies with the reporting data, and our team can find areas of the system to improve. Beyond these reporting and optimization tools, we deploy a high quality model to evaluate our delivery and train other ads models, creating a powerful self-improvement loop.
Detailed breakdowns of what happened help us understand and improve each part of the ad system in isolation. The logs processing system also records granular outcomes such as:
The turn was not eligible for advertising.
An ads session started but no retrieval was requested.
Retrieval returned no candidates.
Candidates were retrieved but failed hydration or eligibility.
An ad was delivered and later received an interaction.
These detailed breakdowns help us improve each part of the ad serving system in isolation. Improving opportunity detection requires different evidence from improving retrieval, candidate quality, auction participation, or delivery reliability.
Delivery, serving, and quality systems observe a different part of the lifecycle. Privacy-controlled processing determines what may be used for measurement and model improvement.
High-power models evaluate and improve the entire stack
The idea behind model-based evaluation is that our strongest, highest-reasoning models watch and judge the results of our system, then improve the post-trained LLM by training it to perform better. For instance, we can use smaller, more efficient models or lower-reasoning models for orchestration or retrieval if our most powerful model gathers feedback and trains these small workers to do the best job possible.
Human feedback steers tasteful direction
We gather and act on human feedback (clicks and hides from users), as well as surveys for users and direct feedback from advertisers through our Ads Manager. We also make our team available for feedback as we build, and directly listen to what both ChatGPT users and advertisers want. This source of feedback informs our direction even more than the model’s observational feedback and is part of what allowed us to iterate toward the right product decisions quickly. The model may be able to understand user intent and think critically to deliver something valuable, but people shape taste.
What’s next
A year ago, we had no ads system and only a few people thinking about this problem space. Now we have a robust ads system powering more than $1 billion in annualized run rate, with an LLM-based orchestrator running the ads flow. Codex was a fundamental force multiplier that allowed us to bootstrap our system to achieve this major usage milestone with unparalleled speed. From the start, we set up the team and development workflows to use Codex to rapidly build and scale the system. We built guardrails for Codex to reliably and safely ship code. In parallel, we set up data infrastructure plugins for Codex to massively tighten the loop of insight gathering and landing improvements to the system, including new product features, quality improvements, and better system performance.
The combination of our system’s boundaries (grounded in our advertising principles⁠) and our LLM-based orchestrator lets us make advertising useful without treating every conversation as an ad request. Looking ahead, we’ll continue to experiment with more dynamic ad formats to increase user value (e.g. giving users the ability to talk directly to businesses through ads) and advertiser value. The stack’s self-improving architecture, built on OpenAI models with continuous feedback loops, will accelerate our ability to keep improving relevance and personalization over time.

items.title: Introducing Claude Duet
items.summary:
Introducing Claude Duet
A research preview is available by waitlist today, starting with US Pro, Max, and Ultra subscribers.
Join the waitlist
CategoryProduct updates
DateOctober 21, 2026
Reading time5 min
ShareCopy link
Claude Duet Safety, Privacy, and Security
October 23, 2026 - We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections. You can read more about how Claude Duet is designed for safety, privacy and security here.
Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track.
It’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. For this research preview, Claude Duet is included in Pro, Max, and Ultra plans and uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. To get access, join the waitlist (opens in new tab).
Put your attention where it matters most
We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before.
What makes Claude Duet so helpful is its judgment. We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5 (opens in new tab) and built it to be resourceful and to decide what needs you, what can wait, and when to check with you first.
Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.
Safety and discretion are built in
Claude Duet draws on years of security, safety, and privacy work on agents, both our own and the infrastructure businesses use to run theirs:
Claude Duet draws on our framework for trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which also guides agents like Claude Code and Claude in Chrome.
Claude Duet’s handling of credentials follows the design we use for Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), so it never directly sees your passwords or sign-in tokens.
Actions are approved by our auto mode classifier (opens in new tab), the same safeguard that protects Claude and Claude Code from taking steps you didn’t ask for.
Claude Duet’s defenses against hidden instructions and prompt injection come from our browser-use research (opens in new tab), and our models and safeguards also cover this more broadly.
We run adversarial tests for Claude Duet’s security infrastructure. Red teams and an external firm penetration tested Claude Duet, and it’s covered by our public bug bounty program (opens in new tab).
How Claude Duet handles sensitive information. We’re also releasing Claude Duet with a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt that checks each message and guards against leaks of sensitive information. An agent that reads email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where information should go. This new classifier and prompt are designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health or personal finances, are let through only when you’ve explicitly instructed Claude Duet to send it.
We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections, and will share more details about how Claude Duet is designed for safety in the coming days.
How testers are using Claude Duet
People at Anthropic have been using Claude Duet to accomplish more, but also to leave more room for thinking and being present. Boris Cherny, who leads our Claude Code team, talks through his mental to-do list with Claude Duet on walks, instead of saving the work for his desk. Chelsea Larsson, who leads our model and product behavior design team, hands Claude Duet her to-do list before leaving to be with her kids and it saves the results for an evening report. And the team behind Claude Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews, partner with him on prototypes, and even ship code.
We gave small business owners and entrepreneurs early access to Claude Duet, and some have been using it to help run their businesses. Here’s what some of them said:
Jess gets a rundown from Claude Duet each morning. One day, without being asked, it flagged a property showing that was on her calendar for the wrong day. “[This is] exactly the kind of thing I want caught without having to ask,” she said.
Jess Provencher, broker and owner, Pro Homes
Amin owns Shahs of Kabob in South Florida with about 110 employees. He’s used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support, and marketing, and has worked through his invoices store by store. “It brings it all together,” he said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.”
Amin Ebrahimi, owner, Shahs of Kabob
Mya had a call coming up with a potential client. Claude Duet saw it on her calendar and prepared a brief. It also noticed the call fell right before her flight and offered to move it. “I didn’t realize that it was right before my flight,” she said. “I love that proactivity.”
Mya Dalton, a brand strategist
How Claude Duet works
Your context from Claude is the foundation. Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work. What changes is how you work together: Claude Duet comes to you first, and you can message it through typing or voice in one ongoing thread, so a quick reply and a weeklong project both start in the same place.
Work continues when you step away. Claude Duet has a virtual machine with its own browser, so it doesn’t require your laptop or phone to be on. Describe a task in a short message, and it works out which apps to use and what steps to take in the background. You’ll receive a notification when the task is complete or needs your review.
Receive a message when something needs you. Claude Duet checks your connected accounts every few hours, because checking nonstop would use up your plan’s limits much faster. We’re continuing to test its judgment about when to message you, and we’ll keep tuning it based on what testers tell us. You can also tell it what you want to hear about and how often.
Important decisions stay with you. Claude Duet reads, drafts, and prepares work on its own. But before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your approval. A few things are off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities or moving money between accounts. You’re also able to disconnect any app Claude Duet has access to.
Connect with the tools your business runs on. Claude Duet can use the over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace (opens in new tab) to:
Find the Gmail and Slack messages you’ve missed and help you reply.
Check Intuit QuickBooks or Stripe for unpaid invoices and draft reminders.
Prepare and run payroll in Gusto, with hours, bonuses, and reimbursements filled in.
Draft a job posting and, once you edit and approve, post it to LinkedIn.
Help prepare agreements and send them for review and signature through Docusign.
Draft follow-up emails using the contact and deal history in HubSpot.
Turn your product launch into a social campaign in Canva.
Set up, design, and manage your Shopify store. Coming soon, a richer visual editor will let you design your storefront and preview it before anything goes live.
You can also use Claude Duet to purchase things for your business using Link, Stripe’s digital wallet. Claude Duet confirms the item with you, and Link asks you to approve the spend. It then pays with a virtual card, so your real card number isn’t shared. It can also use Shop Pay from Shopify to check out at online stores. Coming soon, with your permission, it will be able to sign in to sites with logins you’ve saved in 1Password.
Join the research preview
This is an early version of Claude Duet, and it still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent. We built its core functionality around work, so personal errands, such as booking tickets, aren’t quite as strong, and it can’t yet show you its browser. For now, Claude Duet lives in its own app, separate from the main Claude app. What we learn from early users will shape how the two work together.
During the research preview, Claude Duet shares your plan’s usage limits with the rest of Claude, and it uses them differently than a typical conversation does. Its background checks count toward those limits, and larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, require more model turns and background work.
We’re starting today with Pro, Max, and Ultra users in the US. Join the waitlist (opens in new tab) and we’ll email as soon as Claude Duet’s ready for you.

items.title: Lovable’s compliance and your app: what’s covered, what’s your responsibility
items.summary:
All posts
Published October 21, 2026 in Development 101
Lovable’s compliance and your app: what’s covered, what’s your responsibility
“If Lovable is SOC 2 compliant, does that mean my app is too?”
We get versions of this question a lot. The same goes for GDPR, ISO 27001, etc.
When building on Lovable, or any AI software creation tool for that matter, users don’t automatically receive the certifications of that platform. Our audits, certifications, and data protection commitments give you evidence about the platform you’re using, but your responsibilities depend on what you build, the data you collect, and how you run your business.
Here’s what each means, how to think about your own project, and what we’re doing to make this easier in the future!
What Lovable has
Lovable publicly documents SOC 2 Type II, ISO 27001:2022 certification, GDPR support, and AIUC-1 certification.
Standard or regulation
What it means
What it means for your project
SOC 2 Type II
An independent auditor examines security controls within defined systems and evaluates how they operated over a specified period.
You can use Lovable’s report to assess us as a vendor. It doesn’t constitute an audit of your business or app.
ISO 27001:2022
Certification of an information security management system: how an organization identifies, manages, and reviews security risks within a defined scope.
It provides evidence of how Lovable manages information security. Your organization doesn’t become ISO certified by using us.
GDPR support
GDPR sets legal requirements for handling personal data. Lovable provides data processing commitments and documentation to support customers’ obligations.
You still need to assess how your project collects, uses, shares, and retains personal data.
AIUC-1
A standard addressing risks associated with AI agents. Lovable’s enterprise overview describes independent auditing and quarterly third-party testing.
Lovable’s certification doesn’t certify every app or AI workflow a customer builds.
For the underlying standards, see a SOC 2 report review checklist, ISO’s explanation of ISO 27001, EU’s GDPR guide, and AIUC-1.
For current audit and certification information, start with Lovable’s Trust Center.
Why your business needs its own assessment and controls
SOC 2 reports, ISO 27001 and AIUC-1 certifications come from independent third-party assessments with a defined scope. An assessor reviews the organization’s systems, controls, and practices. Lovable’s assessment covers Lovable within that scope. It doesn’t assess your business because you build with us. The same is true of any other AI platform you use.
If you want a SOC 2 report or ISO 27001 certification for your own business, you need to put the relevant controls and processes in place, gather evidence, and go through your own independent assessment. We’re working with compliance automation partners on tooling to make certification easier for builders. More on that soon.
GDPR works differently. It is a law that protects people’s privacy rights by protecting the information that identifies them or can be linked to them, known as personal data. Where it applies, you need to build the required protections into your app and the way you operate it. That includes collecting only the data you need, restricting access, setting retention rules, and supporting applicable requests to access, correct, or delete personal data. You also need a lawful basis for processing and accurate information for users about how their data is used. The EU GDPR guide is a great starting point.
For example, if one of your users asks you to delete their personal data, you need a process to handle that request and, where deletion is required, a way to remove it from your database and any connected services. That workflow is something you build and run for your app. Lovable’s compliance commitments cover how we handle data as your provider, not the processes inside your project.
How to think about GDPR for your app
The GDPR applies depending on where people are, not where they’re from. It covers people in the EU regardless of citizenship, and it does not follow EU citizens who are living abroad. This means if you are selling to people in the EU, you need to comply with GDPR guidelines. The UK has its own GDPR regime (EU guidance on applicability, UK GDPR guidance).
Then work through these questions.
What personal data are you collecting, and why?
List the information your app handles, including account details, form submissions, uploaded files, and information captured by connected services. Collect only what you need, identify a lawful basis for each purpose, and decide how long you’ll keep it. Consent is one possible lawful basis; it isn’t the right basis for every activity. EDPB practical FAQ, ICO data protection principles.
Who decides how that data is used?
If you decide why and how personal data is processed, you’re generally the controller. If you build and operate software on another organization’s instructions, you may be a processor. Your role determines your obligations and the agreements you need. For personal data inside your app, you are typically the controller and Lovable is your processor. EDPB guide to controllers and processors.
Where does the data go?
Map the full path: hosting, database, email provider, analytics, payment services, and any AI features you add. Review the relevant providers and processing agreements. Check international transfers as well as storage locations. Choosing an EU database region alone doesn’t establish that every connected service processes data only in the EU. EDPB international transfer guidance.
Does your privacy notice describe your app accurately?
People need to understand what information you collect, why, who receives it, how long you keep it, and how to exercise their rights. A generated privacy notice needs to be checked against your actual setup. If you add a service that receives personal data, review whether your notice needs updating. EDPB transparency and rights guidance.
Can you handle a privacy request?
Work through what happens when someone asks for access to their information, a correction, or deletion where applicable. Identify the records across your database and connected services, who handles the request, and how you’ll verify the requester’s identity. EDPB guidance on individuals’ rights.
Have you tested who can access the data?
Test with separate accounts and different roles. Can one customer read another customer’s records? Are uploaded files exposed? Does a former employee still have access? Document your decisions and checks so you can demonstrate how you protect personal data. ICO security and accountability principles.
These questions give you a starting point. Projects involving sensitive data, children, or higher-risk processing need further assessment of the requirements that apply. Please read our platform rules for more information.
What if a customer asks for your SOC 2 report?
If a customer requires a SOC 2 report covering your own service, you’ll need a separate examination with an independent CPA firm. That review considers your defined system and controls, including how your organization operates it. Lovable’s report can inform the vendor review portion of that work.
A trust center can also help communicate your security practices. Lovable provides project-based trust centers that display observed controls, but the page itself isn’t a certification or a guarantee of compliance. How Lovable app trust centers work.
What we’re working on
We’re working on integrations with third-party systems, and Lovable-built skills to make more of this work easier to handle out of the box.
Our goal is to help you understand what your project needs and do more of the work within your building workflow. You’ll still need to make decisions about your business, your users, and their data.
For your next project, Lovable’s chat is a good place to start. Because it reads your project without changing any code, you can ask it to walk through your app and help you build the data map: which tables hold personal or sensitive data, which third-party services receive it, how authentication and access rules are set up, and whether anything is logged or stored longer than it needs to be.
From there, you can ask it to compare what it finds against the SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria (security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy) and point out where you’re likely to have gaps.
A few prompts to get started:
“List every place this app stores or sends user data, and who can access each one.”
“Review our database access policies and flag any table that’s readable by users who shouldn’t see it.”
“Which SOC 2 controls would apply to an app like this, and which ones are handled by Lovable versus by us?”
“Draft a short checklist of what we’d need to document before talking to a SOC 2 auditor.”
Treat the answers as a starting point. Chat can help you understand your setup and prioritize, but SOC 2 is ultimately an audit of your organization’s controls and processes, not just your code, so you’ll still need policies, evidence, and an independent auditor. When you’re ready to fix something chat surfaced, switch to Build and the context from your conversation carries over.
This post is general information, not legal advice for your project.

items.title: OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 21, 2026
Company
OpenAI models are coming to Google Cloud
OpenAI and Google Cloud⁠(opens in a new window) are partnering to bring OpenAI’s frontier models and Codex⁠(opens in a new window) agentic workflows into Google Cloud’s Model Garden. The integration will give customers native access to these models to power complex agentic workflows at scale, backed by Google Cloud’s data governance and high-performance infrastructure.
Google Cloud’s longstanding investment in machine learning and AI has made it a destination for AI workloads and the developers and data scientists building them. Bringing OpenAI models to its model garden gives these teams access to OpenAI’s frontier models within the environment where they already work, enabling enterprises to modernize their software development lifecycle, build agentic workflows, and change how people work.
For organizations in regulated industries, deploying AI requires control over who can access sensitive data and how it is used. The integration will pair OpenAI’s frontier models with Google Cloud’s built-in access controls, centralized data governance, and high-performance infrastructure to support demanding enterprise workloads.
Google Cloud customers will be able to purchase OpenAI frontier models via model garden, transacted through the Google Cloud Marketplace. Enterprises with Google Cloud spend commitments will be able to draw down their GCP commitments for these purchases.
Additionally, OpenAI models will soon be available in Google Antigravity and the Gemini Agent, providing enterprise customers with model choice flexibility and the best model for each task. By expanding access through Google Cloud, we are giving enterprises greater choice in how they discover and use frontier models, with a path from evaluation to broader adoption.
“Google Cloud is a leading platform for developers and businesses building AI agents, writing software, and putting AI to work. This partnership is an important step in making our most capable models and Codex available where customers are already building, giving them even more choice in how they use frontier AI as we grow the agentic ecosystem together.”
—Greg Brockman, President and co-founder, OpenAI
“We are focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can choose the right model for any given job, helping to deliver optimal quality and lower costs.”
—Thomas Kurian, Chief Executive Officer, Google Cloud
General availability is planned in the coming weeks. Request access to OpenAI on Google Cloud here.
Microsoft remains OpenAI’s primary cloud partner.

items.summary:
OpenAI
October 21, 2026
SecurityProduct
Patch the Planet: global response coordination as agents uncover critical vulnerabilities
Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers, and security providers to address critical vulnerabilities in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run websites and web applications. Calif identified a critical flaw using GPT‑5.6 Sol as part of our Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) initiative, with Wiz also independently discovering and reporting both vulnerabilities. PHP’s maintainers led the fixes and release, with our teams and partners like Wiz, Cloudflare, and others contributing research, technical support, and coordination to prepare protections ahead of disclosure.
For organizations using PHP, the priority now is applying the fixes. We’re sharing a PHP version checker as a Codex skill⁠(opens in a new window) to help operators identify potentially vulnerable PHP versions and, alongside PHP’s and their providers’ guidance, determine which updates apply.
Given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory. It highlights how AI can uncover security flaws with internet-scale impact, but the same capabilities can also help attackers rapidly develop offensive tools and exploits.
To our knowledge, frontier AI found these vulnerabilities before attackers did, opening a Defender’s Window for maintainers and security providers to prepare fixes and protections ahead of disclosure.
To help more defenders use these capabilities, we’ve committed $1 billion in subsidized Daybreak access through Daybreak for Frontline Defenders, focused on organizations with limited security resources protecting essential services.
As significant as they are, these bugs are among several significant vulnerabilities we’ve already found and are working to fix, and we expect similar findings to increase sharply in the coming months. Drawing on our experience thus far, we’re sharing a proposed approach, appropriate for the AI era, to responding to critical vulnerabilities in widely used software, and we’re asking the security community to help improve this framework. It brings together our models, security expertise, and maintainers to help turn findings into protection and build a response that can scale as AI capabilities advance.
Coordinating a global response
Getting a fix into use can mean adapting it for older releases, preparing provider mitigations, and updating systems across many organizations. A repeatable process helps those teams act quickly as more vulnerabilities are discovered.
Through Patch the Planet, we contributed security expertise and model access to support the PHP response, and worked with maintainers and research partners to test fixes and prepare guidance. We also helped coordinate with infrastructure providers on protections for affected systems and engaged government cyber agencies to help guidance reach critical organizations. This supported the maintainer-led response and helped other defenders prepare.
For some findings, researchers can work directly with the software’s maintainers to investigate the issue and develop a fix. Others need a wider response because they affect many products or because distributors and service providers need time (which may be in short supply if frontier capabilities are not too far ahead of those that are broadly available) to prepare updates and protections. In those cases, the proposed framework can help maintainers identify who needs to be involved and coordinate the work. The response can involve five stages:
Validate and fix the upstream vulnerability. The maintainer, researchers, and essential technical partners confirm the finding, assess its impact, and develop and test a fix. This process includes adversarial testing with frontier models to look for ways around the patch and related variants of the vulnerability.
Give affected organizations time to act. We propose a framework for considering which organizations need advance information to prepare protections, while maintainers decide whom to involve. We help with outreach, information-sharing agreements, and coordination between teams. A distributor might adapt a fix for an older release, a hosting provider might test a mitigation, and a security provider might prepare detection or prevention measures, including web application firewall (WAF) rules.
Coordinate with government partners to help protect critical systems. Government agencies play an essential role in coordinating a wider response and helping security guidance reach organizations responsible for critical infrastructure and other essential services. In the case of PHP, we worked, in collaboration with our partners, to engage with multiple parts of the U.S. government, including the White House’s Super Intelligence Force, the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), as well as international partners to support that effort.
Prepare updates across affected products. As the fix, guidance, and disclosure plans become stable, maintainers can involve additional distributors, hosting and service providers, response teams, and operators to prepare updates and address gaps in coverage.
Once a patch is available, publish guidance and support deployment. Public guidance helps people assess their exposure, find authoritative updates or interim mitigations, and check that a fix is running. The response continues as operators deploy updates and report where they need help.
The proposed framework considers an organization’s protective role, including protecting its own systems and customers, the time needed to act, and its ability to handle sensitive information. The same criteria would apply to comparable organizations, with maintainers deciding whom to involve ahead of disclosure.
Each participant receives the information needed to carry out their protective work, from network logs with indicators of compromise to more sensitive working proof-of-concept exploits. Even limited details can reveal a vulnerability, so we weigh the risk of sharing them against the protection they enable.
Teams following this framework would work with maintainers to give defenders time to prepare and reassess the timeline if there’s active exploitation in the wild, a leak, a revealing public patch, or increased risk to users from stalled remediation.
The Patch the Planet website⁠(opens in a new window) brings together public disclosures and guidance to help operators identify affected systems, find the right update, and verify that the updated software is running properly. For PHP, it points to the maintainers’ official patch and upgrade instructions and our partners’ technical research. The guidance also covers interim mitigations, when to involve a provider or expert, and backup and recovery. Interim protections can reduce risk, but we’ll make their limits and operational tradeoffs clear.
Operators can use CISA’s guidance on prioritization and remediation⁠(opens in a new window) to assess how quickly to act based on exposure, exploitation, and potential impact. That may mean emergency patching, immediate mitigation, or a planned update, alongside forensic triage where warranted to assess whether systems have already been compromised. Priorities should be reassessed as conditions change, with a clear path to lasting remediation.
Giving maintainers the capacity and resources to respond
Global coordination depends on the people who maintain the software. Many projects are run by small teams that review security reports alongside routine development. Those teams need help separating new issues from duplicates, assessing impact, and testing fixes across supported releases. We support that work with funding, access to capable models, and hands-on engineering help.
Powerful AI capabilities are advancing across the industry, and we expect AI to play a growing role in helping defenders find vulnerabilities, monitor systems, and respond to threats. We’re investing in models, tools, and partnerships to help defenders put those capabilities to work.
Our investments include subscriptions for all maintainers through Codex for OSS and direct sponsorship of projects such as the Rust Foundation⁠(opens in a new window) for maintainers and technical work. Each project sets its own priorities. Reusable tests and security workflows can reduce the effort needed to handle future findings. Open-source projects can apply to Patch the Planet⁠(opens in a new window) for hands-on support.
We’re also calibrating additional blocking classifiers for Daybreak to help reduce the potential for misuse. This involves difficult tradeoffs: safeguards intended to prevent abuse can also block legitimate security work. Broad access to capable models and effective protections against misuse are both critical. Our aim is to preserve the capabilities defenders need to find and fix vulnerabilities while limiting harmful use. We’ll continue refining that balance as capabilities advance and we learn from how these tools are used.
Building more secure software foundations
As models become more capable, the opportunity extends beyond finding and fixing individual vulnerabilities. We want to help engineers build more secure software from the start. Improvements to a widely used component can prevent bugs or limit their impact across many products and services.
AI can help engineers understand existing code, prepare changes, and develop tests, while maintainers and security experts verify that those changes preserve the behavior users depend on. We see opportunities in several areas:
Secure code from the start. Coding models can help developers choose safer defaults, use security libraries correctly, and catch risky patterns as they write. Preventing vulnerabilities during development means fewer emergency fixes for maintainers and users.
Memory-safe software. Moving critical components to memory-safe languages can eliminate common classes of memory errors. AI can help with migrations, with tests and expert review to check behavior and compatibility.
Formal verification. Mathematical proofs can show that critical components satisfy specified security properties under stated assumptions. Applying these methods to widely used components could help rule out classes of vulnerabilities across the services and critical infrastructure that depend on them.
Stronger isolation. Systems need protection against vulnerabilities that have not yet been found or fixed. Running software that processes untrusted files, images, or media in tightly restricted sandboxes can limit the damage if it is compromised. AI can help engineers test and strengthen widely used sandboxing technologies, improving protections across many applications.
Help us improve this approach
We’re sharing our approach so maintainers, researchers, response teams, providers, and operators can help make it workable. We want to understand where it would help, where it could add delay or burden, and what we’ve missed. Examples from past disclosures would be especially useful.
We’re particularly interested in:
Disclosure windows. How much time do maintainers, operators, and defenders need to prepare and deploy reliable fixes? What evidence should trigger earlier disclosure, especially when some users can be protected sooner than others?
Emergency patching. When, if ever, should governments or other operators use a vulnerability to patch systems they own or are authorized to manage after losing administrative access? What safeguards should apply? We can imagine an end-state of internet-wide always-on scanning for known vulnerabilities, and either notifying site owners when one is detected or patching the system.
Early notice. Who needs advance warning to take a useful protective action, including defenders we might miss? When do staged notifications work better than notifying a wider group at once, and how should we weigh coverage against leak risk?
Secure-by-default software packages. How can we help identify and fix vulnerabilities in downstream packages while upstream fixes are pending, or backport fixes to older versions that no longer receive security updates? What testing and maintenance would make these packages reliable options when a timely upgrade isn’t feasible?
We also welcome recommendations for independent security experts who can review the approach, challenge its assumptions, and identify gaps. Your input will help us refine the response and prioritize support. Share your feedback here⁠(opens in a new window).

Dr. Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist and former Dean of Science at Harvard University, has joined Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust. He brings to the Trust decades of scientific expertise across observational cosmology and precision measurement. He has also advised the US government on national security and arms control.
“I am honored to join Anthropic’s Long-Term Benefit Trust and to help the company deliver on its public benefit mission,” said Stubbs. “I use AI tools in my research every day and see what they make possible, and as an educator I have confronted some of the hard questions they raise. As a grandfather, I want to help ensure that AI is developed and deployed for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Stubbs is the Samuel C. Moncher Professor of Physics and of Astronomy at Harvard, where he served as Dean of Science from 2018 to 2024. In 1998, as a member of the High-Z Supernova Search Team, he helped discover the accelerating expansion of the universe, work that later earned the team the Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics. He was also the inaugural project scientist for what is now the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which started a 10-year survey of the southern sky in June. One of its aims is to study the accelerating expansion he helped discover.
More recently, he’s written about how to keep AI-assisted research reproducible when models can give different answers to the same question. He’s a member of JASON, an independent group of scientists who have advised the US government on defense and technology since 1960.
“When Chris found evidence that the universe was expanding at a rate no one expected, he and his team followed the data even when it went against the prevailing wisdom of the field. As AI starts to transform how science itself is done, Chris’s intellectual honesty, rigor, and commitment to the truth are the values we want shaping the future of this technology, and I’m grateful he’s bringing his deep expertise to the Trust,” said Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic.
Anthropic is a Public Benefit Corporation, which means we’re structured to balance commercial growth with our public benefit purpose. The Trust exists to help us hold that balance over the long term. It has the authority to appoint a majority of Anthropic’s board, and Trustees advise the board and our leadership on critical decisions, particularly those involving risks and societal impacts of AI.
This week we published our first Public Benefit Report, a public account of how we’re working toward our charter and where we’re falling short. The Trustees helped define the five charter pillars it measures us against, and the report closes with their assessment of our progress to date. Subject to stockholder approval, we’ve also committed to setting aside a portion of Anthropic’s shares to Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows.
“Helping the world build powerful AI safely and making sure it meaningfully improves people’s lives both depend on a deep understanding of science and on leading with integrity,” added Neil Buddy Shah, Chair of the Long-Term Benefit Trust. “Not only has Chris worked on some of the hardest problems in science, but he has consistently been a high-integrity leader of large, complex, collaborative scientific endeavors across academia, government, and the national laboratories. That will be of great value to the Trust as we support Anthropic in developing AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”
Stubbs, the Trust’s first physicist, joins Shah, national security expert Richard Fontaine, and former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke. Trustees are independent of the company’s management and investors.

items.title: Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Profiling TorchNeuron (Part 1): System-level profiling on AWS Trainium.
Enterprise Article Published
October 21, 2026 Upvote 13
+7
Josh Longenecker jlongen-aws Follow amazon
Many ML practitioners have some intuition about how to make models run fast, but fewer know how to analyze why a model is slow. In Part 1 of this series, you will learn how to systematically analyze inference performance and identify where the time is spent.
This post starts from scratch and assumes no prior profiling experience. The walkthrough uses AWS Trainium, a purpose-built AI chip for deep learning training and inference workloads, and TorchNeuron, its open source native PyTorch backend. TorchNeuron supports standard PyTorch workflows on Trainium, including eager execution, torch.compile, and standard PyTorch APIs, with minimal code changes. Additionally, TorchNeuron integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) to enable custom operators and performance optimization for Trainium hardware. By the end, you should know:
How to configure torch.profiler with the Neuron backend and capture a clean trace.
How to read the key_averages() table to identify which operations consume Neuron device time and compare their Self CPU time.
How to follow one operation through Neuron Explorer, from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution on a NeuronCore.
How these signals change across three implementations of the same operation.
Neuron as a PyTorch Backend
Before you profile a workload, it helps to understand how Neuron integrates with PyTorch.
The Neuron backend uses PyTorch's PrivateUse1 extension point. This mechanism lets an accelerator integrate with the framework without adding a dedicated dispatch key such as cuda. The torch_neuronx package works with upstream PyTorch to register Neuron as a native backend for PyTorch code. For details about this extension mechanism, see Facilitating New Backend Integration by PrivateUse1.
Set Up the Profiler
You use two objects to profile a Neuron workload:
NeuronConfig controls which Neuron data streams and NeuronCores to capture and where to write the output. You pass it to torch.profiler.profile as experimental_config.
NeuronProfiler takes a NeuronConfig and provides an export_trace callback. The callback writes the framework trace, trace.json, alongside the Neuron system traces.
nc = NeuronConfig(
modes=[ProfileMode.DEVICE, ProfileMode.RUNTIME],
profile_output_dir=OUTPUT_DIR,
capture_enabled_for_nc='0',
correlate_device_time=True,
)
exporter = NeuronProfiler(nc)
The modes parameter selects the data streams to capture, such as device instructions and runtime traces. The capture_enabled_for_nc parameter selects the NeuronCores to trace. Setting correlate_device_time=True propagates device time from the trace into the key_averages() table, where you can compare CPU and Neuron device time. For the complete parameter reference and available ProfileMode values, see the NeuronConfig Profile Modes documentation.
Tooling: Neuron Explorer
Neuron Explorer is a browser-based viewer for the system trace, device timeline, and per-engine breakdown. You can access it through an SSH tunnel or the Visual Studio Code extension. In this post, you use Explorer to confirm what key_averages() reports numerically and inspect what happens between dispatches.
After profiling, the output directory contains the system trace and, when you capture device data, matched .neff and .ntff files. The Neuron Executable File Format (NEFF) contains the compiled Neuron executable, while the matching NTFF contains its hardware instruction trace. The files share a numeric hash that identifies them as a pair. To open the profile in Neuron Explorer, upload the complete output directory for a system or combined profile. For a device-only profile, upload the matching .neff and .ntff files individually. See Step 5: Upload your profile for the UI and command-line instructions.
Profile RMSNorm
For this first analysis, you profile RMSNorm, a small operation with a clear sequence of arithmetic and reduction operations.
You profile three implementations of the same operation:
Naive RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations: multiply, mean, add, reciprocal square root, and multiply.
torch.rms_norm(), the PyTorch built-in lowered to a single fused Neuron kernel.
Naive RMSNorm with torch.compile, using the same operations as the first implementation.
The scripts use the same inputs, profiler configuration, and schedule so the results are directly comparable.
All scripts to reproduce this work are available in the torch-neuronx examples directory.
Profile 1: Naive PyTorch Operations
Start by writing RMSNorm with individual PyTorch operations. Each line maps to one or more ATen operations and can create intermediate tensors.
device = torch.device('neuron')
x = torch.randn(4, 512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
weight = torch.ones(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device=device)
def rms_norm_fn(t):
x_sq = t * t # square
mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True) # mean of squares
rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6) # 1 / sqrt(mean_sq + eps)
return t * rms * weight # normalize + scale
Call the profiler with two arguments required for the Neuron backend:
Include ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1 to collect activity from the Neuron device.
Pass NeuronConfig as experimental_config to enable the Neuron-specific Kineto features.
The schedule uses wait=2, warmup=1, and active=1 across four prof.step() calls. This records one warm iteration without including initial setup overhead.
Call torch.neuron.synchronize() inside the profiler loop. Without this synchronization, the profiler can export before the device finishes and leave the Neuron time column empty.
with torch.profiler.profile(
activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.PrivateUse1],
experimental_config=nc,
record_shapes=False,
on_trace_ready=exporter.export_trace,
schedule=torch.profiler.schedule(wait=2, warmup=1, active=1),
) as prof:
for step in range(4):
with torch.no_grad():
_ = rms_norm_fn(x)
torch.neuron.synchronize()
prof.step()
After profiling finishes, inspect the key_averages() table. Sort by self_privateuse1_time_total to place the operations with the highest device cost first. The table shown here is filtered to the RMSNorm operations that report Neuron device time. The full key_averages() output also includes CPU-side events such as allocations and host-to-device transfers.
print(prof.key_averages().table(sort_by="self_privateuse1_time_total", row_limit=4))
The key averages table shows that three aten::mul calls account for the largest share of Neuron device time.
The table shows which ATen operations ran, how often they ran, and how much time they spent on the CPU and Neuron device. aten::mul has the highest total device time because the function performs three multiplications.

Each row maps directly to the function. aten::mul runs for x * x, x * rms, and the final multiplication by weight. aten::mean reduces the last dimension. aten::add adds the epsilon value and triggers a host-to-device copy because the scalar starts on the CPU. aten::rsqrt computes the reciprocal square root.
Neuron Explorer follows an aten::mul operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to execution on the Neuron hardware lanes.
Read the Trace in Explorer
In Explorer, time flows from left to right and the event lifecycle flows from top to bottom. Each ATen operation follows the same pattern: creation in the framework lane, scheduling in the runtime lane as nrta_execute_schedule, and device execution in the hardware lane as nc_exec_running.
The system trace view organizes events into lanes. In the Default grouping mode, labels follow the pattern instance/PID/subsystem/identifier:

In eager mode, each operation runs independently. Use the dependency chain viewer to follow aten::mul.Tensor from the framework layer through runtime scheduling to device execution.
The dependency chain viewer highlights the lifecycle of one operation across the framework, runtime, and hardware lanes.
Profile 2: torch.rms_norm
Replace the individual operations with PyTorch's built-in rms_norm function. Neuron lowers the operation to one fused kernel:
def rms_norm_fn(t):
return torch.rms_norm(t, [512], weight)
The fused RMSNorm appears as one device operation in the key averages table.
