The fused RMSNorm follows one framework-to-hardware path instead of dispatching each arithmetic operation separately.
Compare the Lowering Path
In the naive implementation, each operation crosses the dispatch boundary independently and follows its own framework-to-runtime-to-hardware path. In the fused implementation, one Python call covers the complete computation. The trace contains one dispatch and one hardware event, with no gaps between component operations.
Profile 3: Naive PyTorch with torch.compile
For the final example, compile the original naive RMSNorm function with torch.compile.
With @torch.compile(backend="neuron"), TorchDynamo captures the Python bytecode as an FX graph and AOTAutograd lowers it to ATen operations. The Neuron backend receives the complete graph instead of dispatching each operation separately. It fuses the operations, optimizes memory access, and compiles the graph into a single NEFF artifact. The artifact runs as one hardware dispatch.
@torch.compile(backend='neuron', fullgraph=True)
def naive_compiled(t):
x_sq = t * t
mean_sq = x_sq.mean(dim=-1, keepdim=True)
rms = torch.rsqrt(mean_sq + 1e-6)
return t * rms * weight

Instead of calling a purpose-built fused operation, the compiler discovers the fusion from the original Python function. In this run, the Neuron time is comparable to torch.rms_norm, at 375 μs compared with 403 μs.

Both torch.rms_norm and torch.compile fuse RMSNorm into one kernel dispatch. In these runs, either approach takes about one-sixth of the naive implementation's device time. Fusion removes the gaps between hardware executions and avoids materializing intermediate values such as x_sq and mean_sq between separately dispatched operations.
Conclusion
key_averages() shows which operations consume device time, while its full output also reveals CPU-side setup and transfers. Explorer provides the corresponding visual trace. You can follow one operation from framework dispatch through runtime scheduling to hardware execution and see the gaps that fusion removes.
You can use the same workflow on larger models: find a hotspot in the table, verify it in the trace, and then determine whether a fused operation or torch.compile can reduce its cost.
In Part 2, we will move into the device-level profile. You open the NEFF, inspect the TensorEngine, VectorEngine, and direct memory access (DMA) breakdown, and place the kernel on the roofline to determine whether it is compute-bound or memory-bound.

In Southeast Asia, generative AI has become an essential part of daily life, actively used by 243 million people (58% of the working population) and scaling four times faster than the rollout of the mobile internet. This has major implications for the region’s economy, according to the 11th edition of the annual e-Conomy SEA report
1
. Building the Intelligent Economy, by Google, Temasek, and Bain & Company, finds that widespread AI implementation is propelling the region’s digital economy to grow 17% year-on-year (YoY) to reach $368 billion
2
in Gross Merchandise Value (GMV) in 2026. This puts it firmly on track to exceed $1 trillion by 2035. Using tokens
3
as the new benchmark for the AI economy, the report projects that growing confidence in agentic commerce will drive a 60-fold surge in regional AI usage over the next five years.
Here are the three key takeaways from this year's e-Conomy SEA 2026 report:
1. AI is sustaining growth in every sector.
Across the digital economy, AI is reshaping how people live, shop, and move. E-commerce ($226B GMV, +18% YoY) anchors this shift, as shoppers use multimodal discovery and in-app assistants to confidently navigate complex purchases. These personalized experiences organically drive 10% higher conversions and order volume uplifts as large as 75%.
In online travel ($59B GMV, +10% YoY), traditional search engines remain the top platform people use to plan travel, while generative AI has overtaken social media to become the second-most used tool for organizing complex itineraries.
Online media ($44B revenue, +22% YoY) is personalizing content feeds and connecting audiences with more relevant ads, yielding a 10 to 20% quality engagement uplift as commerce media becomes a $4 billion market.
Mobility and food delivery ($40B GMV, +15% YoY) saves consumers time via predictive suggestions, smarter routing, and AI-powered offerings like pooled rides, fueling healthy transactional growth.
Finally, digital financial services ($1,650B GTV, +16% YoY) help consumers with real-time fraud detection, broader credit access, and personalized financial recommendations that complement human advice, alongside Singapore’s regional leadership in digital wealth platforms.
2. Consumer trust will help unlock the era of agentic commerce.
Digital automation is already well established across the region, where 72% of users rely on everyday features like price tracking. This familiarity is clearing the runway for agentic commerce, with 75% expressing willingness to let AI agents autonomously compare prices and complete transactions on their behalf.
This momentum is rooted in regional optimism: people in Southeast Asia view AI as a net benefit to society, with 62% reporting greater trust in AI tools today than a year ago. Driven by proven track records (56%), rising familiarity (55%), and output accuracy (53%), this trust signals a clear runway for deeper platform integration. To feel comfortable using new agentic capabilities, users expect clarity and guardrails, including robust privacy safeguards (44%), transparent information on what AI can and cannot do (36%), and the ability to reverse agentic transactions (30%).
3. Four major areas must adapt to enable AI adoption.
To support a projected 60-fold increase in regional AI usage by 2030, the region's broader digital ecosystem must systematically evolve across four critical conditions:
Accelerated agentic adoption and sustainable economics: Businesses need to move beyond using AI to answer single questions and start using it to help complete multi-step tasks from start to finish, backed by strong privacy safeguards and clear safety rules. At the same time, running AI models must keep getting more affordable and deliver clear, practical value, so businesses of all sizes can adopt the technology sustainably.
Scaled physical infrastructure: Physical expansion must rapidly keep pace with soaring compute demand. Meeting this trajectory requires a ~3x expansion in data center capacity over the next five years, with AI workloads capturing a dominant share of total infrastructure.
Strict model and energy efficiency: National frameworks, such as Singapore’s binding Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) rules under the Digital Infrastructure Bill, must guide next-generation facilities, paired with expanded clean energy access like Malaysia’s Corporate Renewable Energy Supply Scheme (CRESS) model.
Unified regional governance: Anchoring this trajectory, the upcoming ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) in November 2026 will establish the world's first region-wide digital trade pact, providing a framework that can unlock further growth in the Southeast Asia digital economy.

items.title: Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 21, 2026
PublicationResearch
Using thousands of AI agents to uncover new leads in biological data
How OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research used distributed AI agents to help scientists identify promising research leads in data from millions of brain cells
Read the paper(opens in a new window)
See how OpenAI, PerturbAI, and Scripps Research deployed thousands of AI agents in parallel to identify promising biological connections in complex data from millions of brain cells.
⁠
Video credit: PerturbAI.
What if scientists could uncover new clues about Alzheimer’s and Parkinson’s in minutes instead of months? Working together, OpenAI, PerturbAI⁠(opens in a new window), and Scripps Research⁠(opens in a new window) used thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind⁠(opens in a new window) to analyze and interpret existing experimental data from millions of mouse brain cells⁠(opens in a new window) in just 32 minutes. The agents connected the effects of gene disruptions with findings from scientific literature, uncovering unexpected biological connections that can help scientists understand disease and identify research directions for new treatments. The work shows how AI can help researchers explore more of what large biological experiments reveal.
Modern experiments generate far more data than scientists can thoroughly investigate. Researchers can now alter thousands of genes and measure their effects across millions of cells. But understanding what these results mean for human disease requires connecting complex experimental findings with decades of scattered scientific knowledge. This is where AI can help scientists uncover promising leads that might otherwise be missed.
“We build cell atlases so that other scientists can make discoveries we haven’t imagined yet. AI could help more researchers explore these resources and turn unexpected observations into new questions to test.”
—Sarah Teichmann, Ph.D., Chair in Stem Cell Medicine at the University of Cambridge and founding co-chair of the Human Cell Atlas
The team divided the analysis among thousands of AI agents powered by GPT‑Rosalind, an approach we call distributed biological reasoning. The agents examined a whole-brain CRISPR atlas⁠(opens in a new window), a dataset showing how gene disruptions affect different types of cells across the mouse brain. Each agent investigated a gene disruption, analyzed cellular responses, searched scientific literature, and proposed explanations for the results. Their reports were combined into a reasoning atlas linking genes, cellular effects, relevant publications, and possible biological mechanisms.
The research team estimated that comparable human analysis and literature review, conducted one perturbation at a time, would take months to a year. The agents reproduced findings from human analyses while uncovering additional leads. Their assessments of novelty and scientific value also aligned with judgments from blinded human experts. These findings help prioritize further experiments needed to test the proposed biological mechanisms.
Some of these insights point to new leads for understanding brain disease. The agents identified unexpected differences in how two disease-linked genes affect brain cells differently, as well as a potential connection between cholesterol regulation and neurodegeneration. These findings could help scientists investigate how disease develops and where future treatments might intervene.
“Sometimes the clues are already there, scattered across different fields—we just haven’t connected them. The possible link between neuronal function and cholesterol metabolism shows how those pieces, once brought together, can give us a new way to think about disease biology.”
—Tomasz Nowakowski, Ph.D., associate professor of neurological surgery at UCSF
Researchers can begin exploring these findings today. The reasoning atlas is available⁠(opens in a new window), allowing scientists to compare related genes, investigate unexpected responses, and identify promising leads to pursue. New discoveries often emerge when researchers from different fields bring their expertise together and connect familiar ideas in unexpected ways. AI can significantly scale these connections by linking new data with knowledge scattered across disciplines. The opportunity goes beyond analyzing data faster. By combining AI with experimental biology, human expertise, and scientific literature, we can help scientists turn more of their data into testable ideas.
Big experiments, unexpected clues
Some of an experiment’s most interesting clues lie outside the story scientists set out to investigate. In a dataset spanning thousands of perturbations, those clues can be easy to miss.
The agents identified an unexpected difference between Tsc1 and Tsc2, two genes that work together to control mTOR, a major regulator of cell growth, metabolism, and aging. Disrupting either gene had similar effects in several groups of neurons. But in the cerebellum, which helps coordinate movement, Tsc2 disruption altered the activity of dozens of genes involved in neuronal communication, while Tsc1 disruption produced little change.
That difference may be relevant to human disease. In people with tuberous sclerosis, abnormalities in the cerebellum are strongly linked to TSC2 mutations. While medicines that reduce mTOR activity can treat certain brain tumors and seizures, learning and behavioral difficulties associated with the disease remain challenging to address. The agents pinpointed a specific group of neurons and cellular changes worth investigating: which changes might existing medicines correct, and which might point to new treatment approaches? This gives researchers a more specific set of questions to test in the lab.
Divide the work, deepen the reasoning
Could a single agent given the entire dataset do just as well as thousands of agents working in parallel? We tested this while keeping the model and resources fixed. As the workload grew, the single agent searched less of the literature, citing only 11 references at the largest workload, while the distributed agents cited more than 700 references. Human experts also preferred the distributed-agent interpretations.
Scientists have limited time and often focus on the strongest signals in their data. Distributed agents can help examine a wider range of responses, including subtle or unexpected ones, and connect them with relevant scientific literature. Running the agents in parallel allows many perturbations to be investigated at once. This helps scientists explore more of what an experiment contains and identify promising leads that might otherwise be missed.
At the largest workload, distributed agents cited more than 700 references, compared with 11 for a single agent.
Finding the next experiment worth doing
A finding becomes more valuable when it points to an experiment worth doing. The agents found one such lead in DCTN1, a gene whose mutations cause Perry syndrome, a neurodegenerative disease with Parkinson-like symptoms.
DCTN1 is involved in moving cargo inside neurons. In the whole-brain CRISPR atlas, disrupting Dctn1 increased the expression of genes involved in making cholesterol. The agents connected this observation with research suggesting that problems with cholesterol transport may cause cells to make more cholesterol. This raised a question for follow-up experiments: could DCTN1 disruption change how cholesterol is distributed within neurons, and could those changes contribute to neurodegeneration? If so, could restoring normal cholesterol distribution help protect neurons?
Human experts also considered this hypothesis novel, consequential and worth following up on. This example shows how connecting an unexpected result with existing knowledge can turn a clue into a testable idea, and potentially a new direction for treating disease.
In blinded comparisons, human experts preferred distributed-agent reports over single-agent reports 75% of the time.
Scientists remain at the center of discovery. By uncovering more promising leads, AI can help researchers decide which ideas to pursue, design experiments, and interpret results. The goal is to turn more of the information in biological experiments into knowledge that, over time, can help guide the development of better medicines.

items.title: Which software engineering skills matter in the age of AI?
items.summary: If you ask a developer about their workflow, they can tell you how much faster the latest model is, what their coding agent can now handle, and which new tool has improved the way they work. Kunal Kushwaha has a follow-up question. “What about you?” I recently sat down with Kunal, the founder of WeMakeDevs, at CodeRabbit’s San Francisco office for an episode of *The Merge*. We talked about what software engineers should learn as AI takes on more implementation work and how they can continue improving alongside the tools they use. Kunal’s answer starts with the work that still belongs to the engineer. They need to understand the problem well enough to choose an approach and explain the reasoning behind their decisions. Whatever tools they use, they remain responsible for what ships. He also pointed to a practical way for engineers to develop greater technical depth: running an LLM locally. ![An orange and gray system cutaway with a magnifying glass revealing connected components.](/content/assets/kunal-engineering-skills-1.webp) *Figure 1. Engineering judgment depends on understanding how the pieces of a system fit together.* ## When a 12-year-old can build a product in eight hours At a recent hackathon, Kunal met a 12-year-old who had registered but was still on the waitlist. His dad had already dropped him off, and Kunal let him join the event. The young developer’s project became one of Kunal’s favorites from the past ten hackathons. It could research a user’s idea, generate a website around it, and identify people the user could contact. Kunal was impressed by the interface, documentation, and how the project brought the tools together. The [demo video on LinkedIn](https://lnkd.in/p/gzb6_yZ7) also includes a brief role-play. Kunal said the whole thing came together in eight hours. For engineers who spent years learning languages, frameworks, and the relationship between software and hardware, watching a 12-year-old create a substantial application in an afternoon can be unsettling. It led us into a more uncomfortable part of the conversation: what this shift means for engineers whose roles are centered on implementation. Kunal is enthusiastic about what these tools make possible, but he recognizes that the transition will be harder for some engineers than others. Someone doing narrowly defined implementation work, with few opportunities to move into another role, may be affected very differently from someone with more options. His advice is to examine what you bring to the work as more of the implementation becomes automated. ## Fundamentals help engineers see past the hype Technical fundamentals still matter because they give engineers a way to evaluate what AI tools produce and the claims made about them. When I asked Kunal if learning the low-level details still matter, he put the benefit plainly: “You learn how to escape the hype cycle.” Understanding the basics makes it easier to ask what a tool actually changes, which part of the system it helps, and where its limitations matter. Without that grounding, it is easy to mistake a better demo for a better solution to the problem in front of you. That does not mean engineers need to know everything. Kunal has worked deeply with Kubernetes and still encounters unfamiliar parts of Kubernetes, Linux, and networking. His hands-on experience gives him enough context to investigate what he does not know and make informed decisions. He applies the same reasoning to learning with AI. A student can use an agent to build an entire website, but the learning should not end there. They should read what it produced, ask how the functions work, and use the implementation to deepen their understanding. What matters is whether each project leaves them better able to explain, change, and debug the next one. ## Product judgment matters more as implementation gets easier Kunal proposes a simple way to assess product judgment in an interview: give the candidate a URL and say, “Talk to me about this website.” He wants to hear how the candidate breaks down the product, what they would change with creative control, and how those decisions could affect the business. Their response shows if they can identify what deserves attention and explain why their proposed changes would matter. This echoes [our conversation](/blog/the-last-software-engineer-knows-what-to-build) with Kent C. Dodds about what work will look like for "the last software engineer." Kent argued that as agents take on more implementation, engineers will spend more time deciding what to build, shaping the system, and judging the result. Kunal reaches a similar conclusion through his work with students, engineers, and hackathon teams. He also sees collaboration, empathy, and an understanding of the people who will use the software as essential to the job. Hackathons also give him a practical view of execution. In those environments, Kunal looks for the same kind of judgment in how teams decide what to build and present their work. The strongest teams get one main feature working, save a usable first version, and build from there. They also make the result easy to try. Kunal’s emphasis on execution sparked a discussion about how much weight should be given to the idea. He suggested that ideas matter less than execution, while I argued that as implementation gets easier, choosing a valuable problem should matter that much more. Kunal qualified his point: an ambitious idea still needs a working implementation. A small, well-executed product can beat a bigger idea that never gets built. ![A person approaches a finished application while unfinished interface components lie nearby.](/content/assets/kunal-engineering-skills-2.webp) *Figure 2. A small working product gives people something they can try and respond to.* ## How far automated code review can go Our sharpest disagreement was over how far automated review will go. Kunal expects agents to handle more of it and thinks humans may eventually stop reviewing code altogether. At the same time, he believes the stakes should determine how much attention a change receives. He used a hypothetical Black Friday incident at a large company to illustrate where he would still expect human review. If an agent produced a fix during a major sale, he would still want a person to check it. While we differed on how much review agents will eventually handle, we agreed that responsibility for the result does not shift to the agent. “If something messes up, you’re the one who is responsible,” Kunal said. The conversation turned to what happens as agent-generated changes accumulate in a system. I described a project I had been building with coding agents for about a year. Early on, I understood what they were putting together. As more agents contributed, maintaining that understanding became harder, although the automated checks continued to pass. We discussed maintenance, performance, and security problems that may surface only after a change passes its tests and reaches production. That led us to discuss the blast radius of a change. Reviewers need to see how it affects the wider application, including areas they did not expect the agent to touch. At CodeRabbit, we built [Change Stack](/change-stack) to provide that expanded view. It organizes pull requests into logical groups and layers so reviewers can follow dependencies across the change. ## Learn to run LLMs locally When I asked Kunal for a specific technical skill engineers should learn next, he suggested something quite different from another coding-agent workflow. “Learn how to run LLMs locally.” His recommendation is to run a model locally and then explore fine-tuning and what it would take to run it at scale. Kunal says the exercise exposes engineers to the infrastructure behind the interface, including how the model runs, how its components communicate, and the deployment choices involved. He compared the experience with [learning Kubernetes](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tutorials/kubernetes-basics/). An engineer may use a managed service in production while still benefiting from having built and operated a small cluster. That experience helps them understand what the managed service is doing on their behalf. The same principle applies when a team chooses how to serve a model. An API, company-owned hardware, and a managed platform come with different tradeoffs. Working through a local setup gives engineers more context to ask better questions about the various options. ![An exploded view of a local computer connected by an orange cable to a server rack.](/content/assets/kunal-engineering-skills-3.webp) *Figure 3. Running a model locally exposes the components behind an AI service before you consider deployment at scale.* ## Build experience through open source and sharing Open source gave Kunal a way around a familiar problem early in his career: an internship application asks for experience, but getting it seems to require an internship. Rather than wait for an opportunity, he built experience in public by contributing to Kubernetes, taking part in [Google Summer of Code](https://summerofcode.withgoogle.com/), and eventually mentoring others. He would still recommend that path to an engineer starting today, despite the proliferation of AI tools. Kunal sees projects, open-source contributions, and hackathons as opportunities for developers to build skills and share what they learn. Posting that you completed a tutorial marks your progress, but explaining a concept from it invites feedback that can test and deepen your understanding of the material. For engineers preparing for their next role, Kunal recommends that they study the work the job involves and the AI tools and systems people use to do it, then put that knowledge to work in a project. Sharing that work gives other people a chance to try it and offer feedback. A developer who understands a project well enough to explain it, improve it in response to feedback, and stand behind the result has a concrete answer to Kunal’s opening question: “What about you?”

items.title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
items.summary:
Back to Articles
AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms
Published
October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 7
+1
Mattt mattt Follow
Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog:
a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework
that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses.
We heard from app developers who were curious about local models
but weren't always sure how to get started.
They also wanted to avoid the added complexity
of supporting multiple inference providers.
AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.
Local and hosted inference each have their strengths,
and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps.
A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.
A year and dozens of releases later,
AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out,
along with swift-huggingface 1.0
and swift-xet 1.0.
Here's what changed, and what's next:
A drop-in compatible API
The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same:
use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app.
To get started, change your import statement:
- import FoundationModels
+ import AnyLanguageModel
The same session code then works with the system model,
with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML,
and with the hosted providers below.
Over the past year, we've added several major features:
Tool calling works with every provider.
Guided generation works with every provider, too,
including nested @Generable types and arrays of them.
Image support lets you attach images to prompts
using Foundation Models 27's syntax,
including when you use the system model on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.
On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with
any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol,
including Core AI models.
Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out
swift-huggingface
and swift-xet
to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.
Hosted models, too
Support for hosted models expanded this year, too.
AnyLanguageModel now supports:
OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses APIs
Open Responses,
for any provider with a compatible endpoint
Anthropic's Messages API, with adaptive thinking and effort options
Google's Gemini API
Ollama
Private Cloud Compute, on OS 27
Hugging Face Inference Providers,
and other OpenAI-compatible endpoints such as OpenRouter,
through a custom base URL
With Inference Providers,
you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device
with the same session code:
let model = OpenAILanguageModel(
baseURL: URL(string: "https://router.huggingface.co/v1/")!,
apiKey: ProcessInfo.processInfo.environment["HF_TOKEN"]!,
model: "openai/gpt-oss-120b",
apiVariant: .chatCompletions
)
Hosted providers get the same features as local models:
guided generation, tool calling with streaming,
and token usage on responses.
Reasoning is now part of the transcript too.
When you switch providers,
reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.
API keys come from a closure instead of a string,
so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server.
The README
explains when to let people bring their own keys
and when to route requests through a proxy.
AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux,
so the same code can work on a server.
Open-weight models got better
While we've made local models easier to use,
the models themselves have become more capable,
making the small ones a good place to start.
Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:
Gemma 4 E2B from Google,
in GGUF, about 3.4 GB at Q4_0 with quantization-aware training.
LFM2.5 2.6B from Liquid AI,
in GGUF, about 1.7 GB at Q4_K_M.
Qwen3.8 27B for MLX from Alibaba,
about 16 GB at 4 bits.
The first two fit on an iPhone,
and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more.
Selecting the MLX model takes one line:
let model = MLXLanguageModel(modelId: "mlx-community/Qwen3.8-27B-4bit")
And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy,
GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16.
For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.
Upgrading to 1.0
dependencies: [
.package(
url: "https://github.com/huggingface/AnyLanguageModel",
from: "1.0.0",
traits: ["MLX"]
)
]
If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the
AnyLanguageModel,
swift-huggingface,
and swift-xet release notes
for help updating your code.
Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features.
Thank you to everyone who contributed
for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.
What's next
Language models have proven to be a powerful tool
for building intelligence into products.
They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work.
We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities:
familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device.
Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

items.summary:
All posts
Published October 20, 2026 in Announcements
Enterprise features October roundup
Teams at large companies build working prototypes with AI every day. The ones worth keeping need to go to production. That takes access to real company data and sign-off from security on where the app runs and who can use it.
Many of the enterprises we work with run a federated model. A central IT or AI team sets the guardrails once, like who can build and what needs approval before an app goes live. Teams in each function build inside those guardrails. IT can see everything they ship. Governed sprawl beats shadow sprawl.
We built this month's releases for teams that work this way. Apps can run on sensitive data in your own cloud. Central teams can set up Lovable once for the whole company and decide what goes live. IT can manage all of it from the tools it already uses.
Run your apps in your own AWS or Azure account
Some apps can't go to production until they run inside your own network. An HR app that reads from your HR system is a common example. With Deploy on AWS and Deploy on Azure, Enterprise teams can run those apps and the data behind them in their own cloud account. Both are in private preview.
People keep building in Lovable the same way they do today. Preview sandboxes, published apps, the app database, file storage, and app logs run in a dedicated network inside your account. Apps reach internal systems like your data warehouse over VPC or VNet peering. Those systems stay off the public internet. Lovable installs and updates everything it deploys there. Your Enterprise security controls still apply.
Deutsche Telekom went live in October with its Lovable apps running in its own AWS account.
Read how it works in Deploy your Lovable apps in your own AWS account and Deploy on Azure: keep your Lovable apps in your own subscription. The Azure post also covers the other ways to build with Lovable on Microsoft. To join the private preview, talk to your account team or email byoc@lovable.dev.
Bring your own key
When you deploy in your own cloud, chat and project history still stay with Lovable. Bring your own key puts that history under your control too. Admins connect their own encryption key in Workspace settings. Lovable encrypts the history with it. If you revoke the key, Lovable can no longer read the history.
Bring your own key is in private preview. Today it works with AWS KMS in workspaces that use Deploy on AWS. Azure Key Vault support is rolling out with Deploy on Azure. We're also working on it for workspaces hosted on Lovable. Your account team can walk your security team through how it works.
EU inference
For European companies, the security review often asks where the AI processes requests. By default, Lovable sends AI requests to the standard endpoints of the model providers on our subprocessor list. Those providers can process requests in the U.S. EU inference keeps an Enterprise workspace's AI model requests on model endpoints in the EU, while you build and for the AI features in your published apps. A request that no EU endpoint can serve fails rather than running elsewhere.
A workspace owner or admin turns it on in Privacy & security settings. If you also use Deploy on AWS or Azure, your apps and their data run in your cloud while EU inference covers the AI requests.
Read EU inference: control where AI processes your requests. The EU inference docs list which models and features are available with it turned on.
Organizations
Large companies often run several Lovable workspaces, one for each team or region. In a federated model, the central team still owns identity for all of them. With Organizations, IT sets it up once.
From the organization console, you can:
Set up SSO and SCIM for every workspace in the organization
Map groups in your identity provider to the workspaces people should land in
See every member and the workspaces they belong to
Lock identity settings so workspace admins can't change them
Block people from creating workspaces IT hasn't approved
Review audit logs across every workspace in the organization
Teams can also publish internal apps to the whole company. A workspace owner or admin picks the organization audience in the publish dialog. Only people in a workspace in your organization can open the app. The project stays in its own workspace.
Organizations is also where admins set up Deploy on AWS and Azure workspaces. It's available on Enterprise. Reach out to your account team to turn it on.
Learn how to publish to your organization.
Workspace policies and approvals
Workspace policies are where the central team decides what needs a review before an app goes to production. Admins can let more people publish and still check the apps that matter. A policy either blocks an action or requires an admin or owner to approve it first. The first policies cover publishing. When no policy applies, the app publishes without a review.
You can turn on policies to:
Restrict publishing while a project has unresolved PII findings (this replaces the Block publishing with PII setting)
Require approval when external collaborators publish
Restrict publishing apps publicly
Require approval to publish apps that use connectors
Block publishing from email addresses outside your verified domains
When a policy requires approval, the person publishing sends a request with a note. Every admin and owner gets it in Lovable and by email. Once one of them approves, Lovable publishes the app. Later updates go out without a new request until something the policy checks changes, like the app's connectors or who can view it.
For the connectors and external collaborators policies, the setup dialog shows how often the policy would have required approval in the last 30 days. Policy changes and approval decisions show up in your audit logs. People keep building and previewing while a request waits.
More policies are coming, starting with who can publish and holding apps with open security findings. Later ones go beyond publishing.
Workspace policies and approvals are available on Enterprise. Read the workspace policies docs and Privacy & security settings.
Action center
Admins and owners approve requests in the new Action center. It also flags other things in the workspace that need a decision:
Projects whose owner left the workspace
Projects whose credit usage rose sharply
Public apps with critical security findings
Public apps nobody has edited for months
You can act on each one from there, for example by assigning a new owner or unpublishing the app.
The Action center is available on Business and Enterprise. Approval requests need Enterprise. Read the Action center docs.
The Lovable API for workspace admins
Central teams want to manage Lovable the way they manage every other tool they run. The Lovable API lets them pull usage and security data into their own dashboards instead of exporting it manually. It works from your own scripts and agents. It's available on Business and Enterprise. Admins use it to:
Read workspace settings and list members and groups
Pull project and workspace analytics
Poll security scans and workspace security insights across every project
Publish, unpublish, update, and delete projects
Read PII labels and the project security inventory (Enterprise)
Credit usage and credit limits are coming to the API next. Admins will be able to track spend and set limits from the same scripts.
Owners and admins create API keys in Workspace settings. You can also register OAuth clients so your own apps connect to Lovable with each person's permission.
Learn more:
Lovable API overview
API reference
Create and manage API keys
Audit log export to your SIEM or cloud storage
Security teams can now watch Lovable activity from the tools they already monitor. Lovable sends your workspace's audit logs to Splunk or another destination you own every hour or every three hours. Each run sends only what arrived since the last one.
Logs can go to:
Splunk
Azure Log Analytics
Amazon S3
Google Cloud Storage
Azure Blob Storage
Lovable keeps audit logs for 13 weeks. With an export, you keep your own copy for as long as your policy requires. Lovable signs in to AWS, Google Cloud, and Azure with short-lived credentials your cloud account trusts. There's no long-lived key to manage. Workspace settings has step-by-step setup instructions for each destination.
Learn more:
Data exports overview
Splunk setup guide
Azure Log Analytics setup guide
Amazon S3 setup guide
Audit logs
What's next
We're building settings that apply to every workspace in an organization at once. On Deploy on AWS and Azure, we're working toward full feature parity with hosting on Lovable. Deploy on Google Cloud is on the way.
Workspace policies, the Action center, the Lovable API, and audit log exports are live today. Talk to your account team to set up Organizations or to try Deploy on AWS or Azure. New to Lovable Enterprise? Speak to a member of our sales team.

items.title: Franchisee reconciles cash in 94% less time with ChatGPT Work
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 20, 2026
Franchisee reconciles cash in 94% less time with ChatGPT Work
An independent Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon franchisee cut repricing time by 95% and built a workflow that could free up $100K in cash flow.
Contact salesCompany size: SMBRegion: North AmericaIndustry: Food & BeverageProducts: ChatGPT
95%
Reduction in time required for pricing analysis, from 5 days to 1 to 2 hours
$100K
Maximum annual cash flow that could be freed up with optimized labor workflow
4
Hours of manual work saved every payroll
94%
Reduction in time spent on monthly cash reconciliation
Ted Taylor entered the restaurant business after a 25-year career in the semiconductor industry. Today, he’s an independent franchisee operating three co-branded Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon restaurants across New Mexico.
Running quick-service restaurants means balancing the customer experience with a lot of work customers never see, like menu pricing, staffing, equipment maintenance, and policies. Ted uses OpenAI technology to get through all of it faster.
With ChatGPT, Ted accelerates time-consuming tasks like research and drafting, and he uses ChatGPT Work to gather and analyze volumes of data across pricing, sales, forecasts, schedules, and labor and to get recommendations on where each restaurant needs attention, reducing repricing time by 95% and shaving 4 hours off payroll runs.
“ChatGPT Work’s recommendations are so good that it’s much faster to start there and then make adjustments.”
—Ted Taylor, independent franchisee, Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon
Repricing menus across three markets in minutes
Repricing menus is an annual undertaking that requires a complex analysis of recipe costs, item popularity, local competitor pricing, portion sizes, and the different economics of in-store and delivery orders. Ted uses ChatGPT Work to bring those factors together and get pricing recommendations in 1 - 2 hours instead of 5 days.
“It used to take me a few days of work to analyze and come up with item-level pricing; whereas, ChatGPT Work tears through it in a matter of moments and does it more thoroughly.”
—Ted Taylor, independent franchisee, Schlotzsky’s and Cinnabon
Ted first uses ChatGPT Work to research and establish his pricing targets and pricing strategies based on local competitors’ pricing trends, portion sizes, and relative food quality. He then gives ChatGPT Work a categorized list of menu items with their current in-store and delivery prices. He specifies how much he wants each set of prices to increase overall and which items should receive larger or smaller increases, largely based on the earlier analysis from ChatGPT.
He can make the analysis more detailed by adding item-level sales history and supplier prices. ChatGPT Work can use these inputs to estimate sales impacts from price changes and to optimize item-level pricing around cost of goods targets.
ChatGPT Work returns a spreadsheet with recommended in-store and delivery prices. It will even relate the pricing changes to an overall pricing strategy designed to optimize business outcomes like customer retention, minimizing price shocks, and best positioning of add-ons.
The first time Ted used ChatGPT Work for pricing, he also ran the analysis manually. “ChatGPT Work made a deeper local comparison and helped me avoid increases that would have made some items uncompetitive,” he said. Ted immediately switched to using ChatGPT to develop the first recommendations.
Finding ways to optimize labor and free up cash flow
Ted uses ChatGPT Work to help manage labor costs in two ways: reviewing how labor is tracking across his three restaurants and testing a better way to build the weekly schedule.
For the labor analysis, Ted gave ChatGPT Work read-only access to his sales and labor data. When he runs the analysis, it compares scheduled, budgeted, and actual hours with forecast and actual sales. It also reviews the previous 12 weeks to account for stores that routinely come in above or below their sales forecasts. The resulting report flags overtime, shifts running longer than planned, and gaps in coverage, and highlights what a manager should review.
For the scheduling test, Ted gave ChatGPT Work an employee roster with each person’s role, training, availability, and pay, along with the store’s staffing needs at different sales levels. He and the manager compared ChatGPT Work’s proposed schedule with what she would have built, identified missing rules about when to add staff during busy periods, and refined the instructions for ChatGPT Work.
ChatGPT Work now produces a full schedule for that location. The manager checks it over, makes adjustments if needed, and enters it into the restaurant’s scheduling system. Ted estimates that better scheduling could eventually reduce hourly labor costs by one to two percentage points of sales across all three restaurants, which could add $50,000 to $100,000 in free cash flow annually that can be utilized for increased pay, bonuses, investment in the business, or increased profit distributions.
Accelerating back-office tasks with ChatGPT Work
Ted also uses ChatGPT Work for day-to-day operations, from developing HR policies to reconciling cash and managing supply and repair requests.
When New Mexico started requiring restaurants to keep a written procedure for bodily-fluid incidents, Ted used ChatGPT to write a draft in about 30 seconds. When Ted needed a social media policy for his employee handbook, ChatGPT helped him quickly draft guidance that an outside HR firm later reviewed without making any changes.
Ted uses ChatGPT Work to reconcile cash monthly across his three restaurants. He uploads each store’s cash transaction data and bank records, and ChatGPT Work compares the transactions with the corresponding deposits. Monthly reconciliation used to take three hours, and now it takes 5-10 minutes. He also cut four hours of manual work from every payroll cycle by using ChatGPT Work to summarize payroll inputs.
To help keep restaurants running smoothly, Ted also used ChatGPT Work to build a web portal where employees can request supplies or repairs. The portal notifies him through a dedicated email address and tracks each request’s status.
More time to improve the business, not just run it
Ted’s approach to using ChatGPT Work is practical for any small-business owner. He gives ChatGPT the same data and guidelines he’d use to make a decision and compares its output with how he’d do the work himself. As he gains confidence in the results, he expands his use to more tasks around the business, always reviewing the results before implementing.
For Ted, the value of ChatGPT Work goes beyond hours saved. Now he can do analysis he might otherwise skip and spend more time on customers, employees, and growing the business.

items.title: How Kiro fixes itself, and how we keep the fixes honest
items.summary: One sentence in Kiro’s file-read and search tool descriptions made a false claim about how the harness behaves, and it reached the model 61,742 times across a few hundred sessions. It did nothing useful, and it’s unlikely anyone would have filed a ticket for it. Problems like that are hard to find, and fixes are just as hard to judge. For example, we nearly shipped one that passed more tasks and used fewer tokens, until we split the results by host and found almost all of the gain came from a single run where the agent happened to escape a loop it usually gets stuck in. Without that host, the fix was slower, more expensive, and less accurate. A loop that grades its own fixes would have shipped it.

items.title: Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively
Published
October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 55
+49
Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow Régis Pierrard regisss Follow
If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.
Wait, what's a TPU? 🤔
TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.
TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.
The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.
The old way
Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.
To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.
Enter TorchTPU 🚀
TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:
pip install torch-tpu --extra-index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cpu
The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.
Your favourite libraries, now on TPU
Transformers
Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
model_id = "Qwen/Qwen3.5-9B"
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
model_id,
device_map="tpu", # will load model directly on the TPU
)
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
inputs = tokenizer("The future of AI is", return_tensors="pt").to("tpu")
out = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=64)
print(tokenizer.decode(out[0], skip_special_tokens=True))
The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.
Images? Videos? Diffusers paints them on TPUs 🎨
TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.
import torch
from diffusers import StableDiffusion3Pipeline
pipe = StableDiffusion3Pipeline.from_pretrained(
"stabilityai/stable-diffusion-3.5-medium", dtype=torch.bfloat16
)
pipe.to("tpu") # eager mode: that's the whole change
# optional: compiled mode
pipe.transformer.compile(backend="tpu", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)
image = pipe("a corgi astronaut planting a flag on a pizza moon").images[0]
The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.
Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.
Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:
TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1
MiniMax-H3 (video + audio)
Qwen-Image-2.1
"The fluffy plush Hugging Face mascot from the picture, a round yellow smiling face with rosy cheeks and two little open hands, stands at the prow of an ancient Greek trireme […] Sound of crashing waves, creaking timber, wind in the rigging, distant seagulls, and a low epic orchestral swell." · 1344×768, 5.2 s, 49 steps · 188 s compiled, 262 s eager
"A capybara wearing a wizard hat, reading a book by candlelight, oil painting" · 1024×1024, 40 steps · 3.5 s compiled, 8.0 s eager
"A neon shop sign that reads 'QWEN IMAGE 2.1', rainy night, reflections on wet pavement" · 2048×2048, 40 steps
Kernels
The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.
TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:
from kernels import get_kernel
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.integrations.moe import ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS
repo_id = "tengomucho/ragged-dot-tpu"
kernel = get_kernel(repo_id, version=1, trust_remote_code=[repo_id])
ALL_EXPERTS_FUNCTIONS.register("tokamax_ragged_dot", kernel.experts_forward)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
"Qwen/Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507",
experts_implementation="tokamax_ragged_dot",
)
The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.
Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.
We test it so you don't have to 🧪
We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].
The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!
It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.
If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.
Get started
TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".
TorchTPU on GitHub
TPU kernels on the Hub
Cloud TPU documentation
We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

items.title: Introducing the Agent SDK
items.summary:
Blog / productOct 20, 2026·product
Introducing the Agent SDK
Rustam Lalkaka · 5 min read
Software teams use agents defined as code to handle recurring work across the development lifecycle. These agents connect to the places where a team works and act when relevant events occur, whether that means reviewing a pull request, executing a compliance workflow, or investigating an incident.
The most useful agents are tailored to how a particular team operates. Until now, building one has generally meant adopting a product designed around someone else's workflow or starting from scratch.
Today, we're releasing the Agent SDK, the framework we use to build our own managed agents like Bugbot, Security Reviewer, and Rollouts. Agent SDK allows you to define agents in code and manage them like any other software project. Start from a template or point your coding agent at our docs. When the agent is ready, agent-sdk deploy it to Cursor infrastructure with one command.
#Build around your workflow
The Agent SDK lets you quickly build and deploy agents that work the way your team does. They respond to the events your team already handles and follow policies your team can inspect and change.
Code review is one example. Each team has its own standards for what requires attention and who should review it. With the Agent SDK, you can build an agent that responds to pull request events from GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket. The agent can assess the risk of a change, route it to the right team, and approve changes that meet your policy.
As an example, a team within Cursor had built a large, fast-growing knowledge base of lessons learned and wanted every pull request checked against it. This way, the team's past decisions would hold even as the codebase changed. With the Agent SDK, they built kb-reviewer in about a day. It now runs on every PR in their main codebase, flags changes that contradict a recorded lesson, cites the note behind each finding, and encourages engineers to reconcile the discrepancies it reports.
For more complicated work, agents can hand a task to another specialized agent with its own tools and sessions. They can also divide a job among subagents working in parallel.
The Agent SDK also supports evals and event replay out of the box, allowing for rapid development with assurances that critical workflows execute the way you expect. The PGA Tour uses the Agent SDK to power their software development factory. Evals keep them moving quickly.
The Agent SDK has enabled PGA to build every component of our software factory on Cursor's infrastructure. It provides the flexibility we need to build agents that drive our development process. And built-in support for evals allows us to quickly iterate on new ideas and optimize existing capabilities reliably.
Michael GyarmathyPrincipal Engineer, PGA America
#Define everything in code
An Agent SDK agent is organized like a small software project. The instructions that guide it sit alongside code for its tools, connections to outside services, and the evals used to test it.
Each file represents something the agent knows or can do. Prompts are written in Markdown, while tools are defined as TypeScript functions. Because everything is code, changes can go through the same version control and review process as the rest of your software.
#Deploy agents wherever you need them
When you're ready to put an agent into use, you can deploy it to Cursor by running agent-sdk deploy from the project directory. The command builds the agent, gives it a URL, and starts it on our infrastructure. You can manage secrets and integrations from the dashboard, while continuing to use the same logs, evals, and playground available locally.
You can also run the agent on your own infrastructure. Each agent runs as a single Node process that can be packaged in a container.
#Get started
Getting started with the Agent SDK looks much like starting any other software project. Create a project directory, then launch the local playground:
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { defineAgent } from "@cursor/agent-sdk";
export default defineAgent({
name: "Robo",
model: {
id: "composer-2.5",
params: [
{ id: "effort", value: "high" },
{ id: "fast", value: "true" },
],
},
local: {
cwd: join(homedir(), ".cache", "factory", "robo"),
},
})
From there, you can iterate locally and run evals before deploying with agent-sdk deploy.
The Agent SDK also ships with skills that guide coding agents through the development process. You can point an agent at the docs and have it help build the bot with you.
The Agent SDK is generally available today. Read the docs and get started.

And built-in support for evals allows us to quickly iterate on new ideas and optimize existing capabilities reliably.
Michael GyarmathyPrincipal Engineer, PGA America
#Define everything in code
An Agent SDK agent is organized like a small software project. The instructions that guide it sit alongside code for its tools, connections to outside services, and the evals used to test it.
Each file represents something the agent knows or can do. Prompts are written in Markdown, while tools are defined as TypeScript functions. Because everything is code, changes can go through the same version control and review process as the rest of your software.
#Deploy agents wherever you need them
When you're ready to put an agent into use, you can deploy it to Cursor by running agent-sdk deploy from the project directory. The command builds the agent, gives it a URL, and starts it on our infrastructure. You can manage secrets and integrations from the dashboard, while continuing to use the same logs, evals, and playground available locally.
You can also run the agent on your own infrastructure. Each agent runs as a single Node process that can be packaged in a container.
#Get started
Getting started with the Agent SDK looks much like starting any other software project. Create a project directory, then launch the local playground:
import { homedir } from "node:os";
import { join } from "node:path";
import { defineAgent } from "@cursor/agent-sdk";
export default defineAgent({
name: "Robo",
model: {
id: "composer-2.5",
params: [
{ id: "effort", value: "high" },
{ id: "fast", value: "true" },
],
},
local: {
cwd: join(homedir(), ".cache", "factory", "robo"),
},
})
From there, you can iterate locally and run evals before deploying with agent-sdk deploy.
The Agent SDK also ships with skills that guide coding agents through the development process. You can point an agent at the docs and have it help build the bot with you.
The Agent SDK is generally available today. Read the docs and get started.

items.title: MPS in PyTorch 2.15
items.summary:
Back to Articles
MPS in PyTorch 2.15
Published
October 20, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 37
+31
Khushi Agrawal khushi-411 Follow
If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.
A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.
TL;DR
FP8 comes to the Mac: store float8_e4m3fn values in half the space of BF16 and use scaled matrix multiplication and all other ops which are supported on CUDA/CPU!
MoE models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s on an M3 Ultra, thanks to a native grouped matmul with a dedicated decoding path, fewer GPU-CPU syncs and faster top-k routing.
Less time per token for every LLM: single-row linear layers use specialized matrix-vector kernels, and softmax over the vocabulary is about 8× faster.
More linear algebra on the GPU: complex LU and triangular solves, faster small-matrix inverses, and faster QR decomposition.
Audio, video, and training get attention too: faster paths for convolutions, padding, dropout, interpolation backward and reductions. Wan2.2's video VAE decode now peaks at 8 GiB of memory instead of 270 GiB.
More control from Python: public MPS streams and more reliable event timing.
Updated requirements: MPS now requires macOS 15 or later; PyTorch 2.15 requires Python 3.11 or later.
A peek at 2.16: attention fully on Metal, more MPSGraph-to-Metal migrations and faster LLM decoding.
What this means for you
If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:
Much faster local LLMs. Mixture-of-experts models decode 5–6.5× faster than in 2.14: on an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B goes from 9.4 to 61.3 tokens/s and LFM2.5-8B-A1B from 23.6 to 123.6 tokens/s. Dense models benefit too, from faster linear layers and an 8× faster softmax for sampling. (More)
Video generation that fits in memory. Decoding a video with Wan2.2's tiled VAE used to push driver memory to 270 GiB; it now peaks at about 8 GiB. (More)
Correct image editing with Qwen-Image-2.1. On 2.14, the Qwen-Image-2.1 VAE encoder silently corrupted images on MPS, breaking image-edit workflows (reported in ComfyUI). The same padding change fixes it: an encode-decode round trip now matches CPU at 29.95 dB PSNR, up from 10.06 dB.
FP8 weights on your Mac. FP8 tensors take half the memory of BF16, and F.scaled_mm multiplies them directly on the GPU. (More)
Contents
Getting started
FP8 comes to MPS
Faster language-model decoding
Linear algebra gets a boost
Convolutions, padding, and training
Softmax and reductions
A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding
More control with MPS streams
More operations work on MPS
A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16
Wrapping up
Getting started
You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.
To try the release candidate in a separate environment:
uv pip install torch==2.15.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/test/cpu
FP8 comes to MPS
FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.
You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
def quantize_fp8(x):
limit = torch.finfo(torch.float8_e4m3fn).max
scale = x.abs().amax().clamp_min(1e-12) / limit
return (x / scale).to(torch.float8_e4m3fn), scale
x = torch.randn(1, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
weight = torch.randn(1024, 1024, device="mps", dtype=torch.float32)
x_fp8, x_scale = quantize_fp8(x)
w_fp8, w_scale = quantize_fp8(weight)
y = F.scaled_mm(
x_fp8,
w_fp8.t(),
scale_a=x_scale,
scale_recipe_a=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
scale_b=w_scale,
scale_recipe_b=F.ScalingType.TensorWise,
output_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
print(y.shape, y.dtype)
Faster language-model decoding
Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.
Linear layers
MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.
Mixture-of-experts layers
A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.
In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.
For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
tokens = torch.randn(64, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
weights = torch.randn(3, 128, 64, device="mps", dtype=torch.bfloat16)
ends = torch.tensor([16, 48, 64], device="mps", dtype=torch.int32)
out = F.grouped_mm(tokens, weights.transpose(-2, -1), offs=ends)
print(out.shape) # torch.Size([64, 128])
The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:
Linear algebra gets a boost
Complex-valued computations
Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:
import torch
a = torch.randn(8, 8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
a = a + 8 * torch.eye(8, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
b = torch.randn(8, 2, device="mps", dtype=torch.complex64)
lu, pivots = torch.linalg.lu_factor(a)
x = torch.linalg.lu_solve(lu, pivots, b)
print((a @ x - b).abs().max().item())
Small matrices and larger solves
Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.
Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.
SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.
Convolutions, padding, and training
Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:
Operation
What changes in 2.15
conv1d forward
Specialized kernels replace MPSGraph, plus an im2col-plus-matmul path for short outputs. Useful for audio and streaming-model shapes.
Constant padding
Moves to Metal kernels, fixing runaway driver-memory growth in tiled video VAE decoding (more below).
Reflection and replication padding
New Metal implementations that are faster and fix backward correctness.
Out-of-place dropout
nn.Dropout and F.dropout now use the existing fused kernel.
Upsampling backward
A Metal gather kernel replaces the MPSGraph resize-gradient path.
Channels-last conv2d backward
Stays on an efficient channels-last path instead of an NCHW graph with costly strided access.
Softmax and reductions
Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:
A much smaller memory footprint for video decoding
One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:
Memory metric
MPSGraph padding
Metal padding
Current tensor-allocation peak
4.422 GiB
4.095 GiB
Allocator-reserved peak
8.070 GiB
8.070 GiB
Total driver-memory peak
270.135 GiB
8.108 GiB
More control with MPS streams
You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.
Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:
import torch
x = torch.randn(1024, device="mps")
torch.mps.synchronize()
worker = torch.mps.Stream()
with torch.mps.stream(worker):
y = x.square()
x.record_stream(worker)
del x
worker.synchronize()
print(y.cpu().shape)
More operations work on MPS
Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.
Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.
A sneak peek at PyTorch 2.16
Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.
Faster LLM decoding
Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:
Model
Before
After
Change
LFM2.5-8B-A1B
108.8 tokens/s
126.0 tokens/s
+16%
Qwen3.6-35B-A3B
52.9 tokens/s
62.8 tokens/s
+19%
Qwen3.8-27B
12.1 tokens/s
12.6 tokens/s
+4%
Attention runs entirely on Metal
Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.
More MPSGraph to Metal migrations
The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.
A smaller install
Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.
Wrapping up
PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!
What's next for us
More MPS: 2.16 will run attention entirely on Metal, and we'll keep moving operations off MPSGraph.
torch.compile: we're working on getting rid of graph breaks, so more models compile end to end.
Your ideas: what else should we work on in PyTorch? If something is slow, missing or broken, on MPS or anywhere else, open an issue on GitHub and let us know.
A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.
