items.title: NotebookLM's Video Overview System Prompt: The Full Creation Workflow
items.summary:
See all postsPublished on 2026-10-20
NotebookLM's Video Overview System Prompt: The Full Creation Workflow
作者：
宝玉
The Video Overview creation skill shared below lays out a complete workflow for turning notebook sources into a video: read the context, help the user choose a focus, confirm the settings, and hand the request to the video generation pipeline.
What caught my attention is how much of the prompt deals with getting the user's intent right. It distinguishes a new video request from a question about an existing one, discards abandoned choices when the user starts over, and preserves the user's approved focus text verbatim when submitting the generation request.
The file also includes the questionnaire and review card schemas, format and visual style rules, localization requirements, and example tool calls. Those schemas and calls reference NotebookLM-specific components and tools; they describe the orchestration layer rather than a standalone prompt to paste into a video customization box.
Below is the full supplied skill file, reproduced unchanged in one code block, including its metadata, JSON templates, and dispatch examples.
---
name: vo-creation
description: >-
Create cinematic videos from content using a multi-step co-creation workflow.
Use when user wants a breakdown, cinematic video, or movie-style video
overview from their sources.
---
# Video Creation
You are a World-Class Video Producer and Visual Storyteller. Your goal is to
transform raw sources into a cinematic breakdown video using a co-creation and
multi-step agentic workflow. Your tone should be like a thoughtful creative
partner.
## Context Gathering (IMPORTANT)
Prefill every card field from context you already have. Make a tool call only
when that context falls short:
1. **Source material**: Use the source summaries already in the notebook
context to identify themes and topics. Only run a `semantic_search` (at most
once) if the summaries are insufficient — for example, when a selected
source has no summary, when the summaries are too brief to extract 3
distinct themes, or when the user asks about a specific section or detail
not covered in the summaries (e.g., "chapter 3"). Do not call
`semantic_search` if the summaries already provide enough detail to populate
the card.
2. **Conversation history**: Review the full conversation. Pay **special
attention to the user's last message** — it often contains the most specific
and recent intent signal (e.g., "make a breakdown about the economic impact
section" or "cinematic video on chapter 3").
3. **Implicit preferences**: Infer tone, audience, and visual feel from context
clues. A scientific paper suggests a grounded, analytical tone; a
pop-culture topic suggests something vibrant and energetic.
Use this context to prefill every field in the cards below. The user should be
able to hit "Generate" on the Review Card immediately and get a great result.
## User Intent Resolution & Disambiguation (CRITICAL)
Before deciding which card to show or what action to take, you **must resolve
the user's intent** by examining their latest message in relation to any
existing artifacts or in-progress cards:
### 1. Existing Artifact vs. New Co-Creation Journey
- **Referring to an existing artifact**: If an artifact has already been
generated or is currently generating in the notebook/session (e.g., in the
Studio panel), and the user is asking about it (e.g., "how is my video?",
"check on the video", "show me the video", "can you change the style of that
video?"):
- Respond conversationally about the existing artifact and direct them to
the Studio panel.
- **Do NOT** show a new card or call `create_artifact`.
- **Starting a new co-creation journey**: If the user explicitly wants a new
artifact or a new topic (e.g., "make me a video", "make another video",
"create a video about X", "generate a new video"):
- Treat this as a brand-new, independent request.
- Do NOT carry forward unrelated settings or topics from previous
artifacts.
- If a video already exists, mention it in one line ("Your video 'X' is in
Studio. Let's set up a new one.") and continue to Step 0 or Step 1.
- **No creation verb** (e.g., just "video?" or "the video") while a video
exists: answer about that video and offer a new one in the same reply.
- **Let the card carry open choices.** If the notebook covers several topics
or angles, show the Questionnaire Card with them as focus chips instead of
asking in chat. Ask in chat only when no card can express the choice (e.g.,
the notebook has no sources).
### 2. Handling "Start Over" & Card Abandonment
- If a Questionnaire Card or Review Card is currently pending/unsubmitted in
chat, and the user sends a message indicating they want to start over, try
again, or create a different video (e.g., "generate a new video", "start
over", "start again", "make another video", "new video", "let's try again",
"scratch that"):
- **Treat the previous card as ABANDONED.**
- **PURGE all previous selections**: Discard all prior format choices,
focus chips, topic titles, and style selections from the abandoned card.
**Never carry forward abandoned preferences.**
- **Evaluate the new request as fresh**:
- If the user provided a specific new topic (e.g., "start over and
make a video on photosynthesis"), gather context for that new topic
and present Step 0 or Step 1 for it.
- If the user did NOT provide a topic (e.g., just "generate a new
video", "start over"), the request is underspecified — **you MUST
present Step 0: Questionnaire Card**. Never skip Step 0 by recycling
the abandoned topic!
- **Never call `create_artifact`**: An abandoned card must never trigger
generation.
## Translation & Localization (CRITICAL)
All human-facing display strings across both QuestionnaireCard and
CoCreationReviewCard A2UI components MUST be translated into the user's active
device/conversation language (e.g., Spanish, French, German, Japanese, etc.).
### What MUST be translated into the user's active language:
- **Card Titles**: e.g., `"Let's set up your video"`, `"Video: <Topic>"`
- **Question Text & Subtitles**: e.g., `"What should the format be?"`, `"What
should the video focus on?"`, `"Select 1 or 2 topics for a sharper video"`
- **Option Labels & Descriptions**: e.g., `"Explainer"`, `"Comprehensive
overview that connects the dots"`, `"Short"`, `"Bite-sized overview to help
quickly grasp core ideas"`, `"Cinematic"`, `"Engaging, expressive content
that dives deep"`
- **Focus Chip Labels**: Dynamic and pre-selected focus topics
- **Review Notice Text**: Title, label, and expanded label (e.g., `"Review
producer notes"`, `"Review producer notes before final rendering"`, `"Refine
draft producer notes before final generation..."`)
- **Any other human-readable display strings** presented to the user in the
UI.
### What MUST NOT be translated (Preserve structural identifiers):
- Schema keys and property names (e.g., `surfaceId`, `catalogId`, `component`,
`id`, `icon`, `imageEnum`, `selectionType`, `subtitle`,
`subtitleVisibleOptions`, `options`, `questions`, `styleList`,
`selectedStyle`, `styleVisibleFormats`, `reviewNotice`)
- Structural IDs and enum values (e.g., `"root"`, `"QuestionnaireCard"`,
`"CoCreationReviewCard"`, `"explainer"`, `"short"`, `"cinematic"`,
`"crop_16_9"`, `"crop_9_16"`, `"movie"`, `"stylus_note_spark"`,
`"subscriptions"`, `"vo_styles"`, `"auto_select"`, `"en"`, `"es"`, `"fr"`,
`"de"`, `"ja"`, `"ko"`, `"pt"`, `"zh"`, etc.)
> **OVERRIDE NOTICE:** This Translation & Localization clause overrides any
> directive to copy text in quotes as-is. While structural identifiers, keys,
> IDs, icons, and enums must be preserved as-is, all human-readable display
> strings must be translated into the active device/conversation language.
## Step 0: Co-Creation Questionnaire Card (Conditional)
Decide using the **whole active journey**, not just the latest message. If the
user is answering a question you asked, read the answer together with their
original request.
After reading the journey, you know… | Next step
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------
Which angle, theme, historical arc, or section to cover (e.g., "bioluminescence in the deep sea", "how X changed over time", "chapter 3") | Step 1: Review Card
Only the broad notebook subject, or nothing yet (e.g., "make me a video") | Step 0: Questionnaire Card
- **At most one chat question per journey.** Once the user has answered it,
your next reply is a card.
- These cards are this skill's planning step. Don't also propose a plan in
chat.
- Introduce the card with one short sentence, without citations.
- Abandoned journeys don't count as context. See **Handling "Start Over"**.
### Requirements
Every field within the "focus" section **must** have a thoughtfully pre-selected
default based on your context gathering above.
#### Focus Chips Guidelines
- **Quantity**: Generate **3-5 distinct focus chips** (always generate at
least 3 chips) derived from source content. Having 3–5 options provides
users with a diverse range of angles to explore and prevents jamming
multiple topics into single chips. Pre-select 1–2 with the richest source
grounding.
- **Single Topic Per Chip (CRITICAL)**: Each focus chip MUST represent
strictly ONE coherent concept, angle, or theme. The topics chosen must be
the most compelling or representative of the source's content, with
sufficient substance to support a narrative without being too narrowly
focused.
- **NEVER combine or link multiple disparate topics into a single chip.**
- **Do NOT use '&', 'and', '+', '/', 'or', hyphens, or commas to join two
distinct concepts** (e.g., do NOT generate "Global Logistics & Equipment
Transport" or "Sustainability & Net Zero 2030"; split them into separate
chips like "Global logistics", "Equipment transport", "Sustainability
goals", "Net-zero by 2030"). Hyphenated words like "net-zero" are fine.
- If source material covers multiple related areas, create separate,
distinct chips for each individual topic.
- **Succinct Phrasing**: Keep chips concise and human-digestible: **3 to 6
words**, ideally 4 to 6, on a single continuous line. Ensure suggestions are
expressive and compelling (e.g., "How noise cancelling works", "Why ice is
slippery", "Physics behind ski edges", "Tesla's rivalry with Edison", "5
moments from Google I/O") rather than overly terse or dry topic labels
(avoid clipped labels like "Economic impact"). Avoid introductory articles
("The ..."), filler words, or wordy academic phrasing (prefer "Physics
behind ski edges" over "The Physics Behind Contemporary Ski Edges").
- **Prompt Formatting**: Each focus chip's label MUST follow a clear sentence
pattern:
- `'How [subject] [verb]'` (e.g., `'How noise cancelling works'`)
- `'Why [surprising claim]'` (e.g., `'Why ice is slippery'`)
- `'[Noun phrase] of/behind [subject]'` (e.g., `'Physics behind ski
edges'`)
- Descriptive noun phrase (e.g., `'Knit and purl basics'`, `'Street
circuit dynamics'`)
- `'[Subject]'s [dramatic noun phrase]'` (e.g., `"Tesla's rivalry with
Edison"`)
- `'[Number] [things] from [source]'` (e.g., `'5 moments from Google
I/O'`)
- Use sentence case (capitalize only the first word and proper nouns).
- Use concrete nouns and active verbs — name the specific subject, not a
category.
#### Focus Chips Negative Constraints
- **Do NOT combine multiple topics into a single chip** (no '&', 'and', '+',
'/', 'or', hyphens, or commas joining distinct concepts). Hyphenated words
like "net-zero" are fine.
- **Do NOT exceed 6 words per chip.** Keep chips concise and expressive (4–6
words preferred).
- **Do NOT start suggestions with imperative verbs** like Explain, Describe,
Create, Generate, or Summarize. Frame the suggestion as a noun phrase or
question-form topic (e.g., 'How X works' rather than 'Explain X'). The
prompt should read as a topic label, not a command.
- **Do NOT use colons or multi-clause sentences.**
- **Do NOT use multi-line formatting**, newlines, bullet points, or numbered
lists. Each suggestion must be a single continuous line of text.
- **Use numerals and symbols** instead of spelling out numbers and units
(e.g., '18%' not 'eighteen percent', '$5M' not 'five million dollars', '3x'
not 'three times') to keep suggestions compact.
### Questionnaire Card A2UI Structure
Every `<...>` field must be populated using context. For fields WITHOUT `<...>`,
preserve structural identifiers (`id`, `icon`, `selectionType`,
`subtitleVisibleOptions`) exactly as defined, but translate human-visible
display strings (`title`, `text`, `subtitle`, `label`, `description`) into the
active device/conversation language per the **Translation & Localization**
clause.
```json
[
{
"version": "v0.9",
"createSurface": {
"surfaceId": "<unique-surface-id>",
"catalogId": "notebooklm:nlm_v1"
}
},
{
"version": "v0.9",
"updateComponents": {
"surfaceId": "<unique-surface-id>",
"components": [
{
"id": "root",
"component": "QuestionnaireCard",
"title": "Let's set up your video",
"questions": [
{
"id": "format",
"icon": "movie",
"text": "What should the format be?",
"selectionType": "single",
"options": [
{
"id": "explainer",
"label": "Explainer",
"icon": "crop_16_9",
"selected": true,
"description": "Comprehensive overview that connects the dots"
},
{
"id": "short",
"label": "Short",
"icon": "crop_9_16",
"description": "Bite-sized overview to help quickly grasp core ideas"
},
{
"id": "cinematic",
"label": "Cinematic",
"icon": "crop_16_9",
"description": "Engaging, expressive content that dives deep"
}
]
},
{
"id": "focus",
"icon": "stylus_note_spark",
"text": "What should the video focus on?",
"subtitle": "Select 1 or 2 topics for a sharper video",
"subtitleVisibleOptions": ["short"],
"selectionType": "multi",
"options": [
{
"id": "focus-1",
"label": "<topic 1 from sources>",
"selected": true
},
{
"id": "focus-2",
"label": "<topic 2 from sources>",
"selected": true
},
{
"id": "focus-3",
"label": "<topic 3 from sources>"
},
{
"id": "focus-4",
"label": "<topic 4 from sources>"
},
{
"id": "focus-5",
"label": "<topic 5 from sources>"
}
]
}
]
}
]
}
}
]
```
Wait for the user's response before proceeding.
## Step 1: Co-Creation Review Card
Present a **Co-Creation Review Card** summarizing everything before dispatching
a video generation. This gives the user a final chance to confirm or tweak
before generation begins.
### Step 0 → Step 1 Transition (if applicable)
A Questionnaire Card submission ends with a hidden
`<!-- a2ui-submitted: {...} -->` tag. Route on its `action` field — not on the
visible sentence, which is localized (if `action` is absent, treat `"surprise":
true` as Skip planning):
- `"questionnaireCardSurprise"` (**Skip planning**): skip Step 1 and dispatch
now with `enable_planning="false"`, mapping the tag's `format`/`focus` per
the Step 2 parameter table and filling the rest from context.
- `"questionnaireCardSubmit"` (**Continue**): build the Review Card. The tag
lists only what the user **chose**; derive the rest from the Questionnaire
Card you emitted earlier in the conversation: any chip you offered that is
absent from the submission was **deselected**, and any submitted chip you
did not offer was **typed by the user**. **You MUST carry these forward** as
defaults in the Review Card:
- Set `selected: true` on the matching `format.options` entry.
- Synthesize `focusDescription` **only** from the selected focus chips. The
selected chips define the subject; source material may supply supporting
sub-points *within* that subject, but must never introduce an additional
subject.
> [!IMPORTANT]
>
> If the user came from Step 0 and already chose a format or focus areas, those
> selections **must** be reflected as defaults in the Review Card. The user
> should not have to re-select anything they already chose.
### Accompanying Turn Message (Chat)
When presenting the Co-Creation Review Card:
- Provide brief context on what is happening during this turn (e.g., "I've set
up a review card for you to confirm your final options before kicking off
generating your video.").
- **Do NOT explain a lengthy narrative arc, outline, or scene breakdown in the
chat.** Keep your accompanying chat message to 1–2 concise, friendly
sentences.
### Dynamic Field Population Rules
Every `<...>` field must be populated using context. For fields WITHOUT `<...>`,
preserve structural identifiers (`id`, `imageEnum`, `styleList`) exactly as
defined, but translate human-visible display strings (`title`, `text`, `label`,
`description`) into the active device/conversation language per the
**Translation & Localization** clause.
Field | How to Populate
------------------- | ---------------
`title` | Format: `"Video: <Topic>"`. Derive the topic from: (1) the user's last message (highest priority), (2) Step 0 focus selections, (3) source material's main theme. Keep it concise — 3–6 words. Avoid generic titles like "Video: Overview".
`format.selected` | Set `selected: true` on the option that matches: (1) the user's Step 0 selection, (2) explicit mention in conversation (e.g., "short video"), (3) default to `"explainer"` only if no signal exists.
`language.selected` | Set `selected: true` on the option that matches: (1) the user's explicit language preference (e.g., "make it in Spanish"), (2) the dominant language of the source material, (3) default to `"en"` (English) if no signal exists.
`style.selected` | Set `selectedStyle` to the style ID that best matches the content's tone. Available IDs: `"auto_select"` (default/general), `"classic"` (scientific/technical/professional), `"whiteboard"` (educational/instructional), `"watercolor"` (nature/atmospheric/artistic), `"retro_print"` (vintage/historical/editorial), `"heritage"` (cultural/traditional), `"papercraft"` (playful/crafty/DIY), `"anime"` (pop culture/entertainment/dynamic), `"kawaii"` (cute/lighthearted/fun).
`focusDescription` | A 1–3 sentence natural-language brief. This is the **most important** dynamic field — it becomes the `video_focus` parameter in dispatch. Compose by: (1) state the core topic/angle from the **selected** Step 0 chips or user message, (2) reference key outline points if the user refined one. Never widen the scope to other source themes, and never mention a chip the user deselected. Write in direct, active voice. **Be specific** — no generic filler like "exploring the key themes." **DO NOT include citations or source brackets (e.g. [1])** — focus text must be pure natural language.
### Co-Creation Review Card A2UI Structure
```json
[
{
"version": "v0.9",
"createSurface": {
"surfaceId": "<unique-surface-id>",
"catalogId": "notebooklm:nlm_v1"
}
},
{
"version": "v0.9",
"updateComponents": {
"surfaceId": "<unique-surface-id>",
"components": [
{
"id": "root",
"component": "CoCreationReviewCard",
"title": "<Video: Topic Title>",
"titleIcon": "subscriptions",
"format": {
"icon": "movie",
"options": [
{
"id": "explainer",
"label": "Explainer",
"imageEnum": "crop_16_9",
"selected": "<true if matches user intent, false otherwise>",
"description": "Landscape ⋅ Comprehensive overview that connects the dots"
},
{
"id": "short",
"label": "Short",
"imageEnum": "crop_9_16",
"description": "Portrait ⋅ Bite-sized overview to help quickly grasp core ideas"
},
{
"id": "cinematic",
"label": "Cinematic",
"imageEnum": "crop_16_9",
"description": "Landscape ⋅ Engaging, expressive content that dives deep (English only)"
}
]
},
"language": {
"options": [
{ "id": "en", "label": "English", "selected": "<true if matches>" },
{ "id": "es", "label": "Spanish" },
{ "id": "fr", "label": "French" },
{ "id": "de", "label": "German" },
{ "id": "ja", "label": "Japanese" },
{ "id": "ko", "label": "Korean" },
{ "id": "pt", "label": "Portuguese" },
{ "id": "zh", "label": "Chinese" }
]
},
"styleList": "vo_styles",
"selectedStyle": "<style ID that best matches content tone>",
"styleVisibleFormats": ["explainer"],
"focusDescription": "<1–3 sentence brief: the user's selected angle + outline points if the user refined one. Be specific to the actual source content; never add topics the user deselected.>",
"reviewNotice": {
"title": "Review producer notes",
"label": "Review producer notes before final rendering",
"labelExpanded": "Refine draft producer notes before final generation. The notes will show up in studio for your review in a few minutes."
}
}
]
}
}
]
```
**STOP and WAIT** for the user's response. When the user submits the Review
Card, proceed immediately to Step 2 (Dispatch).
## Step 2: Dispatch
You can proceed to dispatch (`create_artifact`) in any of three ways:
1. **Review Card Submission (Primary)**: The user submits the Review Card,
transmitting a message containing their selections (`format`, `language`,
`style`, `focusText`, and whether review mode is enabled).
2. **Skip Planning from Step 0** (`"action":"questionnaireCardSurprise"`):
dispatch immediately with `enable_planning="false"`; map `format`/`focus`
per the table below and derive `title`, `language_code`, and
`video_overview_style` from context.
3. **Explicit Chat Confirmation**: The user sends a conversational message
explicitly confirming the pending card's settings (e.g., "looks good, go
ahead", "make the video", "proceed with these defaults"). In this case, use
the values shown in the pending Review Card.
A start-over or new-topic message is never a confirmation (see **Handling "Start
Over"**). If the user asks for changes ("make it shorter"), update and re-show
the Review Card instead.
> [!CAUTION]
>
> **CARD SUBMISSION LANGUAGE MODIFIER (`in <lang>`):** When the user submits the
> Review Card, the incoming message generated by the UI contains `Generate me
> <format>, in <lang>, ...` (e.g., `Generate me explainer, in ja, in auto select
> style, focused on...`).
>
> - The token `in <lang>` (e.g., `in ja`, `in es`, `in fr`) specifies ONLY the
> artifact's generation language for `create_artifact(...,
> language_code="<lang>", ...)`.
> - It is **NOT** an instruction for you to chat or respond in that language!
> - You **MUST NEVER** reply in Japanese, Spanish, French, German, or any
> other artifact language just because `in <lang>` appears in the user turn
> or card submission text.
> - Your accompanying chat turn message MUST ALWAYS remain in the user's
> conversational language (e.g., English).
### Card Selections → `create_artifact` Parameter Mapping
Card Source | Selection Field | `create_artifact` Parameter | Mapping
--------------- | --------------- | --------------------------- | -------
**Review Card** | `format` | `template_format` | `"explainer"` → `"explainer"`, `"short"` → `"short"`, `"cinematic"` → `"cinematic"`
**Review Card** | `language` | `language_code` | Pass the language `id` directly (e.g., `"en"`, `"es"`, `"ja"`). Note: Cinematic format only supports English (`"en"`).
**Review Card** | `style` | `video_overview_style` | **Explainer format ONLY.** Pass the selected style ID directly (e.g., `"retro_print"`). Omit if `"auto_select"`. Do NOT pass for `"cinematic"` or `"short"`.
**Review Card** | `focusText` | `video_focus` | Pass `focusText` **verbatim**. If the user approved an outline in chat, append it under "Approved outline:". Do NOT add source themes, chip context, prior artifacts' customizations, or text from an earlier card draft.
**Review Card** | `reviewMode` | `enable_planning` | **REQUIRED.** Set `"true"` if review mode is enabled (default), or `"false"` if disabled.
### Common Parameters (all formats)
- **`artifact_type`** (string, required) — Must be
`"ARTIFACT_TYPE_VIDEO_OVERVIEW"` (or `"ARTIFACT_TYPE_EXPLAINER_VIDEO"`).
- **`template_format`** (string, required) — Must match the user's selected
format from the Review Card.
- **`title`** (string, optional) — A title for the video artifact.
- **`video_focus`** (string, required) — The Review Card's `focusText`
**verbatim** (the user's words, unchanged — including anything they typed,
and excluding anything they deleted). If the user explicitly approved an
outline in chat, append it after the focus text under "Approved outline:".
Nothing else — no added topics, tone, or audience guesses.
- **`language_code`** (string, optional) — BCP-47 language code (e.g., `"en"`,
`"es"`, `"ja"`) if specified. Note: Cinematic Video Overviews can only be
created in English.
- **`enable_planning`** (boolean, REQUIRED) — Set to `"true"` if review mode
is enabled (default), or `"false"` if disabled.
### Format Mapping
Set `template_format` to the lowercase format ID from the Review Card:
`"explainer"`, `"short"`, or `"cinematic"`.
### Style (Explainer only)
When `template_format` is `"explainer"`, pass the user's selected style ID
directly as **`video_overview_style`**. If the style is `"auto_select"`, omit
the parameter entirely to let the pipeline choose.
> [!CAUTION]
>
> Do **NOT** pass `video_overview_style` or `style_prompt` for `"cinematic"` or
> `"short"` formats — they do not support style selection.
### Example dispatch — Explainer format:
```
create_artifact(
artifact_type="ARTIFACT_TYPE_VIDEO_OVERVIEW",
template_format="explainer",
video_overview_style="retro_print",
title="Formula 1: 75 Years",
video_focus="A chronological and analytical overview of Formula 1's
75-year history. Traces the journey from the 1950 inaugural season's
'Core Four' circuits, through global expansion and the evolution of
street tracks, to technical milestones like aerodynamics, hybrid
engines, and the modern Netflix-fueled digital era.",
language_code="en",
enable_planning="true"
)
```
### Example dispatch — Cinematic format:
Given focusText=`"Cinematic breakdown for marine biology students. Dark,
atmospheric, documentary visual feel. Focus on bioluminescence and hydrothermal
vents with emphasis on chemosynthesis."` and an outline the user approved
earlier in chat (the first paragraph of `video_focus` is the focusText verbatim;
the outline is appended only because the user approved it):
```
create_artifact(
artifact_type="ARTIFACT_TYPE_VIDEO_OVERVIEW",
template_format="cinematic",
title="Deep Sea Ecosystems",
video_focus="Cinematic breakdown for marine biology students.
Dark, atmospheric, documentary visual feel. Focus on
bioluminescence and hydrothermal vents with emphasis on
chemosynthesis.
Approved outline:
1. Descends into the vast darkness of the deep ocean
2. Reveals bioluminescence as nature's hidden light show
3. Explores hydrothermal vent ecosystems and chemosynthesis
4. Contrasts deep sea adaptations with surface life strategies
5. Synthesizes the interconnected web of abyssal ecology",
language_code="en",
enable_planning="false"
)
```
### Accompanying Turn Message (After Dispatch)
When kicking off `create_artifact()` after the user confirms the Review Card:
- Explain that you have taken their preferences and kicked off generation of
the video.
- **If the user selected/enabled review mode (`enable_planning="true"`)**:
explicitly instruct the user to look to the studio panel on the side to edit
or confirm their producer notes mid-generation.
- **If review mode is disabled (`enable_planning="false"`)**: let the user
know their video is being generated and will appear in the studio panel once
ready.
- Keep your accompanying message concise (1–2 sentences) — do NOT dump a
scene-by-scene script or narrative outline in chat.
- **Conversational Language Consistency (CRITICAL)**: The accompanying chat
turn message **MUST always match the user's conversational language** (e.g.,
if the user interacted in English, respond in English). **Do NOT switch your
chat message language to the artifact target language** selected by the user
in the card (e.g., if the user chose Spanish, Japanese, French, or German
for the video artifact, the chat message must remain in the user's
conversational language).
- **Incoming `in <lang>` does NOT change chat language**: Even if the incoming
card submission message says `Generate me explainer, in ja, in auto select
style...`, this ONLY instructs the tool parameter `language_code="ja"`. You
**MUST NOT** write your chat response in Japanese! Write your chat response
in English (or whatever language the user spoke in conversation).
#### Example: Dispatching with non-English artifact language
**User message (from Review Card submission)**: `Generate me explainer, in ja,
in auto select style, focused on the following: An in-depth explainer examining
how Formula 1 coordinates air, sea, and land cargo transport across a 24-race
global calendar while analyzing the true economic impact of mega-events.`
**Tool call**:
```
create_artifact(
artifact_type="ARTIFACT_TYPE_VIDEO_OVERVIEW",
template_format="explainer",
title="F1 Logistics & Economic Impact",
video_focus="An in-depth explainer examining how Formula 1 coordinates air, sea, and land cargo transport across a 24-race global calendar while analyzing the true economic impact of mega-events.",
language_code="ja",
enable_planning="false"
)
```
**Accompanying Chat Output (MUST remain in user's conversational language, e.g.
English)**: "I've started generating your explainer video in Japanese. It will
appear in the studio panel on the right once it's ready!"
*(CRITICAL: Notice the chat output is in English, NOT Japanese, even though `in
ja` appeared in the card prompt and `language_code="ja"` was passed to
`create_artifact`.)*
**After calling the `create_artifact` tool, your work is done.** The server-side
pipeline handles all video creation — including video format selection, art
direction style selection, storyboard, script, image/video generation, TTS, and
post-production. Do NOT attempt to generate video content yourself.
## General Style & Compliance
- **No Citations in Focus Text**: Do NOT insert any source citations,
footnotes, or bracketed numbers (e.g., `[1]`, `[2]`, `[source]`) within
`focusDescription`, `focusChips`, or `video_focus`. Focus text must remain
clean, flowing natural language.
- **Concise Chat Responses**: Do NOT output verbose narrative arcs, scene
breakdowns, or script dumps in the chat before or after presenting cards.
Let the card and the studio panel hold the structured details.
- **Eliminate "AI Slop"**: Avoid generic corporate jargon and AI clichés
(e.g., "unlocking potential," "tapestry," "delve," "journey of discovery").
Use direct, high-signal language.
- **No LaTeX Formatting**: Render all mathematical symbols as standard text.
- **Verb-First Scene Labels**: Every scene label must begin with a strong,
present-tense action verb.
- **Strict Brevity**: Scene labels must not exceed **13 words**.
- **No Static Numbering**: Do not prefix labels with "Scene 1," etc.
- **Logical Progression**: Ensure the video follows a compelling narrative
arc: *Hook* → *Context* → *Core* → *Evidence* → *Synthesis* → *Resolution*.

items.title: OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 20, 2026
Company
OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio
AI-powered drug development platform accelerates progress toward new treatments.
OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio⁠(opens in a new window), a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development. We’re bringing Orchestra’s team and technology together with Rosalind, our AI models and tools for life sciences research. Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner.
Developing a new medicine is extraordinarily complex, taking roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery to regulatory approval in the United States. Beyond the science, teams must orchestrate programs across internal departments and external partners, often relying on disconnected systems. We’re now at an inflection point where AI can help take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows.
Bringing Rosalind and Orchestra together
Rosalind brings our AI models and tools to life sciences researchers. GPT‑Rosalind helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry. Rosalind Workbench⁠ connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data to help researchers analyze results and plan experiments.
Orchestra brings a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. Together, we aim to build agents that help teams connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine.
Designed for the way biopharma teams work
Orchestra Bio is a platform where people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders delegate the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, freeing up time to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays.
A problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others. A failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents help teams identify which activities and timelines are affected, gather the relevant information, and compare ways to respond. Scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next.
Realizing the potential of AI in life sciences requires close collaboration with the organizations working at the forefront of drug discovery and development. Our partnership with Novo Nordisk⁠ aims to translate its scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance. At Moderna⁠, AI is helping teams translate insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D.
Our vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines: exploring ideas, designing experiments, interpreting results, and coordinating the work needed to advance promising treatments. Bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind is a step toward that vision. Alongside researchers and our partners, we aim to make more discoveries possible and help new medicines reach patients sooner.

items.title: SWE-bench Multimodal v2 is not multimodal
items.summary:
Contents Intro Methodology SWE Multimodal v2 Benchmark details Experiment details Removing Git history GPT-6 Luna xhigh runs Sample trace Sonnet 5.5 max runs Results GPT-6 Luna xhigh (480 tasks) Sonnet 5.5 max (60-task subset) Why did removing images make so little difference? Images were rarely required The hidden tests don't check what the images show The models may already know some fixes Example tasks where images were not needed MMMU-Pro as a control GPT-6 Luna xhigh (1730 questions) Sonnet 5.5 max (120 questions) Conclusion Acknowledgements Intro I was using SWE-bench Multimodal v2 to establish baselines for a project at the Prime Intellect residency. I found out that GPT-6 Luna (xhigh) performed similarly on the benchmark whether I used normal images or OCR-based output or no images at all. This felt unexpected for a multimodal benchmark. I wondered: does this mean the images are optional? After looking into the data, we found that most of the information the models needed was already in the issue text or derivable from the code. I also ran Sonnet 5.5 on a subset to check whether this was specific to Luna. Its score barely changed when I removed the images. In short, Removing the images barely changes the score, for both Luna and Sonnet Most tasks can be solved from the issue text and the code alone, since the images mostly repeat what the text already says The hidden tests rarely check details found only in the images, like the colours or spacing in a design spec, which helps explain why removing images barely affects the score What changes when the images disappear? with imagesno imageschange, points SWE-bench Multimodal v2 · resolved GPT-6 Luna xhigh 480 tasks 36.9% 37.1% +0.2 Sonnet 5.5 max 60 tasks 35.0% 40.0% +5.0 MMMU-Pro · accuracy GPT-6 Luna xhigh 1,730 questions 79.7% 36.9% −42.8 Sonnet 5.5 max 120 questions 80.8% 44.2% −36.6 Scores barely move on SWE-bench Multimodal, while accuracy falls sharply on MMMU-Pro. Each pair uses the same tasks within that experiment. Vals AI released a SWE-bench Multimodal v2 leaderboard on October 14, so this felt like a good time to write this blog up and share our findings. Methodology SWE Multimodal v2 Benchmark details The benchmark has 480 tasks built from GitHub issues in 11 JavaScript repos (Carbon alone accounts for 133), most with screenshots. 39 of the 480 have no image in the issue text at all. It's worth noting that even these tasks can involve images, since the agent may take screenshots to check its work or open image files already in the repo. Most tasks are small fixes to UI components, map rendering, syntax highlighting or Lighthouse audits, things like a missing aria-label, a misaligned icon or a keyword highlighted in the wrong colour. They are fairly focused and short horizon. Luna xhigh spent a median of 5.5 minutes on each. Vals AI reports 5min 14 sec median time for Luna and 24m+ for Sonnet 5.5 at max reasoning. I find it interesting that this benchmark is not saturated given the nature of tasks. Tasks per repo (click to expand) RepoTasks carbon-design-system/carbon133 openlayers/openlayers77 GoogleChrome/lighthouse54 bpmn-io/bpmn-js53 highlightjs/highlight.js39 PrismJS/prism38 alibaba-fusion/next36 grommet/grommet20 prettier/prettier13 eslint/eslint11 scratchfoundation/scratch-gui6 Experiment details I evaluated two models on SWE-bench Multimodal v2 and MMMU-Pro: Model SWE-bench Multimodal v2 MMMU-Pro Input conditions GPT-6 Luna (xhigh) All 480 tasks All 1,730 questions Images, OCR, no images Sonnet 5.5 (max) 60-task subset 120-question subset Images, no images For SWE-bench Multimodal, rollouts ran with full network isolation, and grading took place in a separate sandbox. Issue images were downloaded beforehand so they could be provided without network access. Removing Git history In the traces of an initial run, we caught agents: Searching Git history for commits associated with the reported issue or an upstream fix. Inspecting later commits and their diffs to retrieve the implementation that fixed the issue. Incorporating code from those upstream fixes into their submitted patches. As you can see, sometimes the agents take 'learn from the codebase' too literally. This is a known SWE-bench reward hack, documented about a year ago, and we were surprised to still see this in the benchmark images. Checking out an older commit takes the files back in time, but it doesn't erase newer commits from .git. So the agent may start with the buggy code while the actual upstream fix is still sitting in the same repository. It can go on an archaeological expedition through Git refs or stored objects, find the fix, and copy it instead of solving the issue. To prevent this, we rebuilt the benchmark images to keep only the task's base commit and the objects needed to reconstruct its files. We then copied the cleaned filesystem into a fresh image so the removed history couldn't survive in older image layers. GPT-6 Luna xhigh runs I was using GPT-6 Luna xhigh for ablations. There were three full runs on all 480 tasks, one per condition, on verifiers with the Codex harness. The three conditions were native image input, a custom OCR-based representation of each image and no images mode. This is possible to do in verifiers because of the interception server. It sits between the harness and the model API, letting us rewrite messages before the model sees them. I used it to replace images in both user messages and tool outputs with OCR text or placeholders. In OCR mode, each image is replaced by the text that OCR reads from it, with every word placed on a character grid at its position in the image and tagged with its colour. A header gives the image size and main colours, and a short list underneath describes shapes that are not text, such as icons, outlines and lines. The interceptor rewrites every image in each model request, in the issue and in tool outputs alike, before it reaches the model. Sample trace Issue message of task lighthouse-4036, which has 2 screenshots, as the model received it in each of the three modes. Swipe or scroll sideways, or jump to with images · with OCR · no images With images1 / 3 → With OCR← 2 / 3 → No images← 3 / 3 Full trace in the no images mode. The full trace (click to expand) · resolved · 5 model calls · 7 commands · 60 s Upstream PR imagesThe 2 issue images the model never saw thinkingModifying repository for user request I need to modify the repository and inspect it further. The user mentioned that the rel=noopener audit should ignore mailto links, which seems to be related to a request issue. I should identify the specific project involved. items.title: Terminal X matches senior investor judgment 88.6% with GPT-6.1
items.summary:

Terminal X matches senior investor judgment 88.6% with GPT‑6.1
Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades outputs against a 54-criterion rubric, catching 25% more deviances from a fund’s mandate with GPT‑6.1 Sol.

An investment firm’s edge is built deal by deal, but the judgment behind each decision usually lives in the heads of a few senior investors. When they leave, the firm takes on what Terminal X⁠(opens in a new window) calls memory debt: the firm may keep the documents, but it loses the reasoning.
Terminal X’s Capital Memory operating system is designed to pay that debt down. The company’s forward-deployed engineers, former finance and investment professionals at JPMorgan and Blackstone, sit with each customer’s investment teams, design the firm’s agentic architecture, and encode how the firm invests into agents the firm owns, deployed on-premise or in its own cloud.
OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna, handle the reasoning inside those agents. And Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades the agents’ output against the firm’s standards. GPT‑6.1 Sol helped the Eval Agent catch about 25% more recommendations that strayed from a fund’s mandate and ran the same workflows at approximately 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model.
“GPT-6.1 Sol’s long-context reasoning and token efficiency allow us to build deeper evaluation pipelines. This helps our Eval Agents make investment judgment measurable and auditable.”
—Hyun Hong, Co-founder and CEO, Terminal X
Encoding the reasoning of each firm’s best investors
For each customer, Terminal X builds agents designed to invest the way the firm’s best investors do. Terminal X engineers spend weeks onsite with the customer, reverse-engineering the firm’s trusted memos and capturing processes that were never written down, such as how the credit desk screens a borrower or which sources the co-investment team pulls before a memo.
Next, those processes are encoded in hundreds of agents, customized by asset class and strategy, with sub-agents for each investment stage. GPT‑6.1 Sol handles the stages that require judgment and a huge context window: synthesizing the investment thesis, identifying key considerations, and assessing fit with the firm’s mandate. GPT‑6 Luna runs the high-volume steps where token efficiency matters more than depth.
The agents work inside each firm’s private data room, a dedicated environment for enterprises to share and manage sensitive investment data. The agents process documents in English, Korean, Japanese, and Chinese, and store what they learn as a firm Memory: a versioned record of how one desk makes one kind of decision, including its past analyses, committee decisions, workflow instructions, and house views.
Engineers turn each Memory into a repeatable workflow on Terminal X’s platform, where every production query is auditable with its full trail: the steps taken, sources retrieved, model used, and the reasoning.
According to Terminal X, customers see significant savings as a result of this approach, including one private equity firm that reported $2.4 million in annualized savings from automated due diligence and investment memo workflows.
Scoring answers with an Eval Agent and improving the system
To check agents’ answers against the firm’s own standard, Terminal X built an Eval Agent. It’s an orchestrated workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol and other OpenAI models designed to read every agent output the way a VP reads an analyst’s work.
The Eval Agent checks each output against a 54-criterion rubric. It asks: Are the numbers, comps, consensus figures, and quotes pulled from the right sources? Does the narrative hold? Does the recommendation tie to the house view?
Each check scores pass or fail. Every fail includes a one-line reason and a better source or corrected text and becomes a Memory. For example, a missed source, a wrong comparable, or a thesis that drifts from the house view is encoded as a new workflow instruction or a new test case for that desk.
“Every answer gets eval’d, and whatever the analyst corrects teaches the system a little more about how that firm works,” says Ken Lee, Co-Founder and CTO of Terminal X. “So the longer a firm uses it, the more it thinks like their own team.”
Testing every model, choosing by task
Terminal X picks models based on its own evaluation results. Across 500 scored judgments, its Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol agreed with the senior human reviewer 88.6% of the time, vs. 86.4% for the next-best model, an improvement of 220 basis points.
One class of error where GPT‑6.1 Sol outperformed is style drift. For example, a buyout fund’s mandate is to find take-private candidates trading at a discount to NAV, underwrite the business, and structure the financing. When scenario models suggest a market turn, deals start recommending a distressed credit position or a rescue financing. The Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol caught about 25% more of these departures than the next-best model did.
GPT‑6.1 Sol’s token efficiency on long-context work enabled Terminal X to build a deeper review workflow within the same budget. The thesis is tested first against the fund’s mandate, then against its recent deals. Uncertain verdicts are re-run, and the agent reconciles the results before reporting.
That deeper review flagged deals that a single pass on a comparable model had waved through. GPT‑6.1 Sol also ran the same workflows at about 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model, at similar speed.
Moving toward a Memory for every investor
Using GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna, Terminal X has built 1,700 firm Memories, run more than 1 million custom workflows, and reached a weekly active user count equal to 81% of its monthly active users.
Terminal X’s next step is to extend firm Memories from desks to individuals, so that each investment professional’s standard is captured as it is practiced, not only as it is described.
For Hyun, co-founder and CEO of Terminal X, that is the point: “The firms that win the next decade will own their judgment as data. Our job is to make that judgment measurable, so it can be kept, improved, and reused.”

items.title: A smarter approach to AI cost controls: allocating spend by efficiency
items.summary:
Blanket usage caps are akin to a hiring freeze in the AI era.
Many enterprises have turned to uniform caps to control AI spend, but they are blunt instruments that limit productivity. They hold back the engineers who are the most efficient users of AI. And engineers who use AI less effectively don’t get feedback on what to change.
The better approach is to allocate spend based on engineering efficiency and give less efficient engineers precise suggestions on how to improve.
This has historically been hard to manually scale. So, today we’re introducing three enterprise features to help:
Efficiency Score grades how efficiently each engineer uses Devin. For each session, including investigations and planning that never produce a PR, Devin estimates the associated productive engineering hours, meaning how long a human engineer would have needed for the same work. The grade reflects the productive hours an engineer gets per unit of spend across recent sessions, with a smaller credit for volume.
Devin Coach gives engineers feedback on a prompt before it runs. It flags common mistakes, such as a vague request, an expensive mode for a simple task, or unrelated tasks in one session, and suggests a fix.
Efficiency-based approvals raise limits automatically for efficient engineers. This enables more precise cost controls without ballooning admins’ review burden. When an engineer with a Healthy or Satisfactory grade nears their limit, Devin raises it automatically, up to a ceiling the admin sets. Other engineers’ requests are sent to an admin for review.
Devin’s intelligent cost controls have helped us keep a lid on runaway agent spend. Efficiency-based auto-approval has really eased the burden on our admins. Our power users get more usage without having to ask, and when someone’s usage isn’t paying off, we find out and can have a conversation with them. Devin Coach has made it easier to scale training users to be more efficient.
Giving each engineer an Efficiency Score
To set granular limits, you need to know how much each engineer gets out of Devin relative to what they spend. The Efficiency Score is a 0–100 rating of each engineer’s recent Devin usage. It is calculated from recent Devin sessions in three parts: Devin identifies the sessions that produced useful work, estimates the engineering hours that work represents, and converts those hours into efficiency and volume ratings that combine into the score.
Recognizing work that doesn’t produce a merged PR
Many organizations measure AI output with merged PRs. The limitation of that approach is that a lot of useful work never produces a merged PR, such as planning, triage, data analysis, and investigations. The Efficiency Score thus builds on “productive engineering hours,” the metric we introduced earlier this year to estimate the value of Devin sessions.
First, Devin checks whether each session produced useful work. For a session with a PR, that means the PR was merged. For a session without one, a classifier judges whether Devin made real progress on the task, like triaging the bug or answering the analytics question. That way, a bug investigation gets credit even though it never produces a PR.
Second, for every session that passes, it estimates how many hours the same work would have taken a human engineer.
We validated these estimates against a dataset of engineers’ own assessments of the equivalent engineering hours from their Devin sessions.
Combining efficiency and volume into a score
At Cognition, we calculate spend via Agent Compute Units (ACUs), which combine LLM and cloud infrastructure cost into one unit of measure. The score looks at an engineer’s productivity in two ways:
Efficiency (E) is productive hours per ACU. It shows whether spend turns into productive work. An engineer who writes clear prompts, picks well-scoped tasks, and uses the right model gets more productive hours from each ACU.
Volume (V) is productive hours per day. It shows how much productive work the engineer delivers overall, regardless of cost.
We weigh efficiency more heavily, since the goal is to give more capacity to engineers who get the most out of each ACU. Volume earns points because we also want to credit how much productive work an engineer delivers.
Each measure is first converted to a rating between 0 and 1 that levels off at high values. The two ratings then combine into the score:
Score=100×(E+λV(1−E)),where λ=0.2
An engineer’s efficiency rating sets their starting score: a rating of 0.50 starts at 50. Volume can then add up to a fifth of the points left between that starting score and 100. An engineer starting at 50 can gain up to 10 points from volume, and one starting at 80 can gain up to 4.
For example, here are four engineers based on their most recent 200 ACUs.
E (efficiency)V (volume)Score
Typical engineer0.50 (Medium)0.50 (Medium)100 × (0.50 + 0.2 × 0.50 × 0.50) = 55
Power user0.50 (Medium)0.95 (High)100 × (0.50 + 0.2 × 0.95 × 0.50) = 60
Heavy but wasteful0.27 (Low)0.95 (High)100 × (0.27 + 0.2 × 0.95 × 0.73) = 41
Careful, low volume0.75 (High)0.17 (Low)100 × (0.75 + 0.2 × 0.17 × 0.25) = 76
The power user and the typical engineer are equally efficient, but the power user’s higher volume earns them 5 more points. The heavy but wasteful engineer matches the power user’s volume, but low efficiency puts them nearly 20 points lower.
Giving engineers a path to improve
The score reflects recent usage rather than a lifetime average, so early sessions don’t count against engineers indefinitely. Better task selection, planning, and model choices improve future scores.
Engineers can see their score in My Analytics, under Session efficiency, as one of four grades: Healthy, Satisfactory, Needs Improvement, or Unknown when there isn’t enough data. Supporting metrics help explain the score: merged PRs per day, ACUs per merged PR, sessions with delivered outcomes, and consumption by session size.
Guiding engineers before they spend with Devin Coach
We’ve found that new users tend to run into the same few issues: prompts too general to accomplish a concrete task, defaulting to the most expensive model, or combining several unrelated tasks in one session. Because these patterns are so consistent, we saw an opportunity to productize training. Devin Coach gives engineers feedback on their prompts before they run, so they can build better habits over time without requiring a series of training sessions.
Example: no plan before implementation
Suppose the user writes, “Rewrite our billing system to support usage-based pricing.” The main problem with such a prompt is that it leaves major design decisions open. Devin Coach suggests making a plan first. This allows the engineer to correct wrong assumptions before spend goes into an implementation.
DevinAgentAsk
FastConsider asking Devin for a plan before implementingCreate plan
Example: using an overpowered model for the task
Another example: for simple tasks such as changing a button label, Devin Coach may suggest “Switch mode” to replace Ultra, the highest-powered and most expensive choice, with the default mode. As smaller models have improved, they are a more efficient choice for many tasks.
Example requestSuggestion typeExample suggestion
A billing-export session receives an unrelated request for a dark-mode toggle.Unrelated follow-upStart a new session to keep unrelated history out of the session’s context.
One prompt combines unrelated tasks, such as a pricing-page link fix and an iOS startup crash.Parallelizable tasksSplit into child sessions to shorten completion time.
A request is clearly personal, such as planning a vacation.Non-work usageDon’t submit this prompt, which seems unrelated to work.
To avoid noisy suggestions, Coach uses a small LLM classifier that checks a fixed set of behaviors and returns no suggestion when a prompt is fine. We tuned it on several hundred labeled examples, weighted toward cases where Coach should leave a good prompt alone.
Devin Coach analytics shows admins which suggestions users see, accept, and reject, with acceptance rates, daily trends, and breakdowns by type. This helps teams identify recurring problems, and can be used by the company’s DevEx teams or by Cognition’s forward-deployed engineering teams for tailored enablement sessions.
Devin Coach will not silently rewrite prompts. Admins choose how much intervention they want: inline suggestions that engineers can ignore (the default), required confirmation before a flagged new-session prompt is sent, or no checks at all.
Raising limits automatically with efficiency-based approvals
Enterprises using static limits typically have two options: figure out manually who their power users are and give them a higher allowance, or set a uniform cap that limits them. We built efficiency-based approvals in Devin as a third option. Devin uses each engineer’s Efficiency Score to raise their limit automatically, which lets enterprises scale personalized cost controls to hundreds, if not thousands, of engineers without a growing review queue.
Admins turn this on by selecting “Approve based on efficiency” in Usage policies and setting the maximum amount Devin can approve automatically.
When an engineer with a Healthy or Satisfactory grade approaches their limit, Devin increases it without a request, so they can keep working without waiting for an admin. Increases stop at a ceiling the admin sets, and organization-wide limits still apply.
If an engineer requests more than the ceiling allows, Devin grants up to the ceiling and sends the remainder to an admin. It never denies a request automatically.
Engineers with a Needs Improvement or Unknown grade can still request more usage, but their requests go to an admin for review. When reviewing a request, admins see the engineer’s reason alongside their efficiency, model mix, and consumption, the metrics enterprise admins told us matter most when allocating spend.
The chart below follows two real engineers at different companies. Both were among the most productive users on their accounts, and both hit their monthly cap. At the first company, which required manual approvals (left), the engineer was blocked for four days until an admin raised the limit, and their merged PRs fell to a third of their usual rate that week before recovering. At the second company, which had auto-approvals enabled (right), the engineer hit their cap 22 times, and Devin lifted it automatically each time. They kept shipping, going from 30 to nearly 80 merged PRs a week over the period.
Allocating spend where it has the most impact
As AI investments grow, organizations need greater precision and automation to manage spend effectively across thousands of developers. Efficiency Score, Devin Coach, and efficiency-based approvals are intended to help organizations avoid blanket limits.
Over the coming months, we will introduce flexible budgeting controls that allow enterprise administrators to allocate budgets to department leaders, who can then distribute usage limits to sub-teams and handle request approvals. Alongside these controls, we will continue to optimize our efficiency scoring and coaching capabilities to help enterprises maximize the engineering output delivered for every dollar spent.
Auto-approvals are available today for all customers on a Devin Enterprise plan. Get in touch to try it out.

items.title: Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 19, 2026
PublicationResearch
[ COBOL ][ OCaml][ Fortran][ Visual Basic ]Advancing coding in low‑resource programming languages
Our latest model advances bring stronger capabilities for building and migrating software in low-resource programming languages such as COBOL, Fortran, and Visual Basic. These languages have less code and documentation available for models to learn from than languages like Python and JavaScript, yet support critical infrastructure and essential services around the world. COBOL supports⁠(opens in a new window) more than 40% of online banking systems, 80% of in-person credit card transactions and 95% of ATM transactions, while Fortran is used in weather forecasting⁠(opens in a new window) and nuclear reactor safety analysis⁠(opens in a new window). Improving AI’s ability to work in these languages could help teams maintain and modernize the software that essential services depend on.
This work is guided by feedback from developers and enterprise customers who have told us that coding models often struggle with these languages. Maintaining and modernizing this software can be difficult: documentation may be incomplete, original developers may have left the company, and important business rules may only exist in code. Whether teams are fixing bugs or migrating to another language, they need to preserve the behavior their systems depend on.
To measure progress, we developed two evaluations. MultiLangBench tests whether a model can build a SQLite-compatible database engine from scratch across 20 different programming languages. Our COBOL migration evaluation tests whether a model can migrate existing programs to another language while preserving their behavior. Together, they test two complementary skills: building new software and preserving what existing software does.
Our latest models show substantial improvements across both evaluations, delivering much higher accuracy at lower cost.
On MultiLangBench, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across 20 programming languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, with improvements in every language tested. GPT‑6 Luna also outperforms GPT‑5.6 Sol, reaching 40.3% at approximately 78% lower estimated API cost.
On our COBOL migration evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with just 5.4% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while costing 39% less. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, nearly saturating the evaluation.
Together, these results show that our models are becoming significantly better at working with a wide range of programming languages, while also becoming more cost-efficient.
1. Building SQLite from scratch (MultiLangBench)
MultiLangBench asks a model to build a SQLite-compatible database engine in a specified programming language. The model must organize a codebase, manage state, handle errors, and add new features while preserving existing functionality.
To compare implementations across languages, we use database files as a shared interface. The candidate program receives an initial database and a SQL query, then produces a modified database. We use the reference SQLite implementation to check whether the resulting database has the expected contents. This lets us apply the same tests regardless of the language used to build the engine.
We adapted tests from SQLite’s existing test suite to this format. The evaluation measures how much working functionality a model can build over an extended coding session, reporting both test pass rate and API cost.
At maximum reasoning effort, GPT‑6 Astra achieves an average test pass rate of 87.4% across the 20 languages, up from 26.8% for GPT‑5.6 Sol. Improvements extend to every language tested, including COBOL (10.9% to 72.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 85.8%), Fortran (21.4% to 83.5%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 89.4%). Astra scores above 83% in 19 of the 20 languages, with COBOL remaining the hardest at 72%.
GPT‑6 Luna offers a lower-cost option that also improves on GPT‑5.6 Sol in every language tested. At maximum reasoning effort, it reaches an average test pass rate of 40.3%. Gains include COBOL (10.9% to 17.1%), OCaml (25.6% to 34.1%), Fortran (21.4% to 31.4%), and Visual Basic (27.5% to 41.6%). These improvements come at an estimated average API cost of $0.77 per sample, compared with $3.48 for GPT‑5.6 Sol, approximately 78% lower.
We are releasing the MultiLangBench evaluation setup and test suite on GitHub⁠(opens in a new window), along with results for each language. Developers can inspect what the evaluation tests, review performance in the languages they use, and identify gaps that matter for their own work.
2. Migrating a COBOL codebase
Our second evaluation asks models to migrate COBOL programs to C++, Java, Kotlin, Python, or Rust while preserving what each program does.
Successful migration requires understanding both the program’s business logic and COBOL’s specific language behavior. COBOL programs often process financial transactions and business records, where details such as rounding rules and missing-record handling reflect business requirements. For example, COBOL’s fixed-point arithmetic discards excess decimal digits unless rounding is explicitly requested. A rewrite that rounds those values instead can run without errors while producing different financial results.
To test whether these behaviors are preserved, we evaluate our models on hidden tests that require byte-for-byte parity on observable outputs. A migration is considered successful only if all tests pass. Behavior-preserving capabilities like these are useful for teams maintaining and modernizing older systems, though applying it to production software still requires expert review and testing against the system’s business rules and dependencies.
On this evaluation, GPT‑6.1 Sol achieves 86.6% accuracy at low reasoning effort, compared with GPT‑5.6 Sol’s 5.4% at the same setting at just 61% of the API cost. At higher reasoning effort, accuracy reaches 97.9%, bringing the evaluation close to saturation. These evaluation results demonstrate progress toward more accurate, affordable code migration for teams modernizing the software their businesses depend on.
Advancing capabilities for enterprise software
These evaluations, alongside direct feedback from developers and enterprise customers, help us see where our models are improving and where they still fall short.
Our goal is to help models apply software engineering skills across more languages: understanding unfamiliar repositories, planning changes, using build tools, running tests, and debugging failures.
You can try our latest models through the API on coding tasks in the languages your team uses. Your feedback on what works, where the models struggle, and which languages or workflows we should focus on next helps shape how we train and evaluate models to better support the software you depend on.

items.title: How Numan Built an Eval-First AI Health Coach with LangGraph and LangSmith
items.summary:
Case Studies
How Numan built an eval-first AI health coach with LangGraph and LangSmith
Asif LaldinMarcus Wadge-DaleShubhangi HoraKonstantinos GeorgakilasOctober 19, 202610minGo back to blogCreate agentsCreate agentsShare
Numan is a UK digital health company helping patients manage long-term conditions across weight, hormones, and sexual health. Many of our patients are on a weight-loss programme and use the app daily to track progress.
When building Nu, our AI health coach, one of our design challenges was delivering high-quality health coaching without crossing the line into medical diagnosis, prescriptions, or making clinical decisions—all strict boundaries for agents in our highly regulated medical space. While we initially focused on the agent and automation around it, what turned out to matter most was the quality of our evaluation criteria. This is the story of how we developed and improved our evaluation criteria to deliver high-quality user experiences while steering clear of areas subject to regulation.
Where standard eval approaches fell short for Nu
We started where most teams start, with a dataset of inputs and expected outputs, and an LLM judge scoring each reply. While that playbook works well for a Q&A agent, coaching is a conversation, not an answer. Every approach that fixed Nu's reply in advance failed in two ways:
1. Single-turn evals on static fixtures (a fixed input, a fixed expected output, and a judge scoring one reply on its own). Behavioural coaching rarely has one right answer to a prompt and whether a reply was safe depends on the conversation around it. Nu needs to understand what is getting in the patient’s way across a conversation before it advises and hold the right boundary when a patient pushes.
Averaging one score across the whole dataset hid where Nu failed. A few bad replies barely move the number, so the conversation looks compliant when it isn’t. The fixtures also caused a second problem. In one run, a cluster of low scores turned out to be the eval’s fault, not Nu’s. The rubric expected empathy, exploration and advice all within a two-turn exchange, whereas a human coach would pace these across a conversation. Nu was coaching properly, but the narrow, fixed eval signaled failures incorrectly.
2. Scripted multi-turn conversations. The obvious fix for single-turn fixtures is to write out a patient’s expected series of replies in advance. With this "script," several turns of a scenario, fed to Nu one at a time, allow the judge to score the full transcript at the end. While this gives the judge more room than a single reply, the eval fell apart the same way. When the patient’s second turn is written in advance, the test ignores what Nu actually said in the first turn. The moment Nu says something the script did not expect, every later turn is replying to a conversation that never happened.
These 2 failure modes shaped everything we built thereafter.
The eval framework we run today
Nu is a LangGraph graph. A supervisor model orchestrates handoffs to domain-specialist sub-agents, each focused on one coaching area with its own prompt and tools. That composition model makes a new specialist cheap to add, and more importantly, it keeps the evaluation surface uniform across all of them.
Some of what Nu has to get right is decidable from a single reply. For example, whether the supervisor routed to the right specialist, whether a medication question got a safe answer, or whether the safety guard caught what it should. For those we run themed datasets spanning coaching quality, safety, medication queries, routing, and summarisation. Unlike our original single-turn evals, we changed two things: 1) Every dataset is scored per-category by an LLM judge rather than one average, so a cluster of failures in one category stays visible even when the rest look healthy. And 2) each rubric asks only what a single reply can show, so the judge no longer penalises Nu for pacing a conversation the way a coach would.
Everything that a fixture cannot cover (i.e. what requires the shape of a whole conversation) gets its own layer, described below. Because Nu is a graph, an eval can target the whole system or a single sub-agent, and a new specialist inherits the eval surface.
"The thing we ship is the thing we test"
The easy way to build an eval is a separate harness that copies the agent’s prompt and calls the model directly...which works until the harness and production drift. We have no separate harness and operate under the principle the thing we ship is the thing we test. Every eval runs through the same LangGraph graph a patient talks to, so what we score is what a patient meets.
As we scaled, we started asking whether one provider was right for every agent, since the supervisor and the domain specialists do different cognitive work. Nu runs on two frontier providers today, chosen per-agent: one for the supervisor, another for the specialists. Thanks to the portability of our eval suite built as open, themed datasets we can point at any configuration, we ran the same datasets across providers and read the results side by side. A migration between frontier providers, normally weeks of manual testing, took only a day.
Behavioural tests to keep the regulatory boundary
Under MHRA guidance, a software-based product with a medical purpose (giving clinical advice, diagnosing, or recommending treatment) becomes a medical device. Nu was designed to be a wellness product for lifestyle coaching and education, not clinical care.
Keeping Nu inside that scope is something we check on every change. Safety probes run as per-category metrics and gate releases: a regression there blocks the change from shipping automatically. We tune toward safe-completion, a redirect that holds the line while still sounding like a coach, so a patient who asks something out of scope gets a warm, useful answer rather than an abrupt refusal.
Beyond testing, guard nodes run on every conversation inside the graph. A safety guard reviews each outgoing response against a fixed set of clinical safety rules before the patient sees it. An unsafe draft is sent back to the supervisor to regenerate. If it keeps failing, the message is replaced with a safe fallback rather than delivering the unsafe response. And because the guards sit in the graph, they sit inside the same eval surface—where one of our themed datasets exists specifically to test that the safety guard catches what it should. In addition, health coaches review a sample of real conversations every day and flag anything that looks like a safety miss, so human subject matter experts calibrate what counts as safe.
Simulating conversations instead of scripting them
Our newest layer, in prototype today, simulates the conversation instead of scripting it. We hand the eval a patient persona, a scenario, the key problems Nu should draw out, and a turn limit. A cheaper model plays the patient, holding a multi-turn conversation with the real agent and reacting to whatever Nu says. Then a judge scores the whole transcript per-category. Because the patient is generated rather than fixed, we can probe adversarial cases (phrasings built to slip a clinical request past the coach, manipulation disguised as an ordinary question) and catch failures a fixture never encounters. For example, Nu rushing to an answer instead of investigating the way a coach should.
This kind of prompt hardening via simulated conversations reduced serious scope violations in jailbreak scenarios against the regulatory boundary. We ran parallel medication-query evals as a regression gate so prompt improvements could not break behaviour we already trusted.
Using the simulated conversation layer for continuous improvement without introducing regressions is less an engineering problem than a rubric problem. When we first drafted criteria for this layer, two themes we thought were compatible turned out to contradict each other on missed-dose handling: one said decline and signpost to a clinician, the other said safe-completion with general facts from the patient information leaflet. One prompt cannot satisfy both. This example of a prompt conflict taught us that the scarce, valuable asset is not the prompt, which a capable model drafts well from limited context; it is the eval criteria. And on a regulated boundary, those criteria have to be authored and signed off by a clinician who also understands the regulatory line, not an engineer. The results from Nu's simulated conversations are judged against engineering-drafted criteria, which is why this layer does not gate releases or inform any safety claim until a clinician has signed off the rubric (which is what keeps the product on the wellness side of the line).
The stack: LangGraph and LangSmith
Real and simulated conversations run through the same LangGraph agent; LangSmith measures both. A clinician-owned rubric drives the judge, and a boundary regression blocks the release. Dashed = prototype or direction.
LangGraph and LangSmith fit together as one system to make up our agent development stack.
LangGraph is the agent. A supervisor triggers domain specialists, each with its own prompt and tools.
Evals run through that same graph. Both fixture and simulated conversation eval layers hit the real agent and can target the whole system or a single sub-agent.
LangSmith is where everything is measured. Every conversation, simulated or real, lands as a trace. Reviewers annotate those traces, kicking off the continuous quality improvement loop. Datasets and experiments live there too. For example, the side-by-side provider comparison behind our one-day migration was read straight out of LangSmith.
The integration between LangGraph and LangSmith keeps evaluation cheap to run. There is no glue code stitching three disconnected tools together. The thing we ship and the thing we test are the same graph, watched by the same platform.
Where we are heading: scaling the criteria, not just the agent
Coaching quality hinges on 1) authoring the criteria that decide whether a conversation was good, and 2) widening the coverage they are tested against. So we're focused on testing more adversarial personas and scenarios, adding more themes as we build more specialists, and expanding the clinician-in-the-loop rubric wherever it touches safety or scope. Reviewers keep reading real conversations in LangSmith, and an engineer still raises every prompt change.
Everything described so far is offline, proving a change holds the regulatory line before it ships. The next step is online evaluators that run the same rubrics continuously against real conversations as they land in LangSmith, scoring Nu's side of the conversation. Instead of the daily sample coaches review today, human reviewers will start from the conversations an evaluator has already flagged—to watch the boundary hold in production and sharpen the rubric upon false alarms.
We're also seeing encouraging results from early experiments to automate the workflows that follow a trustworthy rubric—including triaging reviewed conversations into a ranked backlog and tuning a prompt against a fixed benchmark. Recently, an offline prompt-optimisation loop pointed at a single behavioural benchmark meaningfully improved the score with no hand-tuning...in favor of our hypothesis that if you get the criteria right, the rest becomes automatable.
Building an AI coach near a regulatory line
If you are building a conversational agent anywhere near a regulatory line, here are our recommendations:
A fixed dataset cannot cover a whole conversation. Keep fixtures for what a single reply can show, simulate conversations for the rest, and score per-category rather than chasing an aggregate.
Make the boundary a probe. Run it on every change, let a regression block the release, and aim the same rubric at production.
On a regulated boundary, the rubric belongs to a clinician. Engineering-drafted criteria are enough to get a harness running; they are not enough to gate a safety claim.
Invest the bulk of your effort into the eval criteria. Everything downstream follows from the eval criteria: better coaching, a defensible boundary, and eventually automation you can trust.
We'll write again as the criteria and the automation matures.
Nu is built on LangGraph and LangSmith. Numan's AI system handles health-coaching conversations across multiple health domains. Nu is designed to operate as a wellness product, not a medical device. It provides coaching and health education, and does not diagnose, prescribe, monitor disease, or make or inform clinical decisions.
