items.title: MiniMax M3.1 Flash：重新定义 Agent 的性能与成本
items.summary: 原创 MiniMax 2026-10-19 19:20 上海 今天，我们正式更新 MiniMax M3.1 Flash。 此前以匿名身份处理了超过 200T Token 的 Space Bunny🐰，正是 MiniMax M3.1 Flash 的早期版本。 作为新一代 Flash 模型，M3.1 Flash 在 Agentic 任务、编程、Computer Use 及网络安全能力等方面实现了代际的提升，同时线上推理速度提升了近 3 倍，使用成本降低了 70%。 模型能力全面提升 M3.1 Flash 在多项基准测试中取得了全面进步，在复杂 Agent 任务 (Cowork)、Computer Use、软件开发 (Coding) 及网络安全方面，达到了领先模型水平。 复杂任务与自动化能力： 在 AutomationBench-AA 中位居最前列。在跨 SaaS 系统的真实企业业务工作流中，能完整解决销售、营销、运营、客服、财务、HR 的真实问题。 在 BankerToolBench 中 76.2 分，擅长多步骤规划、跨文档 / 跨文件一致性、金融业务合规、工具链式调用等真实复杂问题。 编程与软件工程能力： 在 DeepSWE v1.1 评测中取得 73.7% 的成绩，达到顶尖模型水平。DeepSWE 聚焦复杂软件任务，要求模型独立完成代码理解、功能开发、问题修复与测试验证。M3.1 Flash 展现出出色的长链路任务执行能力，能够以更低的成本支持复杂的软件开发工作流。 Computer Use 能力： 在衡量 AI 电脑操作与跨应用任务执行能力的 OSWorld V2 中取得 61.7 分，在衡量真实并有经济价值场景下电脑操作能力的 Agents' Last Exam (ALE) 中取得 29.6 分，两项得分均位列国产模型第一。 M3.1 Flash 展现出出色的真实环境交互、工具使用与长链路任务执行能力，能够从理解任务进一步走向实际操作与交付。 网络安全能力： 在 CyberGym 基准测试中取得 82% 的高分，展现出领先的漏洞发现与验证能力。 经内部安全专家深度评测，模型在代码审计、漏洞修补、渗透测试、恶意代码分析与逆向工程等场景下均表现出色，能够以低成本、高效率支持复杂的安全体系建设。 我们进一步优化了 M3.1 Flash 的推理效率，使用了更激进的稀疏注意力架构，日常使用场景下的输出速度可达 200+ TPS (Tokens per Second)，中位数 (P50) 稳定达到 170+ TPS。 模型价格 在 Agentic 类任务中，模型的综合使用成本较前代模型降低了 70%。输入价格为每百万 Token 1 元，输出价格为每百万 Token 4 元，缓存读取价格为每百万 Token 0.1 元。 重新定义 Agent 任务的能力和成本 在衡量复杂 Agent 任务执行能力的 Automation-Bench、衡量真实编程能力的 DeepSWE，以及衡量真实并有经济价值场景下电脑操作能力的 Agents' Last Exam (ALE) 三项基准测试中，M3.1 Flash 以极低的任务成本实现了顶尖模型级别的性能表现，在性能与成本之间建立了极具竞争力的新标杆。 M3.1 Flash 现已正式上线 MiniMax API、MPlan 以及 MiniMax Code 中，并将于稍后开放权重。 MiniMax Code 桌面端下载：https://agent.minimax.cn/download M Plan 订阅入口：https://www.minimax.cn/m-plan API 调用：https://www.minimax.cn/ Flash 是我们对效率与能力平衡的持续探索，而追求智能上限的 Pro 版本也会在稍后与大家见面。 Intelligence with Everyone. 跳转微信打开

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.summary: As merges to Anthropic's monorepo grew from about 2,500 to more than 30,000 a day, source control became the biggest development bottleneck. Here is how the team built Scion, an in-house version control system designed for always-online agents, and migrated off git in five months.

items.title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
items.summary:
Back to Articles
TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
Published
October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 32
+26
Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow
TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.
TorchNeuron
TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP.
Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.
Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.
New backend, native interface in HF libraries
To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.
TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.
For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.
Transformers
Inference
Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.
The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.
import os
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401
from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig
MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B"
MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024
PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron")
world_size = dist.get_world_size()
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
MODEL_ID,
dtype=torch.bfloat16,
distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size),
device_mesh=DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(world_size))),
).eval()
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID)
if tokenizer.pad_token is None:
tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token
tokenizer.padding_side = "left"
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
[{"role": "user", "content": "The future of AI is"}],
add_generation_prompt=True,
padding=True,
tokenizer_kwargs={"pad_to_multiple_of": PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE},
return_tensors="pt",
)
generation_config = GenerationConfig(
max_new_tokens=128,
do_sample=False,
use_cache=True,
pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id,
eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id,
cache_implementation="static",
max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN,
prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE,
compile_config=CompileConfig(backend="neuron", fullgraph=False, dynamic=False),
)
with torch.no_grad():
output_ids = model.generate(
inputs["input_ids"],
attention_mask=inputs["attention_mask"],
generation_config=generation_config,
)
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
print(tokenizer.decode(output_ids[0, prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True))
Training
Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.
Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.
import os
import torch
from datasets import load_dataset
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser
def main(script_args, training_args, model_args):
# The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660)
torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False
training_args.model_init_kwargs = {
"revision": model_args.model_revision,
"trust_remote_code": training_args.trust_remote_code,
"attn_implementation": model_args.attn_implementation,
"dtype": model_args.dtype,
"device_map": None,
}
if int(os.environ.get("WORLD_SIZE", "1")) > 1:
# The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded
training_args.model_init_kwargs["distributed_config"] = DistributedConfig(
tp_size=int(os.environ.get("TP_SIZE", "1")),
fsdp_size=int(os.environ.get("FSDP_SIZE", "1")),
)
# Prepare dataset
train_dataset = load_dataset(
script_args.dataset_name,
name=script_args.dataset_config,
split=script_args.dataset_train_split,
)
# UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset.
train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns(["messages"])
# Training
trainer = SFTTrainer(
model=model_args.model_name_or_path,
args=training_args,
train_dataset=train_dataset,
)
trainer.train()
trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir)
trainer.end()
if __name__ == "__main__":
parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig))
script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config()
main(script_args, training_args, model_args)
Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.
Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:
Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes.
torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure.
Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1.
The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.
TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \
--model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \
--dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \
--dataset_train_split train_sft \
--output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \
--dtype bfloat16 \
--max_length 2048 \
--packing true \
--packing_strategy wrapped \
--learning_rate 2e-5 \
--warmup_steps 0.03 \
--num_train_epochs 1 \
--logging_steps 2 \
--per_device_train_batch_size 4 \
--gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \
--save_only_model true \
--torch_compile true
We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.
Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.
Diffusers
Inference
Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:
import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP
from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP
from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig
# Distributed devices initialization
dist.init_process_group(backend="neuron") # TP
dev = torch.neuron.current_device()
mesh = DeviceMesh("neuron", list(range(8))) # TP=8
# Pipeline initialization
model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1"
transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained(
model,
subfolder="transformer",
torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP
)
pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained(
model,
transformer=transformer,
torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
)
pipe.vae.to(dev)
pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend="neuron", fullgraph=True, dynamic=False)
# Image generation
emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt="A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting", device="cpu") # text encoder stays on CPU
image = pipe(
prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev),
prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None,
height=1024,
width=1024,
num_inference_steps=40,
generator=torch.Generator("cpu").manual_seed(0), # same noise on every rank
).images[0]
if dist.get_rank() == 0:
image.save("out.png")
You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.
More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.
Kernels
Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models.
Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.
You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!
Acknowledgments
Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new wholly owned entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.
As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.
The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.
One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.
We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as an LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.
Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.
This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.
In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

Benefit Street Partners answers questions faster with Codex
Anant Kumar builds tools to compare loan valuations and analyze credit agreements, using Codex for code review and faster follow-ups.
Contact salesCompany size: EnterpriseRegion: North AmericaIndustry: FinanceProducts: Codex

~20 min

At Benefit Street Partners, a credit-focused investment manager, answering an investment committee’s follow-up questions used to take days or weeks. Portfolio manager Anant Kumar says analysts can now turn a round of comments in a day with Codex, and often answer questions during the meeting itself. BSP is using these tools to add more review capacity and rigor to underwriting within the same timeframe, rather than to do more deals.
“I’ve gone from being just an analyst and a portfolio manager to being a developer as well now. I can build things.”
—Anant Kumar, Portfolio Manager, Benefit Street Partners
Building his own dashboards
To create a dashboard he could share with colleagues, Kumar used to need someone with software expertise to build a website and pull in the data. Now he builds his own tools, using AI to draft code and review it for errors.
His tracker uses public SEC filings from business development companies (BDCs) to compare how firms value the same loan. The team can see how its marks compare with other holders’ valuations.
Kumar built the tracker and used Codex for code review. The first version took a day. After adding features and refining the interface over subsequent weeks, he estimates total development time at 10–12 hours total.
Building a credit agreement analyzer
Kumar’s other tool analyzes credit agreements, which are often 300 pages or longer. Investors need to find clauses that could shift value away from lenders, a task that previously meant asking outside counsel to work through the agreement page by page. Kumar brought together memos from leading law firms on clauses and risks to watch for. He describes the analyzer as a “second brain within our organization.”
An uploaded credit agreement takes about 20 minutes to process into a first-pass analysis, followed by an hour or more of human review. BSP has refactored the tool with GPT‑6 Astra, and it is now live in the company-hosted portal.
“The AI is very helpful in collating data, ingesting it, synthesizing analysis, but the ultimate investment decision needs to be made by a human,” he says.
Underwriting is typically a multi-round process. A round consists of further diligence and a revised memo responding to the investment committee’s questions. Deal timelines range from a few days to a few weeks, so the number of rounds varies. Kumar says, “We feel more confident in our decision making because we have more information at our disposal.”
“The quality of my analysis has become so much better and so much faster.”
—Anant Kumar, Portfolio Manager, Benefit Street Partners
Results at a glance
Built the first BDC tracker in a day, using Codex for code review; about 10–12 hours total including later additions.
Produces a first-pass analysis of a credit agreement in about 20 minutes, followed by an hour or more of human review.
Answers committee follow-up questions faster with Codex, often during the meeting, according to Kumar.
What’s next
BSP is working to connect information across deals. Continuous underwriting is a longer-term aspiration: the team could monitor loans as news happens and examine the effects across its portfolio, rather than re-underwriting only after an event.
“Codex has unlocked my day, because I have many more hours in the day to do more high-level work and less routine work,” says Kumar.

items.title: How an Anthropic BDR in Japan runs his day with Claude Managed Agents
items.summary:
How an Anthropic BDR in Japan runs his day with Claude Managed Agents
How one business development representative clears his inbound queue and drafts bilingual customer emails with Claude Managed Agents and Claude Tag.
CategoryBest practices
ProductClaude Managed Agents
AuthorShahboz Ibragimov
DateOctober 16, 2026
Reading time14 min
ShareCopy link
As a business development representative on Anthropic's Japan team, my job is to show Japanese companies how Claude can simplify and automate their workflows, but until earlier this year, most of mine were still manual. I was spending a couple of hours each morning routing and qualifying leads, then writing emails in Japanese or English. In the time I had left, I was updating our CRM, often a day or more behind. Now my agents prepare most of that before my day starts, and I review it.
The first Claude-run workflow I built was pretty scrappy, but it did the job. I'd hand Claude one piece of my work at a time, correct what it got wrong, and save those corrections. Over time, that grew into a handful of agents, each covering a different routine.
Word got around quickly, and teammates started asking for my prompts and skills so they could build their own. All I could send them was a zip file with my skills and a few Markdown files from the knowledge base, which they had to upload to Claude and then answer a round of setup questions before anything worked. My own setup was getting harder to keep track of, too. Each agent was a skill, a scheduled task and a shared folder, and I changed them by asking Claude in whatever chat I had open, so the same skill was being edited from lots of different conversations.
I wanted to define each agent once, in one place, and be able to see every change I'd made to it. So I decided to try Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) (beta), our managed agent infrastructure on the Claude Platform.
I was hesitant to try it at first. The docs talk about schedules, tools, and credential vaults, and I'm a sales rep, so I assumed Managed Agents was for developers who can build and maintain the necessary infrastructure. I tried it anyway because my agents already existed, and I only had to move them over.
It turned out I didn't need to be a developer. I described each agent's job in plain language, Claude wrote a few short setup scripts, and I ran them from the terminal on my laptop. (If you're starting from scratch, the Console also has a quickstart with ready-made agent templates.) Since then, there has been no infrastructure for me to look after.
In this post, I'll walk through how I designed and prototyped the fleet, why I moved it to Managed Agents, how Claude Tag picks up anything that falls outside the routine, how it all changed my week, and what I'd tell sellers who want to build their own agents to automate manual, repetitive workflows.
Designing my fleet of agents
I divided up my workflow across several agents and gave every agent one clear job. A single responsibility keeps each one easy to reason about and easy to track, especially when something is off. I also gave every agent a Japanese name, because they mostly work in Japanese. Together they're called the Nakama, "the crew," or more literally, the companions you work with:
Furiwake ("sorting") kicks off first: it reads the daily inbound queue and routes each lead to the right rep on the team, balancing the number of leads and the priority of each one and checking who's in that day, so every lead has an owner before any of us start our day. At the end of each run it posts a report to a dedicated Slack channel (every lead in, every lead assigned) so I can track the handoff.
Sabaki ("handling") triages the leads that are assigned to me: it qualifies each lead, categorizes it against pre-set criteria, takes the defined next step for that category (draft a reply pointing them to self-serve, craft a customized first email), updates the lead record in Salesforce, and drafts the first-touch email. It sources the draft's contents from the Nakama's shared knowledge base, a memory store (opens in new tab) every agent reads and writes (more on this below).
Henji ("reply") scans my inbox hourly for customer emails that need a response and prepares a draft reply in Japanese or English, depending on the thread, drawing on the same knowledge base as Sabaki. I can review, edit, and send the draft.
Shoudan ("opportunity") reads recent customer interactions and pushes updates into Salesforce, so opportunity records stay current without manual data entry.
Nokori ("what remains") runs at the end of the day: it scans my calendar, reads the attached meeting transcripts, summarizes each meeting, and drafts the follow-ups, again from the same knowledge base.
Each agent runs on a schedule. A sixth agent, the Nakama's coordinator, is the fleet’s operations manager. It updates the agents’ instructions and the shared knowledge base between runs. When I want to change how an agent works, I write what I want in plain language in the Nakama’s Slack channel. Only I can post requests for changes to agents’ instructions and system prompts. The coordinator checks that channel every 15 minutes or so, picks up the request, and makes the update.
Prototyping the fleet in Claude
You don't need Managed Agents to start. I prototyped the whole fleet in Claude first, using the following pieces:
A skill per agent: the instructions for one job.
A scheduled task for each skill, so I don’t need to run it manually.
A shared folder on my laptop as the knowledge base every skill writes its learnings back into: the difference between what it drafted and what I sent, plus anything new it dug up along the way.
On Managed Agents, the skill became the agent's system prompt, the scheduled task became a schedule on the agent's deployment (opens in new tab), and the shared folder became a memory store. I still ask for changes in plain language, but now I do it all in one Slack channel, and each change to an agent's instructions is saved as a new version, so each agent keeps a numbered history of its instructions. I'd suggest starting in Claude and moving your agents to Managed Agents once you have more than you can comfortably keep track of.
Running the fleet on Claude Managed Agents
Three things I got on Managed Agents that mattered most for my workflow:
The agents can run in the background
The agents run on their schedule whether my laptop is open or not, even when it's offline. The schedule is part of each agent's deployment. I could schedule skills in Claude too, but each of those schedules was a task set up in my own app. On Managed Agents, I set the cadence and timezone in the Console, next to the deployed agent's instructions and tools, and I have no cron jobs to maintain on the side. If a run goes wrong, I can open it in the Console and see each step the agent took. And while I'm trying out a change to an agent, the scheduled runs keep using the version that’s deployed, so a half-finished edit doesn't end up in tomorrow's run.
The Nakama shares one memory and learns from my edits
Every agent reads and writes the same memory store (opens in new tab), so any agent can use the others’ learnings. The agents compare the drafts they wrote with the emails I sent, and they save each difference as a note on how I'd phrase it. They also keep whatever new information they dig up while researching an answer, from our internal docs and our official websites. I fix a phrasing once in Henji's drafts, and Sabaki and Nokori stop making the same mistake.
Credentials live in a managed vault with scoped permissions
My agents have access to my email and our Salesforce records, but since these are customer conversations and company records, I wanted that access under control. The credentials live in managed vaults (opens in new tab), which protect credentials agents use to log in to outside services, such as OAuth access and refresh tokens, API keys, and personal access tokens. Each agent’s deployment uses only the vaults its job needs, it never sees the credentials, and I can revoke access in one step.
Handing the next steps to Claude Tag
For most of what the Nakama produces, I only need to read a draft in my inbox and send it, or glance at an updated Salesforce record. But some items need a follow-up step, such as figuring out an upgrade path or a purchasing route, or escalating an issue to another team.
For those, the agents don't stop and wait for me. They hand the item to Claude Tag (opens in new tab) (in beta). Claude Tag is Claude set up as a member of our Slack workspace: anyone in a channel it has joined, a person or one of my agents, can tag @Claude with a request and it picks the request up and works on it in the thread. Once it's configured in your workspace there is nothing new to learn. You tag Claude the way you would a colleague.
In my setup it works like this. An agent posts the action item to the Nakama's Slack channel and tags Claude. Claude reads the thread, checks our rules and the terms that apply, lays out the options, and drafts what's needed. It tags me when a step needs my review or sign-off. When a customer or another team needs to reply first, Claude sets a reminder for itself to check back on a set day. In the thread below, it set a reminder for Tuesday to check whether the customer had replied and whether the deal desk had answered the ticket. When the reminder comes due, Claude checks both and posts where things stand in the same thread. If someone needs a nudge, it drafts the message and tags me to send it.
Claude also posts a morning brief of product and pricing updates. The Nakama coordinator picks up that brief and writes the necessary changes into the shared knowledge base.
What changed in my week
Now that Claude prepares inbound replies and keeps CRM records current (mostly) without my manual input, my role is to review anything that requires human judgment. A written rulebook defines each agent's lane and items like pricing questions, sensitive accounts, or ambiguous asks route to me. Every email draft from Henji, Sabaki, or Nokori arrives with a short summary at the top of what's going on, so I don't have to trace the whole thread to understand the context: I read the summary, confirm, make revisions, and send.
Looking at the weekly log of what the Nakama gets through and counting each task as the time it would have taken me to do manually, the fleet saves me around 60 hours of work. I spend the time that frees up on work that agents can't effectively do (yet): conversations with customers, outbound strategy, cross-functional projects, and helping teammates build their own fleets.
Designing agents to be more efficient
Scheduled agents run every day whether I'm watching or not, so waste can add up, in cost and reliability. Some of the most common mistakes include adding to existing instructions rather than updating them, giving agents more context than they need for their tasks, and running every job on the biggest model at the highest effort level.
Most of what keeps the agents efficient is how I designed the fleet: each agent has one job, so its instructions stay focused on that job; each working agent runs on a schedule, so it wakes up, does its pass, and stops; and the agents share memory, so a correction made once is reused everywhere.
The other big factor is which model each agent runs on. Once an agent's job is well defined, it may not need our most capable model. Furiwake and Shoudan follow a written rulebook, so they run on Sonnet, our smaller model. Sabaki, Nokori and the coordinator run on Opus, our larger model, because their work needs more judgment. The coordinator needs it most, since it edits the other agents' instructions and one bad edit would reach every agent. Henji needs as much judgment as Sabaki, because every customer's email is different, but it also runs more often than any other agent, all through the working day. Running it on Opus every time would be the most expensive option, so I use the advisor strategy (opens in new tab) in Managed Agents: Henji runs on Sonnet, and when it reaches a decision it can't make on its own, it asks Opus for advice. The advisor reads what Henji has done so far and sends back a plan, a correction, or a stop signal, and Henji then finishes the draft for my review. I also set each agent's effort level (how long the model thinks before it answers) separately from its model, and I raise it only where the reasoning is hard, as with Henji's replies.
What I learned
Three things I'd pass on to anyone building their own fleet.
You don't need a detailed prompt every time. Describe the job once, let Claude draft, fix the draft, and let it keep the fix.
The knowledge base matters more than the prompt. Every correction and past interaction is saved where all the agents can read it and write to it, so Claude takes its context from there instead of from a longer prompt. It took a few hundred cheap rounds of drafting, fixing, and saving to get the drafts to sound like me.
Give Claude more room, sooner. At first I kept doing the tasks that I assumed needed me: updating the knowledge base, or editing each agent's instructions by hand. Both worked fine once I let go of them. The agents now write what they learn into the knowledge base themselves, and the coordinator updates the other agents' instructions when I ask in plain English. I had been too cautious with work I could trust the agents to do.

items.title: How Grupo Boticário uses AI to strengthen human connections
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 16, 2026
How Grupo Boticário uses AI to strengthen human connections
Almost 50 years after starting in a compounding pharmacy in Paraná, the group operates a proprietary agent platform that autonomously resolves up to 80% of resellers’ operational requests—enabling the sales force to take on an advisory role.
Contact salesCompany size: EnterpriseRegion: Latin AmericaIndustry: RetailProducts: API
Up to 80%
autonomous resolution of operational requests
100%
of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise covered since November 2025
90%
of direct-sales leads initially received and qualified by AI
30+
agents across the reseller journey
Two things done well, now at scale
Grupo Boticário began in 1977 as a small compounding pharmacy in Paraná. According to Renato Pedigoni, the group’s CTO, the founder did two things very well: he served customers with care and affection, understanding their needs, and created high-quality products.
Almost five decades later, its ecosystem encompasses laboratories, factories, innovation, technology, logistics, marketing, and retail—with a presence in more than 40 countries, more than 4,000 physical stores across more than 1,700 Brazilian cities, and an ecosystem of 200,000 points of sale across retail, partners, and suppliers. It is one of Brazil’s largest beauty franchise networks.
The company’s premise is that technology exists to keep doing those same two things—on a massive scale.
“Today, almost 50 years later, we use technology to continue doing those two things well, and at scale,” says Pedigoni.
This is the origin of the term the company adopted to describe itself: Lovetech—the union of technology and human sensitivity as pillars of its culture, helping the company innovate while preserving the human touch.
“We like to call ourselves a Lovetech, using technology to bring people closer together, encourage self-care, and connect with the people in our ecosystem.”
—Renato Pedigoni, CTO, Grupo Boticário
Why the platform had to be proprietary
The decision to develop solutions internally stems from how the group operates: a vertically integrated chain that runs from research and development laboratories through manufacturing, distribution, and logistics to the final interaction with customers.
That interaction happens on many fronts at once. Beyond being multi-brand, the group is multichannel: physical stores, e-commerce, marketplaces, franchising, direct sales, B2B, and B2P. More than 10 consumer brands—including O Boticário, Eudora, Quem Disse Berenice, Vult, and Truss—operate under different business models, with franchisees, resellers, and beauty professionals in salons.
“Once we have this complexity of multiple brands, categories, and channels, we can build our own technology that brings it all together,” Pedigoni explains.
The return is twofold: better listening to customers at the point of contact and optimization of the production chain—which inputs to buy, where to distribute them, to which store, and how many units of each SKU need to be delivered.
Grupo Boticário was not born digital. But it has reached a stage where it develops critical solutions and processes internally—supported by the premise of digital democratization: making data accessible across the company for analyses, AI models, and dashboards. For the fifth consecutive year, the company was recognized among Latin America’s most admired companies in data, ranking second in State of Data Brazil 2025–2026, by Data Hackers in partnership with Bain & Company.
“With this view of an integrated chain, this mix of channels, and collaboration with other business partners, our own technology allows us to be more effective and closer to the customer.”
—Renato Pedigoni, CTO, Grupo Boticário
An agent platform for the entire reseller journey
OpenAI provides the technology in the group’s proprietary agent orchestration platform, which combines foundation models with business rules to democratize the creation of agents focused on activating and serving its key partners: resellers and franchisees.
“Today we have hundreds of agents in our ecosystem serving customers, partners, franchisees, and resellers,” says Pedigoni.
The reseller journey alone has more than 30 agents, covering everything from registration and the first order to day-to-day operational support—alongside agents dedicated to validating the content and effectiveness of responses, ensuring continuous improvement of the solution. The architecture combines generative and predictive AI.
The journey is divided into two areas.
For reseller onboarding, AI qualifies leads: a lead arrives through a digital channel and is received by AI to clarify questions about joining. When the lead signals an intention to complete an order, it is transferred to human support. This ensures a prompt first response, with service available 24 hours a day, and directs leads ready to advance through the journey to the human team. The solution covers 90% of leads captured in direct sales.
For reseller support, agents autonomously resolve day-to-day operational requests: sending catalogs, answering questions about payment slips, handling app questions, and addressing general topics. Since November 2025, they have covered 100% of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise, with up to 80% autonomous resolution.
“OpenAI helps us enormously by delivering foundation models at scale, so we can focus on our business rules and what our resellers need,” says Pedigoni.
He is careful to shift the interpretation of these figures.
“Sometimes we think of automation as something closely tied to efficiency. We prefer to see this automation as improving the quality of our service and enabling our supervisors to have an even deeper relationship with consumers and resellers, too.”
Repetitive work is removed from the sales force’s routine, allowing it to focus on better understanding resellers, their context, and their customers. On the other side, resellers receive quick answers and gain time to act as advisors within their own businesses.
“Our deal with OpenAI brings to life our vision that AI exists to amplify human talent. By integrating these models into our proprietary platform through multiple agents, we achieved autonomous resolution of up to 80% of operational requests. This frees our sales force from repetitive tasks, enabling them to take on a truly advisory role, focused on what matters most: strengthening connections and growing the businesses of our reseller network.”
—Renato Pedigoni, CTO, Grupo Boticário
The people serving customers write the prompts
One of the operation’s distinguishing features is organizational rather than technical: the business team manages prompts on the platform.
It was not always this way. When the first agents were built years ago, prompts were the technology team’s responsibility—a more technical task in unfamiliar territory. Results were good, but the group saw value in continuous iteration: optimizing prompts every day and running A/B tests between approaches.
“And there is no one better to do that than the team serving customers today,” Pedigoni says.
The change altered the teams’ roles. Sales, customer service, and support teams began managing their own prompts, with continuous incremental improvements based on feedback from daily use. They expanded their focus beyond direct work with resellers to include service systems and models—drawing on their own frontline experience.
“With this, we improved service quality for our resellers and also created new career paths for teams that continue serving customers while also contributing to the creation of a better automated service system.”
—Renato Pedigoni, CTO, Grupo Boticário
Results overview
Since November 2025, agents have covered 100% of conversations generated in appchat and WhatsApp Enterprise, with up to 80% autonomous resolution of operational requests.
The solution covers 90% of direct-sales leads, initially received and qualified by AI, with 24-hour service at first contact and transfer to the human team when there is an intention to proceed with an order.
The group operates hundreds of agents across its ecosystem; the reseller journey alone has more than 30, from registration and the first order to operational support, with agents dedicated to validating content and response effectiveness.
The solution is proprietary, combines generative and predictive AI, and operates with business-team autonomy: the team manages prompts directly on the platform.
Sales, customer service, and support teams began contributing directly to the system’s evolution, creating new career paths.
Lessons for leaders
Automation is about service quality before efficiency. The benefit appears in the deeper relationships that humans have time to build.
Put the agent where users already are. Convenience determines adoption more than technical capability.
Give prompt control to the people who know the customer. Those serving customers daily iterate better and faster than those who only implement the technology.
A proprietary platform makes sense when complexity is your advantage. Many brands, channels, and partnership models require a layer that no one provides out of the box.
Treat the change as career design. New paths keep frontline knowledge involved in building the system.
Tips
Use foundation models to avoid spending energy on areas outside your business rules.
Separate lead qualification from operational support—these journeys have different success criteria.
Define the handoff to humans early; at Boticário, it is the intention to complete an order.
Create dedicated agents to validate other agents’ responses.
Establish a routine of prompt A/B testing run by business teams.
Next steps
The group sees agent adoption as creating space: removing day-to-day operational overload to free up higher-value work—performed by people with practical frontline knowledge.
“The more we invest in AI adoption, the more we can also create new opportunities for both the people on our team and our business, using the knowledge of the people who operate it.”
—Renato Pedigoni, CTO, Grupo Boticário

items.title: How Itaú is building generative AI for its entire customer base
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 16, 2026
How Itaú is building generative AI for its entire customer base
With ia.i, a conversational interface, and the IARA governance platform, Itaú is applying its AI First strategy to customers and employees—in one of Brazil’s most regulated sectors.
Contact salesCompany size: EnterpriseRegion: Latin AmericaIndustry: FinanceProducts: API
~300,000
customers in the first phase of ia.i
100%
of the customer base is the goal by the end of 2026
90M+
documents in the legal solution’s repository
20% to 80%
efficiency gains in the department’s processes
The challenge is to make the technology disappear
Creating a close, personalized experience for millions of customers in a country like Brazil is, first and foremost, a question of simplicity rather than of models.
“Much of it is about making something simple, direct, and useful, delivering a direct benefit to the customer, and making the technology almost unnoticeable,” says Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO of Itaú.
The standard he describes is demanding: the solution must solve a real everyday problem and be direct, simple, and memorable. Technology serves as the means, never as the centerpiece of the experience.
There is demand for this. A study by Itaú in partnership with Grupo Consumoteca shows that 80% of Brazilians want to better organize their financial lives and seek more effective support for decisions, and that 65% would like technologies that act as a financial copilot, providing ongoing guidance.
“OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions.”
—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú
ia.i: from convenience to advice, in one place
The journey began in 2024, when the bank introduced the first Inteligência Itaú capabilities for specific financial needs. ia.i is the next stage: a complete conversational layer, activated by text or voice, bringing interactions related to checking accounts, credit, cards, insurance, and other services into one environment — and connecting customers to specialized human support whenever needed.
This breadth was precisely what guided the choice of models.
“OpenAI’s models were very important in delivering this experience, because they were able to operate across this range of solutions,” Mazzei explains. “From the simplest ones, which need to be efficient in cost and latency, to more complex solutions, where reasoning and all the necessary grounding are required to provide an appropriate answer.”
Having a range of models — rather than a single model — made it possible to deliver the complete solution in one product. At the center of this experience is Customer DNA, a layer of financial context that helps the bank understand the needs, habits, and life stages of approximately 70 million customers. Under governance and responsible AI controls, GPT models are among the components that help maintain and enrich this representation, making interactions progressively more relevant.
The solution rests on three principles: interactivity, multimodality — text, voice, image, and clicks in the same experience — and individualization.
With approximately 300,000 customers in the first phase, the bank entered a period of learning about the real relationship between customer and product.
“We can understand how customers begin to use this product more deeply and see how it can directly benefit each person’s daily financial life,” says Mazzei. Its presence extends across the journey: from a question about an expense in an account statement to investment advice and convenient transactions on WhatsApp.
“The financial world often has products that are not so straightforward and need this context, this simpler relationship with money.”
—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú
IARA: the layer that makes scale possible
Behind the visible experiences is an architectural decision. To operate AI at the scale of a bank, Itaú built IARA — a governance and orchestration platform that gives teams controlled access to different models in line with internal policies. OpenAI is among the model providers available in this environment.
This layer supports solutions such as the legal department’s, where the platform automates document reading, analysis, and interpretation. The solution operates on a repository of more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80% in stages of the department’s processes.
“It is essential that this information be preserved, remain within the bank’s context, and access models in a secure, governed way, with an understanding of token-use efficiency so that the entire solution is economically viable for the bank,” Mazzei says.
IARA addresses three problems at once: cost control per token, accuracy of responses, and application of responsible AI policies. In such a regulated sector, this makes it possible to move quickly while maintaining control.
“When we talk about Responsible AI at the bank, it is a discipline we take great care with,” he says. “We need customers to interact with the bank and our responses to align with our values and culture.” This includes reducing any risk of bias that may arise in frontier models.
Responsible AI principles guide the entire lifecycle of solutions, from development to continuous monitoring, aiming to ensure safety, transparency, ethics, and regulatory compliance as the technology scales.
“IARA is a fundamental platform, because it ensures we can have governance and observability in a highly regulated environment.”
—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú
AI First on the inside, too
The bank’s AI First strategy extends beyond end customers. The same intelligence layer that supports ia.i also assists specialists, managers, and customer service teams.
Mazzei describes a range extending from automating simple tasks to performing work that was previously unfeasible — but adds value to customer relationships: summaries before meetings, meeting preparation, understanding a specific issue, and developing plans and alternatives that were previously less obvious and time-consuming.
The bank has significant expectations for this implementation: three times more time available for customer relationships, service up to twice as fast, and conversations up to three times more effective.
“This set of tools in the hands of relationship managers allows us to focus on what matters most: creating value for our customers.”
—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú
Results overview
ia.i reached approximately 300,000 customers in its first phase, covering everything from convenient transactions to investment advice, activated by text or voice.
The IARA platform makes different models available to the bank’s teams with governance, observability, cost control per token, and enforcement of Responsible AI.
The legal solution operates on more than 90 million documents and executes more than 2 million tasks per month, with efficiency gains of 20% to 80%.
Using a range of models made it possible to serve both cost- and latency-sensitive cases and those requiring deeper reasoning; GPT‑5.x models are part of Customer DNA, which provides financial context for approximately 70 million customers.
Lessons for leaders
Measure the experience by its simplicity, rather than sophistication. The goal is for the technology to go unnoticed and the benefit to be apparent.
Choose a range of models, rather than a single one. Real journeys combine low-latency interactions with decisions that require reasoning.
Build the governance layer before scaling. Observability, cost control, and responsible AI make scale viable in regulated sectors.
Treat bias and cultural alignment as product requirements. Responses to customers must reflect the institution’s values.
Apply the strategy internally, too. Giving time back to teams frees up human relationships where they matter most.
Tips
Start with concrete everyday problems, such as a question about an account statement or a simple transaction.
Launch to an initial customer group and use it to learn actual behavior before expanding.
Centralize model access on one platform to maintain control over costs and quality.
Monitor token efficiency from day one — economic viability is part of the design.
Combine conversation and navigation: not every action is best handled through natural language.
Next steps
ia.i continues to evolve. The bank expects to make the experience available to its entire customer base by the end of 2026. Planned capabilities for the next stages include product simulations and sign-ups, as well as recurring financial analyses of income, expenses, and habits.
For Mazzei, the significance of the initiative goes beyond the product — the bank has navigated decades of transformation, with customers’ habits and expectations constantly changing.
“Leading the AI era is about responding faster to our customers’ needs. It is about understanding how technology can add value and help customers engage with financial products and services in a much simpler, more direct way that helps them achieve what they are seeking.”
—Carlos Eduardo Mazzei, CTO, Itaú

items.title: How Localiza reorganized work around generative AI
items.summary:
OpenAI
October 16, 2026
How Localiza reorganized work around generative AI
For the company, generative AI is more than a productivity layer: it is a new computing interface. That commitment takes shape across three areas—transforming the business, creating new customer interfaces, and building AI-native products.
Contact salesCompany size: EnterpriseRegion: Latin AmericaIndustry: TravelProducts: ChatGPT, API, CodexShare
A new kind of computing, not a new tool
When generative AI arrived, Localiza took a view that defined everything that followed: this was more than another piece of software in the toolkit; it was a change in the way the company operates.
Rather than pursuing isolated use cases, the company organized its collaboration with OpenAI around three strategic pillars: transforming the business through experimentation at scale, creating new customer interfaces, and building AI-native products. What connects all three is the decision to redesign processes around intelligence, context, and speed.
“We see this as a powerful tool that helps our teams do what they already do well. They live our culture, understand our customers’ needs, and know how to deliver great service.”
—André Petenussi, CTO, Localiza
Pillar 1: scale enables learning
The principle guiding internal adoption is straightforward: scale enables learning, and learning creates better products.
In practice, that meant distributing ChatGPT licenses as a resource for experimentation and productivity, rather than simply as an individual benefit. Teams across Localiza, from finance to day-to-day operations, maintain active experiments with custom GPTs, agents, and Codex.
Codex first arrived in the technology department—software engineers, product managers, designers, and data scientists. But adoption did not stop there: analysts, managers, PMOs, lawyers, and other business specialists began building their own prototypes and automations to test hypotheses within their areas of expertise.
This was an effect the company had not anticipated—a redefinition of the stages before development, with multidisciplinary teams prototyping solutions before they enter a development queue.
The bottleneck, he says, is human rather than technical.
“The big challenge is helping a large team learn new ways of working and build new skills, while ensuring that all 19 of our tribes and 130 squads work efficiently and consistently.”
—André Petenussi, CTO, Localiza
Pillar 2: customers describe their needs in natural language
The second area starts with an observation about behavior: people have begun describing what they need in natural language, creating a new entry point for mobility services—at the very moment they express their intent.
Localiza’s internal data confirms this shift: traffic originating from LLMs has been growing rapidly since 2024, with ChatGPT emerging as the main channel.
The company chose to establish a presence in this space early. In March 2026, it became Brazil’s first mobility platform—and one of the first in Latin America—to offer an app integrated directly into ChatGPT. Customers can explore rental, subscription, and used-car options and begin their journey in the conversation, before completing the transaction in Localiza’s secure environment.
“We believe we’ve been able to serve our customers in these new ways because we took on this challenge early and have kept learning at every step.”
—André Petenussi, CTO, Localiza
Internally, Localiza’s app in ChatGPT is treated as what it is: an experiment designed to keep the company close to the frontier of customer behavior, accelerate learning from real interactions, and explore how AI complements the existing ecosystem.
Pillar 3: Liza, a product designed around conversation
The company’s clearest example of an AI-native product is Liza, a conversational assistant that has become an established success story in its operations.
The difference from a traditional chatbot lies in the architecture, not the interface. Rather than following a fixed decision tree, Liza was built around conversation, intent, and context: it combines OpenAI models, Localiza services, and specialized tools to support key parts of the experience, from understanding the initial request to assisting with key stages of the rental journey.
The ambition is to handle repetitive journeys with quality and free teams for complex, higher-value interactions.
But success is not measured by the volume of automation.
Localiza was already mapping and measuring its customer service journeys before it had access to this type of technology—and that foundation made it possible to decide clearly where an agent should step in and where a human needs to intervene.
“We’ve always been committed to making the customer journey as seamless as possible, and we’ve developed metrics to measure the quality of that experience. We track conversion too, of course, but our main focus is the customer experience.”
—André Petenussi, CTO, Localiza
Liza also serves as a continuous learning loop: aggregated, monitored signals from interactions help identify needs, points of friction, and service opportunities. Combined with voice capabilities—voice-to-text and text-to-voice—these signals support its evolution from a transactional chatbot into an AI-native customer interface that can learn and scale across different mobility journeys.
“This frees up much of the team to tackle more meaningful problems with greater confidence and ease, helping us deliver on our mission for our customers.”
—André Petenussi, CTO, Localiza
Learning together, since GPT‑3.5
The partnership with OpenAI began early: the first version of Liza still ran on GPT‑3.5.
For Petenussi, the central value of the relationship lies in active learning between two companies evolving in parallel, rather than in a specific feature—with the partner understanding Localiza’s challenges and the different maturity levels of its capabilities, both within and outside technology.
It is an argument he often makes to other companies in the market: with a technology that is still maturing, trial and error and close collaboration have considerable value.
“We believe we’re still in the early years of a technology that is transforming markets, how we work, and how we use products and services. It will help shape our world over the next 5, 10, and 15 years.”
—André Petenussi, CTO, Localiza
Results overview
In March 2026, Localiza became the first company in Brazil, and one of the first in Latin America, to launch an app integrated directly into ChatGPT; more recently, it joined the platform’s advertising pilot in Brazil as an advertiser.
Traffic from LLMs has been growing rapidly since 2024, with ChatGPT as the main channel.
The Liza assistant operates with more than 60 specialized agents, built on reasoning models, MCP integration, and specialized tools that orchestrate the rental journey.
Teams across the company—from finance to operations—maintain active experiments with custom GPTs, agents, and Codex.
Codex reached the technology department and spread to business areas, with analysts, managers, PMOs, and lawyers building their own prototypes and automations.
The technology operation is organized into 19 tribes and 130 squads.
Lessons for leaders
Treat AI as a new operating model, rather than a productivity layer. The greatest gains come from redesigning processes around intelligence, context, and speed.
Use scale to generate learning. Simultaneous experiments at scale produce more organizational knowledge than a perfect pilot.
Take experimentation beyond technology. When lawyers, PMOs, and analysts prototype within their own areas, the nature of upstream work changes.
Map and measure your journeys before automating them. Having quality metrics in place enables you to decide where an agent should intervene and where a human is indispensable.
The adoption bottleneck is reskilling, not the model. Changing how hundreds of people work is harder—and more decisive—than integrating the technology.
Tips
Start with the customer’s problem and journey, rather than a model feature.
Allocate licenses as an experimentation budget, rather than an individual benefit.
Establish quality metrics before scaling conversational agents.
Treat a presence in new conversational channels as a learning experiment, rather than an acquisition campaign.
Close the loop: use the signals generated by each interaction to improve the product itself.
Next steps
Localiza’s ambition is to put AI at the center of its next experiences and processes—whether in how work is produced, the experience created for customers, or the resolution of an operational problem.
The next areas already being developed with OpenAI include the evolution of Liza and sales-focused agents, the establishment of conversational interfaces as a customer entry point, and the new cycle of agentic software development.
“The main focus is how we create better experiences. Whether that is to improve the profitability of our business, to ensure its health, or, above all, to create delightful experiences for our customers and our employees.”
—André Petenussi, CTO, Localiza
