items.title: How the Claude Code team does code review
items.summary:
How the Claude Code team does code review / claude.dev BlogEngineering
How the Claude Code team does code review
How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents.
AUTHORAddy Osmani, Morgan Westlee Lunt, and Qing WangCATEGORYEngineeringPUBLISHEDOct 15, 2026READING TIME14 minHow the Claude Code team does code reviewTREE└Rethinking the purpose of code review└The scarce resource: human time and attention└The life of a change└Layer by layer└How we make the reviewer better└Where humans stay in the loop└Sharing context across the team└"You land it, you own it"└When we change direction└How you can adopt this process└Where this is going░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░░00%14 MIN READSHAREX.comLinkedInEmailCopy URLCopy markdown
We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?
This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.
We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.
RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW
When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.
Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.
Code review does two jobs:
Find and fix issues before they ship
Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team
This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.
We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?"
Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.
Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.
THE SCARCE RESOURCE: HUMAN TIME AND ATTENTION
We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily.
Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second.
So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it.
THE LIFE OF A CHANGE
A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review.
The life of a changepngA typical Claude Code change, from the author's machine to usersFIG AMost of the path is automated; a person's attention goes where the risk is
LAYER BY LAYER
Layers, not one gatepngSix layers of checks, with rollback under themFIG BEach layer catches some problems and misses others. Few get through all of them, and rollback handles the rest.
1. The work is verified before anyone else looks
Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide.
Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines.
Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator."
When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as:
CLAUDE.md tells Claude what the project is: the stack, the conventions, the goals and the non-goals. Every review loads it, so in a large codebase we keep it short and point to other docs from there. The reviewer also flags code that breaks a convention in it, and changes that make a line in it out of date.
REVIEW.md, written by code owners, tells the reviewer what matters in their part of the code. We check separately whether the reviewer actually follows it. The good ones are short. They say what failure looks like in that repo (for docs it's "it lies," for config it's "it misroutes"), cap the nits, list paths to skip, and ask for a file and line as evidence instead of a guess from a name. They also ask for a summary that starts with a count and says plainly when there's nothing to fix.
2. AI review on every pull request
Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else?
On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally.
When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time.
Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault.
Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round.
3. Security review that can block
Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive.
If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code.
4. Automated checks that block
The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it.
5. Human approval, scaled by risk
A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review.
RiskExamplesHuman approvals
LowDocs, copy, internal-only features, additive changes behind a flagNone required once automated review and security checks are green
MediumOrdinary product changes, and changes to sensitive areas such as caching, the auto-updater, or system promptsOne person
HighThe highest-risk code, plus a small set of paths that always need two peopleTwo people
The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file.
Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human.
Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves.
An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again.
6. Merge queue, flags and a gradual release
The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it.
7. Fast detection, fast rollback
Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue.
Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges.
One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems.
HOW WE MAKE THE REVIEWER BETTER
Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop.
Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily.
Our incidents are the evalpngBuilt from past incidents and reverts, run every dayFIG CThe eval grows with every incident, and every change to the reviewer is scored against all of it.
We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second.
Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review.
Review has to converge. An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it.
When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round.
We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review:
A round cap. After three rounds, the reviewer asks the author to step back and reconsider the approach.
Diff-only re-review after the first few passes.
Flag the class of bug, so the author fixes every instance, not one line.
No repeats of findings already posted.
Review agents also run nightly over existing code, helping us catch old bugs before they show up somewhere else.
Review that convergespngInternal pull requests, before and after the convergence changesFIG DFewer review rounds per internal pull request after the convergence changes
WHERE HUMANS STAY IN THE LOOP
Pulling a senior engineer out of deep work to catch a routine mistake costs far more than an automated review. People on the team are still responsible for:
Deciding whether to build it. Direction, taste and scope. One team that declared its review bottleneck solved still kept human review for changes from outside the team, so someone asks "should we even do this?"
Reviewing risky code such as billing, the auto-updater and CI workflows.
Reviewing architecture that sets a pattern others will copy.
Reading the evidence. Test output, the command that ran and what it returned, a screenshot, the reviewer's findings. If you can't say what the checks would miss, ask for a real review rather than a quick approval.
Owning the outcome. A person is accountable for every change that ships, whoever typed it.
SHARING CONTEXT ACROSS THE TEAM
Code review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code?
We don't have a formal process for this. Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today.
Some of us go a step further and have Claude build a small artifact that visualizes that part of the code and teaches it the way that person likes to learn.
If the goal is to spend human attention well, this beats reading trivial diffs line by line. A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer for the module you're about to change teaches you a lot. Our culture of defaulting to working on open Slack channels helps too, since you see what others are building while they build it.
"YOU LAND IT, YOU OWN IT"
If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly:
Changes are small, so they're easy to review, debug and revert.
Everything is reversible. Flags, reverts and staged releases undo most mistakes in minutes.
Blast radius sets the bar. Expensive code gets more people and more checks.
Regressions surface fast through telemetry and internal use.
It isn't blame. Owning a fix means you have the most context; incident reviews look at the system.
Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line.
WHEN WE CHANGE DIRECTION
Agents make it cheap to start things, so some work shouldn't land. Usually someone in the channel asks why, points at an earlier decision, or suggests a simpler route, and the author closes or reshapes the PR.
Since the code was fast to write, closing the PR doesn't feel like a loss. The trick is to raise a different direction in the thread early, not as a blocking comment on a finished PR.
HOW YOU CAN ADOPT THIS PROCESS
Most of the pieces to do this with your team exist today.
Before the pull request
Give your agent checks it can run, listed in a short CLAUDE.md, plus hooks that run formatters and linters.
Run /code-review and /security-review locally, or a fresh-context subagent review.
Add a REVIEW.md, and move repeated review comments into it.
On every pull request
Require CI, and add "Testing", "Risk" and "How to revert" to your PR template.
Add an AI reviewer (Code Review for Claude Code, or the Claude Code GitHub Action) on one repo, tune REVIEW.md for a few weeks, then widen.
Add automated security review, and require every review thread resolved before merge.
Match review effort to risk: a quick pass on routine changes, a deep one where a missed bug is expensive (Quick, Standard or Deep in Code Review).
Cap review rounds; after the first few, re-review only the new diff.
Approval
Write down risk tiers, set from the change rather than the author; start strict and loosen with evidence.
Keep the lighter approval paths for authors you trust.
Use CODEOWNERS and branch protection so auth, billing, CI and release workflows, and installers always need a person.
Never let a bot's approval replace a required human's; dismiss approvals on new commits.
Merge and after
Use a merge queue, feature flags, internal use first, staged releases and one-step rollback.
Turn incidents and reverts into an eval set, and rescore the reviewer whenever its prompts, tools or model change.
Measure human time, with revert and incident rates as the guardrail.
WHERE THIS IS GOING
Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving.
When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a CLAUDE.md, a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before.
If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong.
With thanks to Emma Webb, Michael Segner and Amie Rotherham for their reviews.

items.title: Navan cuts a month-long migration down to a week, without freezing the codebase
items.summary:
Blog / customersOct 16, 2026·customers
Navan cuts a month-long migration down to a week, without freezing the codebase
Navan's latest migration touched 8 applications and 15 libraries and finished in about a week, without freezing development.
4 min readContact sales
Navan is a global AI-powered business travel and expense management company.
~1 weekTime to complete a Spring Boot migration across 8 apps and 15 libraries.~200Engineers actively using Cursor's Cloud Agents, a 10x increase since April 2026.36%Share of merged core-repo pull requests authored with Cursor over a 30-day period.
Navan is a global AI-powered business travel and expense management company.
~1 weekTime to complete a Spring Boot migration across 8 apps and 15 libraries.~200Engineers actively using Cursor's Cloud Agents, a 10x increase since April 2026.36%Share of merged core-repo pull requests authored with Cursor over a 30-day period.
Navan's most recent migration touched 8 applications and 15 libraries, and finished in about a week without freezing development. Two years ago, a comparable migration took over a month, and a bad merge locked the master branch for a day. The difference is Cursor's Cloud Agents, which let Navan plan the migration once and run it across 8 applications in parallel on its own self-hosted machines, instead of one engineer working through it alone.
#An 8-app migration finishes in a week instead of a month
Two years ago, moving Navan's codebase to a new Spring version took Rahul Popuri, Sr. Staff Software Engineer, over a month. Incomplete pushes and reverts locked the master branch for a day during that stretch. The disruption didn't end when the lock lifted: other engineers were still catching up on landing changes days later. The bigger cost wasn't the lock itself. It was the month of an engineer's time spent on the migration instead of shipping features or fixing bugs.
Navan's most recent migration, to Spring Boot 4, finished in about a week, with less disruption to ongoing development. With Cursor, Rahul planned the upgrade in advance, then delegated each component to Cloud Agents running on Navan's self-hosted machines, so 8 applications and 15 libraries moved at the same time instead of one after another. The agents used Navan's internal tooling and spun up browsers on those same machines to click through flows and verify their changes.
In the past, one bad merge brought workstreams to a standstill. This time I had eight apps moving at once while minimizing any disruption to ongoing development.
Rahul PopuriSr. Staff Software Engineer, Navan
Rahul wasn't watching a single job run. He was monitoring multiple agents upgrading different applications at once, a scale of parallel work he says wouldn't have been possible even a few months earlier.
#Cloud Agents run the real workload
Rahul moved almost all of his work onto Cursor's Cloud Agents. GitHub work runs on Cursor-managed infrastructure. Internal MCPs for Snowflake and Slack run on Navan's own self-hosted machines, where agents can also spin up a browser to verify their own changes. Automations, Skills, and Memories run on top of that setup, so eval loops and migrations continue asynchronously without someone watching them.
That pattern has since scaled well past one engineer: roughly 200 people at Navan now actively use Cursor's Cloud Agents, a 10x increase since April 2026.
Before Cursor, Navan's engineers had built real infrastructure around their previous coding agent, but it required someone at one desktop with the session open the whole time. That ruled out the parallel, asynchronous work Navan needed.
#The same leverage shows up on product teams
On the product side, Elton Yang, Staff Software Engineer on expense and billing, builds new agents for expense and billing workflows starting from a plain description. Cursor follows the team's existing design patterns and writes the agent's prompts itself, which means testing starts the same day instead of after hours spent writing the initial prompt by hand.
We don't even have to write out the agent prompt ourselves anymore. Cursor follows our prior designs and gets an agent working the same day.
Elton YangStaff Software Engineer, Navan
That shift changed what a small team can carry. After many engineers moved off Navan's dedicated AI-agent team, one engineer took over feature work that previously needed 2 or 3 engineers across multiple sprints. One of the clearest examples is manual bank linking: the one engineer recreated an Angular form in React and built the backend to connect it, moving from backend-only into full-stack work when the task required it. The individually owned workstream stayed focused on new features instead of sliding into pure maintenance.
Cursor also changed what covering for a teammate looks like. When Elton had to take over two codebases he did not know well while a colleague was on leave, Cursor handled the investigation for him, pulling logs and database records and laying out the issue before Elton opened a single file.
I wasn't too familiar with either codebase. I said, 'Here is the issue, help me figure this out.' It pulled the logs and the database and walked me through it like I had been living in that repo for months.
Elton YangStaff Software Engineer, Navan
This saved roughly two days of ramp-up time across the two codebases, plus the stress of learning them cold.
Review still rests with people. Elton treats the agent as a pair programmer, not a coding oracle: he watches the agent's reasoning as it runs and corrects wrong assumptions as soon as he sees them. Once code is generated, it goes through the same human and AI review, testing, and staging process as anything else, and complex changes are verified in staging before production. Agents plan and execute the work, but engineers make the judgment calls and own the final merge.
If you're running migrations or parallel workstreams that used to need a full team and a locked codebase, reach out to start a Cursor trial.

items.title: See Your Runner's Desktop
items.summary: You can now see and control your macOS or Linux runner's desktop. This is nice for trying native apps that Amp builds for you, such as iOS apps: Turn on Share This Mac's Display under Settings › Runner in the macOS app, or start your runner with amp --no-tui --desktop. Your Amp client connects directly to the runner, so it's nearly instant when the runner is on your local network or nearby. Read See and Control the Runner's Desktop for more details.

items.summary:

Stack Overflow for Agents triples signups with ChatGPT plugin
Two engineers shipped Stack Overflow for Agents in a few weeks with Codex, and its ChatGPT plugin helped drive up to 10× growth in agent creation.

More signups for Stack Overflow for Agents overnight with the ChatGPT plugin

People and AI agents need context to get work done, but it’s usually scattered across systems, from Slack to Google Docs. Finding it and understanding how it all fits together can be a challenge.
That’s why Stack Overflow⁠(opens in a new window) is building a knowledge intelligence platform that unifies those sources and turns raw context into verified knowledge available wherever people and agents work.
OpenAI models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6 Sol power the platform’s AI, with tasks routing to different models based on the reasoning required and cost. Codex helps the company’s engineers build the products, while a ChatGPT plugin makes their newer agentic product, Stack Overflow for Agents, easier to discover and use.
“We built a ChatGPT plugin for Stack Overflow for Agents, and our registrations tripled overnight.”
—Alexandra Lato, VP of Product, Stack Overflow
Two engineers ship a net-new product in a few weeks with Codex
Stack Overflow for Agents, which extends Stack’s intelligence layer to agents, began with a hypothesis and two engineers using Codex. The engineers gave Codex a development environment and a plan, and then worked with it to build the product. Within a few weeks, Alex says, they had a full-fledged product.
“So it really made their team feel bigger,” Alex says. “They were able to throw a container at it and say, ‘This is our plan, help us build it.’”
Developing connectors in days, not weeks, with Codex
Stack Internal, Stack Overflow’s enterprise product, needs to connect to all the systems where organizations keep their knowledge. Building this capability requires more human involvement than the two-engineer effort behind Stack Overflow for Agents, but Codex is accelerating this work, too.
Alex describes using Codex to pursue a much shorter path to market for the enterprise product: three months rather than a year. Building connectors is one concrete example.
“On average, it takes us 3 to 6 weeks to build one connector. With Codex, we were able to build it within 4 days.”
—Alexandra Lato, VP of Product, Stack Overflow
More recently, the team built a connector in a single day. By accelerating connectors, Codex helps Stack Overflow bring enterprise products to market faster.
Increasing agent creation and signups with a ChatGPT plugin
Once Stack Overflow for Agents was ready for distribution, the team needed a way to get it into people’s workflows. It built a ChatGPT plugin so users could discover and set up the product in ChatGPT, with fewer steps than a traditional Model Context Protocol (MCP) setup.
“Once you have a plugin, it becomes a frictionless setup with ChatGPT.”
—Alexandra Lato, VP of Product, Stack Overflow
Alex says the plugin tripled registrations and accelerated agent creation: “I think we were up to 10X last time I checked.”
Reducing configuration work with the Decisions API
Stack Overflow manages its own model routing and configuration, but Alex hopes to explore using the Decisions API to reduce some of that work and put more engineering capacity into the product.
“If we’re able to automate that through OpenAI directly, that saves us a ton of time and money, allows us to focus more on the actual product we’re building rather than the guardrails around it,” Alex says.
Expanding across the full knowledge lifecycle
Stack Overflow is also working on expanding its knowledge product to enable sharing of what people learn. To date, its focus has been pulling information in. Now, Alex is closing the loop so knowledge gained in a one-to-one session with a developer or someone outside engineering can help others, too.
“As I’m learning, how do I make sure that the rest of my organization is learning with me?”, said Alex. “I’m really looking forward to building a product that allows for that full knowledge life cycle.”

items.title: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale
Published
October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 82
+76
ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow
Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license.
Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model.
Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it.
TL;DR
501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token.
Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens.
Checkpoint formats: BF16, FP8, and NVFP4
Reasoning that can stay in context across turns (preserve_thinking), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max".
Response template in the tokenizer.
Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2
Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles.
Ships with a Rust-based custom harness.
Apache 2.0.
Build with Beam
Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub:
You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces
You could quantize it for your favorite hardware
You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem
You could build an RL environment with or for Beam
You could benchmark Beam and share the results.
You could surprise us!
If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts.
What is Beam?
Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one.
Attention
The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones.
Inside the attention block (both layer types)
The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding. Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1. It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling.
Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection.
Mixture of Experts
The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters.
The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5.
Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips.
If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below.
Residual Stream
The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth.
Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k). The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state.
Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap.
Long Context
Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate.
Context
If all 52 layers were global

Benchmark Results
Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team.

Hardware Requirements
The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell.
A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection.
Inference Support
Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM.
Transformers
Install the latest version of transformers.
pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1"
The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline:
from transformers import pipeline
pipe = pipeline(
"text-generation", model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B", device_map="auto"
)
messages = [
{"role": "user", "content": "Write a limerick about Python exceptions."}
]
output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens=2000)
output[0]["generated_text"][-1]
The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template.
Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer.
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
model_id, dtype="auto", device_map="auto"
)
Chat
messages = [
{"role": "system", "content": "You should only answer with a number."},
{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 * 23?"},
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
messages,
add_generation_prompt=True,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
return_tensors="pt",
reasoning_effort="medium" # by default
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=2000)
tokenizer.parse_response(
outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0]
)
Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see.
Tool calling
Complete tool-calling example
def get_weather(city: str, unit: str = "celsius"):
"""
Get the current weather for a city.
Args:
city: The city to look up.
unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit".
"""
...
tools = [get_weather]
messages = [
{"role": "user", "content": "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?"}
]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
messages,
tools=tools,
add_generation_prompt=True,
tokenize=True,
return_dict=True,
return_tensors="pt",
).to(model.device)
input_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[-1]
outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=1000)
message = tokenizer.parse_response(
outputs[0][input_len:], prefix=inputs["input_ids"][0], tools=tools
)
message.get("tool_calls")
Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type.
Multi-GPU and multi-node
Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig:
import os
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
"reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B",
distributed_config=DistributedConfig(
tp_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), ep_size=int(os.environ["WORLD_SIZE"]), tp_plan={}
),
)
Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256.
vLLM
Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API:
vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam
For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter:
vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
--tensor-parallel-size 16 \
--speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }'
Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1. For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM.
SGLang
Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s:
python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 4 \
--attention-backend trtllm_mha \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000
On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell):
python -m sglang.launch_server \
--model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \
--served-model-name beam \
--tp 8 \
--attention-backend fa3 \
--page-size 64 \
--context-length 1048576 \
--mem-fraction-static 0.85 \
--enable-unified-memory \
--speculative-algorithm DFLASH \
--speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \
--speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \
--tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \
--host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000
Inference Providers
Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon.
import os
from openai import OpenAI
client = OpenAI(
base_url="https://router.huggingface.co/v1",
api_key=os.environ["HF_TOKEN"],
)
completion = client.chat.completions.create(
model="reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto",
messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the capital of France?"}],
)
print(completion.choices[0].message)
Inference Endpoints
We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4, or install with the hf cli like so:
hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam
What we tested
We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses.
Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket.
Category
Prompt Description
Low reasoning (tokens)
High reasoning (tokens)

Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket, rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit.
Post-training Beam
You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.
SFT with TRL
The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters:
We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen.
The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes.
After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself.
Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR.
GRPO with Miles
Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe.
Workload
Reference configuration
Inference / eval, BF16
16x H200 per engine
Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles)
96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated.
LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles)
32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout.
Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles)
48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint.
The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes:
docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam .
python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \
--model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \
--model-dir /root/models/Beam \
--data-dir /data/datasets
export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1
export RAY_ADDRESS=http://${MASTER_ADDR}:8265
python scripts/run_beam.py execute \
--model-dir /root/models/Beam \
--data-dir /data/datasets \
--output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
--num-rollout 100
What happens in a rollout:
Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each.
Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit.
Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty.
Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute.
Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch.
Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty.
The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn.
Train with LoRA
You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading.
python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \
--model-dir /root/models/Beam \
--data-dir /data/datasets \
--output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \
--num-rollout 100
Build with Beam: Demos
If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page. To inspire you, here are a few things we built.
Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application!
At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out.
We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text.
Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account.
Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery.
We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements.
You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace. If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions.
Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents?
We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API.
For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset.
Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes.
You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard, explore the published result data, and reuse the study harness.
Hey Beam, finetune a decision model for my code base!
Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage.
We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly.
First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster.
For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup.
If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results.
Wrapping Up
Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8, NVFP4. If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab.

items.title: Amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine
items.summary:
Amazon Polly Generative engine now offers more natural and accurate speech output. We’re introducing an upgrade to the Amazon Polly Generative engine that delivers more expressive, more accurate speech output with low latency. The upgrade adds 14 new voices across 9 locales, including general availability of Generative voices in Hindi and Finnish for the first time. The upgrade is now generally available in production.
Importantly, this is a drop-in upgrade for existing generative voices. Voice names and API calls are unchanged, so your existing applications continue to work as they do today.
Amazon Polly is a fully managed AWS service that converts text into natural-sounding speech for contact centers, large language model (LLM)-based agentic applications, media and entertainment, e-learning, accessibility, and other applications that require reliable voice output at scale.
Hear the difference
You can use sample audio to evaluate the improvements directly.
The more natural, authentic, and expressive voices. Hear how Tiffany welcomes you in a delightful tone.
“Hi there! I’m Tiffany, one of Polly’s generative voices. I was built to sound natural, expressive, and a little bit delightful. What should we talk about?”
Accurate speech generation for numbers, currency, addresses, and so on. Kenneth reads back an order confirmation, including the tracking number, date and time, currency and address accurately.
“Thanks for calling. Your order, number 4471 9902 ships today to 85 Harbor View Drive, Apartment 4B, Portland, Oregon 97209. It should arrive on Thursday, October 22nd, between 9 AM and 1 PM. Your total was $1,284.50 and your confirmation code is K-7-Q-2-X-9.”
Net new languages. Arjun and Kiara for Hindi, and Suvi for Finnish. Hindi and Finnish are generally available for the first time on the Amazon Polly Generative engine.
Arjun: नमस्कार, आप सुन रहे हैं आज की मुख्य ख़बरें। देश के कई हिस्सों में मानसून की विदाई के साथ मौसम सुहाना हो गया है। (Hello, you’re listening to today’s top stories. As the monsoon retreats across much of the country, the weather has turned pleasant.)
Kiara: नमस्ते! मेरा नाम कियारा है। आइए, आज मैं आपको एक छोटी सी कहानी सुनाती हूँ।(Hello! My name is Kiara. Come, let me tell you a little story today.)
Suvi: Majakanvartija ei ollut nähnyt laivaa yhteentoista päivään. Sitten, vähän puolenyön jälkeen, horisontissa välähti yksi ainoa valo. Kerran. Kahdesti. Ja sitten, uskomatonta kyllä, se vilkutti takaisin hänen nimensä. (The lighthouse keeper hadn’t seen a ship in eleven days. Then, just after midnight, a single light blinked on the horizon. Once. Twice. And then, impossibly, it blinked back his name.)
Different styles of speech delivery based on textual context. Powered by the new Amazon Polly Generative engine, the voices can reflect emotion and prosody even better based on the text input, without manual setup.
Neutral: “Your package arrived early.”
Uncertainty: “So, um… your package arrived early. I think?”
Surprised: “Wait, what? Your package arrived early?”
New voices, languages, and Region availability
A larger catalog overall for Amazon Polly Generative engine – Totaling 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales.
14 new voices across 9 locales – US English (Kenneth, Nate), Australian English (Russell, Curtis), Indian English (Kiara, Arjun), German (Tina), US Spanish (Carlos), Brazilian Portuguese (Leo, Carolina), Korean (Hyunduk), Hindi (Kiara, Arjun) and Finnish (Suvi).
Net new languages generally available in Generative engine – Hindi and Finnish.
Region expansion to AWS GovCloud (US-West) – Totaling 11 AWS Regions.
Built for production-ready speech workflows for enterprise
The upgraded Amazon Polly Generative engine uses a standard Amazon Polly API call to build your speech applications. With Amazon Polly, you can continue to build with familiar AWS patterns: call the same Amazon Polly API, manage access with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), use the output in your existing applications and contact-center flows, and monitor the workloads that synthesize speech for your customers.
This launch is designed to elevate the speech output quality that you can hear with your existing Amazon Polly implementation. No changes to your code are required to get the upgraded voices. For applications that already use Amazon Polly Generative voices, the upgrade happens in place. For new applications, the same SynthesizeSpeech API gives you access to a larger set of generative voice catalogs. With the Bi-Di Streaming API StartSpeechSynthesisStream, you can stream text to Amazon Polly and receive synthesized audio back simultaneously. This is well-suited for real-time applications like voice agents and bespoke characters in games.
Competitive price-performance
The Amazon Polly Generative engine offers competitive pricing on a pay-as-you-go basis. With this model upgrade, you get improved voice quality and accuracy at the same price. There’s no cost increase, no new SKU, and no changes to your existing integration. You can cache and replay synthesized static prompts with no additional cost. Refer to Amazon Polly pricing for complete cost information.
The Amazon Polly Generative engine now delivers more natural, expressive speech alongside low-latency streaming for real-time applications, Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) support for fine-grained control, and the operational reliability of a fully managed AWS service. This combination of quality, performance, and cost efficiency supports a wide range of production use cases.
What you can build
Contact centers. Accuracy matters most in customer service conversations. When a caller checks an order, a voice that reads back the tracking number, address, and confirmation code correctly helps resolve the call in self-service rather than escalating to a human agent. Amazon Polly Generative voice’s accurate entity pronunciation and low-latency generation make automated interactive voice response (IVR) interactions sound more conversational.
Cascaded voice agents. Using Amazon Polly in a voice agent framework, you can convert LLM response text into clear, natural-sounding speech and stream it back to users in near real time over WebSockets or telephony channels. This makes live conversational voice possible. The primary benefits are low-latency playback, high scalability, and cost efficiency.
Media, localization, and dubbing. Convert scripts into finished audio for video, advertising, podcasts, product overviews, and audiobooks. You can use one voice or many, without a studio session. More natural intonation reduces post-production. The expanded locale coverage, including first-time generative Hindi and Finnish, means you can localize a single piece of content into more markets from the same pipeline.
E-learning and training. Narrate courseware, onboarding, and knowledge-based articles at scale, and update them as soon as the source text changes. No re-recording is required. More expressive delivery supports engagement through long-form material.
Accessibility. Provide a clear, natural spoken version of articles, documents, and applications so more people can consume your content by listening: read aloud, on the go, or with a screen reader.
Interactive and transactional experiences. Voice-enable games, kiosks, IVR menus, and IoT devices with responses generated on demand. Use Amazon Polly when the voice needs to sound natural and read names, numbers, product details, addresses, and confirmations reliably.
“At Sanoma Media Finland, we use Amazon Polly to turn our real-time news articles into audio, giving the listener the choice to listen whenever it suits them better. Today we publish over 10,000 articles per month using Polly’s Finnish neural voice. Based on our testing, Suvi’s new generative voice is a clear improvement over the previous neural voice – it sounds noticeably more natural and makes for a more enjoyable experience for the listener.”
— Justus Reinikainen, Product Manager, Sanoma Media Finland
Getting started
You can access the new voices using the AWS Management Console, AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), or the AWS SDKs.
Prerequisites:
Active AWS account with Amazon Polly access.
AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) installed and configured.
Python 3.10+.
Boto3 installed: pip install boto3.
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions: polly:SynthesizeSpeech.
Here’s a quick example using the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with the SynthesizeSpeech API and a generative voice:
import boto3
polly = boto3.client("polly", region_name="us-east-1")
response = polly.synthesize_speech(
Text="Hello! This is Amazon Polly's next-generation generative voice.",
VoiceId="Kenneth", # any generative voice in the catalogue
Engine="generative",
OutputFormat="mp3",
)
with open("speech.mp3", "wb") as f:
f.write(response["AudioStream"].read())
You can also make the same request with the AWS CLI:
aws polly synthesize-speech \
--region us-east-1 \
--voice-id Kenneth \
--engine generative \
--output-format mp3 \
--text "Hello! This is Amazon Polly's next-generation generative voice." \
speech.mp3
To retrieve the full, current voice list programmatically, call DescribeVoices. You can use this in deployment checks to confirm that a selected generative voice is available in the Region where your application runs.
Availability
The next-generation Generative engine and the new voices are now generally available. The 14 new Generative voices are available in the following AWS Regions: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Zurich), Europe (London), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Canada (Central), and AWS GovCloud (US-West). Getting started, by audience:
Developers – Call synthesize_speech with Engine="generative" in your existing application. No other changes are required.
Contact-center teams – The improvements reach Amazon Connect and Genesys flows automatically.
Everyone – Access any voice in the Amazon Polly console.
A few things to know:
Standard and neural voices are unaffected.
Speech marks are not available on generative voices (unchanged from today). If your application requires them, standard and neural voices continue to support them.
Generative engine continues to support SSML tags. See supported SSML tags for more details.
Use current voice availability at runtime. Call DescribeVoices or check the console when deploying across Regions.
Conclusion
The next-generation Generative engine of Amazon Polly is available today, delivering more natural and more accurate voices, adding 14 new voices, including generative voices generally available in Hindi and Finnish for the first time, and requires no change to your code. See Amazon Polly pricing page for pricing information. To get started, open the Amazon Polly console to try the voices, and see the Amazon Polly documentation to build with them.

items.title: How IskayPet unified corporate knowledge with Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases
items.summary:
IskayPet’s office teams had a knowledge challenge. Answers to everyday operational questions, such as a return policy, a veterinary protocol, or an onboarding step, lived in hundreds of Microsoft SharePoint documents spread across four languages and three countries. Finding the right information in large document repositories took a long time. Every new store, country, or procedure made the problem bigger.
Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) is the usual way to solve this. But running RAG in production normally means operating vector databases, embedding pipelines, and ingestion jobs yourself.
In this post, we show how IskayPet, a leading pet care company in Iberia, built a corporate knowledge assistant on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases. The assistant answers employee questions across retail operations, veterinary care, people and onboarding, and procurement, in four languages and across three countries, with no RAG infrastructure to manage. The team built the whole solution, from the store-facing frontend to the AWS architecture and deployment, using Kiro with Claude Haiku 4.5. We cover the architecture, the SharePoint integration, the retrieval configuration decisions, and the results in production.
About IskayPet
IskayPet is a leading pet care company in Iberia. It operates more than 330 stores across Spain, Portugal, and France under the Kiwoko, Tiendanimal, Kivet, Clinicanimal and Animalis brands. With more than 4,500 employees and 7 million customers, IskayPet runs operations that span retail, veterinary clinics, animal care, procurement, and people and onboarding. Each area has its own policies and procedures, in Spanish, Portuguese, French, and English.
The challenge
Across every business area, IskayPet office staff searched hundreds of SharePoint documents by hand to answer operational questions about procedures, policies, contracts, and onboarding. With operations in three countries and four languages, this took real time, and the answer was often outdated or wrong.
There was no reliable way to query corporate knowledge, and the problem grew with every country, area, or document added. IskayPet needed a solution that could do the following:
Answer natural-language questions grounded in their own corporate documents.
Work across four languages without maintaining separate systems.
Route each question to the right body of knowledge (an area, a country) without cross-contamination.
Scale to new areas and countries without re-architecting.
Cite its sources so employees can trust and verify answers.
Reuse their existing SharePoint repositories without a costly migration.
Why Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases
IskayPet chose Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases for its managed RAG infrastructure, which removed the need to run vector stores, embeddings, or ingestion pipelines. The main reasons were:
Managed RAG: Amazon Bedrock handles data ingestion, multimodal parsing, vector storage, embedding generation, and retrieval. IskayPet pays only for what it stores and retrieves.
Native SharePoint connector: The connector ingests documents directly from IskayPet’s existing SharePoint environment, which avoided a data migration. With advanced indexing enabled, it also processes content from images embedded in documents.
Built-in hybrid search: Combining semantic and keyword (BM25) search at no extra cost recovers exact terms, such as product codes and references, that pure semantic search can miss.
Managed reranking: Retrieved passages are reordered by relevance at no additional charge.
Document-level access control: The knowledge base can enforce the source system’s own permissions at retrieval time, so a query returns only passages from documents the requesting user is already allowed to read. This lets IskayPet reuse SharePoint permissions instead of rebuilding an authorization model.
Model flexibility: IskayPet can start with a cost-effective model and change it later without rewriting infrastructure.
Native RAG evaluation: The team measured quality at each step with the built-in evaluation tools.
Solution overview
The following diagram shows the end-to-end flow, from the employee’s question through permission-aware retrieval to the grounded, cited answer.
Figure 1: Solution architecture
The solution is an assistant that employees reach through their existing channels. When an employee asks a question, the assistant retrieves the most relevant passages from its knowledge base, restricted to the documents the employee is allowed to read. It then generates a grounded, cited answer in the employee’s language.
At a high level, the flow works as follows:
An employee submits a natural-language question through the chat interface.
The application calls the knowledge base for the requested assistant, passing the employee’s identity so that document-level permissions are applied to the retrieval.
The knowledge base runs hybrid search (semantic and keyword) over the indexed content, reranks the results, and returns the most relevant passages with their source references.
A foundation model (FM) generates a grounded answer from the retrieved passages. The prompt requires source citation and tells the model to say when the answer isn’t in the retrieved content.
The employee receives the answer along with the source documents and can leave feedback (thumbs up or down) that feeds the evaluation set.
Building the solution with Kiro and Claude Haiku 4.5
IskayPet built the whole solution, from the store-facing frontend to the AWS architecture and service deployment, using Kiro, the agentic development environment, running on Claude Haiku 4.5 on Amazon Bedrock. As new models become available on Amazon Bedrock, IskayPet plans to evaluate and adopt them for each use case.
For model availability by AWS Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
Store-facing frontend – The team used Kiro to build the frontend that store employees use to interact with the assistant, generating and iterating on the UI code with Claude Haiku 4.5.
Architecture and deployment – Kiro also helped design the AWS architecture and provision the services behind the solution: knowledge base configuration, data sources, AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, and the application layer.
An agentic workflow with Kiro and a fast, cost-effective model like Claude Haiku 4.5 helped a small team move from concept to production quickly. It also kept the application code and the infrastructure consistent and maintainable.
Ingestion: The SharePoint connector with advanced indexing
IskayPet’s documents already lived in SharePoint, organized by area and country. Rather than migrate them, the team used the native SharePoint connector in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases.
In the data source’s Advanced configurations, under Content indexing and Advanced indexing, IskayPet enabled Visual content in documents. This setting extracts content from images embedded in documents (PDF, DOCX, PPTX) and from standalone images. Figures and scanned content inside procedure documents became searchable without a separate preprocessing pipeline.
The connector syncs incrementally, so new and updated documents are picked up on each sync.
Multi-country, multi-area architecture
A key design decision was how to structure knowledge for four languages, several business areas, and three countries. IskayPet weighed two approaches:
A single shared knowledge base, with every document tagged by country and area and a retrieval filter applied per query. This maximizes reuse of shared content but couples all domains into one index.
A dedicated knowledge base per assistant, each scoped to the relevant SharePoint sites or libraries. This keeps each body of knowledge isolated end to end and lets each assistant be tuned independently.
IskayPet chose a knowledge base per assistant. Each assistant points at specific SharePoint sites and can be narrowed further to specific document libraries or folders through inclusion paths, so it indexes only the intended content and not the whole corporate site. Adding a new area or country means adding an assistant and pointing it at the right content, not re-architecting the system.
Access control
Access is governed by the users’ existing SharePoint permissions. The assistant doesn’t grant access to anything new: It only makes it more straightforward to query documents an employee could already open. This works on two levels.
Which assistants a user sees – An employee is shown only the assistants whose underlying documentation they’re entitled to read, whether that entitlement comes from direct permission, group membership, or access to a specific folder. If access can’t be confirmed, the assistant is hidden rather than shown.
Which documents inform an answer – Access is enforced again at retrieval time, per document: The employee’s identity is passed to the knowledge base, which returns passages only from documents that person is authorized to see. Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases supports this document-level access control natively, so the same answer to the same question can legitimately differ between two employees with different permissions.
Because permissions are read from SharePoint on every access check, revoking or granting access in SharePoint is reflected in the assistant without changes to the application.
Retrieval and generation configuration
The quality of a RAG system is decided mainly at ingestion, retrieval, and generation. Fine-tuning is a complementary technique. For this use case, IskayPet tuned the following settings:
Chunking – Handled by the managed knowledge base, so the team didn’t build or tune a chunking pipeline. This removed a component that’s usually significant operational effort in a self-managed RAG.
Hybrid search – The knowledge base combines semantic and keyword retrieval, which recovers exact terms such as product codes that pure semantic search can miss.
Number of results – Tuned against an evaluation set. The assistant retrieves 25 passages and, after removing duplicates and fragments too short to add context, injects up to 15 into the prompt. This number is the main cost lever, because it multiplies input tokens on every question.
Generation prompt – Enforces a corporate tone, requires source citation, and tells the model to say when the answer isn’t in the retrieved content, which reduces hallucination and adds traceability.
As a production control, the team is adding Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to apply content filtering and responsible AI policies to the generated answers.
Evaluation– Native Amazon Bedrock RAG evaluation, using the thumbs up and down feedback from real usage as an evaluation set to measure quality before and after each change.
Generating the response
For answer generation, IskayPet uses a cost-effective foundation model on Amazon Bedrock. Because the knowledge base decouples retrieval from generation, IskayPet can switch or upgrade the generation model without touching the ingestion or retrieval layers. This lets the team balance cost and answer quality as usage grows.
Cost efficiency
The knowledge base includes multimodal parsing, embedding generation, and reranking at no additional charge, so IskayPet’s ongoing cost comes mainly from index storage, retrieval API calls, and generation-model tokens. In production, input tokens dominate that cost, because of the passages injected into each prompt. The team is evaluating further optimizations as usage grows, including prompt caching for the stable part of the prompt and batch inference for non-interactive workloads.
Results
In roughly the first two months in production, IskayPet has seen:
Faster answers – Time to find an operational answer dropped from 3–5 minutes to about 7 seconds.
Higher productivity – Around 95 percent less time spent searching for procedures and policies.
Scale – The solution is expected to handle roughly 100,000 queries per month across all business areas and countries.
Conclusion
IskayPet built a production corporate knowledge assistant on Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Bases that serves three countries, four languages, and several business areas, with no RAG infrastructure to run. The native SharePoint connector reused their existing repositories. A dedicated knowledge base per assistant gave them a clean multi-country design with each domain isolated end to end. Managed parsing, embedding, and reranking kept both operational effort and cost low. Building the frontend and the AWS architecture with Kiro and Claude Haiku 4.5 lets a small team reach production quickly.
If you’re facing a similar knowledge-retrieval challenge, you can start on the AWS Free Tier and build your first knowledge base on the Amazon Bedrock console. To go deeper, see the following resources and try the SharePoint connector and document-level access control against your own documents.
To learn more, see Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base and Evaluate the performance of RAG sources using Amazon Bedrock evaluations.

Daniel is a Senior Solutions Architect at AWS, where he has been focused on guiding enterprise customers in Iberia in their cloud adoption, as well as implementing artificial intelligence use cases. He is passionate about solving complex business challenges with cloud technology.
