items.title: Pegasus 1.5 from TwelveLabs is now available in Amazon Bedrock
items.summary:
On Oct 9, 2026 we announced the availability of TwelveLabs’ Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock. Pegasus 1.5 is a video language model that turns long-form video into structured, timestamped metadata. You describe the moments that matter to your workflow, and the model returns every matching segment as JSON.
Video represents a significant and complex category of unstructured data, yet most of it remains unsearchable and underutilized. Extracting structured, actionable insights from that content has historically required labor-intensive manual review or fragmented toolchains.
With earlier versions of Pegasus, you can point the model at a clip, ask a question, and get an answer. Now, Pegasus 1.5 analyzes the entire video, finds every segment that matches user-defined criteria, and returns structured, timestamped metadata. It also introduces video segmentation, multimodal prompting with reference images, and on-the-fly processing.
With Pegasus 1.5 on Amazon Bedrock, you can analyze videos directly from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) URI or a base64 string with no pre-indexing required, and your data remains within the AWS data boundary.
In this post, we cover what’s new in Pegasus 1.5, how the model is packaged on Amazon Bedrock, and how to send your first request. We then walk through video segmentation, structured JSON output, and multimodal prompting.
What’s new in Pegasus 1.5
Pegasus 1.5 has the following changes compared to previous versions:
Time-based metadata generation. You define the segments, events, or domain-specific cues that matter to your workflow, such as editorial segments, sports plays, speaker changes, or brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns every matching segment as JSON, with start and end times and the requested fields populated.
Multimodal prompting. A segment definition can combine a text description with a visual reference. This makes it possible to locate a specific product, logo, or person, along with what they are doing on screen.
On-the-fly processing. No ingestion pipeline or pre-indexing step is required. Videos are sent directly from Amazon S3 and results are returned in the response.
Extended processing capacity. Pegasus 1.5 analyzes videos up to two hours long in a single request, up from one hour in Pegasus 1.2.
Pegasus 1.5 retains and enhances the core capabilities that made Pegasus 1.2 a powerful tool for video understanding, including:
Video-to-text generation: Creates detailed textual descriptions based on video content.
Granular visual comprehension: Analyzes objects, on-screen text, and numerical content within video frames.
Temporal grounding: Accurately identifies timestamps of specific events within videos.
Multimodal understanding: Combines visual, audio, and textual information for comprehensive analysis.
Multilingual support: Full support for English, with partial support for Arabic, Chinese, French, German, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese, Russian, Spanish, Thai, and Vietnamese.
How Pegasus 1.5 works on Amazon Bedrock
Pegasus 1.5 takes a video and either a text prompt or a set of segment definitions, and returns text or JSON. You call it on the bedrock-runtime endpoint with the InvokeModel API, or with InvokeModelWithResponseStream when you want the response streamed as it’s generated.
Setting
Value
Model ID
twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0
AWS Region
US West (Oregon), us-west-2
Inference
On-demand
APIs
InvokeModel, InvokeModelWithResponseStream
Each request runs in one of two analysis modes, chosen with the analysisMode field:
Analysis mode
analysisMode
You send
You get back
General
general (default)
A text prompt in inputPrompt
A text answer in message, or JSON when you supply a schema
Time-based metadata
time_based_metadata
Segment definitions in responseFormat
A segments list with start and end times and the fields you asked for
You can point the model at video in two ways. An S3 location (s3Location) takes the object’s uri and the bucketOwner account ID, and suits long-form video. A base64 string (base64String) embeds the video in the request body, up to 25 MB, and suits short clips.
To track cost by application, create an application inference profile from the Pegasus 1.5 model, tag it, and call it by its Amazon Resource Name (ARN) in place of the model ID.
Getting started with Pegasus 1.5
The following section outlines how to get started with Pegasus 1.5.
Prerequisites
Before you begin, make sure you have:
An active AWS account with Amazon Bedrock access.
Python 3.10 or later, with the AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) installed.
AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions for bedrock:InvokeModel and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream.
Model access enabled for TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in the Amazon Bedrock console.
Videos stored in an Amazon S3 bucket, or short clips you can send inline.
The following policy grants both invoke actions on Pegasus 1.5.
{
"Version": "2012-10-17",
"Statement": [
{
"Effect": "Allow",
"Action": [
"bedrock:InvokeModel",
"bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream"
],
"Resource": [
"arn:aws:bedrock:us-west-2::foundation-model/twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0"
]
}
]
}
Boto3 signs requests with your usual AWS credentials. You can also authenticate with an Amazon Bedrock API key by setting it in the AWS_BEARER_TOKEN_BEDROCK environment variable. For production, prefer a short-term key generated from your IAM credentials with the aws-bedrock-token-generator package, because it expires automatically. Bearer-token authentication also requires the bedrock:CallWithBearerToken permission.
Send your first request
Install Boto3:
pip install boto3
The following example analyzes a video stored in Amazon S3 in general mode. This example uses the global Cross Region Inference (CRIS) endpoint. To target the US geographic endpoint instead, replace “global.” with “us.” in the endpoint URL.
import boto3
import json
from botocore.config import Config
AWS_REGION = "us-west-2"
MODEL_ID = "global.twelvelabs.pegasus-1-5-v1:0"
bedrock_runtime = boto3.client(
service_name="bedrock-runtime",
region_name=AWS_REGION,
config=Config(
# keep a longer read_timeout for lengthier invocations such as video segmentation
read_timeout=900,
retries={"max_attempts": 0},
connect_timeout=10,
),
)
# Analyze a video stored in Amazon S3
payload = {
"inputPrompt": "Summarize this video and identify the key topics discussed.",
"mediaSource": {
"s3Location": {
"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-pegasus-15/your-video.mp4",
"bucketOwner": "your-account-id"
}
},
"temperature": 0.2,
"maxOutputTokens": 4096,
"includeMetering": True
}
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(
modelId=MODEL_ID,
body=json.dumps(payload)
)
result = json.loads(response["body"].read())
print(result["message"])
The response carries the answer in message, the token counts in input_tokens and output_tokens, and the reason generation ended in stopReason. A stopReason of length means the answer reached maxOutputTokens before it finished, so check it before you rely on the output:
if result["stopReason"] == "length":
print("The answer was cut off. Raise maxOutputTokens and try again.")
print("Tokens in:", result["input_tokens"], "out:", result["output_tokens"])
Request fields for general mode:
Field
Required
Description
inputPrompt
Yes
The question or instruction about the video
mediaSource.s3Location.uri
One video source is required
S3 URI of the video
mediaSource.s3Location.bucketOwner
With uri
AWS account ID that owns the bucket
mediaSource.base64String
One video source is required
Base64-encoded video, up to 25 MB
temperature
No
Randomness of the output, from 0 to 1. Default 0.2
maxOutputTokens
No
Maximum tokens to generate, from 512 to 98,304
responseFormat
No
A JSON Schema the answer must follow
analysisMode
No
general (default) or time_based_metadata
For a short clip, you can send the video inline instead of from S3:
import base64
with open("your-video.mp4", "rb") as f:
video_b64 = base64.b64encode(f.read()).decode("utf-8")
payload["mediaSource"] = {"base64String": video_b64}
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload))
print(json.loads(response["body"].read())["message"])
Note that the preceding example uses the optional includeMetering attribute. includeMetering: True makes Pegasus 1.5 add two billing-usage fields to the non-streaming response: outputTokenCount and inputVideoSecond (the analyzed video’s duration in seconds).
Stream the response
For interactive applications, InvokeModelWithResponseStream returns the answer in chunks as it’s generated. Each chunk carries the next piece of text in message:
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model_with_response_stream(
modelId=MODEL_ID,
body=json.dumps(payload)
)
for event in response["body"]:
chunk = json.loads(event["chunk"]["bytes"])
print(chunk.get("message", ""), end="", flush=True)
print()
Return structured JSON
In general mode, you can constrain the answer to a JSON Schema so downstream code can parse it directly. Set responseFormat.type to json_schema and put the schema under jsonSchema. The answer arrives in message as a JSON string:
payload = {
"inputPrompt": "Analyze this video and return a structured summary.",
"mediaSource": {
"s3Location": {
"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-pegasus-15/your-video.mp4",
"bucketOwner": "your-account-id"
}
},
"temperature": 0,
"maxOutputTokens": 2048,
"includeMetering": True,
"responseFormat": {
"type": "json_schema",
"jsonSchema": {
"type": "object",
"properties": {
"summary": {"type": "string"},
"key_scenes": {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"}},
"setting": {"type": "string"}
},
"required": ["summary", "key_scenes", "setting"]
}
}
}
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload))
summary = json.loads(json.loads(response["body"].read())["message"])
print(summary["summary"])
for scene in summary["key_scenes"]:
print(" -", scene)
Video segmentation: Turning video into structured data
Time-based metadata generation is where Pegasus 1.5 differs most from earlier versions. Instead of a prompt, you send one or more segment definitions, and the model returns every segment of the video that matches each one.
Set analysisMode to time_based_metadata and responseFormat.type to segment_definitions. The definitions take the place of inputPrompt, so leave that field out. Each definition has:
id: a name for the definition, returned on every segment it matches.
description: what a matching segment looks like.
fields: the values to extract for each segment, each with a name, a type (string, boolean, number, integer, array, or timestamp), and a description.
The following example identifies each editorial section in a news broadcast and returns a title, summary, and key topics for each one:
payload = {
"analysisMode": "time_based_metadata",
"mediaSource": {
"s3Location": {
"uri": "s3://amzn-s3-demo-pegasus-15/news-broadcast.mp4",
"bucketOwner": "your-account-id"
}
},
"responseFormat": {
"type": "segment_definitions",
"segmentTimeFormat": "hh:mm:ss",
"segmentDefinitions": [
{
"id": "editorial_section",
"description": "A distinct editorial section of the broadcast, "
"such as a new story, topic, or segment of the program.",
"fields": [
{"name": "segment_title", "type": "string",
"description": "A descriptive title"},
{"name": "summary", "type": "string",
"description": "A brief summary of the segment content"},
{"name": "key_topics", "type": "array", "items": {"type": "string"},
"description": "Main topics discussed"}
]
}
]
},
"temperature": 0,
"maxOutputTokens": 32768,
"includeMetering": True
}
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(
modelId=MODEL_ID,
contentType="application/json",
accept="application/json",
body=json.dumps(payload)
)
result = json.loads(response["body"].read())
for segment in result["segments"]:
print(segment["start_sec"], "-", segment["end_sec"], segment["segment_title"])
print(" ", segment["summary"])
print(" topics:", ", ".join(segment["key_topics"]))
The previous sample code when tested against a sports clip may produce an output like the following sample.
{
"segments": [
{
"start_sec": "00:04:24",
"end_sec": "00:05:22",
"segment_title": "Substitutions and Added Time",
"summary": "The referee announces three minutes of added time, and both teams make substitutions in preparation for a potential penalty shootout.",
"key_topics": ["Substitutions", "Added time", "Penalty shootout preparation", "Tactical changes"]
},
{
"start_sec": "00:05:22",
"end_sec": "00:08:57",
"segment_title": "Last Gasp Attempts and Final Whistle",
"summary": "The final minutes of the match see intense action from both sides, with several close calls before the referee blows the final whistle, ending the game in a 3-3 draw.",
"key_topics": ["Final whistle", "Draw"]
},
{
"start_sec": "00:08:57",
"end_sec": "00:09:29",
"segment_title": "Match Conclusion and Penalty Shootout Setup",
"summary": "The match concludes with a 3-3 draw, leading to a penalty shootout. Players from both teams shake hands and prepare for the decisive moments.",
"key_topics": ["Match conclusion", "Penalty shootout", "Player handshakes", "Final"]
}
],
"definition_errors": [],
"input_tokens": 249408,
"output_tokens": 802,
"stopReason": "stop",
"finish_reason": "stop"
}
Each segment carries start_sec, end_sec, and the fields you defined. segmentTimeFormat controls how the times are written: seconds returns numbers you can do arithmetic on, while hh:mm:ss and hh:mm:ss.fff return readable timestamps as strings. The response also includes a definition_errors list, which is empty when every definition was processed.
A single request can include multiple segment definitions, for example one for editorial sections and another for on-screen brand appearances. Pegasus 1.5 returns the matches for all of them in one segments list, and tags each segment with _definition_id so you can tell them apart. The following example adds a second definition to the previous request and groups the results:
from collections import defaultdict
payload["responseFormat"]["segmentDefinitions"].append({
"id": "brand_appearance",
"description": "A shot where a company logo or branded product "
"is clearly visible on screen.",
"fields": [
{"name": "brand", "type": "string", "description": "The brand shown"},
{"name": "is_prominent", "type": "boolean",
"description": "Whether the brand is the main focus of the shot"}
]
})
response = bedrock_runtime.invoke_model(modelId=MODEL_ID, body=json.dumps(payload))
result = json.loads(response["body"].read())
by_definition = defaultdict(list)
for segment in result["segments"]:
by_definition[segment["_definition_id"]].append(segment)
for definition_id, segments in by_definition.items():
print(definition_id, len(segments), "segments")
Because the schema is defined once, the same definitions can be applied across an entire video library, producing consistent metadata for every asset.
Multimodal prompting: Adding visual context to your queries
Pegasus 1.5 introduces multimodal prompting, so you can include reference images alongside your text prompts. This is useful when you want to ask the model about specific objects, people, or scenes that are easier to show than describe.
For example, you can provide a product image and ask the model to identify every moment where that product appears in a video. Or you can provide a reference image of a specific logo and ask the model to detect brand appearances and their timestamps. This capability enhances the precision of video analysis, and opens up use cases such as visual brand monitoring, product placement analysis, and image-guided content search.
Reference images attach differently depending on the mode. In general mode, put them in promptV2.mediaSources, alongside the question in promptV2.inputText. In segmentation mode (analysisMode: time_based_metadata), attach them to the mediaSources of each segment definition inside responseFormat.segmentDefinitions. A definition can then match a visual reference as well as a text description. Each image needs a name, a media_type of image, and exactly one source: either an inline base64String or an s3Location with uri and bucketOwner. A single request can carry up to 30 reference images.
A general-mode request asks the model about an object shown in a reference image. The following sample payload and response provide an example in general mode.
payload = {
"analysisMode": "general",
"mediaSource": {"s3Location": {"uri": "s3://...", "bucketOwner": "..."}},
"promptV2": {
"inputText": "Does the object in the reference image appear in this video?",
"mediaSources": [
{"name": "ref1", "media_type": "image", "base64String": "..."}
]
}
…
}
{
"input_tokens": 144,
"output_tokens": 11,
"message": "Yes, the green canoe appears in the video.",
"stopReason": "stop"
}
In segmentation mode, the reference image lives inside the definition, so Pegasus returns only the segments where that product appears. The following sample payload and response provide an example in segmentation mode.
payload = {
"analysisMode": "time_based_metadata",
"mediaSource": {"s3Location": {"uri": "s3://...", "bucketOwner": "..."}},
"responseFormat": {
"type": "segment_definitions",
"segmentTimeFormat": "hh:mm:ss",
"segmentDefinitions": [
{
"id": "product_appearance",
"description": "A shot showing the product in the reference image",
"fields": [
{"name": "what", "type": "string", "description": "what is on screen"}
],
"mediaSources": [
{"name": "ref1", "media_type": "image",
"s3Location": {"uri": "s3://...", "bucketOwner": "..."}}
]
}
]
}
}
{
"segments": [
{"start_sec": "00:00:00", "end_sec": "00:00:02",
"what": "A family of four in a green canoe, paddling on a calm river surrounded by towering red rock formations."},
{"start_sec": "00:00:09", "end_sec": "00:00:10",
"what": "The family back in the canoe, paddling away from the shore, with the children smiling and enjoying the serene surroundings."}
],
"definition_errors": [],
"input_tokens": 4498,
"output_tokens": 292,
"stopReason": "stop",
"finish_reason": "stop"
}
Monitoring usage
Pegasus 1.5 publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics in the AWS/Bedrock namespace under its model ID, including Invocations, OutputTokenCount, InvocationLatency, and InvocationClientErrors. Use them to track volume and latency. Pair them with application inference profiles when you need usage broken down by application.
Use cases
Pegasus 1.5 is designed for organizations that manage large volumes of long-form video:
News and broadcast archives: Teams can define editorial segments, topics, and speaker changes once, then catalog years of footage that was previously searchable only by transcript keywords.
Sports broadcasters and leagues: Detect plays, scoring events, and other key moments across full-length game footage, speeding up highlight production.
Streaming applications: Scene-level metadata supports moment-based recommendations, contextual ad placement, and segment-level brand safety review.
In each case, people remain part of the workflow. Their work shifts from finding and tagging every moment by hand to reviewing and refining the metadata generated by the model.
Input requirements
Pegasus 1.5 supports the following video specifications:
Duration: Up to 2 hours.
File size: Up to 2 GB from Amazon S3, or up to 25 MB as a base64 string.
Resolution: 360×360 to 5184×2160.
Aspect ratio: Between 1:1 and 2.4:1, or their inverses.
Formats: FFmpeg-supported formats.
Now available
TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 is available today on Amazon Bedrock in the US West (Oregon) AWS Region. Check the full Region list for future updates, and visit the Amazon Bedrock pricing page for pricing information. Pegasus 1.5 is billed through AWS Marketplace, so its charges appear on your AWS bill and in AWS Cost Explorer under TwelveLabs rather than Amazon Bedrock.
To get started:
Visit the TwelveLabs models page on Amazon Bedrock to learn more about the model family.
Review the Pegasus 1.5 model card for feature support, Region availability, and sample code.
Send us feedback at AWS re:Post for Amazon Bedrock or through your usual AWS Support contacts.
We’re excited to see what you build with TwelveLabs Pegasus 1.5 in Amazon Bedrock.

items.title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
items.summary:
As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI.
For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription.
The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability.
In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription.
Optimizing Nova-3 to Trainium2 with native PyTorch
Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile. We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile. The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected.
We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile. Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target.
From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution.
We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size.
Kernel-level tuning with Neuron Explorer and NAD
Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills.
In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels.
Layer
What we found and changed
Gain
FFN
The reference kernel’s tiling schedule reloaded the full set of projection weights from off-chip memory for every token tile, so memory bandwidth limited throughput as the token count grew. Our hand-tuned kernel loads each weight tile once, reuses it across multiple token tiles, and pipelines weight reads with on-chip compute.
2.0x lower latency compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96
Depthwise conv1d
The experimental NKILib kernel framed the operation as an implicit general matrix multiply (GEMM), which left Tensor Engine utilization low. We rewrote it as a broadcast multiply-accumulate loop on the Vector Engine, reaching full engine utilization, enough to more than offset the Vector Engine’s lower peak throughput.
1.5x speedup compared to the reference kernel at batch size 96
Conv2d
The model’s conv2d layers hit a compilation bottleneck: beyond batch size 32, these layers prevented the model from compiling as a single graph. Since NKILib had no conv2d kernel, we wrote one from scratch in NKI. The kernel went through several profiler-informed iterations following the flywheel described earlier, unlocking batch sizes above 32.
Up to 50x on the convolution module at batch sizes ≤32
Data-parallel runtime in Rust
Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, we reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one (LNC1). This configuration lets us host eight model replicas (DP8) per Trainium2 device. Inputs are processed concurrently while maximizing per-device throughput. The data-parallel runtime is driven by a work-stealing queue with one thread per replica.
Deepgram’s production serving stack is written in Rust, so porting Nova-3 to Trainium2 required more than compiling the model: it also had to run without Python or PyTorch in the serving path. We therefore built a lightweight runtime in which Rust coordinates model replicas through a shared work-stealing queue. A C layer loads and executes ahead-of-time-compiled Neuron Executable File Format (NEFFs) directly through the Neuron Runtime API (libnrt). The runtime integrates directly with Deepgram’s serving architecture and reproduced the reference token sequences exactly at every tested batch size.
We benchmarked it against multithreaded (MT) and multiprocessing (MP) Python data-parallel runtimes. Compared with the MP baseline, the Rust runtime removes the overhead of the Python interpreter entirely. Compared with the MT baseline, it further alleviates global interpreter lock (GIL) serialization, so dispatch calls from concurrent worker threads are no longer contended within a single process. These gains matter because Nova-3 performs a sequence of small decoder calls for each audio chunk, making host-side dispatch the bottleneck at low batch sizes. The throughput improvement is therefore largest there, and remains meaningful even at the throughput-maximizing batch size. There, the Rust runtime delivered a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline.
Figure 1: Deepgram Nova-3 on AWS Trainium2, compiled ahead of time and served from Rust
Cost saving impact
We measured price-performance as audio processed per dollar. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, the single-device Trainium2 setup (trn2.3xlarge) processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running.
Conclusion
In this post, we demonstrated how Deepgram and the AWS FDE ported the Nova-3 speech-to-text PyTorch model to Trainium hardware using TorchNeuron, which provides native PyTorch framework integration for AWS Trainium. We improved performance by replacing layers directly with pre-built kernels from NKILib. We then assessed performance using Neuron Explorer and used the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) profiling skills to query profiling data and accelerate performance troubleshooting. Building on these insights, we adapted kernel source code using the NAD kernel-writing skills. Finally, we built a lightweight Rust data-parallel runtime for AWS Trainium, calling the Neuron Runtime API from Rust. Our setup demonstrated cost savings in offline, throughput-oriented scenarios, validating AWS Trainium as a viable and efficient option for Deepgram’s inference workloads.
To try this approach on your own models, start with the AWS Neuron documentation, which covers the compiler, the runtime, and the supported frameworks. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) guide explains how to write the kernels described in this post, and the NKI samples repository holds the reference kernels we started from. The Neuron developer tools documentation covers the profiling and agentic tooling we used here, including Neuron Explorer and Neuron Agentic Development. For instance sizes and pricing, see Amazon EC2 Trn2 Instances. For help scoping a similar port, contact the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering.

items.title: OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
items.summary:
Back to Articles
OlmoEarth v1.3: State-of-the-art embeddings for the whole planet
Community Article Published
October 22, 2026 Upvote 15
+9
Kyle Wiggers Ai2Comms Follow allenai
🤗 Models | 📄 Tech Report | 📊 Data | 💻 Code | 🌎 Embeddings Explorer | 🗺️ Interactive story
Today, we’re releasing OlmoEarth v1.3, a state-of-the-art satellite embedding model. Alongside OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re sharing precomputed, annual embeddings for the whole planet (10m, 64- and 128-dimensions), plus a new browser-based tool to explore and customize maps based on those embeddings — the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer. This means anyone can put OlmoEarth v1.3 to work right away, from tracking change over time to finding similar places—no sign-in, and no advanced technical knowledge required.
Until now, the primary way to use OlmoEarth was fine-tuning in OlmoEarth Studio: training a model for each task and running it over satellite imagery to make a map. That requires GPU access and the ability to download and store the imagery. Embedding models compress satellite data into ready-to-use features that can be reused cheaply for many tasks.
With OlmoEarth v1.3, we’re excited to give users more ways to explore and engage with planetary artifacts in whatever way suits them best.
Compute once, reuse everywhere
An embedding represents what the model learned from millions of images. OlmoEarth v1.3 reads a year of radar (Sentinel-1) and multispectral (Sentinel-2 and Landsat) satellite time series and produces one 128-dimensional vector for every 10-meter pixel on Earth; the first 64 dimensions also work on their own as a smaller embedding.
Foundation models and global embeddings are expensive to produce, and to make sure everyone is able to access the benefits, we’ve computed these embeddings for the entire planet and shared them with the community on Source Cooperative. From there, a crop map, a land-cover map, or a change analysis becomes a lightweight modeling problem: train a small classifier on top and run it locally.
How OlmoEarth v1.3 makes an embedding: a vision transformer reads the satellite data, an Attention Pooler pools it into one vector per patch of land, and a linear layer reduces it to 128 numbers.
State-of-the-art embeddings
We evaluated OlmoEarth v1.3's embeddings against AlphaEarth Foundations (AEF) and Tessera v2 across 27 evaluations, covering six continents and many different tasks. OlmoEarth’s 128-dimensional embeddings score highest on 20 of 27 evals and rank highest overall. The 64-dimensional version, at half the size, still leads on 18 of 27 evals. As part of this evaluation, we introduce PLANTEUR, a new crop-type benchmark for tropical farming, and the embeddings generalize best to places a classifier has never seen (PLANTEUR technical report is available here). Everything behind them is fully open: the model weights, the pretraining data, and the pretraining code.
In practice, this means a small classifier trained on the OlmoEarth embeddings is enough to map what’s on the ground: think classifying smallholder crops in Kenya, detecting brick kilns west of Dhaka, assessing fire damage in Indonesia, and tracking gold mining in the Peruvian Amazon.
Compared to previous generations of OlmoEarth models, OlmoEarth v1.3 was also our cheapest model to train. It took 53% of the computing time of our last version (v1.2) and 18% of our first (v1), with 50% and 22% of the carbon emissions. And it also remains a strong fine-tuning model, matching v1.2's performance across research and partner labels. Our latest model builds on the same foundation as earlier OlmoEarth versions, tuned so the embeddings stay lightweight without giving up accuracy across tasks, and that efficiency work carries forward into the versions ahead.
Full results and methodology are in our technical report.
If you wanted to reproduce it, pre-training OlmoEarth v1.3 Base would cost roughly $2,720 of rented H100 time for the final run. The weights, data, and code are all open.
One place, nine years
How much each pixel’s embedding changed between 2017 and 2020 (left) and 2020 and 2025 (right). Magenta is the largest change. Left: mining spreading southeast, the big patch at lower right. Right: that corner has gone quiet; the change now sits in the older mining zone to the west, part regrowth, part renewed digging. Explore it yourself in the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer.
In Peru's Madre de Dios region, illegal gold mining around La Pampa peaked in 2017 and 2018, clearing more than 1,200 hectares of forest in the buffer zone of the Tambopata National Reserve, according to Amazon Conservation's MAAP monitoring program. In February 2019, Peru's Operation Mercurio shut most of it down. The question ever since has been, did it stay down?
The embeddings help answer that. Compare each pixel's vector across years, no model training required, and the 2017 to 2020 pair lights up where the mining was spreading to the southeast. Run the same comparison from 2020 to 2025, and the signal shifts. The crackdown is visible in the embeddings.
The more interesting part is what the second map still shows. It is not dark. According to MAAP, pockets in the northwest kept operating, and the old mining zone keeps changing as the land recovers. The embeddings register that too. The reprieve was brief, and the pressure is building again. In August 2026, the Associated Press reported, Peru sent navy patrols back into the reserve after prosecutors found mining had crossed into Tambopata itself.
Our interactive story opens on this stretch of Madre de Dios, and walks through several other examples from there.
The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer
The OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer is an interactive analysis tool built from the embeddings themselves, rendered as a false-color map of the planet. Pan anywhere, flip between years to see how landscapes have changed, and pull up the underlying Sentinel-2 imagery to check the map against the real thing. Then start asking questions: click a place to find others that look similar, or drop a few labeled points and train a small classifier on the spot, then export the result as a GeoTIFF. No account, no setup required.
For many teams, testing an idea against OlmoEarth has meant a fine-tuning run, on the order of hours. In the explorer, a first pass takes seconds. You can analyze entire regions from a handful of labels, no GPU needed. When a task calls for fine-tuning, the embeddings can help you decide whether it deserves the compute, and where the model falls short.
The archive behind the Explorer holds embeddings at 10-meter resolution, roughly 150 TB per year, covering land and adjacent coastal waters. At launch, 2025, 2024, and 2023 are global, and 2017 to 2022 cover select countries, with more coverage on the way. You can retrieve the embeddings in the full 128-dimensional version or the lighter 64-dimensional version. Every embedding also comes with a record of where it came from. For each 20-kilometer tile and year, open provenance tables list the Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, and Landsat scenes the model read, with links to the public catalogs that host them, so you can trace any pixel back to the imagery behind it.
Get started
This release includes the OlmoEarth v1.3 Base model, the precomputed global embeddings, the OlmoEarth Embeddings Explorer, and the technical report. If your work needs a specific time window, OlmoEarth Studio runs the same model over the dates, modalities, and resolution that you choose, and a tutorial shows how to generate embeddings on your own compute. These tools work together: explore in the Embeddings Explorer, fine-tune in Studio when a task calls for it, and take your map from there. Everything is published under the OlmoEarth Artifact License, the same open license as v1 and v1.2.
Pull the embeddings for a place you care about, put your question to them, and show us what you find.

items.title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
Community Article Published
October 22, 2026 Upvote 26
+20
Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research
Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less
guesswork about which model to use.
Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task.
Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed.
The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast.
Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble
Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from
Hugging Face:
pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11"
import pandas as pd
from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster
df = pd.read_csv(
"https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv",
parse_dates=["date"],
)
ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
"ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
)
result = ensemble(
df.tail(1024),
timestamp_column="date",
target_columns=["OT"],
context_length=1024,
prediction_length=24,
)
print(result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast
print(result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles
The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card.
result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage.
The ensemble members
The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures:
Model
Architecture
Granite PatchTST-FM-r1
Patched Transformer
Granite PatchTST-FM-r2
Patched Conformer
Granite FlowState-r1.1
State-space model
Granite TTM-r3
Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer)
For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper,
PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview,
FlowState paper, and
Tiny Time Mixers paper.
These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast
combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter.
Two ways to combine the forecasts
Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median.
Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default
The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series.
The forecast combination puzzle
offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations
have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above.
IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative
The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing.
A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight.
Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder:
ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained(
"ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1",
subfolder="recipes/granite-iqr",
)
Which method should I use?
Your goal
Start with
Why
A simple default
Probabilistic Ensemble
Equal influence, no fitted weights
Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread
IQR Ensemble
Influence varies with each member's predicted spread
Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon.
Does the ensemble improve on its members?
We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models
forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit
the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results
with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026.
GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's
mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores
are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations.

Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard.
Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data.
PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices.
In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member.
Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values.
Extend the recipe to other forecasters
The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve.
The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them.
For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing.
Evaluate the recipe for your application
GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data:
Match your use case. Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve.
Compare like with like. Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows.
Look beyond point error. Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%.
Measure the cost. Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload.
Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment.
Try it on your data
The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe:

TL;DR
NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers historical examples as context examples and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models and kumo-engine libraries, or as an NVIDIA NIM.

The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models
Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications.
The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons:
Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational.
Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization.
Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions.
Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational (Paper, GitHub, HuggingFace), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required.
How Kumo Relational Works
Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation (e.g., "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort.
Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning by reasoning over context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target (e.g., "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units").
Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference.
To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works:
Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables.
Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL), a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage.
Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently via column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates.
Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, followed by cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs.
How Kumo Relational Was Built
Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures.
The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited. Pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases.
Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations.
Performance
In the paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. It is the top-performing in-context learning model on the RelBench leaderboard. On RelArena-α, it sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front:
Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard as of 2026-09-21: Elo across tasks versus total task runtime (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than rtl-plurel at similar accuracy.
On the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when noisy columns are added.
Limitations
Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions. Predictive signals must be reachable within a limited number of hops.
Demo
Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory, through database and warehouse connectors, or through kumo-engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. The model itself is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular. The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The interface is designed to naturally extend tabular foundation models to relational signal by passing additional related multi-table context and query information:
import sdm # pip install structured-data-models
model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device="cuda")
pred = model(
# In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets):
x_context=sdm.TableTensor(...),
y_context=sdm.TableTensor(...),
# Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps):
x_query=sdm.TableTensor(...),
# Multi-table information for context/prediction entities:
related_context_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}),
related_query_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}),
)
See the library's relational examples for RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines.
To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request:
import sdm_client # pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]'
client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url="http://localhost:8001") # NIM URL
query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery(
# Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL):
"PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id",
# Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred):
{"users": ..., "orders": ...},
)
pred = client.predict(
# Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict:
query.materialize(indices=[1, 2, 3]),
model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(),
)
See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks.

We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, granite-speech-5.0-2b, and revised versions of two models the community already uses, granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus. Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said.

Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control
granite-speech-5.0-2b is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation.
What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech:
More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech.
Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription.
Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences.
Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language.
Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets.
The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon.
Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are official, as of 21 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets.
Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster
When we introduced Turbo CTC in August, it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most:
Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese.
Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step.
More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings.
It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level.
Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale.
Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when
The updated granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas:
Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall.
Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review.
Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%.
Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists.

items.title: Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
items.summary:
