Scaling Indic Pretraining: 2.8 Trillion Tokens and an Open Data Generation Pipeline
Community Article Published
October 16, 2026 Upvote 45
+39
Will Jennings WillJenningsDC Follow nvidia Kiran Praveen kipraveen Follow nvidia Sriharsha Niverty sniverty Follow nvidia Raviraj Joshi ravirajoshi Follow nvidia Markus Kliegl mkliegl-nv Follow nvidia Yev Meyer nv-3mei Follow nvidia Utkarsh Vaidya uvaidya Follow nvidia Niket Agarwal niketagarwal Follow nvidia
Native-script data for 22 languages, romanized data for twelve, and a reusable GPU-accelerated pipeline for translation, quality assessment, and repair.
Authors: AI4Bharat — Sumanth Doddapaneni, Thanmay Jayakumar, Mohammed Safi Ur Rahman Khan, Mitesh Khapra, Anoop Kunchukuttan, Rudra Murthy, Ujjwal Sharma. NVIDIA — Niket Agarwal, Ramani Akkati, Mohammad Qazim Bhat, Aishwarya Chhabra, Shuoyang Ding, Raviraj Joshi, Anusha Kamath, Abhinav Khattar, Markus Kliegl, Vitaly Lavrukhin, Yev Meyer, Sriharsha Niverty, Brandon Norick, Sai Nishanth Padala, Mostofa Patwary, Kiran Praveen, Kanishk Singla, Rajpreet Thethy, Utkarsh Vaidya, Ameya Velingker.
We're excited to introduce Nemotron-pretraining-Indic-v1 approximately 2.8 trillion tokens across 22 Indian languages, releasing soon alongside the open, GPU-accelerated data generation pipeline used to create it. These are the 22 languages listed in India's Constitution: the first languages for 97% of Indians, or nearly 1.2 billion citizens at the 2011 Census. Developed by NVIDIA with IIT Madras, India's premier engineering institute, and its AI4Bharat lab, this release gives model builders a substantial new resource for Indic pretraining. The pipeline captures the full generation recipe, including prompts, LLM workflows, and quality checks, so developers can adapt it to their own source material and generate more data for their needs.
AI4Bharat, IIT Madras' Indian language research lab, builds open-source datasets and models for Indian languages. Its resources, such as Sangraha, an open pretraining corpus for 22 Indian languages, have helped lay the foundation for open Indic language-model research. Our joint open-source release represents a substantial expansion of the open synthetic Indic training data that will be available to the community. It brings a broad mix of curated English material, including mathematics, code, and question-answer content, into Indian languages, giving teams more training material for building models that can explain technical concepts, work through problems, and answer questions in those languages. Every record traces back to a curated source document, and each output is checked against its input, so the synthetic text stays grounded in real information.
Mitesh Khapra, who heads AI4Bharat and made the 2025 TIME100 AI list, has named the core problem: Indian language technology trails English because "we do not have enough data for Indian languages." We're answering that call with more data, plus an open recipe for generating more.
The corpus also accounts for how people write. It includes native-script data for all 22 languages and romanized text for twelve, spanning 34 language-script configurations. Our workflows combine document-level translation, quality assessment, and targeted repair, with checks to preserve content such as equations, tables, and code. This data complements naturally authored Indic text, which remains essential for local knowledge and cultural context.
We're sharing the open generation recipe so the community can not just reproduce the data but take this work further. Teams can use the corpus directly, adapt the prompts and quality checks, or bring their own source documents to the workflow. By opening up both the data and the process, we aim to make large-scale Indic data generation more accessible and enable more developers to contribute to stronger models across Indian languages.
Continued pretraining for Nemotron 3.5 Super VL added 10 billion Indic tokens, drawn from a twelve-language subset of this corpus and natural Indic text. Our technical report on the model covers the full story. We plan to build on this corpus in future Nemotron models.
What is in the corpus?
Figure 1. The corpus contains 2,601.0 billion native-script tokens and 224.6 billion romanized tokens. Counts use the Gemma-4 tokenizer. Document records include translations and script variants of shared sources; they are not counts of unique English documents.
The corpus has two groups of language configurations:
Native-script and romanized data: Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Nepali, Odia, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu, and Urdu.
Native-script data: Assamese, Bodo, Dogri, Kashmiri, Konkani, Maithili, Manipuri, Sanskrit, Santali, and Sindhi.
Here, native-script describes the writing system: the text is still translated from English. Romanized means Indic-language text written in Latin script, not an English translation. For each of the twelve dual-script languages, romanization covers a subset of the accepted native-script translations.
This distinction matters when constructing a training mixture. Native and romanized records offer different script exposure, but can express the same underlying content. The token counts describe the retained corpus, including accepted rewrites, rather than a training run's token budget. Counts also depend on the tokenizer used, so corpus inventory and training-token counts should be read separately.
From English source documents to Indic training data
To build this corpus, we start with documents from 15 Nemotron-CC-v2 subsets, covering web text, question-answer material, mathematics, code, and other specialized content. We use NeMo Data Designer, NVIDIA's open-source framework for generating synthetic data, to run translation, quality checks, and targeted repair. Throughout the workflow, we retain each source identifier so developers can trace an output back to its original document. Clear provenance like this is part of what makes open data practical to audit and build on. Figure 2 shows the workflow for twelve languages.
Figure 2. Four-stage Indic synthetic-data pipeline for twelve languages, implemented using NeMo Data Designer and Gemma-4-31B-it. We translate English documents, assess translation quality, repair low-scoring outputs, and convert a subset of accepted translations into Latin script. The other ten languages use the separate Indic Translate workflow described below.
The twelve-language workflow
For these twelve languages, we translate documents in full so the model can use context across paragraphs, tables, and equations. We selected Gemma-4-31B-it by comparing models on complete documents, checking translation quality and preservation of technical content. Our prompts distinguish prose to translate from content to preserve, including code, equations, URLs, and formatting.
After translation, we use the same model to assess each output against its English source. A rubric inspired by Multidimensional Quality Metrics (MQM), an open framework for classifying translation errors by type and severity, covers meaning, fluency, terminology, style, and formatting. We retain only outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 (a rubric score, not an accuracy percentage). For lower-scoring outputs, we use the assessment feedback to guide repairs, then reassess them against the same threshold. This process recovered 438.4 billion tokens across native-script and romanized data, already included in the corpus total. Sampled human reviews and tests with deliberately introduced errors helped identify omissions and residual English, informing improvements to our prompts and checks.
Accepted native-script translations also provide the starting point for romanized data. We convert a subset into Latin script and check each result against its native-script input. This separates translation from script conversion. In our initial human comparison, this two-step approach produced fewer hallucinated additions and less residual English than generating romanized text directly from English.
The ten-language workflow
For the other ten languages, we adapt the workflow to address long-document quality and script-stability issues observed in our comparisons. We translate with Indic Translate, a document-level translation model for English and 22 Indian languages from Bodhan AI, a nonprofit center for AI in education incubated at IIT Madras. Gemma-4-31B-it then assesses each translation against its English source. For eight languages, we keep the whole-document approach. For longer Santali documents, we translate overlapping windows and reconstruct the document; for Manipuri, we translate into Bengali script before converting to Meitei Mayek, its native script. These workflows retain outputs scoring at least 75 out of 100 and produce native-script data only, without feedback-based rewriting.
What changed after Indic continued pretraining?
The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report compares the checkpoint immediately before Indic continued pretraining (CPT) with the checkpoint after that stage. The configured budget was 100 billion training tokens, with 10% (10 billion tokens) allocated to a mixture of synthetic and natural Indic text. The remaining 90% maintained the preceding training mixture's relative proportions.
Scores increased on all five reported Indic knowledge and reasoning benchmarks: MILU, Indic MMLU-Pro, Indic ARC-Challenge, Indic ARC-Easy, and Indic GSM8K.
Figure 3. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL before and after the Indic CPT stage. Gains range from 4.98 to 9.82 percentage points. The comparison reports the change across a training stage that combines synthetic and natural Indic data, rather than isolating the synthetic corpus's contribution. Language coverage differs by benchmark; these are stage-level checkpoints, not a comparison of final model releases.
Source: Nemotron 3.5 Super VL technical report, Table 2. GSM8K excludes Odia because evaluation exceeded the serving context limit.
These gains support the combined synthetic-and-natural Indic CPT recipe, while leaving the choice of mixture for other models and languages to further study.
The companion Indic report examines source mixtures, synthetic-data pool size, and script coverage using first-pass accepted data for the twelve-language group. Evaluating the full corpus, including recovered rewrites and the other ten languages, remains a next step for those controlled studies.
Broader Indic capabilities in Nemotron 3.5 Super VL
Beyond the CPT-stage results, how does the released model compare with the previous generation? Figure 4 compares Nemotron 3.5 Super VL with Nemotron 3 Super across Indic task performance and language quality. These results reflect the released model's full training pipeline, including Indic CPT and post-training.
Nemotron 3.5 Super VL scores higher on five of the six task benchmarks shown, spanning knowledge, reasoning, mathematics, code, and translation. Instruction following on IFEval 1.5 dipped 2.04 points. It also improves across all four IndiVibe dimensions: usefulness, fluency, language and script fidelity, and appropriate verbosity. IndiVibe is Sarvam AI's open benchmark of assistant-style prompts in Indian languages. Together, these evaluations examine both what the model can do and how well it communicates in Indian languages.
Figure 4. Indic task performance and language quality across Nemotron Super generations. Left: six task benchmarks. Right: preliminary IndiVibe conditional preference scores, not direct head-to-head win rates. Labels show changes in percentage points, except WMT24++, which uses chrF points. See the companion Indic technical report for benchmark and evaluation details.
Start building
Load the corpus
Start with the languages and scripts your model needs, inspect a sample, and review the dataset card and license before training. Configurations use language, script, and region tags: for example, hi-Deva-IN denotes Hindi in Devanagari, while hi-Latn-IN denotes romanized Hindi.
The example below asks for the repository ID from the dataset card, then discovers the available splits and streams a sample.
from datasets import get_dataset_split_names, load_dataset
dataset_id = input("Repository ID from the dataset card: ").strip()
config = "hi-Deva-IN"
splits = get_dataset_split_names(dataset_id, config_name=config)
print("Available splits:", splits)
data = load_dataset(
dataset_id, name=config, split=splits[0], streaming=True
)
print(next(iter(data)))
Hugging Face Datasets supports streaming so readers can inspect records without downloading the entire corpus. Once the release is available, pin a dataset revision for reproducible experiments.
For a first training study, compare mixtures at a fixed token budget and record the natural/synthetic and native/romanized shares. Track per-language results alongside English capability retention and language/script quality. When creating held-out splits, account for records derived from the same source across languages and scripts.
To build a fuller recipe, pair the corpus with Nemotron post-training data, such as the Chat & Instruction or Post-Training Blends collections. For India-specific synthetic data, seed NeMo Data Designer with Nemotron-Personas-India, synthetic personas in English and Hindi grounded in real-world distributions for India.
Adapt the generation recipe
The open-source Nemotron Bharat translation plugin for NeMo Data Designer provides translation and evaluation prompts, optional feedback-based rewriting, document windowing, and script-remapping support. Use its configuration reference to choose models and languages, adapt prompts to your domain, and set rewrite parameters. The accompanying developer note explains the workflow and engineering choices.
Start with a small sample of your own source documents. Inspect translation quality and preservation of code, mathematics, and formatting, then refine the prompts and checks with native-language reviewers before scaling up. Treat generation and corpus acceptance as separate steps: the plugin returns candidates and scores, while your filtering policy determines which records enter the training corpus.
Scope and limitations
Translation broadens access to the source material, but does not replace text originally written in Indian languages or guarantee coverage of local knowledge and culture. We recommend combining this corpus with appropriately sourced natural Indic text and evaluating the resulting mixture for the intended use case.
Quality assessment is primarily automated, complemented by sampled human review whose coverage varies across languages. For the twelve-language workflow (Figure 2), the translator also serves as the judge. Retained text can still contain errors, and the ten-language workflow needs broader native-speaker validation. Source-ID checks remove processing duplicates; they are not semantic deduplication of similar content.
Alongside the corpus, AI4Bharat at IIT Madras, with support from NVIDIA, is building Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite, an open and evolving collection of benchmarks for Indic model capabilities. It helps model builders assess both task performance and language quality. See the companion blog, Better Models Need Better Benchmarks: Introducing Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite.
Explore the language configurations, test a training mixture, or adapt the open recipe to a new domain. Sharing per-language results and improvements to the generation workflow can help the community build on this work.
Further reading and acknowledgments
The companion reports, Scaling Synthetic Pre-training Data and Evaluation for Indic LLMs and the Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Lightning technical report, provide the corpus accounting, generation methods, experiments, and evaluation details. Evaluation is the other half of this work. For the benchmark side, see the companion blog from AI4Bharat and NVIDIA, Better Models Need Better Benchmarks: Introducing Indic-LLM-Eval-Suite.
This work brings together NVIDIA, IIT Madras, AI4Bharat, and Bodhan AI. We also acknowledge the model and tooling contributions used in the pipeline: Google's Gemma, Bodhan AI's Indic Translate, and NeMo Data Designer. Additional NVIDIA data resources are available in the Nemotron Pre-Training Datasets collection.

items.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed, Rerank, and Parse: Advancing Agents with World-Class Retrieval Models
items.summary:
Back to Articles
NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed, Rerank, and Parse: Advancing Agents with World-Class Retrieval Models
Community Article Published
October 21, 2026 Upvote 68
+62
Yauhen Babakhin ybabakhin Follow nvidia Ryan Chesler emelryan Follow nvidia Jiarui Cai jiaruic Follow nvidia Sean Sodha ssodha-nv Follow nvidia Isabel Hulseman ihulseman0220 Follow nvidia
An agent’s answers depend on the evidence it can retrieve. When that evidence is incomplete or irrelevant, the agent will repeat searches and inspect additional documents, consuming more inference tokens before completing the task. Better retrieval can help agents reach grounded answers with fewer wasted tokens. At enterprise scale, that waste leads to massive inefficiencies. Agents need the right retrieval models and systems to reach insights faster.
Today, we are expanding the Nemotron Retriever collection with new open, commercially available models for embedding, reranking, and document extraction. The new models include Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B BF16, 1B BF16, 1B NVFP4, Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B BF16, and Nemotron 3.5 Parse at 631M parameters.
Together, these state-of-the-art models bring multimodal retrieval, relevance ranking, and document processing to enterprise agent workflows.
Better Retrieval for More Efficient Agents
Retrieval quality affects both the answers an agent produces and the LLM inference cost. Relevant evidence can help the agent answer a question or better decide its next step, and reranking improves the quality of evidence that enters its context.
Consider an agent asked to identify products at risk of stockouts next quarter and explain why. It must combine demand forecasts in charts, inventory levels in tables, and supplier lead times in reports, then reason about whether replenishment will arrive before inventory runs out. Completing the task requires finding the relevant evidence across documents and using it together in the analysis.
To understand how retrieval affects the agent’s ability to combine evidence and complete a task, we evaluated Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank across ViDoRe v3, BRIGHT, and BrowseComp-Plus. ViDoRe v3 uses combined text and image inputs, while BRIGHT and BrowseComp-Plus use text-only inputs. In this pipeline, an agent queries the corpus using a search tool, inspects the evidence, and refines its next search attempt to find the most relevant information to a given query. The experiments below vary how the search tool is implemented: embedding only, embedding plus reranking, and with different models for each. The LLM powering the agent, tools, task set, corpus, and execution policy remain fixed while the retrieval configuration changes. We measure the agent's ability to find the relevant information for each task and total agent inference tokens per task, including input and output tokens across all turns.
Figure 1. End-to-end task success versus total agent inference tokens per task across retrieval configurations.
Lower agent inference cost: Adding Nemotron 3.5 Rerank reduces agentic token cost per query by approximately 14% with Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B, and 13% with Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B, while improving retrieval accuracy in both configurations.
Better evidence within the same agent budget: With Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B as the retriever, Nemotron 3.5 Rerank delivered approximately 0.9 points higher nDCG@10 than Qwen3-VL-Reranker-8B at a similar agentic token cost.
Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank
Behind these agent successes are Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Nemotron 3.5 Rerank, which retrieve evidence across text and images and prioritize it for the agent’s context. Nemotron 3.5 Embed builds on the previous generation’s Nemotron 3 Embed text embedding models to retrieve evidence from document images, including tables, charts, infographics, datasheets, and schematics. This allows applications to search information conveyed by visual content alongside document text.
The four models provide different options for retrieval and second-stage ranking:
Model
Role
Deployment focus
Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B-BF16
Retrieves evidence across text and images, with strong multilingual retrieval capabilities.
Quality-focused search over text and visually rich documents
Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16
Distills the 8B model’s multimodal retrieval capabilities into a compact model.
Multimodal indexing and query serving with a smaller model footprint
Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-NVFP4
Applies NVFP4 quantization to both text and image encoders for efficient multimodal inference.
Large-scale document indexing and high-throughput retrieval on supported hardware
Nemotron-3.5-Rerank-8B-BF16
Jointly evaluates query–document pairs to refine relevance ranking across text and image candidates.
Selecting relevant evidence from retrieved candidates for RAG and agentic workflows
Table 1. Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Nemotron 3.5 Rerank model capabilities and use cases across various sizes and variants.
Key features include:
Text and image retrieval: Search document text and images containing tables, charts, infographics, datasheets, and schematics.
Multilingual support: Text retrieval was evaluated across 34 languages, while multilingual visual retrieval was evaluated on MIRACL Vision (18 languages) and KoViDoRe. The model may support additional languages beyond those evaluated.
Multimodal reranking: An 8B cross-encoder scores query–document pairs across text and image inputs.
BF16 and NVFP4 deployment: The 1B embedding model is available in BF16 and NVFP4, with quantization applied to both text and image encoders.
Domain adaptation: Nemotron embedding fine-tuning recipes support custom document collections, with a 18% relative nDCG@10 gain for both Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16 and Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B-BF16 in our chart and infographic experiments.
Leading Multimodal Dense Retrieval on ViDoRe v3
On ViDoRe v3.1, Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B BF16 achieves 61.17 nDCG@10, ranking first among dense retrieval models. This is an 8.94-point improvement over the 52.23 score achieved by the Llama Nemotron Embed VL 1B model. The 1B model brings most of this visual retrieval quality into a smaller model. Distilled from the 8B teacher, Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B BF16 scores 58.38 nDCG@10, retaining 95.4% of the teacher’s score.
Figure 2. Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B BF16 ranked first among dense retrieval models on the ViDoRe v3.1 leaderboard as of 10/20/2026.
We also compare the models with Qwen3-VL-Embedding, EmbeddingGemma-2, and the previous-generation NVIDIA model across ViDoRe v3, Korean ViDoRe and MIRACL Vision. The chart below reports retrieval accuracy for image-only and combined image-and-text inputs.
Figure 3. Text and visual retrieval performance of Nemotron 3.5 Embed compared with prior-generation models and selected baselines.
The multilingual results show how the models retrieve evidence across different language settings. On MIRACL Vision, the 8B model achieves 72.6 nDCG@10, exceeding Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 4.3 points. We also evaluate the models on KoViDoRe; both Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B and 1B outperform the Qwen baselines when using combined image and text inputs.
Reranking the Evidence for Agent Tasks
Embedding models make large collections searchable by representing content as vectors. After retrieval returns a candidate set, Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B BF16 evaluates each candidate against the query to refine the ordering across text and image inputs. By distinguishing broadly related content from evidence that directly answers the question, the reranker helps agents use their context budget more effectively and focus on information needed to complete the task. For agentic retrieval systems, surfacing the strongest evidence earlier can reduce distracting context and help agents produce more grounded, efficient responses.
In collaboration with the MTEB team, we are launching the ViDoRe v3.1 reranking leaderboard to benchmark rerankers on document retrieval across image-only, text-only, and combined image-and-text inputs. Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B BF16 achieves 60.49 nDCG@10 with combined image-and-text inputs compared with Qwen-3-VL-Reranker-8B’s 59.17.
Figure 4. Nemotron-3.5-Rerank-8B-BF16 ranked first on ViDoRe v3.1 Reranking leaderboard as of 10/20/2026.
Figure 5. Text and visual reranker performance of Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B compared with Qwen 3 VL Reranker 8B. Both models reranked the top 50 candidates retrieved by the Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B model.
Scaling Multimodal Retrieval with NVFP4
Retrieval quality is only part of the equation for production agentic systems. As document collections and query volumes grow, teams must balance accuracy, throughput, and infrastructure requirements.
Nemotron 3.5 Embed 1B NVFP4 provides an optimized deployment option for high-throughput multimodal retrieval. On NVIDIA GB200, it delivers 27.1% higher throughput compared with the 1B BF16 model, increasing from 101.3 to 128.8 documents per second while retaining 99.85% of its retrieval accuracy on ViDoRe v3 with combined image and text inputs. As Figure 6 shows, the NVFP4 model offers a strong accuracy-throughput tradeoff for teams scaling retrieval across production workloads.
This deployment flexibility complements domain-specific customization: teams can select the data type of model weights that fits their infrastructure, then adapt the embedding and reranking models to their own terminology, documents, and retrieval tasks.
Figure 6. ViDoRe V3 retrieval accuracy versus serving efficiency, comparing Nemotron 3.5 Embed with selected smaller open embedding baselines.
High-Performance Serving with NVIDIA NIM
NVIDIA NIM provides a high-performance deployment path for Nemotron 3.5 Embed. In testing on an NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition, NIM delivered 6,031 query requests per second—approximately 2.9× the throughput of a comparable vLLM configuration at 2,099 requests per second—while maintaining comparable passage-processing throughput. This optimized serving stack helps enterprises scale retrieval workloads with production-ready deployment and support.
Figure 7. Nemotron 3.5 Embed NIM serving performance compared with the vLLM checkpoint on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs.
Adapting Retrieval to Domain-Specific Tasks
Enterprise agents often search documents containing specialized terminology and company-specific information that general-purpose retrieval models may not fully capture. Fine-tuning allows teams to adapt Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank using their own documents, queries, and relevance labels to their specific domains and use cases.
The Nemotron multimodal embedding fine-tuning recipe combines synthetic data generation, hard-negative mining, fine-tuning with NVIDIA NeMo AutoModel, and evaluation in one workflow. Teams can generate queries and relevance labels from their own documents to build training data for their retrieval tasks.
We evaluated the recipe on 8,202 chart and infographic images using 8,591 synthetic queries generated with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, focusing on enumerative and open-ended queries with multiple relevant images. Fine-tuning the Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16 on 6,872 queries for one epoch increased nDCG@10 from 37.34 to 44.12, a 18% relative gain over the base model, on 1,719 held-out synthetic queries. Using the same synthetic queries set, fine-tuning Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B-BF16 for one epoch increased nDCG@10 from 41.44 to 48.98, a 18% relative gain. [updated 8B finetuning results on Oct 29, 2026]
How We Built the Embed and Rerank Models
Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B builds on Ministral-3-8B-Instruct, with its language component initialized from Nemotron-3-Embed-8B-BF16. The model is trained on image and text corpora using contrastive learning to produce representations for multimodal retrieval.
The Embed 1B models are distilled from Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B, with their language component initialized from Nemotron-3-Embed-1B-BF16. Distillation combines cosine and mean squared error (MSE) losses to align the student’s embeddings with the teacher’s.
The language component remains frozen throughout embedding-model training. Text-only embeddings are therefore expected to remain unchanged from the corresponding Nemotron 3 Embed models, allowing existing text embeddings and vector indexes to be reused.
Nemotron 3.5 Rerank uses the same backbone architecture as Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B in a cross-encoder configuration. While the embedding model encodes queries and documents separately and scores their similarity, the reranker jointly encodes each query–document pair. A final multilayer perceptron (MLP) scoring head produces a scalar relevance logit.
All models are trained on a mixture of publicly available and synthetic multilingual, multimodal data, and their final released weights are produced through checkpoint ensembling. Further details on the training data are available in each model’s Hugging Face model card.
Nemotron 3.5 Parse
Enterprise knowledge often arrives in PDFs whose embedded text captures only part of what is on the page. Extracting that text can lose reading order, separate table values from their headers, or omit information conveyed in charts. Scanned documents and image-based PDFs may contain no usable text layer at all. Before this information can support search, retrieval, or automated document workflows, the pixels need to become structured content.
Nemotron 3.5 Parse converts document images into machine-readable text while preserving the structure that gives the content meaning. It identifies document elements, their locations, and reading order, and extracts tables and charts into structured representations. The resulting Markdown, HTML tables, and structured blocks give developers content that is better suited to indexing, search, and downstream processing. Applications can retrieve a passage with its surrounding context, process a table as rows and columns, and link extracted evidence back to its location on the original page.
At 631 million parameters, Nemotron 3.5 Parse brings this capability to document pipelines at scale, complementing Nemotron 3.5 Embed and Rerank with structured information for retrieval and agent workflows.
Leading Accuracy with Faster Document Processing
Figure 8. Nemotron 3.5 Parse ranked first on ParseBench leaderboard among models with fewer than 1 billion parameters as of 10/20/2026.
Nemotron 3.5 Parse ranks #1 on ParseBench among models with fewer than 1 billion parameters, achieving a score of 75.20 while processing 10.5 pages per second on one NVIDIA H100. It delivers best-in-class speed with well optimized parameter allocation, multi-token prediction, speculative decoding and flexible native-resolution handling. ParseBench tests table and chart extraction, content faithfulness, semantic formatting, and visual grounding.
Developers can scale processing toward speed or accuracy using the same model. Single-pass inference extracts each page once for the highest throughput. Double-pass inference revisits tables and charts identified in the initial page parse. Triple-pass inference adds a detection pass to find additional regions for refinement. This approach concentrates additional processing on document regions that benefit from a closer look.

All three configurations are Pareto optimal within this comparison: no other compared configuration achieves both higher accuracy and higher throughput. Teams can choose the operating point that fits their workload, from rapid ingestion of large document collections to more detailed extraction of complex pages.
Figure 9. Nemotron Parse 3.5 achieves pareto optimal performance on ParseBench leaderboard.
How We Built Nemotron 3.5 Parse
Nemotron 3.5 Parse is trained on a diverse mixture of enterprise documents, scientific papers, forms, tables, charts, and multilingual text. A strong synthetic data engine expands the range of layouts, structures, and languages the model sees, complementing automatically labeled documents and human-labeled data. Synthetic multilingual data helps build broad OCR capability, with strong performance in evaluations spanning 163 language and script combinations. This diversity prepares the model for the varied content found in enterprise document collections. Model card and multilingual coverage.
We further improve robustness and reliability through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), using custom reward functions to reinforce correct document structure and penalize failures. This post-training reduces repetitive generation loops and unclosed blocks, improves table consistency, and strengthens adherence to chart schemas, making extracted information more reliable for downstream document workflows.
Thank you to LightOn for raising the open-source bar with their models and technical blog. The shared techniques were pivotal in improving our model.
Early Enterprise Partner Evaluations
Elastic customers can access NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever embedding and reranking models through Elasticsearch’s Inference API using NVIDIA inference endpoints. Nemotron 3 will be available via Elastic Inference Service (EIS) soon, while support for Nemotron models on-prem deployment is on the roadmap.
Vectorize evaluated NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed using Hindsight Agent Memory, and it ranked first on two long-conversation memory benchmarks: achieving 93.8% recall@10 on LoCoMo and 65.9% on BEAM 100K against seven other embedding models. It also delivered the highest MRR and recall@5, highlighting its strength for retrieving relevant memories across long, complex conversation histories.
Perplexity saw strong results from NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed on Q2D-Web, its benchmark for first-stage retrieval in agentic search. On Perplexity's private 72-task reranking benchmark, NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Rerank 8B achieved the highest average score of the rerankers evaluated, with strong results across all six domains. These results show the value of specialized retrieval models alongside decision models like pplx-decider-v1.2. Perplexity looks forward to evaluating the Nemotron 3.5 retrieval suites, and the two companies are in ongoing discussions about deeper technical collaboration.
Turbopuffer evaluated NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Embed 8B on the enterprise PDF search benchmark and found that it provided ~5% more relevant results at Recall@20 than the next best model. These models are SOTA for common business tasks, like searching through PDFs with complex images, and are now available in Turbopuffer native embedding.
Getting Started
Developers can access the open weights, data, training recipes, and more on Hugging Face, deploy the NVIDIA NIM for production inference, or deploy the models through leading AI Cloud and Inference Partners including Baseten (Embed, Rerank, Parse), DeepInfra (Embed 1B, Embed 8B, Rerank 8B), FriendliAI (Embed 1B, Embed 8B, Rerank 8B), and OpenRouter (Embed 1B, Embed 8B, Rerank 8B).
Nemotron-3.5-Parse: Hugging Face, NIM
Nemotron-3.5-Embed-8B-BF16: Hugging Face, NIM
Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-BF16: Hugging Face, NIM
Nemotron-3.5-Embed-1B-NVFP4: Hugging Face, NIM
Nemotron-3.5-Rerank-8B-BF16: Hugging Face, NIM
For domain adaptation with NVIDIA AutoModel, we provide fine-tuning support for multimodal embedding and reranking, enabling teams to adapt the models to their own document collections and relevance requirements. Get started with the Nemotron embedding and reranking fine-tuning recipes.
Choose a model based on your workflow: Parse for extracting structured information from documents, Embed for searching text and images, and Rerank for improving the ordering of retrieved results. Combine them to build retrieval pipelines that deliver stronger evidence to AI agents.

items.title: ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model
items.summary:
Back to Articles
ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model
Community Article Published
October 20, 2026 Upvote 28
+22
Ashwath Vaithinathan Aravindan ashwath-vaithina Follow ibm-research Vatche Isahagian Vatche Follow ibm-research Vinod Muthusamy vinodmut Follow ibm-research Jayaram Radhakrishnan jayaramkr Follow ibm-research Evelyn Duesterwald evduester Follow ibm-research Gaodan Fang gaodan-fang Follow ibm-research Punleuk Oum illeatmyhat Follow ibm-research G Thomas gsthomasx Follow ibm-research Michał Ulewicz Michal Follow ibm-research Merve Unuvar mrvnvr Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research
ALTK-Evolve learns and applies a playbook using GPT-4.1, outperforming the retail entries on τ²-bench, a customer service agent benchmark—without updating model weights.
Learned memory takes a basic ReAct agent with GPT-4.1 to the top
Using GPT-4.1, an older, non-reasoning model, a basic customer-service agent reaches 67.5% Pass^4 on τ²-bench retail — meaning it solves the task on all four independent attempts for 67.5% of tasks. It scores above every retail entry in our October 12, 2026 leaderboard snapshot. It runs on the benchmark's stock ReAct scaffold, with learned guidelines appended to its system prompt.
ALTK-Evolve builds that playbook using GPT-4.1. It analyzes the agent's training-task attempts and uses the model to distill successes and failures into short behavioral rules: how to authenticate a customer, confirm a transaction, or handle a return. Those guidelines are then added to the agent's prompt for subsequent conversations. The same model powers both guideline extraction and the agent; no weight updates or human annotation are needed.
Our previous work demonstrated this approach on coding agents. Here, we test it on customer service, where success requires following domain policies, understanding a customer's request, and executing the right tool actions.
τ²-bench tests policy-bound customer service
τ²-bench (from Sierra) measures how well an agent handles customer-service conversations under real constraints. Each task pairs the agent with an LLM-simulated customer who has a goal in mind, a set of domain tools (look up an order, issue a refund, rebook a flight), and a written policy document the agent must follow. The agent has to draw out the right details, stay within policy, and take the correct — often irreversible — actions; a task counts as solved only when the final database state matches the expected outcome, a strict binary reward. We use its two customer-service domains, retail and airline.
We run τ²-bench's own implementation of a basic ReAct agent with a two-phase THINK → ACT loop, using gpt-4.1 as the agent model and gpt-5.5 as the customer-simulator model; 4 trials per task. The only change we make is a block of learned guidelines appended to the system prompt — everything else (policy, tools, scaffold) is stock τ²-bench. Concretely, the learned guidelines are tacked on after the domain policy as a plain markdown list:
You are a customer service agent that helps users according to the policy below.
Always follow the policy strictly. Use the provided tools when needed.
<policy>
# Retail agent policy
As a retail agent, you can help users:
- cancel or modify pending orders
- return or exchange delivered orders
- modify their default user address
…
</policy>
## Guidelines learned from past task attempts (follow these carefully):
- Authenticate the user before taking any order-related action. If email is unavailable, verify identity via full name and zip code using the find_user_id_by_name_zip API.
- Always confirm all intended changes (modify, cancel, return, exchange) with a clear, structured summary, and require explicit user approval before executing any database-updating action.
- When processing a return or exchange, communicate the refund with an itemized breakdown and clarify refund timing — don't wait for the user to ask.
- Take one action per step: never combine a tool call with a user-facing message in the same turn, and wait for the tool's result before replying.
- Before looking a user up, parse and clean their name — e.g. split a combined handle like `daiki_johnson_9523` into first/last name — and after a couple of failed lookups, state the exact format you need.
…
We extract guidelines from the agent's trajectories on τ²-bench train tasks using gpt-4.1, the same model that powers the agent, then apply them unchanged on the held-out test set.
Guidelines improve capability and reliability
In a prior post, we talked about how different models / tasks require different dosage of guidance. Inline with the idea, we also evaluate different amounts of guidelines provided to the model.
Each guideline carries a support count — the number of distinct training tasks it was extracted from, so higher support means a rule that generalized across more tasks rather than a one-off. We compare three configurations: baseline (no guidelines), sup3 (keep only guidelines with support ≥ 3 — a small, high-confidence core), and lossless (keep every guideline retained after consolidation, i.e. support ≥ 1).
Table 1. Guideline configurations and retained guideline counts by domain.

The metrics we track. Every task is attempted 4 times, and we read those trials two ways:
Mean Accuracy — the average success rate across the 4 trials. This is the capability axis: how often does the agent get this right?
Pass^4 — the percentage of tasks that passed across all 4 trials. This measures along the reliability axis and the metric the τ²-bench leaderboard reports. It matters here because a support agent that resolves a refund 3 times out of 4 still fails a quarter of real customers — Pass^4 asks whether you can trust the agent every time, not just on average.
Figure 1. Mean Accuracy and Pass^4 on held-out retail and airline tasks for agents using gpt-4.1 across four trials per task.
Agent model: gpt-4.1 (user simulator: gpt-5.5).

Mean Accuracy climbs in both domains — retail +4.4 pts (78.1 → 82.5) and airline +7.5 pts (57.5 → 65.0). Reliability moves further: the strict Pass^4 rises +10 pts in retail (57.5 → 67.5) and +10 pts in airline (35.0 → 45.0). And the gains come from better-informed calls, not longer conversations — we look at conversation length directly in Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns below.
The best amount of guidance depends on the domain
The two domains disagree about how much guidance pays off. In retail, more is better on every metric — the small sup3 core barely beats baseline on accuracy, and you need the full lossless set for the real jump. In airline the picture flips at the reliability end: lossless leads on accuracy (65% vs 60%), but the compact sup3 core (14 guidelines) is the more reliable one, taking Pass^4 to 45% against lossless's 40%. Echoing the earlier finding that delivery is a dial, not a constant, support count is a knob worth tuning per domain, not a value to hard-code.
Better performance costs more tokens, not more turns
Guidelines aren't free, but the cost lands where you'd expect — in prompt input tokens, not in a longer, more meandering conversation:
Figure 2. Total LLM cost per conversation by domain and guideline configuration on the full base split.

Does the agent get there by talking longer? To answer that cleanly we compare like for like: the task runs solved under both baseline and the guideline variant — identical scenario and seed, a true "same task, done right" set — and count assistant turns on each side.

The agent isn't talking longer — on the shared set, guidelines make conversations slightly shorter: lossless trims ~0.3–0.4 turns in both domains (retail 10.59 → 10.16, airline 9.15 → 8.82), and no variant lengthens them. That matters beyond cost: each turn is a sequential LLM round-trip, so fewer turns means lower end-to-end latency — a faster time-to-completion for the customer, not just a cheaper one. The only real price is on the input side — the larger system prompt riding on every LLM call: retail's 292-guideline prompt pushes cost from ~$0.084 to ~$0.139 per conversation, while airline's smaller playbook is cheaper. And in production even that is largely reclaimable with prompt caching, since the guideline block is identical across every call.
So the trade is a favorable one: for a slightly higher input cost (much of it cached away in practice) the agent lands higher accuracy, higher reliability, and lower time-to-completion at once — not the usual quality-for-latency tradeoff, but all three moving the right way together.
Learned guidelines also improve agents using frontier models
So far, we have used an older, non-reasoning model — gpt-4.1. A fair objection is that learned guidelines might have less to add to an agent using a frontier model: maybe they only patch the gaps of a weaker model. So we tested it directly — we reran airline using gpt-5.5 for both the agent and guideline extraction, on the same τ²-bench ReAct scaffold, with guidelines re-mined from the agent's own runs. One detail changes with the model: none of the guidelines extracted in this setup reached support ≥ 3 (they top out at support 2), so the high-support core here is sup2 rather than sup3.
Table 5. Held-out airline performance for the gpt-5.5 agent across four trials per task.

The learned guidelines improve this setup too. On the same held-out test tasks, appending them to the prompt lifts accuracy +10 pts (72.5 → 82.5) and the strict Pass^4 by +15 pts (55.0 → 70.0) — a larger reliability gain than we observed with gpt-4.1 on these very tasks (+10 pts), and from a much higher floor. Learning guidelines around the model can improve an agent even when it starts from a stronger base. And where the baseline's reliability swung between reruns, the lossless configuration reproduced exactly — the gain it buys is dependable, not a lucky draw.
ALTK-Evolve tops the leaderboard comparison
Submissions are scored on the full base split (train ∪ test), as τ²-bench requires, and reported at Pass^4. Because that covers the full task set rather than the held-out test split, these figures differ from the test-task numbers reported above. This is where the practical upshot shows up — prompt-level memory carries agents using each base model into, or past, current frontier company:
Retail: #1. On the base split the agent with learned guidelines reaches Pass^4 = 67.5%, ahead of every frontier model and ahead of RAFT-30B-A3B (61.4%), a model fine-tuned on synthetic τ²-bench retail data. Using stock gpt-4.1 and a prompt-appended playbook, it outperforms that fine-tuned system by +6.1 points.
Airline: #1 using gpt-5.5, #8 using gpt-4.1 Against the published board, the compact sup3 core gives the agent using gpt-4.1 Pass^4 = 44% — 8th, beating GPT-5.2 (no reasoning) and nearly matching Claude Sonnet 4.5. Swap in the stronger base and the same approach tops the field outright: the agent using gpt-5.5 reaches 82.0%, clearing every frontier entry (66–72%).
Figure 3. Pass^4 comparison between ALTK-Evolve runs and the τ²-bench leaderboard snapshot from October 12, 2026.
Same message in both domains: learning guidelines around the model works across different base models — bringing an agent using an older, non-reasoning model into frontier company on retail, and taking an agent using a frontier model to the top on airline.
Agents can improve without weight updates
Fine-tuning a model on a benchmark is expensive, brittle, and doesn't transfer to the next domain. Here, ALTK-Evolve improves a stock agent on a stock model in both domains — and matches or beats a fine-tuned system on retail — using only prompt-level guidelines extracted from the agent's own runs, automatically, without human annotation, and without any test-set leakage.

items.title: Announcing SimReady Central: An Open Library of Simulation-Ready 3D Assets for Robotics and AI Factories
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Announcing SimReady Central: An Open Library of Simulation-Ready 3D Assets for Robotics and AI Factories
Community Article Published
October 21, 2026 Upvote 68
+62
John Kosnik jkosnik Follow nvidia Frank DeLise delisef Follow nvidia Pomi Lee pomilee Follow nvidia
Building robotics simulations and high-fidelity AI factory digital twins takes more than 3D models. Developers often need to add properties such as collision geometry, mass, and friction. SimReady assets are 3D models that come prepared with the properties required for simulation workflows, reducing that manual work.
SimReady Central brings together more than 2,000 simulation-ready (SimReady) OpenUSD assets on Hugging Face, giving developers a free, ungated starting point for physical AI training environments and AI factory digital twins. The library includes a variety of infrastructure and equipment assets from robot arms and grippers to warehouse equipment, racks, and cooling infrastructure. Developers can check which capabilities each asset supports, then combine assets from different suppliers into a scene.
Equipment manufacturers (OEMs) can now prepare and validate assets against SimReady requirements and use SimReady Central to reach developers and allow their end customers to test and simulate scenarios faster and accelerate decision making. This enables industries to build simulations around their products while managing their own Hugging Face datasets.
We’ll cover what makes an asset SimReady and how OEMs contribute to SimReady Central, then show how developers can use those assets to build a robotic pick-and-place scenario and compare AI factory layouts.
What makes an asset SimReady?
SimReady assets are OpenUSD assets prepared with the properties required for simulation workflows. A detailed 3D model, such as CAD, is a useful starting point. Simulation requires additional information about how that object should be interpreted and used.
For a robot manipulation task, that might include the object’s mass, collision geometry, and friction properties. For AI factory workflows, it might include equipment geometry and the electrical or thermal metadata required by the application.
OpenUSD is an open, extensible framework for describing and composing 3D scenes. Using those scenes to train and evaluate autonomous machines also requires information about physical behavior, collisions, and sensor interactions.
SimReady Foundation provides specifications, profiles, and validation tools that make these requirements explicit. A profile defines the logical grouping of features and capabilities an asset needs for a particular use case.
Figure 1. SimReady Foundation defines asset representation requirements for specific simulation use cases, while developer libraries help prepare and validate OpenUSD assets against those requirements.
Depending on the asset and profile, those features can include:
Asset structural elements
What it enables
Collision geometry and physical properties
Contact and physics simulation in a supported runtime.
Joint structure and limits
Articulated robot and equipment movement.
Semantic labels
Object identification and annotated synthetic data.
Materials and sensor attributes
Rendering and supporting sensor simulation.
For the requirements associated with each simulation use case, see the SimReady Foundation requirements and profiles. Developers should select assets from SimReady Central whose profiles match their workflow needs and compose them into an OpenUSD scene.
Why publish OEM assets to SimReady Central?
OEMs can turn their CAD equipment models into SimReady assets for developers building simulations around their products. SimReady Central makes those assets discoverable on Hugging Face, helping manufacturers reach teams building robotics simulations and AI factory digital twins.
For AI factory OEMs like Vertiv, the library provides a path to distribute assets such as warehouse equipment racks, server racks, cooling equipment, and supporting infrastructure for AI factory digital twins. Developers and frontier agents can incorporate these assets into AI factory digital twins reusing the geometry and properties specified by their SimReady profiles.
For robotics OEMs like Comau, FANUC, Franka Robotics, Robotiq, Standard Bots, and Universal Robots, the library makes robot arms and grippers discoverable by teams building training and evaluation environments. Developers can combine these assets with industrial equipment to build warehouse and factory scenarios.
For simulation asset providers like Palatial the library features the NVIDIA Robotics 1K Dataset released in collaboration with NVIDIA Robotics, alongside complex articulated assets generated from text, images, scans, datasheets, and CAD. Developers can build assets and scenes for robot training and evaluation.
For OEMs like LG Electronics (LGE) that develop robots for the home alongside the appliances they work with, the library provides a path to share assets such as refrigerators and dishwashers. Developers can use assets informed by LGE’s experience in both appliances and robotics to build household simulation environments for robot training, evaluation, and synthetic data generation.
For AI-assisted CAD providers like ForgeCAD, the library makes articulated robotics props with high-quality textures available, which developers can use to build environments for robot perception and manipulation training, as well as synthetic data generation.
To contribute, OEMs can use the SimReady Central submission skill to validate assets against the relevant SimReady profiles, package them, and submit them for inclusion in the library.
Figure 2. OEMs prepare and validate OpenUSD assets against SimReady profiles and then submit the asset to SimReady Central. Developers and AI agents discover assets in the library and use them to build simulation environments.
Build simulation environments with SimReady assets
SimReady Central gives robotics and industrial developers a reusable starting point for robot workcells, industrial environments, and AI factory digital twins. Developers and AI agents can find assets in SimReady Central that meet the profiles required by their workflows and compose them into OpenUSD environments.
Developers can use SimReady assets to populate training environments with objects and obstacles, then vary their placement to evaluate robot behaviors. These environments can support projects such as Microduck, an open-source robot from Hugging Face and Pollen Robotics.
Figure 3. Asset datasets connect through SimReady Central on Hugging Face, using its USD search service to support Isaac workflows, SimReady Central library search, and AI agent workflows.
NVIDIA USD Search powers natural-language search in SimReady Central, helping developers and AI agents find assets across participating datasets. Hugging Face has also integrated USD Search into their platform search with indexed USD properties and simulation metadata, helping agents discover SimReady assets suited to their physical AI simulation tasks.
AI-assisted authoring adds another way to build with those assets. Developers can use frontier models like OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra combined with asset search and scene-authoring tools to build environments using SimReady Central. Given task requirements and spatial constraints, Astra can help find suitable assets, write code to assemble a scene, and create scenario variations.
OEMs can also use Astra to help prepare and refine OpenUSD assets against SimReady Foundation requirements before validating and submitting them to the library.
Build a robotic pick-and-place scenario
For example, a developer building a robotic pick-and-place scenario could start with this prompt:
Using SimReady assets from SimReady Central on Hugging Face, create a basic warehouse pick-and-place scenario in Isaac Sim using PhysX.
Use the nvidia-simready-central.hf.space to find a FANUC robotic arm, a compatible Robotiq gripper, and suitable warehouse assets. Generate the Python code to assemble the scene and configure the pick-and-place task. Render a .mov preview so I can review the results.
Include the scripts, asset versions, and runtime versions so I can reproduce the scenario.
In this workflow, we expect Astra to do the following:
Query the SimReady Search API to find relevant assets distributed on Hugging Face
Reference/Payload them into an OpenUSD stage
Generate Python code to assemble the workcell
Configure the Pick-and-place task
Render a preview for user review
Figure 4. A robotic pick-and-place workcell assembled from SimReady assets illustrates how AI-assisted scene authoring can turn developer requirements into a simulation scenario for review and refinement in Isaac Sim.
Compare AI factory layouts
The same approach can support an ISV (independent software vendor) building an AI factory digital twin. The task shifts from robot interactions to equipment placement: arranging racks, cooling equipment, and supporting infrastructure within specified spatial constraints.
Using SimReady assets from SimReady Central on Hugging Face, create two alternative AI factory layouts with racks and cooling equipment.
Use the supplied equipment dimensions and aisle-clearance requirements. Check for equipment overlaps and clearance violations, and report any issues.
Save each layout as an OpenUSD scene. Include the scene-building scripts, asset versions, and runtime versions so I can reproduce and compare the results.
In this workflow, Astra would assemble the selected SimReady assets into two OpenUSD layouts, followed up by generating scripts to check equipment overlaps and aisle clearances against the supplied requirements. Developers could then inspect the layouts in their simulation application, compare equipment placement and access paths, and review any flagged issues before refining the preferred configuration.
Figure 5. An AI factory layout assembled from SimReady assets illustrates how AI-assisted scene authoring supports equipment placement, aisle-clearance checks, and layout refinement in OpenUSD.
In either example, developers can extend their environments in a few ways:
Reuse the environment: Keep layout and task-specific changes in separate OpenUSD layers so the same source assets can support multiple experiments.
Vary the scenarios: Introduce additional assets from the library and vary object placements, equipment configurations, or surrounding infrastructure to evaluate different conditions.
Build application-specific tests: For robotics, configure training and evaluation tasks in Isaac Lab. For AI factories, connect the scene to the equipment data and simulation tools needed for analyses such as power distribution or cooling performance.
Carry validated layouts into operations: For AI factories, connect the scene to live BMS and IT telemetry to keep the digital twin synchronized with an AI factory facility.
Help shape the next wave of assets
SimReady Central’s roadmap includes more OEM partners and a growing asset library, expanding the equipment and environments developers can assemble from reusable content.
Community feedback will help identify which additions matter most. Tell us in the comments which assets you need, which runtimes you use, and where you encounter integration gaps.
Submit OEM assets for inclusion in SimReady Central using the asset submission guide.
OEM contributions can broaden the available content, while developer examples can show how assets work in different applications. Share examples of what you build in the comments and open an issue in SimReady Foundation for bugs or SimReady requirements feature requests.
Start building on Hugging Face 🤗
Choose an asset from SimReady Central Library for your next robotics simulation or AI factory digital twin. Use the resources below to find assets, build a scene, or contribute equipment models.
Discover assets
Find assets for your task: SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face
Search with natural language: Describe the assets you need through the SimReady Central search endpoint powered by USD Search.
Build your own asset browser: Explore the index-to-library skills in the SimReady Central GitHub repository.
Build a scene
Learn to assemble OpenUSD scenes: Follow the free OpenUSD learning path.
Develop your robotics and digital twin skills: Explore the free physical AI courses.
Build robotics simulations: Start with the Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab.
Build AI factories: Start with an agent-assisted digital twin workflow.
Prepare and contribute content
Start the OEM contribution process: Follow the onboarding guide and find FAQ answers in the SimReady Central Library documentation.
Choose the requirements for your asset: Review the profiles in SimReady Foundation.
Prepare CAD models for simulation: Use the CAD-to-SimReady skills.
Validate, package, and submit your assets: Follow the SimReady Central submission skill.
Happy building, we can’t wait to see what you create!

items.title: bekko-static-embedding-v1: State-of-the-Art Retrieval for Multilingual Static Embeddings
items.summary:
Back to Articles
bekko-static-embedding-v1: State-of-the-Art Retrieval for Multilingual Static Embeddings
Community Article Published
October 21, 2026 Upvote 18
+12
Yuichi Tateno hotchpotch Follow
I've released bekko-static-embedding-v1, a multilingual static embedding model.
It achieves state-of-the-art retrieval among static embeddings: about 11 points above the other multilingual static models on multilingual retrieval, and about 2 points above English-only static models on English retrieval.
Static embeddings skip the Transformer: each token maps to a fixed vector, and a sentence embedding is their average.
They need no GPU and can run 100x to 400x faster on CPU than models like multilingual-e5-small.
bekko-static-embedding-v1 uses a custom 200k-token tokenizer and was trained contrastively on about 814 million text pairs covering 40 languages, with a batch size of 16,384.
It also performs close to Transformer models.
On MMTEB's retrieval tasks, bekko-static-embedding-v1 comes within about 1 point of multilingual-e5-small, a 12-layer Transformer model.
Performance comparison
Against other static embedding models
bekko-static-embedding-v1 leads every public static model I compared, on both multilingual and English retrieval:
Multilingual retrieval. On MNanoBEIR (14 languages × 13 tasks, nDCG@10 × 100) it scores 43.76, about 11 points above static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1 (32.29) and potion-multilingual-128M (32.23).
English retrieval. On NanoBEIR-en (13 tasks) it scores 53.71, above the English-only stable-static-embedding-fast-retrieval-mrl-en-v2 (SST-v2 below, 51.57) and static-retrieval-mrl-en-v1 (50.35). Truncated to 512 dimensions (52.82), it still beats both.
MMTEB. Across 131 tasks the average is 50.18, about 3 points above both multilingual static models. In the Retrieval category the margins are 8.75 and 12.10 points.
Matryoshka dimensions. Truncating to 512 dimensions costs about 0.9 points of average retrieval score.

I trained bekko-static-embedding-v1, and I also develop HAKARI-Bench, the retrieval benchmark used in this post.
How static embeddings work
A static embedding model splits text into tokens with a tokenizer and gives each token a fixed vector.
Encoding a sentence is just a table lookup for each token followed by a mean.
With no Transformer layers to run, vectors come out fast.
Usage with Sentence Transformers
The model loads directly with Sentence Transformers.
This example encodes "sushi is delicious" in English, French, Spanish and Chinese.
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
model = SentenceTransformer("hotchpotch/bekko-static-embedding-v1", device="cpu")
vectors = model.encode(
[
"Sushi is delicious.",
"Les sushis sont délicieux.",
"El sushi es delicioso.",
"寿司很好吃。",
],
normalize_embeddings=True,
)
print(vectors.shape) # (4, 1024)
print(model.similarity(vectors, vectors))
Queries and documents are encoded the same way; no query: or passage: prefixes are needed.
For shorter vectors, pass truncate_dim (32, 64, 128, 256, 512 or 1024):
compact = model.encode(["A short query"], truncate_dim=512, normalize_embeddings=True)

Should you use a static embedding for retrieval?

In this evaluation BM25 beats bekko-static-embedding-v1 on 21 of 37 benchmark averages and on 342 of 550 tasks.
It wins by a wide margin on the long-document NanoMLDR and NanoLongEmbed and on Japanese NanoJMTEB-v2.
On NanoMIRACL, where natural-language questions are matched to documents, the static model wins: 68.03 for bekko-static-embedding-v1 against 57.15 for BM25, a 10.88-point gap.
For some retrieval tasks, a static embedding is the better choice.

Loading only the weights you need
Sentence Transformers' truncate_dim truncates the output vectors, but it still loads the full 1,024-dimensional table.
If you only ever use 512 or 256 dimensions, that memory is wasted.
So the repository also ships ONNX and OpenVINO files that contain only the weights for one dimension.
The model card provides a small get_model() helper to pick the backend, dimension and precision:
from transformers.dynamic_module_utils import get_class_from_dynamic_module
def get_model(backend="onnx", dim=512, precision="int8", revision="main"):
repo = "hotchpotch/bekko-static-embedding-v1"
ext = {"onnx": "onnx", "openvino": "xml"}[backend]
return get_class_from_dynamic_module(
"bekko_static_backend.BekkoStaticBackend", repo, revision=revision,
).load_sentence_transformer(
repo, revision=revision, backend=backend,
file_name=f"{backend}/model_{precision}_dim{dim}.{ext}",
)
model = get_model(backend="onnx", dim=512, precision="int8")

Which model should you pick?
Based on these results, this is how I would choose:
For cheap multilingual embeddings, start with bekko-static-embedding-v1 at 512 dimensions.
If retrieval is the only goal, compare it against BM25 with a tokenizer suited to your language.
For bitext mining or pair classification, also evaluate static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1.
If retrieval quality matters most and you can afford Transformer inference, consider multilingual-e5-small or bekko-embedding.
bekko-embedding is a contextual embedding family that uses Transformer attention, unlike bekko-static-embedding-v1.
Its Transformer part is kept small: bekko-embedding-v1-a8m has about 7.7M active parameters and runs on CPU.
In this comparison it scores 60.34 on NanoBEIR-en and 52.65 on MNanoBEIR, both above multilingual-e5-small.
If you want a balance of retrieval quality and inference speed, bekko-embedding is worth a look.
How I trained it
A custom tokenizer
In a static model, the tokenizer's units are exactly the units whose vectors get averaged.
So besides the existing vocabularies of multilingual BERT and Gemma 2, I tried vocabularies fitted to the training data.
bert-base-multilingual-uncased, used by static-similarity-mrl-multilingual-v1, is among the baselines.
The custom vocabularies use WordPiece.
I first trained a 30k English vocabulary on equal numbers of Wikipedia and FineWeb documents.
I then added vocabulary for 39 more languages while keeping the English token IDs, for 200k tokens in total.
To choose, I trained 8 models, one per tokenizer, on 10% of the training data.
I evaluated them on 200 retrieval tasks: MNanoBEIR (14 languages × 13 tasks) and NanoMIRACL (18 languages), nDCG@10 × 100 averaged with equal weight.
"uncased" ignores letter case and "cased" keeps it.
"script-balanced" is a candidate that rebalances vocabulary across writing systems.
"200k, 30k English" means 200k tokens in total with a 30k English core reserved first.

Training data and hyperparameters
Training uses the bekko-embedding unsupervised dataset, the multilingual corpus described in the Bekko Embedding paper.
From its roughly 1.15 billion rows, I selected 265 data configurations targeting 40 languages, about 814 million text pairs in total.
The 40 target languages are English, Arabic, Bulgarian, Bengali, Catalan, Czech, Danish, German, Greek, Spanish, Estonian, Persian, Finnish, French, Hebrew, Hindi, Croatian, Hungarian, Indonesian, Italian, Japanese, Korean, Dutch, Norwegian, Polish, Portuguese, Romanian, Russian, Slovak, Slovenian, Serbian, Swedish, Swahili, Telugu, Thai, Turkish, Ukrainian, Vietnamese, Yoruba, Chinese.
The pairs include titles and bodies, questions and answers, generated search queries and translation pairs.
For translation data I kept NLLB English HQ and dropped the other bitext sources.
The selection also includes data derived from the MIRACL train split and from NLI.
The embedding table starts from random initialization and learns to pull matching pairs together.
The loss is Multiple Negatives Ranking Loss (MNRL), which contrasts each pair against the other candidates in the batch, applied at the full 1,024 dimensions and at every Matryoshka dimension.
There is no distillation from a teacher model.

items.title: NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation
items.summary:
Back to Articles
NVIDIA Cosmos3-H-Dreams: Bringing Clinical Surgery to Life Through Generative Simulation
Community Article Published
October 20, 2026 Upvote 14
+8
Lukas Zbinden lzbinden Follow nvidia Javier Gamazo javirk1 Follow nvidia Nigel Nelson nigeln Follow nvidia Mostafa Toloui mtoloui Follow nvidia Sean Huver shuver Follow nvidia
Picture moving the Cadiere grasper, grasping the gallbladder, and lifting it, all within a generated surgical scene that responds in real time. Today, we take the next step and introduce Cosmos3-H-Dreams, bringing interactive generative simulation to the visual and procedural complexity of clinical surgery with our most convincing in-body imagery to date.
Our first Cosmos-H-Dreams release, built on Cosmos-Predict2.5, brought interactive generative simulation to dVRK tabletop suturing, a foundational proving ground for surgical robotics. As world foundation model (WFM), Cosmos-H-Dreams demonstrated an alternative to numerical simulation: rather than explicitly modeling scene geometry, tissue deformation, and physical interactions, it learned visual dynamics directly from synchronized video and robot kinematics, yielding interactive tabletop task simulation with high realism.
Today, Cosmos3-H-Dreams advances this capability by learning from video and robot kinematics recording during clinical procedures on the CMR Surgical Versius platform. To our knowledge, this is the first real-time generative surgical simulator trained on clinical cholecystectomy recordings to support live kinematic control. Powered by Cosmos 3 and accelerated with FlashDreams, NVIDIA’s accelerated streaming-inference library, Cosmos3-H-Dreams runs interactively on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 GPU.
1. From Tabletop Tasks to Clinical Scenes
In a controlled tabletop environment like that of Cosmos-H-Dreams, instruments operate against a relatively simple background. Inside the human body, however, small instrument movements can affect an entire scene: tissue stretches under traction, reflections shift, structures become occluded, and smoke changes visibility. Given an initial image and supplied tool actions, a generative simulator must capture these responses while preserving the anatomy and instruments as it generates each new block of video. Small errors can accumulate over time, gradually changing instrument geometry or anatomical structure, making temporal consistency essential.
Visual realism is therefore a starting point for validation, not proof of biomechanical accuracy. The generated scene must also follow the controls: translation, rotation, and gripper commands should produce coherent anatomical consequences. A plausible-looking rollout that ignores those commands cannot serve as an interactive environment.
Maintaining this fidelity and responsiveness in a live control loop requires low latency generation. Cosmos3-H-Dreams addresses this setting through a model specialized for clinical cholecystectomy and distilled for real-time generation, bringing action-conditioned interaction into scenes with complex anatomy, tissue motion, and occlusion.
2. What is New in Cosmos3-H-Dreams?
2.1 A Cosmos 3 Foundation and Richer Surgical Controls
Cosmos3-H-Dreams builds on Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano, a 16-billion-parameter model pretrained on Open-H-Embodiment, and specializes a bidirectional teacher on curated cholecystectomy video and kinematics. Sample selection targets two visible, engaged instruments, a left Cadiere grasper and a right monopolar hook, and limits camera commands to emphasize instrument-driven interaction.
The model uses 28 action dimensions: pose and gripper information for both arms, plus energy controls, thumbstick axes and thumbstick buttons. Training uses 832 x 480 video with actions aligned at 10 Hz; that sampling rate is distinct from runtime generation throughput.
2.2 From Teacher to Four-Step and Two-Step Students
Cosmos3-H-Dreams combines a teacher-to-student training pipeline designed for long autoregressive rollouts with accelerated streaming inference through FlashDreams.
We first adapt the bidirectional teacher on 24 future frames, then extend the horizon to 72 frames, 2.4 and 7.2 seconds at 10 Hz. This gives the teacher longer sequences over which to learn surgical dynamics.
Next, distillation turns the bidirectional teacher into a causal student that can generate video in short blocks as new actions arrive. Causal teacher forcing prepares the student for sequential generation using recorded context. Self-Forcing then trains it on its own generated context, guided by the teacher and a learned critic. This helps address the accumulation of errors during interactive rollouts.
The first released student uses four denoising steps per generated block. We then train that student further with a two-step schedule to produce the second release checkpoint. The two-step model is separately trained, not simply the four-step model run with fewer sampling steps.
Fewer denoising steps results in faster inference time at the expense of lower visual quality. Both checkpoints let developers explore the balance between visual quality and inference cost.
2.3 Streaming through FlashDreams
FlashDreams supplies the accelerated streaming runtime. Long rollouts also require managing the model’s attention history. The Cosmos3-H-Dreams integration uses an adapted FadeMem module that consolidates the growing key/value cache during long rollouts. This complements Self-Forcing: distillation addresses how the model learns from its generated history, while cache consolidation addresses how that history is stored during streaming generation.
3. Exploring Unseen Trajectories
During a clinical procedure there may be complications or some room for the surgeon to perform “novel” movements. Therefore, a simulator must be able to generalize beyond the training data, and produce coherent frames with unseen movements. The demonstrations below show Cosmos3-H-Dreams generating different cholecystectomy scenes conditioned on instrument actions recorded with a VR headset.
The two videos begin with the same initial frame but follow different action sequences illustrating how instrument control leads to distinct continuations of the same scene with physically accurate tissue deformations.
Furthermore, these rollouts allow us to inspect whether instruments follow the controls, whether tissue responds coherently to interaction, and whether anatomical and instrument appearance remain consistent over time.
4. Adapting to Your Own Data and Controller
Cosmos3-H-Dreams includes four-step and two-step checkpoints for cholecystectomy. The system can be adapted to other datasets and embodiments with synchronized video and compatible action representations. To train a real-time student model on your own dataset, we provide a complete recipe for teacher fine-tuning and Self-Forcing distillation in our step-by-step guide. It describes data preparation, public teacher-training tools, and the distillation stages. Controller integrations must use the same action conventions and normalization as training.
5. What is Next
The advance in visual realism opens several research directions:
Model the full procedure. Expand coverage and temporal consistency so all phases of cholecystectomy can be explored systematically, with clear task boundaries and success criteria.
Connect generative and numerical simulation. Combine learned visual realism with explicit geometry, contact and tissue mechanics. Numerical models and measured data could help constrain and validate deformation, making simulation behavior inspectable as well as convincing.
Evaluate with surgeons. Assess anatomical accuracy, instrument behavior and tissue response, turning expert feedback into reproducible benchmarks.
Support more instruments. Move beyond two controlled tools to richer coordination, occlusion and interaction.
Develop autonomous surgical policies. Couple world action models to Cosmos3-H-Dreams in a closed loop, so policies can learn defined cholecystectomy subtasks.
These are research directions, not established clinical capabilities. Cosmos3-H-Dreams is a research simulator, not a validated system for patient care. It offers a foundation for studying surgical interaction in an increasingly realistic environment.
6. Get Started Today
Explore the models, data, and runtime behind Cosmos3-H-Dreams:
Cosmos3-H-Dreams code and examples: GitHub repository
Cosmos3-H-Dreams model: Hugging Face checkpoint
Cosmos3-H-Embodied-Nano: Hugging Face model and GitHub repository
Adapt to your own data: Step-by-step recipe for teacher fine-tuning and self-forcing distillation
Open-H-Embodiment: Hugging Face dataset
FlashDreams: GitHub repository
NVIDIA Cosmos 3: GitHub repository
Bring your controllers, your trajectories, and your research questions. We look forward to seeing what the community builds inside these new surgical worlds.
