items.title: Do we really need bigger AI weather forecasting models to improve resolution?
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Do we really need bigger AI weather forecasting models to improve resolution?
Community Article Published
October 20, 2026 Upvote 14
+8
Emma Scharfmann EmmaScharfmann Follow Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow Kashif Rasul kashif Follow
Applying the downscaler we trained on AIFS-ENS's output to improve the forecast resolution from ~ 28km to 5.5km. Ensemble mean of the forecast over France, valid Wednesday 13 August 2025 at 12:00 UTC (+60 h from initialisation). Ocean grid points are masked.
TL;DR
In this blog, we want to share something research and AI have taught us: you don’t always need a bigger model; often you need to adapt the model to your task. The same idea applies to AI weather forecasting. If you need forecasts at a higher resolution, you can take an existing global model and train a small downscaler on top of it to learn the local details, like the effects of orography or coastlines. We trained one in about an hour to downscale AIFS-ENS temperature forecasts over France from ~28 km to 5.5 km. Against Météo-France weather stations, it reduced the error by 14% in RMSE and 21% in CRPS over the first two days, and by 9% and 14% over ten days (as shown in the demo space).
Table of Contents
Intro
What is a downscaler & demo
Downscaler components
Running a downscaler for temperature over France
Training the downscaler
Conclusion and some notes worth sharing
References
Intro
AI weather models are very good at forecasting large-scale weather patterns. But they see the world as a grid, often at 0.25° resolution (roughly equivalent to a grid of 28km in central Europe), where each cell holds a single value for temperature, wind, and every other variable. Anything smaller than a cell gets averaged out, so local effects from valleys, mountains, islands, or coastlines are lost.
Big labs are tackling this by building models that work at finer resolution. Google DeepMind's WeatherNext 3 for example, which is unfortunately not open source, forecasts surface temperature and humidity at around 5 km (~0.05°). But building and running such models require a huge amount of compute and storage, and engineering resources that only a few organizations have.
A cheaper way to do this is to train a downscaler (i.e. an AI model that predicts at a local scale starting from data at a larger scale) on top of an existing model. A downscaler learns local details to predict what happens within a cell, and therefore improves the resolution. And it runs in seconds, on top of an existing model forecast. In this post, we explain how a downscaler works, then we show how to run, train and evaluate one on weather-station observations for 2m temperature over France.
What is a downscaler?
A weather forecasting model predicts the weather at a specific resolution. A downscaler is an ML model that takes a low resolution forecast and fills in the local details. The downscaler learns these local details from static information such as elevation and the coastline. For example, it learns that within a coarse cell, a mountaintop is colder than the valley below and the coast is milder than inland. Once trained, it can be plugged on top of a coarse forecast to produce a high-resolution forecast at low cost.
You can try out the downscaler we trained on AIFS-ENS (ECMWF) [1] and GEFS (NOAA) forecasts and see how it compares against Météo-France temperature observations in our demo space below.
Like all ML models, downscalers are not magical. So, before training one, check that what you want to improve is something a downscaler can improve. Below is our summary of what a downscaler can and cannot improve.
What a downscaler can improve
What a downscaler can't improve
Add the patterns due to the terrain (valleys, mountains, coastlines)
Fix global errors in the coarse model: if the coarse is too warm in one region, the downscaler will not fix it
Produce a single or an ensemble of fine fields from one coarse field
Add details that the inputs do not contain (it cannot add the effect of mountains without an input that identifies them, like the elevation)
Work behind any coarse model
Reduce the uncertainty of the large-scale forecast
Run in seconds, once trained
Exceed the quality of the fine field used during training
Downscaler components
Training
During training, we show the model the same weather at two resolutions with some additional details (static data). It learns what the coarse version systematically misses by predicting the error between the coarse and fine weather.
Two datasets: the downscaler needs a coarse dataset and a fine dataset covering the same place and times. We used ERA5 [2] at 0.25° for the coarse dataset and CERRA [3] at 5.5 km for the fine dataset. For each time step, the coarse field is interpolated onto the fine grid. The model learns to predict the difference between this interpolated field and the fine field.
Static data: In addition to the field to predict, the downscaler needs additional information to infer what is happening within the cell. These fields are static and therefore easy to learn from. We add the season and the time of day, so the model can also learn how that correction varies through the day and through the year. In our example, we’re using the elevation of the fine-scale field, the height difference between the real surface and the coarse model’s surface, the land fraction and the distance to the sea of the cells, the longitude/latitude and the season and time of day as static data.
Loss function: We made the choice in our example of building a downscaler for an ensemble model. So, we use fair CRPS[4], which scores an ensemble rather than a single field. It rewards being close to the truth and having realistic spread. Note that the loss in our example is computed over land only, since the target reanalysis produces sea surface temperature differently from the land temperature.
Noise: For one large-scale state, there are several possible fine-scale states. So instead of asking for one prediction, we train the downscaler to predict multiple outputs. Each forward pass draws fresh noise and produces a different fine field. Therefore, the downscaler produces an ensemble of forecasts from one coarse field.
Downscaler: The model that learns to predict the difference between the coarse field and the fine field from the coarse field and the static data. In our example, we train a U-Net with about 2M parameters, which took around an hour to train on a GPU.
Inference
Once trained, the downscaler can be added on top of any forecast model (AI-based or physics-based) which outputs the same variable at the same resolution and covers the same region as the training data. In our example, that means that our downscaler can be used with any model producing 2m temperature at 0.25° over France. In this blog post, we apply it to AIFS-ENS. It could equally be applied to other 0.25° models such as Microsoft’s Aurora, GEFS (NOAA) or NVIDIA’s Atlas. Note that one of our static inputs (the height difference) is frozen against ERA5’s terrain. That is right for AIFS-ENS, which is initialised from ERA5, but not GEFS, which runs on its own. This may be part of why the downscaler performs less well on GEFS (see the demo space).
Input data: the downscaler takes the coarse ensemble forecast as input, as well as the same static data used during training, which is stored inside the model. Each coarse member is interpolated onto the fine grid before the forward pass. In our example, ten members from AIFS-ENS at 0.25° are used as input.
Downscaler: it takes the interpolated coarse field, the static data and a draw of noise, then predicts the correction to add to the coarse field. Since the noise is drawn on each pass, running the same member several times gives multiple fine fields.
Output: the model outputs multiple members at fine resolution. In our example, each of the ten coarse members yields four samples, giving forty members at 5.5 km. Note that in our example, running the downscaler takes only a few seconds per forecast.
Running a downscaler for temperature over France
This section walks you through how to use the downscaler we trained to improve the resolution of the temperature predicted by a model (here AIFS-ENS 0.25°)) over France. You can follow the steps below or run this tutorial.
Set up
Clone the repo and install dependencies.
git clone https://github.com/EmmaScharfmann/weather-forecast-model-downscaler
cd weather-forecast-model-downscaler
uv sync
The forecasts are fetched from the Earthmover Marketplace,
which needs a free account and a free subscription to the AIFS-ENS dataset. Subscribing creates a repository under your organisation. Put the repo name in FORECASTS below, then authenticate once.
We also recommend having a free Hugging Face account (sign up here) to download the model's weights and data.
uv run arraylake auth login # or export ARRAYLAKE_TOKEN=ema_xxxxxxxxxxxx
uv run hf auth login # or export HF_TOKEN=hf_xxxxxxxxxxxx
Then, import the packages and set the config.
See packages and config
from pathlib import Path
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import xarray as xr
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
from downscale.constants import COARSE_CROP_MARGIN_DEG, ZERO_C
from downscale.downscaler import Downscaler
from downscale.evaluation import at_valid_times, lead_scores, stack_members, station_rmse
from downscale.fetch import get_target
from downscale.inference import downscale_forecast, save_downscaled
from downscale.plots import map_grid, maps, native_cells, station_maps
from downscale.regions import parse_region
from downscale.sources import (
available_inits, fetch_forecast, forecast_box, open_forecasts, save_forecast, store_name,
)
from downscale.station_interp import curvilinear_for
from downscale.stations import load_published_stations
MODEL_REPO = "EmmaScharfmann/france-temperature-downscaler"
FORECASTS = "<earthmover-org>/ecmwf-aifs-ens-forecast-subscription" # your Earthmover subscription
FORECASTS_2020 = "hf://datasets/EmmaScharfmann/aifs-ens-france-aug2020"
CERRA_REPO = "EmmaScharfmann/cerra-france-t2m-2014-2020"
STATIONS = "EmmaScharfmann/france-stations" # Météo-France, Aug 2020, Aug 2025, Jan-Jun-Jul 2026
MEMBERS = 10 # AIFS-ENS members to downscale (out of 51)
MAX_LEAD_HOURS = 240
SAMPLES = 4 # members out of the downscaler (total 4 x 10 = 40)
EVAL_SAMPLES = 1 # both ensembles keep 10 members, and downscaling is 4x faster
BOX = forecast_box(parse_region("france"), COARSE_CROP_MARGIN_DEG)
OUT = Path("outputs/tutorial") # every forecast is fetched and downscaled once, then read from here
Fetch the coarse forecast
archive = open_forecasts(FORECASTS)
inits = available_inits(archive)
INIT = pd.Timestamp("2025-08-11 00:00")
coarse = fetch_forecast(archive, INIT, BOX, members=MEMBERS, max_lead_hours=MAX_LEAD_HOURS)
Run the downscaler
The model needs a fine grid as input, so the coarse field has to be interpolated first. The static data are part of the model's checkpoint on the Hub. Here, we choose to predict 4 fine members from the coarse field.
model = Downscaler.load(hf_hub_download(MODEL_REPO, "model.pt"))
LAND = xr.DataArray(model.static["land_sea_mask"] > 0.5, dims=("y", "x"))
downscaled = downscale_forecast(model, coarse, samples=SAMPLES)
fine = stack_members(downscaled)
save_forecast(coarse, OUT / "forecasts")
save_downscaled(downscaled, OUT / "downscaled" / store_name(INIT))
fine is the output of the downscaler: its shape is (time, lead_time, member, y, x), with 40 members (10 coarse members × 4 samples), and it holds the temperature in kelvin over France at a resolution of 5.5 km. On a GPU, the downscaler takes seconds to run.
We can plot the coarse forecast and the downscaled forecast:
LEAD = 60 # hours: 12 UTC on 13 August
k = int(np.flatnonzero(coarse.lead_time.values == np.timedelta64(LEAD, "h"))[0])
valid = pd.Timestamp(downscaled.valid_time.values[0, k])
raw_mean = native_cells(coarse.isel(time=0, lead_time=k).mean("ensemble") - ZERO_C, model.lat, model.lon, LAND.values)
fine_mean = fine.isel(time=0, lead_time=k).mean("member").where(LAND).values - ZERO_C
interp_mean = downscaled.t2m_interp.isel(time=0, lead_time=k).mean("ensemble").where(LAND).values - ZERO_C
elevation = np.where(LAND, model.static["cerra_orography"], np.nan)
LABELS = {
"title": f"Ensemble mean 2m temperature, valid {valid:%d %B %Y %H} UTC (+{LEAD} h)",
"coarse": "(a) AIFS-ENS, 0.25° (~28 km)",
"downscaled": "(b) AIFS-ENS + downscaler, ~5.5 km (~0.05°)",
"added": "(c) Correction added by the downscaler: (b) minus (a)",
"elevation": "(d) Elevation of the 5.5 km grid",
"temperature_unit": "2m temperature (°C)",
"correction_unit": "correction (K)",
"elevation_unit": "elevation (m)",
}
low, high = np.nanpercentile(np.concatenate([raw_mean.ravel(), fine_mean.ravel()]), [1, 99])
fig = map_grid([
dict(title=LABELS["coarse"], lon=model.lon, lat=model.lat, values=raw_mean,
vmin=low, vmax=high, label=LABELS["temperature_unit"]),
dict(title=LABELS["downscaled"], lon=model.lon, lat=model.lat, values=fine_mean,
vmin=low, vmax=high, label=LABELS["temperature_unit"]),
dict(title=LABELS["added"], lon=model.lon, lat=model.lat, values=fine_mean - interp_mean,
cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-6, vmax=6, label=LABELS["correction_unit"]),
dict(title=LABELS["elevation"], lon=model.lon, lat=model.lat, values=elevation,
cmap="terrain", vmin=0, vmax=3000, label=LABELS["elevation_unit"]),
], title=LABELS["title"])
We see on panel b) that the resolution is improved everywhere but it is especially obvious in the mountains. On panel c) and d), we see that the main corrections are added where the orography is (Massif Central, Alps, Pyrenees) and on the coast (especially in Brittany).
Compare forecasts against CERRA
CERRA is what the model learned to reproduce during the training. Comparing against it shows how much the model actually learned.
Expand to see the details of the evaluation code
def run(archive, init):
"""The coarse and downscaled forecasts of one initialisation, computed once and saved."""
name = store_name(init)
path = OUT / "downscaled" / name
if not path.exists():
coarse = fetch_forecast(archive, init, BOX, members=MEMBERS, max_lead_hours=MAX_LEAD_HOURS)
save_forecast(coarse, OUT / "forecasts")
save_downscaled(downscale_forecast(model, coarse, samples=EVAL_SAMPLES), path)
return xr.open_zarr(OUT / "forecasts" / name)["t2m"], xr.open_zarr(path)
def score(downscaled, stations, cerra=None, short_leads=48):
"""Score one downscaled run against the stations and, when given, against CERRA."""
downscaled = downscaled.isel(sample=slice(0, EVAL_SAMPLES)) # the run from section c has more
forecasts = {
"AIFS-ENS": downscaled.t2m_interp.rename(ensemble="member").load(),
"AIFS-ENS + downscaler": stack_members(downscaled).load(),
}
read = curvilinear_for(model.lat, model.lon, stations).apply
observed = at_valid_times(stations.t2m, downscaled.valid_time) # (time, lead_time, station)
out = {"stations": {}, "means": {}}
short = downscaled.lead_time <= np.timedelta64(short_leads, "h")
for name, forecast in forecasts.items():
at = read(forecast)
out["stations"][name] = lead_scores(at, observed)
out["means"][name] = at.mean("member").sel(lead_time=short).values
out["observed"] = observed.sel(lead_time=short).values
if cerra is not None:
truth = at_valid_times(cerra.t2m, downscaled.valid_time) # (time, lead_time, y, x)
out["cerra"] = {name: lead_scores(f, truth.where(LAND)) for name, f in forecasts.items()}
at = read(truth) # CERRA at the stations
out["stations"]["CERRA"] = lead_scores(at, observed) # same valid times: the floor
out["means"]["CERRA"] = at.sel(lead_time=short).values
return out
archive_2020 = open_forecasts(FORECASTS_2020)
inits_2020 = available_inits(archive_2020)
cerra, _ = get_target(inits_2020[0], inits_2020[-1] + pd.Timedelta(hours=MAX_LEAD_HOURS), repo=CERRA_REPO,
load=True) # about 30 MB, read once rather than streamed
stations_2020 = load_published_stations(STATIONS, start="2020-08-01", end="2020-08-31")
print(f"{len(inits_2020)} initialisations, {inits_2020[0]:%d %b} to {inits_2020[-1]:%d %b %Y}; "
f"{stations_2020.sizes['station']} stations")
runs_2020 = {init: run(archive_2020, init) for init in inits_2020}
results_2020 = [score(downscaled_2020, stations_2020, cerra) for _, downscaled_2020 in runs_2020.values()]
coarse_first, first = runs_2020[inits_2020[0]]
k = int(np.flatnonzero(first.lead_time.values == np.timedelta64(36, "h"))[0])
valid_2020 = pd.Timestamp(first.valid_time.values[0, k])
raw = native_cells(coarse_first.isel(time=0, lead_time=k).mean("ensemble").load() - ZERO_C,
model.lat, model.lon, LAND.values)
interp = first.t2m_interp.isel(time=0, lead_time=k).mean("ensemble").where(LAND).values - ZERO_C
down = stack_members(first).isel(time=0, lead_time=k).mean("member").where(LAND).values - ZERO_C
truth = cerra.t2m.sel(time=valid_2020).where(LAND).values - ZERO_C
when = f"valid {valid_2020:%d %b %Y %H} UTC (+36 h)"
fig = maps([
("AIFS-ENS - coarse dataset, resolution 0.25° (~28 km)", model.lon, model.lat, raw),
("CERRA - fine dataset, resolution: 5.5 km (~0.05°)", model.lon, model.lat, truth),
("AIFS-ENS + downscaler - resolution: 5.5 km (~0.05°)", model.lon, model.lat, down),
], width=4.4, title=f"Ensemble mean 2m temperature, {when}")
fig = maps([
("AIFS-ENS minus CERRA", model.lon, model.lat, interp - truth),
("AIFS-ENS + downscaler minus CERRA", model.lon, model.lat, down - truth),
], cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-5, vmax=5, label="K", title=f"Error against CERRA, {when}")
for name, error in [("AIFS-ENS", interp - truth), ("AIFS-ENS + downscaler", down - truth)]:
print(f"{name:24s} RMSE against CERRA over land {np.sqrt(np.nanmean(error ** 2)):.2f} K")
Above, we plot the coarse forecast (AIFS-ENS), the fine field (CERRA) and AIFS-ENS + downscaler on summer 2020 (which was not used for training). We see that the error of AIFS-ENS against CERRA is very high in the mountains, which is pretty well corrected by our downscaler.
Compare forecasts against observations
We used observations from Météo-France weather stations to evaluate the model against an independent ground truth. Downloading the station data takes around 1 hour for 1 month, so we cached the stations' data on the Hub (EmmaScharfmann/france-stations) to save some time: load_published_stations in the evaluation code above reads them from there.
# Ensemble means and observations at every station, first 48 h of every run
names = ("AIFS-ENS", "AIFS-ENS + downscaler")
fields = {name: np.concatenate([r["means"][name].reshape(-1, r["means"][name].shape[-1]) for r in results_2020])
for name in names}
observed = np.concatenate([r["observed"].reshape(-1, r["observed"].shape[-1]) for r in results_2020])
rmse_2020 = {name: station_rmse(fields[name], observed) for name in names}
fig = station_maps(stations_2020.longitude.values, stations_2020.latitude.values, rmse_2020,
title="RMSE against each station, first 48 h, August 2020")
Again, we see that the downscaler corrects pretty well the error in the mountains (Alps, Massif Central, Pyrenees) and on the coast (Brittany, Normandy), as we expect it to do.
You can run more forecast and evaluation against observations on our demo space.
Training the downscaler
You can train your own downscaler (you can change the data, resolution, variable, region...) following what we did to train our own downscaler. We will walk you through the main steps in this blog, but you can find a complete tutorial here.
Set up
You need to clone the github repo and log into your Earthmover free account to fetch the coarse field (ERA5 in the tutorial). Then, you need to adapt the configuration for the training (number of epochs, steps per epochs, starting and ending dates of the data for training and validation).
Building the training pair
You need to build pairs of coarse field - fine field. In our tutorial, we're using ERA5 for the coarse field and CERRA for the fine field from 2014 to 2019 for the training and 2020 for the evaluation. ERA5 is fetched from Earthmover while CERRA is cached on the Hub. Then, the static data (at the resolution of the fine field) are added to the pairs: orography, longitude/latitude, land-sea mask, time of the year/day and distance to the coast. The model has to learn to predict the difference between the two maps below:
Training the model
We train a small U-net to learn to predict the difference between the coarse and the fine field.
Random noise is added to predict a probabilistic correction. A CRPS loss is used to train the ensemble downscaler. 2014-2019 is used for training. We train the model for 20 epochs.
Evaluating the model
We evaluate the model against CERRA (year 2020). We plot the difference between the coarse model (ERA5) and ERA5 + downscaler. As expected, we see that local errors in the mountains or the coast are corrected by the downscaler while global errors of the coarse model are not corrected by the downscaler (error in Normandy).
We can also plot the power spectrum of the forecasts. The power spectrum shows how much detail a field has at each scale. The right panel shows the same, but divided by CERRA, so 1 means “as detailed as CERRA”.
ERA5 runs out of detail below ~100 km. A downscaled member follows CERRA, so the model adds the right amount of detail at the right scales. The ensemble mean is slightly smoother than the single member as it averages the details that are uncertain.
Conclusion and some notes worth sharing
Training a downscaler takes a GPU and a couple of hours. It does not make a forecast better globally, but it makes it (way) better locally. Comparing against CERRA tells us whether the downscaler learned what it was trained to learn, comparing against stations tells us whether the final forecast is good. Scoring CERRA itself against stations gives an upper bound on what the downscaler can achieve. And our downscaler gets surprisingly close to that bound (as shown in the figure below)!
RMSE by station elevation and by time of day for AIFS-ENS, AIFS-ENS + downscaler and CERRA, August 2020, all lead times. From the demo space.
Notes worth sharing
This is a demonstration, not a robust evaluation. We chose temperature because it is a smooth variable, summer somewhat arbitrarily (we started out looking at heatwaves and drifted towards training a downscaler), and AIFS-ENS because its forecasts were available on Earthmover and it runs fast (0.5 s per 6-hour step on a GPU).
The power spectrum was our most useful diagnostic. It showed that noise drawn at a single scale piles up spread at that wavelength, and changing the scale only moves the excess. Drawing noise at several scales reduces the problem but doesn't fully solve it.
All errors have a strong daily cycle, because of effects that CERRA, AIFS-ENS and the downscaler all struggle to predict, such as inversions at night and surface heating in the afternoon.
Only about 10–30% of the difference between the coarse and fine fields is predictable from our inputs. The rest would need more inputs, such as wind.
Next steps: we'd like to try precipitation and wind, temporal conditioning instead of treating each time step independently, and a GNN trained directly on station observations instead of a reanalysis. We'd love your feedback on what was useful and what we should do next, in the comments or by email. The model, code and demo are all available.
Acknowledgements: thanks a lot to Quentin Nicolas for sharing his climate expertise and for the many comments that made this post clearer and more accurate.
References

items.title: A curriculum for post-training agents
items.summary: Back to Articles A curriculum for post-training agents Community Article Published October 20, 2026 Upvote 118 +112 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow huggingface Sergio Paniego sergiopaniego Follow huggingface merve merve Follow huggingface Post-training refers to the training stages that follow pretraining, such as supervised fine-tuning, distillation and reinforcement learning. These stages turn a pretrained model into one that follows instructions, uses tools or solves a specific task. When a model acts as an agent, it works over many turns. It calls tools, reads the results and decides what to do next. Agentic post-training applies these stages to agents, so training has to account for the whole sequence of turns instead of a single answer. This page is organized in five steps, after an introductory section. Every step includes a diagram of the method, a livestream or slides, a blog post that explains the idea and the relevant documentation. Some steps add example projects built with that method. The table below summarizes, for each step, what the model learns from, the TRL trainer and what you need to prepare. The order of the steps follows Training Agents, a livestream series on the Hugging Face YouTube channel. Each session covers one post-training method, with training a coding agent as the running example. The Post-training Agents playlist has the four sessions plus two related workshops. Steps at a glance Step The model learns from TRL trainer What you need 1. SFT agent traces from a stronger model SFTTrainer a dataset of agent traces 2. Distillation a teacher's tokens or probabilities DistillationTrainer prompts and a teacher model 3. RL a score for each answer GRPOTrainer prompts and a reward function 4. RL environments the outcome of acting in an environment GRPOTrainer tasks and an environment (OpenEnv) 5. Harnesses and scale full runs of a real agent AsyncGRPOTrainer tasks, an environment and an agent harness 0. Before you start The terms used in the rest of the page (agent, harness, scaffold) and an overview of all the steps. Read: Harness, Scaffold, and the AI Agent Terms Worth Getting Right Overview deck: Train the agent, not just the model (20 slides covering all the steps) If fine-tuning is new to you: LLM Course 1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) The model learns to copy agent traces, recordings of an agent solving a task with every tool call and its result, usually produced by a stronger model. It's cheap and stable. The model only sees correct traces, never its own attempts. When it makes a mistake while solving a task, it has not learned how to recover from it. On-policy distillation and RL address this by training on the model's own outputs. Watch: Training Agents 1: fine-tune a coding agent (code) Read: Training Agents: Class 1, SFT from scratch Docs: SFT Trainer 2. Distillation A teacher model supervises the student, either through the data it writes or through its probabilities on the student's own tokens. The teacher is usually a larger model, several expert models distilled into one student (as in MOPD), or the same model with extra context in the case of self-distillation. The signal is dense, one value per token, so training needs fewer samples than RL. On the other hand, the student is limited by what the teacher knows, and on-policy distillation has to run the teacher at every training step. RL replaces the teacher with a reward that only checks the result. Watch: Training Agents 2: distillation (collection) Read: A brief history of distillation in AI Distillation in 2026 (so far) Docs: Distillation Trainer 3. Reinforcement learning (RL) In reinforcement learning, the model learns from a score on its own outputs. It writes an answer, a reward function scores it, and training makes high-scoring answers more likely. This removes the need for a teacher. A way to check the answer is enough. The algorithm used in this step is GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization). For each prompt it samples several answers, scores them all, and raises the probability of the ones that scored above the group average. Comparing answers within the group tells the model which attempts were better, without training a separate model to estimate that. The signal is weaker than in distillation, one number for the whole answer instead of one per token, so the model needs many attempts to learn. With a plain reward function each answer is a single turn, scored once. Environments let the model act several times and see the result of each action. Watch: Training Agents 3: reinforcement learning (collection) Read: How frontier models train on outcomes in 2026 Projects: Fine-tuning a 350M model for structured outputs in 100 GRPO steps Docs: GRPO Trainer 4. RL environments The reward comes from acting in an environment that keeps state, exposes tools and answers back over several turns. The environment runs the tools, keeps track of what changed and checks the final result, for example by running the tests of a coding task. Each episode is longer than a single answer, so generating rollouts becomes the slowest part of training. Watch: Training Agents 4: from reward functions to environments (collection) RL for Agents Workshop Read: Why RL environments work now (and could not in 2016) Projects: Paint watercolours with code Autonomous driving with CARLA Docs: TRL + OpenEnv OpenEnv docs 5. Harnesses and scale Each rollout is a full agent run through an existing agent harness inside a remote sandbox. Training through the same harness the agent uses in practice means the model learns in the setting where it will run. Generation and training run on separate GPUs, so long episodes don't leave the trainer idle. The trainer then sends the updated weights back to vLLM. items.title: Sort your prompts: a free speed-up for MoE batch inference
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Sort your prompts: a free speed-up for MoE batch inference
Community Article Published
October 19, 2026 Upvote 10
+4
Abdennacer Badaoui badaoui Follow
TL;DR. In a mixture-of-experts model, each decode step has to read the weights of every expert that any request
in the batch routes to. If you run a big offline job (evals, synthetic data, labelling) over prompts from several
domains, mixing them in each batch makes the model read more experts than it needs to. Just sorting the prompts
before calling llm.generate, so that similar requests end up decoding together, made unmodified vLLM
+12–17% faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and +7–12% faster on gpt-oss-120b (one AMD MI300X). On unlabeled chat traffic,
grouping by a 0.6B embedding model still gives +5% on Qwen and up to +4% on gpt-oss.". No model change, no kernel change, no custom scheduler:
one argsort.
Real recorded routing of Qwen3-30B-A3B. Each cell is one (layer, expert) pair; lit = its weights are read at this
decode step, for a batch of 32 requests. Left: random order. Right: the same requests sorted by domain.
Why batch composition matters for MoEs
During decoding, a GPU spends most of its time reading weights, not computing. For a dense model the bytes read per
step are fixed: all weights, once. For an MoE it depends on the batch. Every expert chosen by at least one token in
the batch must be streamed from HBM once per layer; experts nobody picked cost nothing.
Qwen3-30B-A3B has 48 layers × 128 experts, and each token picks 8. A single request touches 8 experts per layer. A
batch of 32 random requests touches about 94 of 128, because their choices barely overlap. But expert choice is not
random: code tokens prefer some experts, French tokens others. Put 32 code requests together and they overlap a
lot more.
Each domain uses its own subset of experts
We counted which experts each domain's generated tokens pick in one layer. Each domain concentrates on its own group:
its 32 favourite experts (a quarter of the layer) receive 68–80% of all its routing decisions, against 25% if
routing were uniform. Code, math, prose, French, Arabic and Chinese each light up a different corner.
Decode time follows the number of experts touched
We measured that link directly. With a vLLM-style fused-MoE Triton kernel on real routing, the MoE layer time is a
straight line in the number of distinct experts the batch touches: about 2.9 µs per extra expert, which is just
9.4 MB of expert weights at ~3.3 TB/s.
How many experts does a batch touch?
We recorded the routing of every prompt and generated token for 768 prompts across 6 domains: code (MBPP), math
(GSM8K), creative writing (no_robots), and French, Arabic and Chinese (Aya). Routing is computed per token, so we
can replay any batch composition exactly, offline.
With 128 fine-grained experts (Qwen3-30B-A3B), one-domain batches read 19–25% fewer experts per step than
mixed batches, at every batch size from 8 to 128.
With only 32 coarse experts (gpt-oss-20b), the gap is 8–11%: there is less room to specialise.
The savings grow with depth. Later layers are the most domain-specialised.
Does it survive end to end?
Fewer bytes in the MoE layers don't automatically mean faster generation: attention, the KV cache, sampling and
scheduling don't care about expert locality. So we measured in stock vLLM 0.27 (ROCm, CUDA graphs, its own
fused-MoE kernels). Setup:
768 prompts, each generating exactly 256 tokens (ignore_eos=True), greedy decoding.
The two runs do identical work. The only difference is the order of the prompt list.
vLLM's offline engine is first-come first-served, so the order decides which requests share a decode batch.

outs = llm.generate(sorted_by_domain_prompts, sp) # same prompts, sorted

Two GPUs, expert parallel. With the experts split across both MI300X (tensor_parallel_size=2, enable_expert_parallel=True), sorting still gives +12.9% at batch 64 (3,440 → 3,885 tok/s) and +8.7% at batch
128 (6,835 → 7,431 tok/s). With experts sharded, each GPU only waits for its own distinct experts, and grouping
lowers that count on the busiest GPU too (~22% fewer in replay).
Each cell is 3 alternating repeats. Run-to-run spread is below 1% for Qwen and up to 4% for gpt-oss-120b. Every sorted run beat every shuffled run, except for gpt-oss on UltraChat at batch 128, where the gain is within noise.
For Qwen, the gains are about half of what the bytes-read model predicts (+20–27%). That is expected, because only the MoE part of each step gets cheaper.
Outputs. Reordering doesn't change what each request computes, but it changes which requests share a batch,
and in bf16 that can flip a near-tie in greedy decoding. That holds for any change of batch composition. To put a
number on it, we compared the sorted run against a shuffled run, and one shuffled run against a different shuffled
run: sorting changes outputs about as much as reshuffling does.

These differences come from ordinary batch nondeterminism: none of these requests computes anything different.
If you need bit-exact outputs, you need batch-invariant kernels, whatever order you use.
No labels? Use the router, or a tiny embedding model
Real traffic doesn't come with domain labels. There are two label-free ways to group it.
Router fingerprint. After prefill, every prompt has a vector of how often it used each expert in each layer.
k-means on these vectors recovers our 6 domains with 100% purity, and it gives the same savings as the true
labels. It needs access to the router, though.
Text embedding. Embed each prompt with Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B
and run k-means. This needs nothing from the MoE, runs before inference, and works for any model.
On the multi-domain workload, the embedding clusters are as good as the labels up to batch 32. On
UltraChat, where no domains exist, clustering
still cuts experts read by 7–12%. End to end in vLLM: grouping UltraChat with the embedding model gives +5.1-5.5% throughput on Qwen3-30B-A3B at every batch size, and +2–4% on gpt-oss-120b (nothing measurable at batch 128).
On the 6-domain set, embedding clusters give +13.0% at batch 64, slightly above the true labels (+12.6%).
The whole recipe:
from sort_prompts import expert_friendly_order
order = expert_friendly_order(prompts, n_clusters=16) # embed + k-means + stable argsort
outs = llm.generate([prompts[i] for i in order], sampling_params)
outs = [o for _, o in sorted(zip(order, outs))] # restore the original order
What if I can't sort the whole dataset?
A streaming job or a server can't see all requests in advance. It can, however, reorder within a window of the
next W requests, which bounds how long any request waits.
Measured in vLLM at batch 32, sorting every chunk of 128 prompts gives +11.7%, every chunk of
256 gives +14.8%, and sorting the full 768 gives +17.3%. A reorder window of 4–8 batches keeps most of the
gain.
Natural output lengths
With EOS enabled, sorting also groups requests of similar length (math answers are short, stories are long), which
changes how the batch drains. With natural lengths (EOS on, up to 512 tokens, batch 32), the sorted job finishes 16.6% sooner in
wall-clock time: 1,810 → 2,104 output tok/s. The gain survives the realistic setting.
Where this doesn't help
Dense models. Every weight is read at every step anyway.
Prefill-heavy work. Thousands of prompt tokens touch nearly every expert regardless of order. This is a decode
effect.
Coarse MoEs. With few experts (gpt-oss-20b, 32 experts), there's less to gain.
Very large batches. Once even a one-domain batch touches almost every expert, there's nothing left to save,
and the step becomes compute-bound.
Latency-sensitive online serving. Holding requests back to group them costs queueing time. The natural home
is offline batch jobs, or a scheduler that picks similar requests from its existing waiting queue.
Related work
The underlying observation, that decode cost tracks the number of distinct experts and that similar requests share
experts, is not new, and others have built systems on it:
ELDR (Choi et al., 2026) routes requests to decode workers by a prefill
"expert signature" in disaggregated serving. They report 17–21% fewer activated experts for same-domain batches
and 5.9–13.9% lower TPOT in vLLM, which agrees with our numbers.
Bambhaniya et al., 2026 groups micro-batches by expert activation to cut
multi-node all-to-all traffic.
Sem-MoE schedules requests onto the expert-parallel ranks that host their
likely experts.
ExpertFlow groups tokens by predicted routes in an offloading setting.
Read-ME uses a decoupled router to do expert-aware batching, but needs a
model change.
Lynx, Opportunistic Expert Activation
and XShare reduce distinct experts per batch by changing routing. That is
complementary, but it changes outputs.
Our point is the minimal version of this: no new system, no predictor, no model change. One sort before an offline
job, measured end to end in unmodified vLLM.
Reproduce
Everything (routing capture, replay simulator, Triton kernel, vLLM benchmark, figures) is in
the repo. Hardware: AMD Instinct MI300X; software: vLLM 0.27.1, ROCm 10, PyTorch 2.12.

items.title: Train in Simulation, Deploy on a Real Robot: Microduck with Isaac Lab 3.0
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Train in Simulation, Deploy on a Real Robot: Microduck with Isaac Lab 3.0
Community Article Published
October 21, 2026 Upvote 29
+23
Oluwaseun Doherty seun-doherty Follow nvidia Oyindamola Omotuyi OOyindamola Follow nvidia Richard AntRi31 Follow nvidia Asier Arranz asiernvidia Follow nvidia
This post was written in collaboration with Antoine Pirrone, Augustin Crampette, Matthieu Lapeyre, Coralie Deplanne, Anne-Charlotte Passanisi, and Thomas Wolf.
TL;DR
Microduck is a newly released affordable open-source bipedal robot by Pollen Robotics and Hugging Face. And now you can train Microduck to walk with Isaac Lab and Newton. Test the policy, export it as ONNX, and deploy it on the real robot. Share it on the Hugging Face Hub or validate it for competition in Microduck Arena, then explore more advanced tasks with NVIDIA Isaac Lab.
Introduction
A walking policy trained in simulation must also handle the friction, delays, and mechanical play of real robot servos.. NVIDIA Isaac Lab is an open-source framework for training policies across thousands of GPU-parallel simulations. With Newton, actuator modeling, and domain randomization, developers can prepare policies for real hardware. Microduck brings this workflow to life: train a walking policy in simulation, export it as ONNX, and deploy it on a real biped robot.
This tutorial walks you through training and evaluating Microduck with Isaac Lab and Newton, then exporting the policy for deployment. From there, you can share your model on the Hugging Face Hub, test its compatibility and compete in Microduck Arena, or put it to work on your own Microduck. Walking is the starting point—with linked examples to help you explore more of Isaac Lab 3.0.
1. Install Isaac Lab and prepare for Microduck training
For the simulation and training portion, you’ll need:
A Linux workstation with a supported NVIDIA GPU and driver. See requirements.
Git and uv.
For deployment, you’ll also need:
A configured physical Microduck.
Its onboard robot software is installed and working.
A supported control interface, such as a paired gamepad.
Quick install
On Linux with a supported NVIDIA GPU and driver, install uv (skip the first two lines if it is already available), clone Isaac Lab, and install its dependencies:
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
source "$HOME/.local/bin/env"
git clone --branch main https://github.com/isaac-sim/IsaacLab.git
cd IsaacLab
uv sync
Confirm that the Microduck tasks and presets are available:
uv run isaaclab list_envs --keyword MicroDuck --show_presets
2. Understand the ready-to-train Microduck environment
Isaac Lab already provides Microduck’s robot model, scene, observations, actions, rewards, and domain randomization. Start with the flat-walking task; the rough variant adds stairs, slopes, and uneven terrain.
Figure 2. Microduck environments side by side: flat terrain (left) and uneven terrain (right).
The policy takes 61 observation values and outputs 14 joint-positions. Keep the observation order, normalization, and action scaling consistent when exporting and deploying. See the Microduck task configuration for the full observations, rewards, and simulation settings.
3. Accelerate locomotion training with parallel Isaac Lab environments
Isaac Lab accelerates Microduck locomotion training by running simulated environments in parallel on the GPU. Isaac Lab can also run distributed training across GPUs, for instance training with 16 GPUs to speed-up the training and increase robustness. In this configuration, we can reach up to 1.25M steps per seconds with rough terrain and backlash enabled.
In this tutorial, we use Newton with the MJWarp solver and Newton-based Better Actuator Models (BAM) to model servo response, together with the backlash preset to turn position targets into realistic servo torques by modelling the firmware controller, motor electrical limits, friction and delay. To allow the policy to transfer from simulation, we make use of domain randomization. On each duck we randomize the mass/centre of mass, ground friction, joint inertia, encoder offsets, battery voltage/sag and command latency. We also vary terrain and apply pushes; as well as backlash independently per joint to represent uneven wear.
Backlash is the mechanical play in a gearbox, when a joint changes direction, the transmission can move slightly before engaging. Modeling this effect and varying it across joints during training exposes the policy to differences it may encounter on the real robot.
Run this command to start training:
uv run isaaclab train \
--rl_library rsl_rl \
--task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
--num_envs 4096 \
presets=backlash
We used the rough terrain for deployment but alternatively you can train the flat terrain environment with this command:
uv run isaaclab train \
--rl_library rsl_rl \
--task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Flat-MicroDuck \
--num_envs 4096 \
presets=backlash
4. Evaluate the Microduck walking policy and export it to ONNX
To deploy a Microduck walking policy on the physical robot, export it to ONNX after evaluating it in simulation. Isaac Lab’s RSL-RL playback workflow automatically exports both TorchScript (policy.pt) and ONNX (policy.onnx) files. Use policy.onnx with Microduck’s onboard runtime, keeping the observation order, normalization, and action scaling consistent with training.
Run the latest checkpoint in the Newton visualizer:
uv run isaaclab play \
--rl_library rsl_rl \
--task IsaacContrib-Velocity-Rough-MicroDuck \
--checkpoint latest \
--num_envs 16 \
--viz newton_gl \
presets=backlash
Replace latest with the path to a specific checkpoint.
Figure 4. Microducks execute a walking policy across uneven terrain in simulation.
Export the policy for Microduck
For deployment we will be using the policy for the rough-terrain environment. The current RSL-RL playback implementation exports both TorchScript and ONNX files to an exported directory associated with the selected run:
exported/
├── policy.pt
└── policy.onnx
Microduck’s onboard runtime loads ONNX policies. Use policy.onnx for the hardware handoff. The automatic export is implemented in Isaac Lab’s RSL-RL playback backend.
5. Share policies on Hugging Face and evaluate them in Microduck Arena
With policy.onnx exported, you can:
Compare it in Microduck Arena, a Hugging Face Space for testing compatible policies on shared challenges and comparing leaderboard results. Arena accepts models with 61 observation values, 14 action values, and a maximum size of 64 MiB. Follow the submission guide to check compatibility and enter a challenge.
Run it on the real Microduck. After checking the observation and action interface from section 4, use the ONNX file with the robot’s onboard runtime; section 6 covers transfer to hardware.
Share it on the Hugging Face Hub. Upload your policy so others can discover and download it. We recommend adding a short model card explaining how to use it. You can also include the training configuration to help others reproduce your results.
6. Deploy the ONNX locomotion policy on a real Microduck
After validating the policy in simulation and checking its interface (section 4), deploy policy.onnx to a configured Microduck:
Copy the policy from your workstation, replacing ROBOT_HOST with the robot’s hostname or IP address:
scp exported/policy.onnx microduck@ROBOT_HOST:/home/microduck/my_walking.onnx
Connect to the robot and inspect its current policies:
ssh microduck@ROBOT_HOST
robotctl policy list
Support the robot on its stand, then load the walking policy. If it is already walking, loading returns it to its home pose and resumes motion.
sudo robotctl policy load walk /home/microduck/my_walking.onnx
Use the documented controls to test standing, slow walking, turning, and stopping. Monitor its state; restore the default walking policy if needed:
robotctl monitor
sudo robotctl policy reset walk
Follow the Microduck policy-loading guide for runtime setup and behavior. Figure 5 demonstrates the deployed policy’s robustness to falls: Microduck recovers its footing and resumes walking after being knocked over.
Figure 5. Real Microduck walking with the locomotion policy trained in Isaac Lab.
7. Extend Microduck training to rough terrain and perception tasks with Isaac Lab
Isaac Lab 3.0 unlocks GPU-parallel robot learning across locomotion, dexterous manipulation, and vision-based tasks, with extensible environments and configurable physics and rendering backends. Explore these examples and tools:
More complex locomotion: Adapt Microduck’s rough-terrain task for stairs, slopes, and uneven ground, with a curriculum that increases terrain difficulty.
Perception and navigation tasks: Extend Microduck’s walking policy with head-camera depth and robot-state observations to explore perception-based tasks in simulation. The GIF below shows ramp traversal. Explore camera-based observations in the Kuka–Allegro examples for vision-enabled manipulation.
Dexterous manipulation: Try the Kuka–Allegro lift and reorient tasks to train an arm and multi-fingered hand to manipulate objects.
Custom environments: Use the project generator to build your own task, then add simulation-ready (SimReady) assets from SimReady Central Library, and tailor observations and rewards to new challenges.
Figure 7. Parallel training in NVIDIA Isaac Lab lets simulated Microducks practice traversing different ramps and platforms, while learning to maintain balance and avoid falls
Figure 8. Microduck perception task in simulation, with an external view above and RGB, depth, and segmentation views below.
Build your next walking policy
Start with the Microduck task in Isaac Lab, train your first walking policy, and share the exported ONNX model on the Hugging Face Hub. Validate it in Microduck Arena, enter a challenge, and see how your policy compares. Then build on what you learn—try rougher terrain, add perception, or create your own task.
Resources

Isaac Lab installation guide
Microduck training environments and configuration
Newton-based BAM actuator documentation
Microduck Arena and ONNX submission guide

Microduck robot software and deployment guide
Isaac Lab Learning Path
Acknowledgments
This workflow builds on Pollen Robotics’ Microduck hardware and software, the original Microduck reinforcement-learning project, BAM actuator modeling work, and the Isaac Lab and Newton integrations.

items.title: NVIDIA Kumo Forecast Combines Pretrained Time-Series Representations with Historical Pattern Retrieval and Interpretability
items.summary:
Back to Articles
NVIDIA Kumo Forecast Combines Pretrained Time-Series Representations with Historical Pattern Retrieval and Interpretability
Community Article Published
October 21, 2026 Upvote 9
+3
Saira Qureshi sairaq Follow nvidia Aditi Gautam adgautam Follow nvidia Manikandan Ravikiran mravikirannvidia Follow nvidia Sena Ekiz neptunel1 Follow nvidia Viraj P Modak vmodak Follow nvidia
Highlights (TL;DR)
NVIDIA Kumo Forecast (formerly known as NV-Tesseract Forecasting) is a multi-variate time-series forecasting model that combines a pretrained Transformer backbone with Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR), a context-enhanced forecasting mode that blends direct model predictions with patterns retrieved from historical data. This includes interpretability of the results. Built on the MOMENT-1-large backbone, Kumo Forecast uses an approximately 340-million-parameter base encoder plus a trainable forecasting head.
The library provides a DataFrame-first API, configurable forecast horizons, optional historical context for retrieval, and an interpretability framework that produces horizon-specific explanations without modifying the underlying forecaster.
Kumo-Forecast is available under Apache 2.0 license.
Model code: NVIDIA/Kumo-TS
Model weights: nvidia/Kumo-Forecast
The Shift to Context-Enhanced Time-Series Forecasting
A forecasting system can draw on two different sources of information: representations learned during pretraining and historical observations available for the current application. Kumo-Forecast brings these together through a pretrained forecasting model and an optional retrieval pathway over historical context.
In its direct forecasting path, Kumo-Forecast uses a MOMENT-based Transformer and a trained forecasting head to predict future values. In Domain Aware Representation and Retrieval (DARR) mode, it also retrieves related patterns from historical data using a nearest-neighbor approach and combines that information with the direct forecast.
This creates a distinction between the model’s input window and its retrieval context. The input window supplies recent observations for the forecast; a separate historical DataFrame can supply additional context for pattern retrieval. Developers can adjust how strongly the final prediction relies on each pathway through the library’s configuration options.
Further information on DARR mode can be found in this published paper, Memory-Augmented Forecasting: Scalability and Generalization Across Temporal Domains
How Kumo Forecast Works
Kumo-Forecast combines four main components: a pretrained temporal encoder, a trainable forecasting head, historical-pattern retrieval mechanism and an interpretability framework.
Pretrained Temporal Representations: The model uses the MOMENT-1-large Transformer encoder as its backbone. The architecture keeps encoder and embedder weights frozen while training the forecasting head, separating the pretrained representation model from the task-specific prediction layer.
Direct Forecasting: The forecasting head maps the model’s representations to future values for the requested horizon. For horizons beyond the model’s native capability, there is support for autoregressive extension. This distinguishes a directly generated forecast from a longer forecast that extends predictions recursively.
Domain-Aware Representation and Retrieval: DARR augments direct forecasting with k-nearest-neighbor retrieval from historical context data. This process combines direct forecasts with historical-pattern retrieval, while the SDK accepts the historical context through a separate context_df argument.
Interpretability: Kumo-Forecasting also includes a model-agnostic interpretability framework. When enabled, it produces an explanation bundle containing lag and feature attributions per forecast horizon, semantic-flow diagnostics, trajectory-stability diagnostics, and optional embedding Integrated Gradients.These outputs accompany the forecast rather than requiring a different forecasting architecture.
Further details on interpretability can be found in this paper, NVExplain: Explaining Time Series Forecasting with Latent Trajectory Analysis and Structure-Preserving Surrogates
Limitations
Data must be numeric, temporal data. Supported input sequence lengths include 256, 512, 1024, and 2048 observations. Inputs consist of a timestamp column and one or more numeric value columns, represented as a pandas DataFrame or a CSV/JSON input. When leveraging DARR mode, the dimensions of the context must be similar to the context of the input.
Demo: Predictive Maintenance
The Factory Operations (FOX) Blueprint includes Early Access to the Predictive Maintenance module which leverages Kumo Anomaly and Kumo Forecast. It analyzes real-time data to predict future anomalies.

items.title: Estimating physics from images: what real measurements reveal
items.summary:
Back to Articles
Estimating physics from images: what real measurements reveal
Community Article Published
October 16, 2026 Upvote 8
+2
Luca Cilio lucakae Follow projectsim
Reconstructing an object's 3D shape and appearance from images leaves its mass and contact properties unresolved. In physics engines such as PhysX and MuJoCo, those properties affect how the object responds when a robot pushes, grasps or drops it [8].
We evaluated ProjectSim’s image-based physical property estimates against measurements from three research datasets: YCB, NeRF2Physics and IDPP. The comparisons cover mass, sliding friction, indentation hardness and restitution, which describes rebound at impact. Our mass and friction estimates agreed more closely with the measurements than the simple density and constant-value assignments we tested. We also evaluated restitution from a single still frame against references obtained from recorded motion.
A separate experiment examined how friction values should be assigned to an asset. An object can have different measured friction on different surfaces, so one coefficient used directly for every contact cannot express all of those measurements. We fitted two ways of assigning coefficients to known contact measurements, examining this limitation separately from the accuracy of image-based estimates.
Comparing estimates with measurements
ProjectSim builds 3D assets from images and uses a vision-language model to estimate physical properties from rendered views of the resulting asset. The four evaluations use different sources of ground truth: scale measurements for objects in the YCB collection [1], sliding friction and indentation hardness measurements from NeRF2Physics [2], and bounce recordings from IDPP [3].
To score agreement, we use the min ratio error (MnRE) metric used in NeRF2Physics and PhysGS [2, 4]. Higher scores mean closer agreement. For a positive reference value p and a nonnegative estimate p̂, the score is the smaller value divided by the larger:
MnRE⁡(p^,p)=min⁡(p^,p)max⁡(p^,p).
\operatorname{MnRE}(\hat p,p)=\frac{\min(\hat p,p)}{\max(\hat p,p)}.
MnRE(p^​,p)=max(p^​,p)min(p^​,p)​.
An exact estimate scores 1; an estimate twice or half the reference scores 0.5. We report the mean across the evaluated items.
The mass comparisons come from our reruns of selected research methods. The friction and hardness comparisons use the external results published in PhysGS [4].

Baselines: density and constant values
We compared the estimates with three simple parameter assignments. For mass, we tested an assumed density multiplied by the volume of the 3D mesh. For friction, we assigned 0.5 to every tested contact. For restitution, we assigned zero, corresponding to no rebound along the direction perpendicular to the contact surface. Those friction and restitution values appear in Isaac Lab's documented material defaults [10].

Mass: agreement with scale measurements
For a broader comparison, we reran four research methods on YCB objects and scored their mass estimates against measurements from a digital scale. ProjectSim achieved the highest mean MnRE in this comparison (Table 3). We then examined individual predictions and found that 51 of 61 predicted masses were within a factor of two of the measured mass (Figure 2).

Friction and hardness: interpreting the measurements
The coefficient of kinetic friction is the sliding friction force divided by the normal force, the force perpendicular to the contact surface. The NeRF2Physics reference measurements used an iOLab cart fitted with fabric pads on six surfaces [2]. Each coefficient describes a fabric-pad–surface contact.
On those six contacts, our mean MnRE was 0.833. PhysGS reports 0.805, alongside the NeRF2Physics, CLIP and GPT-4V comparisons reproduced in Table 4 [4].
Fitting friction to object–surface pairs
To separate the choice of coefficients from image inference, we examined another set of measured contacts. In IDPP, objects were pulled across horizontal surfaces at steady speed with a spring dynamometer, giving the kinetic-friction coefficient as pulling force divided by weight [3]. Our diagnostic used 28 measured contacts involving five objects and six surfaces. The same LEGO brick had different measured friction on paperboard and on a grey towel. One coefficient attached to the brick cannot reproduce both contacts directly.
The OpenUSD physics schema stores friction coefficients on materials and describes combining the coefficients of contacting materials, including by averaging [9]. We fitted two representations to the known measurements and scored them on those same contacts. Assigning one coefficient per object gave a mean MnRE of 0.794. Assigning five object coefficients and six surface coefficients, with each contact predicted by their arithmetic mean, gave 0.931:
μ^ij=ai+bj2,
\hat\mu_{ij}=\frac{a_i+b_j}{2},
μ^​ij​=2ai​+bj​​,
where aᵢ is the fitted coefficient for object i and bⱼ is the fitted coefficient for surface j.
The second representation has more freedom to capture differences between contacts and fits these measurements more closely. To validate estimates for this representation, we need to compare the combined contact coefficient with the real measurement.
Hardness: resistance to indentation
The hardness evaluation uses Shore durometer readings at 31 measurement points on 11 NeRF2Physics objects [2]. Shore A and Shore D use different scales and indenters.
For the published comparisons, NeRF2Physics and PhysGS use an index that leaves Shore A readings unchanged and maps a Shore D reading to 100 + D [2, 4]. Our hardness evaluation reports 0.807, compared with PhysGS's published 0.839.

For this evaluation, the reference coefficients came from tracked bounce recordings in IDPP [3]. Conclusion
Our mass and friction estimates were closer to real measurements than the simple baselines and the research methods compared here. We also obtained close agreement for restitution using one still frame per clip. For robotics teams, these results point towards simulations that better reflect the objects a robot will handle. Better estimates could help recreate how those objects respond to a push, grasp or drop.
As we improve our ability to create 3D objects with realistic physical properties, we want robotics teams to be able to use simulation for more of their training. Reproducing a wider range of real interactions could give robots more varied practice, helping them learn, adapt and improve before they face the real world.

items.title: In financial services, the AI question is moving from the model to where it runs
items.summary:
Back to Articles
In financial services, the AI question is moving from the model to where it runs
Community Article Published
October 22, 2026 Upvote 9
+3
Kunal Tangri ktangri Follow Farsight-AI Adrian Lepers AdrianLepers Follow Farsight-AI Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow Farsight-AI
Open models are now good enough for real work in financial services, and efficient enough to run on hardware a firm can justify. How valuable AI becomes inside a firm now depends less on the model and more on where it's allowed to run.
Until recently, financial firms had two good reasons to rule out open models: they weren't good enough, and the ones that came close were too expensive to run. That case no longer holds. Open models now meet the bar for demanding financial work, including multi-step agentic tasks, and they run efficiently enough that a firm can serve them on hardware it already owns or could reasonably buy.
So the constraint has moved. What decides how far AI gets inside a financial institution today is less how good the model is and more where it's allowed to run.
For that to work, open models have to make it through a firm's governance process, and there has to be an application that makes the effort worthwhile. Hugging Face sees the challenge from the model side via access, approval and governance. Farsight sees it from the application side, running inside firms' own environments and putting those models to work on pitch books, memos, and financial models. That's why we wrote this together.
Why financial institutions want the model inside their walls
When financial institutions talk to Farsight about running models in their own environment, they tend to give the same two reasons.
The first is data. The work that makes AI worth paying for at a financial firm runs on its most sensitive information. That material is what lets a system produce work that reflects how a particular firm thinks, instead of a competent generic draft. It's also what confidentiality obligations and data-residency rules keep from leaving the institution. A model hosted by an outside provider can be very capable and still never be allowed to see it, so the only way to use that data is to run the model inside the firm.
The second is control. Financial institutions, particularly in Europe, are watching how regulation and politics could change which providers and jurisdictions they can depend on, and which models stay available to them at all. Pricing is set by the provider, and a firm that has built its workflows around one API has little leverage when the price moves. Security is the newest worry. AI has made attacks cheaper and faster to mount, and each external dependency adds a route for data to leave the firm and a vendor whose security it has to take on trust. Models running internally sit behind the same controls as the rest of the firm's systems.
Wanting the model inside still doesn't get the budget approved. In our experience, it gets funded when an application people already use every day is creating the demand. Once that's true, the question changes from whether to try open models to how fast the firm can get them approved.
Bringing open models into the firm's governance framework
For financial institutions, putting open models to work starts with a practical question: how do teams access the models they need while meeting the firm's security and governance requirements? Hugging Face Enterprise Plus provides the controls to do that, connecting the open AI ecosystem to the identity systems, access policies and approval processes the firm already uses.
It starts with company-managed identities. With Managed SSO, employees access Hugging Face through the firm's own identity provider, which controls their accounts from creation to deactivation. Enterprise Managed Users keep their work within the organization: these accounts cannot publish models or datasets to a personal profile or join another organization. The firm can give its teams access to Hugging Face while retaining control over their accounts and collaboration.
The next step is deciding which resources teams can use. Enterprise Plus Network Security lets firms require authenticated access from their corporate network and define policies for models, datasets and applications. A firm can make only approved resources available, or allow broader access while restricting specific repositories or publishers.
These policies can fit directly into existing technical, security and legal reviews. For example, a firm can let engineers browse model descriptions while restricting downloads to approved models. When a new model clears review, the firm can update its access policy through the Hub API. Teams have a clear path from discovering a useful model to requesting and gaining access to it.
Governance also extends to the work teams create. Resource Groups let firms assign access to private repositories by team or project, while token management gives administrators control over programmatic access. Audit Logs record changes to membership, repositories and security settings, giving the firm visibility into who changed what and when.
Good governance should give teams a clear path to put open models to work. We built Enterprise Plus so companies can use Hugging Face with the security and accountability they expect from enterprise software, while giving their builders access to the innovation happening across open AI.
Jeff Boudier, Hugging Face
That creates a practical foundation for applications like Farsight. Hugging Face Enterprise Plus helps financial institutions govern access to open models, and Farsight puts those models to work on pitch books, memos and financial models inside the firm's own environment. Together, they help connect model access and approval to the everyday work that makes AI valuable, with the firm retaining control over its data and deployment.

items.title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
items.summary:
vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT).
One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector, which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (AWS EFA, the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types, AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based: After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline.
Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token
This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates.
In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration.
We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark.
Push-based KV transfer
This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path.
Architecture overview
Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons:
It removes the serialization of the pull model by overlapping producer and consumer work. The decode instance registers its target blocks in advance while the producer is still computing KV. The transfer then begins as soon as the producer’s blocks are ready, rather than after a consumer-side ID-discovery round trip, removing that round trip from the path to first token.
It moves the transfer-setup time off the decode instance. That setup runs on the prefill side and on a background thread. It prepares the NIXL descriptors and submits the transfer, so the decode instance does not spend those cycles during its latency-critical token-generation phase.
The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance.
The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together.
Figure 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture, showing how the decode instance, prefill instance, and background transfer thread coordinate
Implementation details
The protocol has three logical steps.
1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill.
2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests.
3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode.
Threading model
The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution.
The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request.
Figure 3: Main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request in the push-based threading model
Timing comparison of pull and push
The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner.
Figure 4: Pull and push transfer flows compared, highlighting how push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill
The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.
Performance data
For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B model on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA. To isolate P→D transfer performance, we configured the benchmark to disable prefix caching with --no-enable-prefix-caching. This configuration makes the decode node retrieve the full KV cache from the prefill node for every request. Otherwise, overlapping prompts could reuse the decode node’s local cache and bypass the transfer, which would produce misleading comparison results.
The following chart compares TTFT for push and pull KV transfer. We sweep input lengths 1k–16k and request rates of 1–8 queries per second (QPS). At low load and short prompts, the two modes perform almost identically. As QPS and input length grow, pull mode degrades sharply, reaching about 1,744 ms at 8 QPS and 16k. Push mode stays far lower at roughly 540 ms, around 3x reduction. The gap opens because pull mode posts NIXL descriptors inline on the decode worker, synchronously within its engine loop, so that work stalls token generation. Push mode moves it to a background thread, off the critical path.
Figure 5: TTFT for push compared to pull KV transfer across input lengths and request rates (1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, prefix caching disabled on the decode node)
This chart shows TPOT under the same conditions. The pattern mirrors TTFT. At light load, push and pull are close, around 5.6–5.8 ms. As load and input length rise, pull climbs to about 10.4 ms at 4–8 QPS and 16k, while push holds near 7 ms. The reason is that push offloads descriptor preparation and transfer submission from the decode worker. Token generation is not starved, so per-token latency stays flat even at high concurrency and long contexts.
Figure 6: TPOT for push compared to pull KV transfer across input lengths and request rates (1P1D topology, 128 output tokens, prefix caching disabled on the decode node)
How to run benchmark
To reproduce our 1P1D benchmark configuration, one prefill node and one decode node, using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, refer to the detailed instructions in the Reproducing our results guide. The guide covers environment setup, launching the vLLM prefill and decode servers, running the benchmark, and collecting results. The feature can run on other supported configurations, but performance results will vary depending on the hardware, model, workload, and network configuration.
Conclusion
In this post, we showed how the push-based KV connector overlaps prefill computation with decode-side block allocation and registration, removing the post-prefill router round trip and decode-side transfer setup from the critical path. This reduces TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our Qwen3-32B benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode provided up to a 3x improvement in TTFT and 30 percent improvement in TPOT compared with pull mode. Results vary by workload and configuration. To use push mode, configure both the prefill and decode servers to use NixlPushConnector instead of NixlConnector.
Choose the push-based connector when early decode node selection is acceptable and lower TTFT is the priority. The pull-based connector remains the better fit for workloads that require bidirectional KV transfer or defer decode-instance selection until after prefill for load-aware routing. vLLM supports both push- and pull-based KV connectors, so you can select the approach that best fits your deployment.
As a future improvement, we are exploring bringing the background NIXL threading model to the pull-mode connector, moving NIXL setup off the critical path so that pull-mode workloads could benefit from the same optimizations. We have opened a pull request to explore this.
